summary: The Food Inspector, P.W. 4, took a sample of Lalacheroo Mal 's Food Inspector on analysis by the Public Analyst. The Public Analyst found that the sample contained nine living meal worms. There was no other evidence in support of the case of the prosecution that the Lal Public Analyst had not examined the Food Analyst and the High Court held that the prosecution has failed to prove that the Food Inspector was adulterated and accordingly acquitted the respondent. Dismissing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: 1. The report of the Public analyst that the article in question was found unfit for human consumption is a must for bringing the case within its purview. [470D] Dhanraj 's case (supra) does not support the case as the report of Public Analyst did not support it. [471F] 2.1 In the instant case, the Food inspector had found that a proportion of nine living meals wormed was adulterated. The food contained nine live meal wained wormons or four tins. The sample there was at best a good deal of difference between worm 's and insect infested. [473F] Dhan Raj vs Corporation of Calcutta, ; , referred to. 2.2 In the present case, though the Food Inspectors in the case were found to be present and that in the absence of clear proof of the sample being unfit for life, it could not constitute a valid basis for holding that the Article was adulterated within the meaning of section 2(1)(f). [473G] Dhanaraj 's Case (supra), referred to and distinguished.

The appellant was convicted under section 7 of the Essential Commodities Act, 1955. He was convicted and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for six months. The High Court dismissed his appeal in respect of the conviction under section 3(2) of the Act but did not accept the ground that he was an agriculturist. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the presumption under para. 3(1) could not be drawn against him because the presumption was in the course of business and (ii) the appellant had successfully proved that he is an agriculturist and the presumption thereunder cannot be drawn. HELD : The High court was right in holding that the presumption tinder para.3(2), could not have been drawn against the appellant. [90 D] Manipur Administration vs M. Nila Chandra Singh, ; , followed. (i)(a) In the present case the appellant produced a number of lease deeds in which leases of various parcels of land were shown to have been granted to him. He also produced receipts of payment of rent and he cited witnesses who deposed on oath that he and his brother cultivated 80 90 bighas of land. No doubt, the lease deeds are not registered but for the purpose of a criminal prosecution, it is easy to see that the evidence which wasbrought for ward of witnesses deposing orally was not concocted to set up a false defence. [91 F G] (b) The presumption under paragraph 3(3) couldnot be drawn from proof of storage only. It is obvious that sub para speaks of storage for sale as a dealer although the words "as a dealer" are not there, because storage has reference to business as a dealers and that is the essence of the Order. [92 F G; 93 A] (c) The High Courts have held in this case that the appellant was an agri trator and was not liable to the penalty under section 49 of the Registration Act.

The appellant was the lessee of a certain land in Bihar. He died in 1917 leaving behind him a will which provided that he would be entitled to fresh settlement on payment of rent and on such terms as might be then agreed upon between the parties. The respondent instituted a suit for ejectment against the appellant on the ground that the lease was void and inoperative because it had been granted by the Receiver without his consent. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court in appeal reversed the decree holding that the notice to quit was insufficient for the purpose of determining the tenancy. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The question whether there was a contract to the contrary is essentially one of fact and cannot be answered in the negative. It is one thing to say that in the absence of a valid agreement, the rights of the parties would be regulat ed by law in the same manner as if no agreement existed at all; it is quite another thing to substitute a new agreement for the parties which is palpably contradicted by the admit ted facts of the case. It would be pertinent to point out that in such cases the duration has to be determined by reference to the object or purpose for which the tenancy was created. The rule of construction embodied in this section applies not only to express leases of uncertain dura tion but also to leases implied by law which may be inferred from possession and acceptance of rent, and other circum stances. It cannot therefore fulfil the requirements of section 107 of the Transfer of Property Act. [280 D F] (ii) The High Court was right in holding that there was no contract to give a fresh notice of termination of tenancy as contemplated by section 106 of the Act. The fact that the rent paid here was an annual rent and he was not entitled to any tenancy rights under the same is altogether different from that of a monthly lease. [281 E F] Debendra Nath vs Syama Prasanna, A.I.R. 1933 Pat. 485, Debendra Narain vs Sharmasree Prasad, A I. R.

The appellant assessee, a firm carrying on business in the years 1964 65 to 1971 72, filed a suit for recovery of Rs. 1,39,722/ from its assessee firm and claimed that the said amount was privileged under section 137 of the Income Tax Act, 1961. The Income Tax Officer rejected the claim on the ground that the record, documents etc., were not available to the assessee. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the question of privilege as claimed by the Income tax Department was important and likely to arise in the course of trial of suits in future also, and that the finality attached to an order of the Commissioner with regard to claim of privilege under section 138(1) could not be questioned. The Appellate Tribunal dismissed the appeal holding that the omission of Section 137 did not make any difference and that it was only a procedural restriction on the power of the Court to summon such documents, record etc. as is found relevant to the case. In reference, the High Court held that when a party to a proceeding in a court applies for production of documents, the same should be in public interest so to do and that, therefore, the finality attaching to an earlier order by the Act was not affected by section 137(1). The High Court also took into account the fact that the provisions of section 138 were almost identical with those of section 139 of the 1961 Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the jurisdiction of the courts to call for production in a case where the documents, records etc., from the income tax authorities had been produced before the IncomeTax Authorities after April 1, 1964; and (ii) the finality which has been attached to the order if the Commissioner under section 136(1)(b) is applicable only in cases where application is made to the Commissioner by a party or any other person for receiving documents or information. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The finality which had been attached under section 139(1), and after its repeal by the 1961 Amending Act, was not enlarged by the substitution of section 137 by the High Courts in respect of the documents filed prior to April 1. 1964. [562D] 2. Section 138(2) of the 1922 Act and section 138 (1)(a) of 1961 Act cannot extend the ban on the courts as contained in section 137, unless a different intention appears, shall not affect any right, privilege, obligation or liability acquired, accrued or incurred under the repealed enactment. [561E] 3. The bar contained in Section 138 of the Act on the exercise of the powers by the Courts to summon the production of the document before the income Tax authorities after April I, 1964 relating to assessment proceedings for 1964 65 onwards and that ban came to an end in respect thereof, without any specific prohibition under any law for the time being in force. [560F] 4. The effect of introduction of Section 138 into the 1961 Income Tax Acts is that it is entitled to a person to make an application to the Commis sioner in the prescribed form and pay the prescribed fee for information as to the amount of tax determined as payable by an assessee under sub section (1) of Section 139. [559G] 5. The right to apply for information only as to transactions past and closed, as if it had never existed.

The plaintiff appellant was the widow of one Seinaba and her husband. Seinba had two sisters, son and daughter. Seins were born in the house of Seinbi and they were governed by the Muhammadan Law. Seisinbai died on May 3, 1946 without leaving any issue. She accepted the gift on behalf of Seins and filed a suit for partition and possession of the property which she claimed as an heir under the Muhammadans. The trial court decreed the suit but the first appellate court did not accept it. In second appeal the High Court held that a gift by the husband to his minor daughter was completed ordinarily by the acceptance of the guardian of the person after the celebration of marriage, a husband can receive a gift in respect of minor wife even though her father be living; and that even if the gift was accepted on behalf the minor son and the donee, the widow could have made a declaration of gift and take possession on behalf Of his wife who had attained puberty and had lived with him for a long time. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf (1) that the gift in question was not void under section 6 of the Muhammada Act; (2) that there was no rule of Muhammadan law which permitted such acceptance and the decision of the High court was right; (3) that even a change in the mode of enjoyment is sufficient evidence of such intention. HELD: (1)(a) The gift in the present case was a valid gift. Mammotty was living at the time of the gift, in the House of his mother in law and was probably a very sick person though not in marzulmaut. His minor wife who has attained discretion was capable under Muhammadan laws to accept the gift. [557 D] (b) The rule about possession is relaxed in certain circumstances by the Mussalman Law and in deciding cases of undoubted authority. In the present ease there is good authority for these propositions in the ancient and modern books of Muhammadans, but the question is whether there was a complete intention to divest ownership on the part of Mammottty and to transfer the property to the donee. If the property is with the donor he must depart from it and the donor must enter upon possession. [558 E F] (c) The test for determining the transfer of possession is whether the donor and donee intended at the moment that the title to the property should pass from the donor to the donor. If there is no such person one can be said to have exercised the power to accept gift on his own behalf. [559 G H] (d) In the instant case, there was complete intention of the donor making the gift and the gift must be accepted as valid and complete. The gift was a proper gift. The donee must not leave behind even a straw belonging to him to show his ownership and possession. Exceptions to section 6(1)(b) are not a condition of its validity in certain cases. One such case is gift by a husband to the wife and another where there is gift to a minor who has no guardian of her property in existence. In such cases the benefit to the minor and the completion of the gifted for his benefit is the sole consideration. [560 B C] (e) The donee 's father was living in the same house and was perhaps a very poor person though he was not in Marzulnaut. He had attained discretion under Muhammadans and the intention to make the gift would be clear and manifest because it was made by a deed which was registered and handed over by Mammots to his mother.

The Madras Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1951 was enacted to provide for the better administration of Hindu religious and charitable institutions and endowments in the State. The Act provided for the proper administration of temples governed by the Act. Section 76(1) provided that the trustee of every religious institution shall keep regular accounts of all receipts and disbursements. In exercise of this power the Government framed rules under section 100(2) of the Act prescribing a minimum fee of Rs. 1,000/ for meeting expenditure incurred on account of expenses incurred by the management of the temple. The respondents who were trustees of the Venkataramana Temple at Mulki, District South Kanara, moved the High Court for an order restraining the Commissioner of Hindu Religious and charitable Endowments from enforcing the provisions of the Amending Act 27 of 1954. The High Court held that sections 21, 30(2), 31, 63 to 69 of the Madras Act 19 of 1951 were ultra vires the State Legislature and directed the Commissioner to pay the arrears of contribution and audit fee under section 76(2). In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the provisions in the Act imposing a duty on the administration of religious endowments have to be made, and not rules governing individual endowments; (ii) the Commissioner had not determined the cost of auditing the accounts of the respondent temple and proceeded to observe "that the Commissioner has not determined any audit fee. He has not fixed the method for determining contribution. (iii) The Commissioner has failed to determine the cost in accordance with section 76 (2). (iv) The order passed by the High court upholding the claim of the respondents was illegal. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (i)(a) The High court erred in holding that appropriate rules were not in existence at the time when the demand was made and on that account the demand is premature. If services are provided, assuming that the Venkataramanana temple either does not need the services or does not obtain the same degree of service as others may. " [923 B C] (b) The power to make rules was not restricted nor were the rules framed by the Government rendering invalid the rules. The order of the High. Court upholding the claims of the res pondents on this part of the case must therefore be set aside. [924 D E] (c) The rules under the Act have to he general and such rules were in fact framed and were in operation. Therefore, the Commissioner was not bound to frame separate rules in respect of each individual religious institution. [936 F G] (d) The rule being a matter to be decided on evidence, it is not necessary that the Commissioner should frame separate Rules in respect thereof for meeting the cost or expenses incurred for rendering the service.

The appellant, a contemner under section 19(1) of the , was served with an order dated 2nd April 1975 directing him to show cause why he should not be proceeded against for committing contempt. The notice was issued in accordance with the procedure prescribed under section 17 of the Act to showcause against the appellant 's alleged liability to be punished under section 15. A preliminary objection raised by the respondents that no appeal lies to this Court under section 20 of the . Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) An order merely initiating the proceeding without anything further, does not decide anything against the alleged contemner and cannot be appealed against as a matter of right from any kind of order made by the High Court in the proceedings for contempt. [512 B] (2) The preliminary objection is well founded and must be accepted as correct. Section 19(i) says that no court shall initiate any proceedings for Contempt either on its own motion or otherwise after the expiry of a period of one year from the date on which the contempt is alleged to have been committed. [511 C] (3) The order or the decision must be such that it decides some bone of contention raised before the High Courts affecting the right of the party aggrieved. Mere initiation of a proceeding for contempt by the issuance of the notice on the prima facie view that the case is a fit one for drawing up the proceeding, does no decide any question. This Court, for the first time, cannot be asked in such an appeal to decide whether the person proceeded against has committed contempt of the High court or not. [ 512 E F] (4) The matter has to be decided either finally or, may be even at an earlier stage an order is made which does decide a contention raised by one party asking the High. Court to drop the proceeding on the ground of its being barred under section20 of the Contempt Act but the High 'Court holds that the proceeding is not barred. [612 G H] (5) The proceedings are initiated under section 18 by issuance of a notice. Thereafter there may be many interlocutory orders passed in the said proceeding by the Court. It could not be the intention of the legislature to provide for an appeal against the order of the Court merely initiating tho proceeding without any question, and cannot therefore be asked, in such a case, to decide that matter. [613 A B] Baradakanta Mishra vs Orissa High Court, ; , referred to.

The appellant was prosecuted along with another under section 6(1 A) of the , for possessing a wireless transmitter in contravention of the provisions of section 3 of the Act and was convicted by the Magistrate. The High Court confirmed both the conviction and sentence. On appeal to this Court, HELD : Section 4 of the Repealing and Amending Act of 1952 applied only to cases of a later amending Act inserting new provisions in an earlier Act, for where an earlier enactment is amended by a later Act, it cannot be said that the earlier Act applies, incorporates or refers to the amending Act. The earlier Act cannot incorporate the later Act but can only be amended by it. [760 F G] In the present case, the insertion of section 6 A in the Act of 1933 was not a textual amendment but a substantial one. The text of an enactment, the argument proceeds on the basis that the word " text " is comprehensive enough to take in a wireless telegraphy transmitter " and therefore the legislature though by the amending act of 1949, inserted the said section in the new Act of 1932, removed it in the year 1952 as the said amendment was unnecessary and redundant. [761 D E] The Amending Act did not indicate any intention different from that envisaged by the said Section. This principle has been succinctly stated in Halsbury 's Laws of England, 2nd Edition Vol. 31, p. 406, thus: "The main object of the repealing and amending Acts is to expurgate section 6 (1 A), which has been applied, incorporated or referred to. The section does not prohibit the possession of a wireless apparatus. It only regulates the import dead matter from the statute book. The offspringe is not comprehensive enough for taking in a telegraphy transmissionter, but can merely be amended so as to include the amending provisions of the new Central Act.

The appellant was the managing Shebait of a deities from 1926 to 1930 and as Shebait he executed a Hatchita in favour of one Nanitosh Chakraborty who died in March 1930. The last entry in the Hatchati in favour Of the appellant was made on the basis of which he received advances of money from time to time from the latter. The appellant claimed that the properties described in Schedules Ka and Kha were purchased ostensibly by her husband as Shebaits for a certain sum and that the appellant had no title to them. Held, that the property described in Schedule Ka was not the property held by the appellant as Shebaita for another person in respect of the decree holder. The fact that the object of restoring possession of the properties sold in execution of the decrees to the judgment debtor was to enable the latter to pay off the decretal dues thus ascertained by instalments does not come within the purview of those provisions. Renula vs Manmatha, (1876) 1 K.B. 171 and Renula v Manmathas 72 I.A. 156, referred to. Held further, that in making a new decree under cl. Ka and Sch. Ka it is only for the purpose of substituting the method of accounting sanctioned by the Act for the calculation upon which the original decree was passed and to give an opportunity to the decree debtor to pay the decretal amount thus ascertained. The subsequent conveyance of these properties in favourof Oramba Sundari, the appellant, has been held by both the courts below to be a fictitious transaction.

The respondent, who was the assignee of a decree in a suit filed by the appellant against the respondent for recovery of certain amounts due to him from his debtor on the ground that he had been granted a decree on the basis of an unregistered document dated July 7, 1949. The trial court decreed the suit and the High Court confirmed the decree. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the words "decree holder" must be construed as meaning decree holder in fact and not as including a party who in equity may afterwards become entitled to the rights of the actual decree holder and therefore, the words 'decree holder ' must be interpreted in their ordinary or natural sense; (ii) if the respondent could not avail himself of the provisions of Order XXI, rule 16 of the Code of Civil Procedure, he was not entitled to apply for execution under Order XXI. Rule 16 of that Code; (iii) the High Courts had consistently taken the view that there could be no assignment of the decree by the transferee in writing within the meaning of Order 21, rule II of the code and therefore the respondent was not a transferee of the original decree; (iv) the expression "decreeholder" must mean a person who claims to be entitled to receive the benefit of a judgment and decree passed in a court of law either in a pending litigation or by institution of a suit for recovery or an application for execution of a debt which may be passed in future. HELD: (i)(a) The words "judgment holder" in Order XXI must mean the judgment debtor in fact, and not a person whose rights and remedies of the transferor in respect thereof including the right to prosecute the claim to judgment in a Court of law whether by an assignment in writing or by operation of law, from making an application which was made before it. [1423 B] (b) The respondent could only make one application for executing the decree on his own behalf and not for an assignment of that decree by an assignee in writing. [1524 C] (c) The expression "judgment" occurring in Order 21 of the Civil Procedure Code means a judgment or order made in a proceeding before a court which is passed in his favour, in a case where the decree is passed by the Court of appeal and the moment a decree is executed in his favor by the court of Law. [1624 D] (d) The word "decree" in O. XXI, r. 16(2)(j) means a decree or order of a court coming within the definition of actionable claim. It would have been open to the transferee after the execution of the deed of assignment in his own favour to take steps under Order XXI, rule 11(2) for execution and obtain a decree against the transferee on the strength of the document for the purpose of section 146 of the C.P.C. [1724 F H] (e) The fact that the respondent had not filed an application under O.XXI, r., 16(1), C. P.C., for execution was not material because the respondent did not take any steps in existence at the time of the assignment and this position was not affected by operation Of Order XXI rule 16(3) of the Act. [1824 F G] (f) The High Court had consistently held that the document under which the assistance of the court was required to be given by the respondent, was not merely a legal assignment but also an assignment made in writing and the matter resting on it could not be said to have been transferred by the assignment in the present case. [1924 F] (g) The transfer of the execution proceedings was not an assignment under O XXI, R. 16 of C.Ps. Act, but only a declaration that the respondents were the assignees of the decrees and the order for their substitution was made on the same day.

The respondent, a manufacturer of steel doors and door leaves, was fabricating steel doors, windows, sashes etc. and making no charge for that service. The Sales Tax Officer included in the taxable turnover of the respondent Rs. 23,480/ received under the contract. He held that the contract was one of sale of goods and the respondent had with a view to promote sales of its manufactured goods undertaken to fix the windows without demanding any charges for that services and that the High Court was in error in holding that the contracts were not "a contract of service" within the meaning of section 2(6) of the . The State appealed. HELD: (i) The object of the Act was to enter into a works contract. That clearly appears from the terms of the tender and its acceptance. [512 B] (ii) The words "the work and labour bestowed and in anything that can properly become the subject of sale" in section 2 (6) are wide enough to include windows, etc. [511 C D] (iii) The contract in question is of the second variety. Counsel for the respondent contended that the terms were not decisive and the Court was entitled to ascertain the true effect of the contract as disclosed by the nature of the work, and the intention of the parties gathered from the term of the Contract, the circumstances of the transaction and custom of the trade and no universal rule applicable to all transactions may be evolved. [506 E F] (iv) The High Court erred in holding on a consideration of the evidence that the respondent was not a contract of sale. [500 G H] (v) It is only upon the "fixing" of windows as provided by the specifications with glass plain or ground as decided by the Engineer in Charge, and were to be "fixed" within six months from the date of its acceptance "to the building with rawl edge and not before. [525 G H; 527 A] (vi) The State of Madras vs Richardson & Cruddas Ltd., ; , referred to.

The prosecution case was that the appellant and his brother were charged with having committed an offence under section 420 of the Indian Penal Code read with section 120B I.P.C. for selling adulterated goods to M/s. Ashoke Trading Corporation of Indore. The prosecution case against the appellant was that he had entered into a taxi with one Shanker Lal and told him that S had arranged for a transaction of sale of foreign goods which would result in good profit to the complainant. The complainant agreed to purchase 200 pieces of the washer plates from S.A. The appellant and Raj Kumar Agarwalla were thereafter arrested by the police. The trial court convicted the appellant under section420 I. P.C., read with s.120B IP. C. and sentenced him to pay a fine of Rs. 3200/ . On appeal, the High Court acquitted S. Avtar but on revision petition to the High court it was allowed. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (1) no case had been made out against him; (2) charges framed against him were consequently quashed. HELD: The report which was lodged by Ram Avtar in the very nature of things made no mention of the name of Raj Kumar Aggarwala respondent because it is the case of the prosecution itself that Raj Kumar appeared on the scene only subsequent to the lodging of the report and the accused were discharged; (3) charges under sections 420, 468 and 471 I.p.C read with S.120 B I. p.C were framed against all the three accused. The part which was attributed to Raj Kumar is that he was present along with Shankar Lal when the latter brought the appellant into the shop of Ram Avtar. That circumstance as pointed out by the High Courts in the case would hardly warrant an inference that Raj Singh respondent too was a party to any conspiracy to defraud or cheat Ram Avtar; (4) charges were consequently not made out and no case has been made against him.

The petitioner, a citizen of India, was employed in the Indian Railways as a commuter of the Indian Railway. He was served with an order dated December 9, 1970, by the General Manager, Railway Safety, directing him to provide for such level crossing of railway vehicles and to remove the posts of Motor Vehicles Inspector, to make periodical inspection of carriages, engines, tracks etc., at different levels. The petitioner challenged the said order in a writ petition before the High Court contending that the Railways had violated the fundamental rights guaranteed under Articles 14, 19(1)(f) and 31 of the Constitution inasmuch as the Railway Board was not functioning properly and efficient. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the Railway Administration was justified in India in passing an order dealing with a great deal of safety and whistlefulness. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The Railways are a public utility service run on monopoly basis. Since it is a public sector service run by the Government, the Railway administration should be free to collect the entire operational cost which would include the interest on the capital outlay out of the national exchequer. Small marginal profits cannot be ruled out. The massive operation will require a margin of adjustment and, therefore, marginal profits should be admissible. [723D E] 1.2 It is true that the accident has occurred as a result of the growth of the Railways and their functioning in view of the trends being started and many other factors which are relevant to the Railways must be briskly adopted. The Indian Constitution has definitely rejected the authority, which is a socialised public utility undertaking, and has also upheld the authority 's action. [700F G] 1:3 It is not necessary for the Supreme Court to give any directions to the opposite parties. No dispute regarding maintainability having been raised, that question also did not arise for consideration. The Railways have a great impact on the rights of the citizens to a matter of that, is entitled to demand that the State shall provide adequate facilities and create an environment in which its fruits can be harvested and shared. [623G H] 1 :4. It is of paramount importance that every citizen must get involved in the determined march to resurrect the society and subordinate his will and passion to the primordial necessity of order in social life. [ 700H; 700A] 1 5. The Union Government should be directed to bring about harmony and ensure profits. [750B] 1 6. It shall be a challenge to improve this great public utility in an effective way and with an adequate sense of urgency. If necessary, it shall set up a high powered body to quickly handle the many faced problems standing in the way. giving directions in a matter like this where availability of resources has a material bearing, policy regarding priorities is involved, expertise is very much in issue, is not prudent and we do not propose to issue directions. [800C D] 7. The Court is directed that he shall be entitled to consolidated cost of Rs.

The appellants filed applications under section 13 of the Bombay Merged Territories and Areas (Jagirs Abolition) Act, 1953, for restoration of their proprietary jagirs. The application was dismissed by the Tribunal on May 6, 1961. On a reference made at Bombay, the High Court held that the applications for restoration were barred by limitation. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that since the orders passed dismissing the appeals were received by them on April 9 and April 20, 1961, the application for restoration should have been made within 30 days from the date of the order of dismissal. HELD: (i) The Tribunal had no power to dismiss an appeal for non prosecution in a case where the appellant did not appear either in person or through his agent or lawyer when the appeal was called for hearing. [144 C] (ii) Section 14 of the Act provides that any jagirdar entitled to compensation under section 11 or 12 shall, on or before the 31st day of July 1958 apply in writing to the Collector for determining the amount of compensation payable to him under the said section. The proviso to section 14(1) lays down that in computing the compensation under this section the Tribunal shall follow the procedure as far as it is applicable laid down in the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. [145 E F] (iii) Section 20 of the Abolition Act provides for restoration to an appeal against the Collector 's award and does not provide for restoration on merits. The reason is that in Regulation 19(1), it is open to the Tribunal to dismiss the appeal for noncompliance with the provisions of Regulation 20(1). If an appeal is dismissed for want of prosecution under Regulation 19 (1) the application of restoration made by the appellants in all the four cases was well within the period of limitation prescribed by Regulation 21.

The appellant 's father was the owner of a temple in the village Telibandha. He had three sons, one of whom was the son of one of the sons. The first appellant was appointed as the manager of the temple and the second appellant was the manager. The respondent filed a suit for declaration that the temple was held by him in trust for the temple of Shri Ramchandra Swamy and that he had committed breach of trust by transferring the trust properties to his own name. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that there was no trust, either express or implied, created in favour of the appellant. On appeal the High Court set aside the judgment and decree of the trial court and ordered the dismissal of the suit. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants (i) that the use of the words "myself" in the gift deed showed an intention to give an absolute interest of ownership in the property to Ramsaran Lal, (ii) that these words were not intended to be used for the maintenance of the deity and therefore they did not make an absolute dedication of the village to the temple. HELD : (i). The High Court was right in holding that the dedication made by the Panch Faisla must be held to be valid. [431 D] (ii).

The appellants were the President of a High Court and Chairman, Action Committee of the High Court described as contemner No. 2 was actively associated with the passing of the resolution which contained disparaging remarks about the Chief Justice and since he also issued that resolution for publication in newspapers he was guilty of contempt. The High Court discharged the notices. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High Courts had not committed any contempt and that the appellants were guilty of contumacious conduct and were guilty under section 2(1) (c) of the Contempt of Court Act, 1971. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The High Courts have found the contemners guilty of criminal contempt. It is true that the Judges of the Division Bench of the Allahabad High Court referred to the contumacious act of the appel lants but the High court did not wish to proceed against the appellants. The appellants were also guilty of wilful conduct and the HighCourt gave the ground that they were responsible for the passing offi cial contempt. [602C D] In view of the fact that the notices were discharged, the appeal is disposed of with the directions that the notice should be issued to the appellants within three months from today. The judgment of the Court below is set aside and the proceedings are dropped. [ 602D E] (a) The High court was right in holding that since the resolution was passed under the Presidentship of the first appellant described as contempt No. 1, it was a matter of regret that the contem ners who were prominent members of the Avadh Bar, should have themselves embarked on the path of vilifying the Chief justice of this Court and that they had not acted in their duty with dignity decorum and discipline. [312E F] (b) The contempt is a matter which must be of such a character as to amount to contempt. In view Of the fact, the High COurt did not intend to punish contemners Nos. 1 & 2 for the contumaious conduct of which we have adjudged them guilty though it express its disapproval of that conduct and hope that the indiscretion will not be repeated.

The three appellants and their eldest brother, respondent No. 1 filed an application under Section 14 of the , before the Sub Judge, Hooghly for a direction on the arbitrator to file the award in the Court in Misc. Case No. 74 of 1977. The learned Sub Judge fixed the hearing of the arbitrators ' application to return the award to enable them to present the same before the sub Registrar for registration. On or about November 28, 1977, the appellants filed an applica tion under Section 15 of the . The Sub Judge ordered interim injunction on the parties including the arbitrators to maintain status quo till the disposal of Misc. case No.74 of 1977 initiated by the appellant No. 2. On appeal, the High Court set aside the order of the Sub judge holding that during the subsistence of the interim injunction order on the arbitrators, to maintain Status quo till date, the award was in court and this was manifest from the order in Misc Case No 74 of 1978. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The two legal maxims of equity which are well settled, namely, "ACTUS CURIAE NON COGITAD AD lMPTION" and "LEX NON OCITAD ORDER, 1939 at page 73 are well established, namely "Allowing a safe and certain guide for the administration of law. The above maxim should however be applied with caution. [123B] 2. In Broom 's Legal Maxims, the law does not compel a man to do that which he cannot possibly perform. The law itself and the administration is understood to disclaim, as it does in its general aphorisms all intention of compelling exemp tion no man. In the instant case, admittedly during the period from 26th July, 1978 to 24th November, 1983 there was subsisting injunction preventing the arbitrators from taking any steps. Furthermore, as noted before the award directed to keep the award stayed, the Court granted time till 28th December, 1982 to reconsider the question of limitation and found that the award had been presented within time as the period during which the judicial proceedings were pending. [124C D] 3.

The appellant was the owner of a building in Kalyan. The respondent gave notice to the appellant to vacate the premises on the ground that he had sublet it to him. The appellant filed a suit for ejectment on the grounds of non payment of rent and sub letting. The trial court held that the sub letting was lawful and that the appellant did not occupy the premises as required by section 15 of the Bombay Hotel and Lodging Houses Rates Control Act, 1947. On appeal the Assistant Judge held that section 15 was applicable to a case where the tenant had made default in payment of the rent and the sub let was for a period exceeding three months and dismissed the suit. The High Court on appeal affirmed this decision. Held, that the respondent was not entitled to the protection of section 15(1) of the Act because he had failed to make payment of arrears of rent within the meaning of section 13(1)(e). Section 15(2) of Bombay Hotel & Lodging Houses (Control) Act, 1946, as it stood before its amendment in 1948 provided that " notwithstanding anything contained in any law for the time being in force, a tenant may sublet any portion of his premises to a sub tenant. Provided further that the provisions of section 14 shall not apply to such a lease. " The respondent was only seeking to enforce his rights under the statute and not to seek eviction under section 13 (1) (e). The appellant could not be permitted to assert in a court of justice any right founded upon or growing out of an illegal transaction.

The respondent No. 1 Board, in the month of March 1990, invited applications for admission to the M.D.B.S. course in the months of March, 1990 and March, 1991. The results were declared on August 8, 1989. The result was published on June 30, 1990. After the date of recounting, the respondent No 1 Board received a notice dated August 8.1989 from the examiners that the answer books of the subjects in question had been tampered with, and that the marks initially obtained by the candidates were tampered with. The examiners gave their explanations and thereafter they were informed that the answers given were not correct. After considering the explanation offered by the examiners, the Board decided to cancel the results of the examination and to debar the students from appearing in the supplementary examination to be held in October 1990. The respondent No 2 Board, however, did not apply for and obtained the approval of the Divisional Board and therefore, the impugned notification was issued on August 29, 1990, which was published in the Gazette dated August 29.1990. The respondents challenged the validity of the impugned order by filing a writ petition before the High Court. The High Court held that the Standing Committee had no power to enquire into the use of unfair means at the final examination and Regulations were not complied with. It further held that there was no dispute that the examiners were appointed on July 30,1990 in accordance with the procedure laid down by the State Board for conducting the examinations and that they were entitled to adduce evidence on their behalf and if the witnesses were examined on behalf of the Board they would be permitted to cross examine them. The writ petition filed by the respondents was dismissed by a Single Judge. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1. The procedure adopted at the inquiry is fair and just and it is not vitiated by any procedural irregularity or violation of principles of natural justice. [893F] 1.2. The findings recorded by the Board are based on no evidence. It has no power under article 235 to differ from the conclusions arrived at by the authorities. [794G] 1:3. The control which is vested in the High Courts is complete control subject only to the power of the Governor in the matter of appointment including initial posting and promotion of the District Judges within the exercise of the control vested in it. [789H; 790A] 1st respondent Board, while exercising its powers under article 226, has no jurisdiction to quash the impugned Notification dated August 31, 1990 issued by the High Commissioner. The power of superintendence is vested with the High court under Article 227.

The appellants were charged with offences under section 120 B of the Indian Penal Code for abetment of criminal misconduct by a firm. The prosecution case was that during the progress of the investigation, and after the houses and shops of the accused persons had been searched, the three accused were found to have exported potatoes at concessional rates on false declarations or certificates that they were seed potatoes. The appellants were tried under section 5(2) Of the Prevention of Corruption Act for abetment thereof. The trial court convicted them but acquitted them. On appeal by the State, the High Court reduced the sentence on the ground that the offence was not established against them and that the conviction was unsustainable. Held, that the prosecution case as set out in the judgment of the High court was correct. The object of the Act was to make more effective provision for the prevention of bribery and corruption and therefore section 5 (2) of the Prevention Of Corruption Act was not applicable to the facts of the case. The offence under section 6 read with section 116 of the Code of Criminal Procedure was committed when the talk about the bribe took place. The definition of criminal conspiracy in section 161 of the Penal Code, if it is habitual, falls within clause (a) of that section and therefore the offence charged as defined in cl. (d) does not come with in the meaning of bribery. The word "obtains" has been used in sections 161 and 165 of the Criminal Procedure Code to place too narrow a construction on the sub clause. It is not necessary for an offence under cl. 161 to prove all this. The offences committed in the course of traps are less grave and call only for lenient or nominal sentences.

The appellant Bank filed a suit for recovery of Rs. 76,368/13P/ with interest at the rate of 14 per cent from the date of default in payment of principal debtor as in the circumstances mentioned in the letter dated December 24,1957 addressed to the surety. The principal debtor executed a demand promissory note and on his failure to pay the outstanding balance of Rs 70,879/ in cash credit account, the Bank instituted a suit against him for recovery. The legal representative of the principal debtor also filed an application under section 144 of the Code of Civil Procedure seeking permission of the General Manager of the Bank to extend the facility to the extent of Rs 75,000/ by executing a bond exhibit 31 and on the same day the principal creditor executed a bond Ext. 83 in favour of the bank. The surety alleged that the pledge of groundnut oil tins was lost on account of negligence of the appellant Bank. The defence raised by the surety was that the Bank had agreed to grant cash credit facility to deceased principal debtor on the security of goods by way of pledge and that though the goods were to be kept in the godown in the compound of Vijay Oil Mills, but the godown was to be retained under lock and key of the same bank. It was also contended that the principal debtors had offered two securities one of which being to be opened under the lock and the key of their Bank, the surety would provide such quantity of goods as would provide full cover to the outstanding security and that since the goods are to be keep in the godowns in the custody of the creditor bank, the sureties were discharged. The trial court decreed the suit against the surety but the High Court held that the surety had agreed and had not exercised such care as a prudent man would in the circum stances of the case which resulted in loss of security, namely, pledged goods and therefore, in view of the combined operation of sections 139 and 141 of the Indian Contract Act, the appellant was discharged. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The surety would be discharged in entirety because it is crystal clear that the Principal debtor had agreed & had in fact pledged 5,000 tins of oil which even if sold at the then current market price would have satisfied the Bank 's entire claim. [927C] 1.2 In order to attract section 141 of Indian Contract, it must be shown that the creditor has taken more than one security on the basis of which advance was made and the surety gave personal guarantee on the good faith of other security being offered by the principal or that the sureties would nonetheless be liable even if the Bank has guarantee, security or remedy, guarantees securities or remedies from the principal. [936E] 1:3 The expression 'any other guarantee, guarantee or remedy ' therein mentioned must be security other than the pledged goods. In an almost identical situation with regard to an identical clauses in Amrit Lal Goverdhan Lalan vs State Bank of Travancore and Ors., ; , this Court held as under: "The expression ' any other guarantee security ' in cl. 5 of exhibit 31 is not assist able to the Bank in this case. [830F] 1 :4 The surety will be discharged on the ground that it is found as a fact that negligence of his creditor bank was responsible for the loss of guarantee, yet the surety will not be discharged. [ 925G H] 2.1 In the instant case, the respondent surety had offered to pay security in respect of the pledged gold and the personal guarantee of the surety and the Bank would be satisfied on the surety 's furnishing personal guarantee and the creditor by its own negligence lost one of the securities. Acceptance of such a contention would tantamount to putting a premium on the negligence of creditor to the detriment of the sureties who is usually described as a preferred debtor.

The appellant was the holder of a village in Berar. He was granted a Sanad in 1948 and he continued to be in possession of it till 1949. In 1927, the Government passed an order under section 3 of the Patels Abolition Act, 1928, declaring that the lands were liable to be resumed and regranted to the respondent No. 1. The appellant challenged the validity of the order on the ground that (1) the patelki inam was not a "patelki" within the meaning of section 3 Of the Act, and (2) the Patelki Inam was not included in the definition of "poli inam" as defined by section 2(IA) of the Act. Held, that the patels were not entitled to claim as of right the share of the p Patel which was granted to him on condition that he would render certain services and incur expenditure for the benefit of the community or any section thereof and the pawaldar had no right to resume "phaiki inam" lands. The Patelkam lands were not liable to attachment or sale, and therefore, the pawaki inam could not be resumed by the Government under section 1O Of the Palels Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1927. Venkatagiri vs Veerabadrayya, (1921) L.R. 48 I.A. 244, referred to. The right of adoption to an inam is not recognised. The grant was not one of a patelkai inam but only a hereditary inam. The patel katels could be granted as of the princely origin and their conditions on the basis of which they were granted the service of patelka mate rials. The fact that the Palias were granted by the panedar did not affect the validity or the validity Of the grant.

The respondent was the karta of two Hindu undivided family. The respondents were the descendants of one R who died intestate in 1947 and his three sons, who were the appellants before the High Court, filed a suit for partition of their properties claiming that the entire estate devolved on R and that R had settled down in Madras and thereafter they had been converted into a caste by survivorship. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the respondents were not entitled to any share in the property as they were Hindus governed by the Hindu law of succession, and that the appellants were entitled only to maintenance and marriage expenses. On appeal, the High court held that the respondent was not a Hindu widow within the meaning of section 3 of the , and dismissed the suit. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants (1) that the definition of joint family property in section 3(a), that the rule of Hindu law applicable to the Khooshal community as well as the Memons would be subject to the same force as a customary law in matters of inheritance and succession, (2) that in view of the provisions of the Act which were consistently held by this Court in the Bombay case, the definition could not apply to the khooshala. HELD: (1)(a) The rule of survivorship is applicable only where there are two different procedures and each one has to be determined according to the circumstances of each case. [512 B] (b) The fact that a Khoonn had settled in Madras, which was not recognised by the law as customary law, would not make any difference because the rule applies only to cases where there is no such custom or usage and the law applicable thereto must apply and govern the case unless there was a pre vailing understanding that that was their customary law. [511 C] (c) The question as to which customary law is applicable depends upon the consideration of the decisions in the earlier case, and the decision in the present case has no application. [612 G H] (d) The definition of "Hindu Law" in section 2(a) of the includes a reference to Hindu Law. The definition is not exhaustive but only indicates what the law applies. It is the law laid down by the High Courts of Madras and Bombay that the law declared by this court would apply to all cases of succession and inheritance. [1212 B C] In the present ease, the Khernavva was a Brahmin community called the Brahmins and the Brahmin Community was governed by it. The Brahmins settled down amongst Hindus, Hindu Law, the Hindu Law as regards succession and the right of a son in it by birth was recognised under the Muslim law. It was not proved that he had ever adopted the custom of adoption according to Hindu law which they had retained while in Cutch and to which they were already accustomed. [1312 C D] (e) The High Court erred in holding that as the Brahmen settled down among Hindus, who settled down between them, the Bombarenna and the minor children would get a share as against the respondent. It had not been proved that the Brahman community of the village had settled the matter of inheritance. The fact of the Khizawar 's case was not relevant for deciding whether the Bombay view of law applicable in all matters relating to succession to their properties, or whether it was open to objection as to the bar of limitation under section 3, Evidence Act, 1908, to the contrary. [1512 C E] (f) The evidence on record did not establish that the Bombay High Court had upheld the custom prevailing in Madras. It would be wrong to say that the custom was not applicable to it unless there were a previ ous custom or custom.

The appellants are manufacturers of different types of fabrics. The appellants filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the circular dated May 11, 1968 issued by the Central Government under rule 9(1) of the Central Excise Rules, 1944, as amended by the Notification No. 9(I) of Central Excise and Salt Act, 1944. The High Court held that the appellants were not liable to pay excise duty on yarn manufactured in their factory at the time of their manufacture or for sale outside the factory and that the notification was valid. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the Notification did not require the specification of place of manufacture and also that the words "which may be specified by the Collector in this behalf" occurring in rule 9 (1) were not intended to be only when the goods are removed from the factory premises. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The notification dated May II, 1968 is valid and valid. [717D] 2. The words "whoever any place where they are produced, cured or manufactured" in the Explanation to rule 9 of the Rules cannot be read as "any place where They are produced", cured or manufac tured or manufactured or any premises appurtenant thereto. [815C D] 3.1 The expression "place of removal" is not defined in the Act. It must be given a meaning and its meaning must be ascertained and regarded as removed. It has been stated that the definition of "place" in Rule 9(i) does not require that the Collector should specify the place where the excisable goods are produced. [617D E] 3:2 The expression 'place of manufacture ' is used in the context of the Act, and it must be subject to the provisions of section 49 of the . [718F] 3(a) It is not necessary that the factory of production should have removed from a place where goods are manufactured, in the factory, so as to give rise to an obligation on the excise authorities to make any demand beyond the period mentioned in section 11A of the Excise Act. The expression has been used in relation to the manufacture within the meaning of section 2(e) of that Act. [700H; 700A] (b) It cannot be said that the expression 'premises ' in the definition is not required to be made by the authorities under the Act or Rules. Rule 9 of a Central Excise Rule, 1944 requires the Collector to specify the places where the goods manufactured are produced and also specify the premises appurtenant thereof if any. [ 700D] (c) The words 'which may he specified by notification in this respect ' occurring in r. 9 (i) mean the goods which may be mentioned by the manufacturer in the Schedule thereto, or is called. [750E] (d) The expression used in r.(1) must be read with the context and the meaning given to it in the rule. [751F] (e) The word 'premises" in r(1), has been given a wider connotation than that of an explanation. It means any physical or actual removal of the goods from a factory or production or manufacture of the excisable good etc., and as such, there is no cause for such apprehension. [753G H] (f) The Explanation to r.9(i), does not qualify the words 'any place ' where they occur, cured, or manufactured. The explanation to r, 9(ii) cannot be so construed as to qualify the word 'place ' in r,9(1).

The petitioner, a holder of a permit issued under Chapter IVA of the , to ply a stage carriage on Bulandshahr Siana Garh Bugrasi Brijghat Bhasians Shambhaoli Babugarh Jadol Jahangirabad route in the State of Uttar Pradesh, challenged the validity of the scheme published under section 68 C of the Act by filing a writ petition before the High Court. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the jurisdiction of the civil courts was impliedly barred from entertaining suits of the present nature. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the suit was not maintainable in a civil court for an injunction restraining the hearing Authority from proceeding with the hearing and approving the scheme either with or without modification. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The jurisdiction of a civil courts is impliedly barred under article 19(6) of the Constitution. [544F] 2. Section 68 D of the U.P. Act provides that where any State Transport Undertaking is of opinion that for the purpose of providing an efficient, adequate, economical and properly co ordinate road transport service it is necessary in the public interest that road transport services in general or any particular class of such service in relation to any area or route or portion thereof should be run and operated by the State Transport undertaking whether to the exclusion, complete or partial, of other persons or otherwise. After the scheme became final, as provided in sub section (iii) of section 68 D, the transport authorities concerned can issue permits only in accordance with the scheme and the other provisions contained in Chapter IV A of the Motor Vehicles Act. This Court in H. C. Narayanappa & Ors. vs The State of Mysore & Ors., ; at page 753 has observed that on the publication of the Scheme under section 69 C of Act any person who is aggrieved by the proposed introduction of the schemes is entitled to file his representations and objections and to appear before the hearing authority under section68 D of tho Act and make his submissions in support of his objections or representations. Sub section (ii) of Section 68D authorises the hearing of the applications for a suit in which the validity or the scheme of a C.P.,C. is called in question. The scheme as approved or modified as stated above shall then be published in the official Gazette and on such publication it becomes final. It is thus seen that Parliament has created a special machinery by the provisions contained therein for bringing jnto force an approved or modify scheme which would have the effect of excluding completely or partially other persons from operating motor service vehicles on any route or in any area.

The appellant was a public servant within the meaning of section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. He was convicted under section 161 Indian Penal Code and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for two years and to pay a fine of Rs. 5001 or in default to undergo further period of six months under section 5 (2). The appellant contended that the concealment of his birth of an illegitimate child was not an offence under the Indian Penal code or any other criminal statute and that the High Court had erred in holding that the appellant was guilty of grossly abusing his position as public servant. Held, that the order of sanction did not amount to a sufficient compliance with cl. 23 of the Indian Police Regulations and was therefore illegal. The order of the sanctioning authority did not suffer from any infirmity or illegality. The Order of sanction was bad in law as all the relevant papers were not placed before the D.I.G. Police, but were kept before the police for verification. The appellant had obtained money from Russel Nathaniel and his wife and also a gold ring from Roshan Lal. The currency notes of the denomination of Rs 100/ each were noted and the numbers of those currency notes were noted. The number of currency notes was noted and Russel was then instructed to pass on the money to the appellant. The fact that the currency notes had been seized from the pocket of the appellant did not make him liable for any offence under section 6(1)(d) of Prevention of Corrupt Practices Act.

The appellant was convicted under section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. He was acquitted by the trial court but on appeal the High Court confirmed his conviction and sentence. The appellant contended that the sanction granted by the Chief Commercial Superintendent of the Eastern Railway was not a valid sanction as it did not give his mind to the facts and circumstances of the case and that the prosecution had failed to prove that he merely put in the witness box before the trial judge, and that therefore the sanction accorded by him was not valid. Held, that the appellant was rightly convicted under the Prevention Of Corruption Act. The sanction clearly stated all the facts which concern the prosecution case alleged against the appellant with reference to his acceptance of Rs. 100 from Venkatachala on May 12, 1952 in circumstances which, if established, would constitute offences under section 161 Indian Penal Code and section 5 (2) Of the Prevention Act. Gokulchand Dwarkadas Morarka vs The King, , approved. Gokul Chand Dwarkadis Morarkka vs State of Bombay, ; , referred to. Held further, that in view of the provisions of the Moraraka 's case, the sanction given by the appellant could not be said to have been a valid one and the sanction was valid. The only point which had been argued before the High court was whether there had been a proper sanction in the present case. Gokul Chandra vs State, A.I.R. (1948) L.R 75 I.A. 30, referred to and distinguished.

The appellant was the holder of life interest in the property. The respondent landlord filed a suit for eviction against the tenant on the ground of demolition and reconstruction. The tenancy under the landlord was admitted by the tenants there. The tenant contended that the landlord had only a life interest and that it was inherent in such a life estate that it is not permissible for the landlord to invoke section 14(1)(b) as grounds for eviction of the tenants by demolition of the property for the purpose of reconstruction. Rejecting the contention, the appellate authority allowed the appeals filed by the tenant holding that the requirement of the landlords bona fide and ordered eviction of tenants was not bona fide. The High Court in revision set aside the order of the appellate court and restored the orders of eviction. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant tenant that a single petition with regard to two different tenancies, although in the same premises one for residential purpose and the other for non residential purpose, is not maintainable. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The rights between section M. Gopalakrishna and the remainder man with regard tO the terms of the Deed of Settlement win have to be worked out in appropriate proceedings, if necessary and the general law win govern the matter if any occasion arises. On the other hand, the Act with which we are concerned is a self contained and complete code for regulation of the rights between landlord and tenants as defined in the Act (See M/s Raval and Co. vs K. G. 276 Ramachandra and others) [275E F] 2. The right between sectionM. Gopalakrnan and the rest man with regards to the terms o f the Deed, of Settlement cannot be characterised as mala fide on the part of the landlord. There is no merit in this contention. A landlord has every right to demolish his property in order to build a new structure on the site with view to improve his business or to get better returns on his investment. Such a step per se cannot be regarded as mala fides on the side of the Act. [275G H] M/S Raval and Company vs K G.V. 276, followed.

The respondent decree holder obtained a decree against the appellant and the respondent. The execution court held that certain trees, which were deemed to be part of 'land ', vested in the State free from all encumbrances. The executing court also held that after vesting of all the rights mentioned in section 6(a)(i) of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, the only way in which a mortgagee could enforce his right against the mortgage or after the Act came into force is provided in section 4(1)(a) of Act. The respondent decree holders ' appeal before the executing court was dismissed. In second appeal before this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that since the respondent decreeholder 's decree holder 's suit had been decreed, the right in trees of groves as these contin ued to vest in the intermediary could not be proceeded against trees in groves and the view taken by the executing Court that there is a distinction between trees and grove land should have been upheld by a Division Bench of the High Court. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The position taken by both the parties was that after the coming into force of the Act, what could still be sold in execution of the decree was the right of the respondent to trees on the 'land" and not the land which were part of the 'estate '. [5E F] 2. The definition of intermediary 's grove under section 3(13) of U. P. Zamindari abolition and Land Reform Act, 1951, shows that trees, before they are cut, form parts of 'a grove '. And an inseparable part is always included in the whole. In view of this very clear legal position, it is not necessary even to consider previous definitions or to make out specious or unrealistic distinctions between standing uncut trees, and grove lands.

The appellants were charged with offences punishable under Sections 302, 324, 323, 341, 148 and 149 read with Section 149 IPC. The trial court convicted them under Section 302 IPC and sentenced them to suffer rigorous imprisonment for life. Accused No. 1 Subran was acquitted of the charge under Section 326/149 IPC. On an appeal by accused Nos. 2 to 6, the High Court acquitted two of the accused and convicted accused No. 4 and 5 for offences under Sections 143, 341 and 323 read with section 149 IPC but no separate sentences were awarded on any of those counts. The High Court also found that clear evidence of eye witnesses was only against accused Nos 2 to 3 and acquitted accused No 1. Hence this appeal by the State. Allowing the appeal partly, this Court, HELD: 1.1 There is a concurrent finding of the acquittal of the two accused persons by the High court and without the High Courts finding that some other known or unknown persons were also involved in the assault, would be that for all intent and purposes the two acquitted accused persons were not members of the unlawful assembly. Thus only four accused could be said to have been the members of an unlawful assembly but such an assembly which comprises of less than five members is not an unlawful one within the meaning of Section 141 IPC. [93F G] 1.2 The intention to cause murder of Suku by the four appellants with the chopper and those injuries "could" have resulted in the death of the deceased, but looking to the weapon with which he was armed and the nature number and seat of injuries inflicted by him though not on any vital part, he can certainly be attributed with the knowledge that with those injuries it was likely that death of Suhu had been caused and therefore he could very well have considered it unnecessary to concentrate on that part of the prosecution case during the cross examination of the Prosecution witnesses. Therefore, the conviction of appellants 2 to 4 for an offence under Section 325 IPC is not sustainable in law. [94F G; 95A] 1:3. The intention of causing murder of S was not attributed to him and the medical evidence also shows that the injuries caused were cumulatively sufficient to cause death and the death had occurred due to multiple injuries which were found sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause his death. [95B C] 2.1 The intention is a necessary postulate for invoking Section 149 I.P.C. Where the existence of such an unlawful unlawful assembly is not proved, the convicted person may be guilty of the offence of murder under Section 304, IPC without a specific charge having been framed against him as envisaged by law. Conviction for the substantive offence in such a case is unjustified because an accused might be misled in his defence by the absence of the charges for the ' substantive offence under section 302 I. P.C., and also because he may not be guilty to be convicted of the substantive offences under Section 307, IPC, without a specifically charge having being framed against the accused as envisaged in law, [95F G]. 2.2 In the instant case, the injuries inflicted on the deceased had been inflicted by all the four accused and that the death was caused due to receipt of multiple injuries.

The appellant assessee, a non resident company, entered into a collaboration agreement with the Standard Motor Products of India Ltd. (Indian Company) in November 1939 whereunder the assessee was entitled to royalty of five per cent on all sales effected by it. This amount was to be remitted to the assessee in the Sterling currency. The assessee 's accounting year was the year ending 30th September, 1966. In the assessment years 1967 68 and 1968 69, the assessee claimed that it was maintaining its accounts on mercantile basis alone and accordingly brought to tax the royalty amount disclosed. The Income Tax Officer completed the assessment for the first two assessment years on the basis of the returns filed by the assessee. For the assessment year 1969 70, the appellant claimed a deduction of five percent of five% of the Indian tax paid in the Supreme Court. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner dismissed the appeals holding that the assessee had not been following any particular method of accounting regularly over the past years. The Tribunal held that the question of method of accountancy adopted by the appellant must be examined afresh and for that purpose allowed the appeals and remanded the matters to the Income Tax officer. In these appeals, it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that the appellant had not maintained its accounts in regard to royalty and that the Indian Company was not aware of the assessee 'Sangamese business in regard of royalty and therefore it had committed a mistake in filing the returns for the assessment. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Court was right in answering the question against the assessee on the facts of the case. It must be held that in the circumstances of the ease, the method of accounts adopted by assessee for the relevant accounting years is really irrelevant. As soon as the monies were credited to the account of the non resident (Japanese) com pany, it must be hold that it "received" the same in U.K.

The appellant was convicted of murder and sentenced to death. The High Court on appeal found corroboration in material particulars, from the evidence of an accomplice, that he made a confessional statement to his brother and that the knife was used by him for the murder. In appeal to this Court it was contended that there was no corroboration of the approver 's story and that his conviction was unsustainable. HELD : (i) The High court had not been oblivious of the rule of prudence and practice which in the words of Martin B in Res. vs Boyes, , laid down as follows: "A conviction based merely on the uncorroborated testimony of an approver may not be illegal, the courts nevertheless cannot lose sight of the rules of prudence, and practice, which in fact and law, for the judge to warn the jury of the danger of convicting a prisoner on the recorder of the court. to advise them not to convict upon such evidence but the judge should point out to the jury that it is within their legal province to convict on such unconfirmed evidence. The rule of guidance is to be found in illustration (b) to section 114 of the Evidence Act which is as follows : "The Court may presume that an accomplice is unworthy of credit unless he is corroborated in material particular". [835 B C] In re Rajagopal, , referred to. (ii) Under section 133 of the Indian Penal Code a conviction based only on the ac quiry of the accused on the testimony of a witness without corroboration in materials particulars. The law may be stated in the language of that section, as follows, : "A person who is a wrestler and he and his brother used to sleep in the offence and afterwards to save himself betrayed his former associates, and who has placed himself in a classison with the former associates and who had placed himself into a classice. . . . A conviction based on the evidence by an accomplice cannot be said to be illegal yet the courts will, as a matter of practice, not accept the evidence Of such a witness, without corroboration In material particulars.

The appellant was a servant of the State Electricity Board constituted under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. He was charged with having committed offences punishable under section 5(2) read with section 5 (1) (d) of the Prevention Of Corruption Act and section 161 of the Indian Penal Code. The trial court accepted the prosecution case as true and convicted him under section 161 I.P.C. and sentenced him to undergo rigorous imprisonment for two years. On appeal, the High Court dismissed his appeal holding that he could not be deemed to be a public servant within the meaning of section 21 of the Act or section 21 Of the Indian . The appellant contended that (i) the prosecution was not a 'public servant ' within the definition of section 2(1) of that Act and (ii) the appellant was not an officer in the service or pay of a Government or of a corporation engaged in any trade or industry which is established by a Central, Provincial or State Act or of the Government company as defined in section 617 of the . HELD : The appellant was an officer of the Corporation within the terms of section 1 of the , and therefore a public servants within the purview of that section. [687 G] (i)(a) The officers and servants of the Board are deemed to have been public servants only when acting or purporting to act in pursuance of any of the provisions of the ; . Therefore, the appellant could not he deemed to he a public Servant within the mean time of section 6 of the General Clauses Act. [688 B] (b) The word 'officer ' in section 21, cl. (12), Indian Penal code is used in the widest sense and applies to all public servants. In view of Explanation 4 to section 21 Indian Penal C.P.,C., it cannot be said that the appellant is a public officer within the contemplation of section 7(1)(d) because he was not acting or purported to act as such.

The appellant was convicted under section 3 of the Maharashtra Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1962. The High Court set aside the conviction and sentence passed on him in respect of contravention of the provisions of the Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended that r. 141(2) was ultra vires because it lays down a rule of evidence contrary to the law contained in section 114 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872. HELD: The order of the High Court maintaining the forfeiture of the seized stock of juar set aside and instead of the sentences awarded by the lower courts sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for six months and fine of Rs. 500/ in default further rigorous imprisonment. [273 G] Rule 141(1) is within the powers conferred by section 3 (1). The rule contemplates that the rules may be inconsistent with existing legislation but by virtue of section 43, if otherwise valid, they would have effect notwithstanding that they are inconsistent with old legislation. Therefore r.141(2), which is within powers conferred under section3 (1) of the Defence of India Act, is within its powers. [272 G] The rule must necessarily provide for the publication of orders made under the Rules and they must also provide for proof in judicial proceedings of the fact of publication. The rules must necessarily be provided for the proof in the judicial proceedings. [274 A B] In the instant case the order of conviction was not vitiated by any error apparent on the face of the record. [275 C D] The High court has rightly set aside that conviction and sentences passed on the appellant.

The appellants were convicted under section 302 read with section 109 and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence of Sia Ram and Violet. On appeal by special leave, it was contended that (i) the evidence of identification was inadmissible because the witnesses did not identify the accused persons; (ii) the only inference which arose from the fact that the crime charged could not have been committed without the interposition of the alleged abettor is that by so doing the witness knew the accused prior to the occurrence and therefore he should be put up for being identified in an identification parade. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The High court was right in holding that no rule of law requires that the oral testimony of a witness should be corroborated by evidence of identifying witnesses. [626 D] (2) In order to constitute abetment, the abettor must be shown to have "intentionally" aided the commission of the crime. Mere proof that the offence charged couldnot have been done without the consent of the accused is not enough compliance with the requirements of section 107. A person may, for example, invite another casually or for a friendly purpose and that may facilitate the murder of the invite. But unless the invitation was extended with intent to facilitate the commission Of the crime, the person inviting cannot be said to have abetted the murder. It is not sufficient if an act on the part of the committing officer or illegal omission, is done by him in the case of a particular accused. [625 E F] (3) The fact that he was a colleague of the deceased who was working as a Nurse with a doctor was likely to have the knowledge of the commission. But the High Court was not impressed by his evidence.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 read with section 34, I.P.C., and sentenced to imprisonment for life. The High Court confirmed the conviction of the appellant under section 307 read with sections 34, Indian Penal Code. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) when three of the four named accused were acquitted by the trial court, the court could not convict only one of them on the basis of constructive liability; and (ii) when the High Court convicted the appellant for having committed the murder of another person, the Court could not convicting him under section 34. HELD : The judgment of the High court must be set aside. It is well settled that common intention within the meaning of section 114 of the Indian Penal code implied a pre arranged plan and the criminal act was done pursuant to the prearranged plan. The said plan may also develop on the spot during the course of the commission of the offence; but the crucial circumstance is that the said plan must precede the act constituting the offence.
