If that be so, before a court can convict a person under section 304, read with s 34, of the Penal Code, it should come to a definite conclusion that the accused had a prior concert with one or more other persons named or unnamed for committing the said offence. A Court cannot obviously make out a case for the prosecution which is not disclosed either in the charge or in regard to which there is no basis in the evidence. There must be some foundation in the Evidence that persons other than those named have taken part in the commission Of the offence and if there is such a basis the case will be covered by the third illustration. In the first instance, the courts cannot make out any case for tho prosecution which was not disclosed in the chargesheet or the evidence was adduced to prove that the appellant along with others named or unidentified persons participated jointly in the offence, nor is there any evidence in that regard. The effect of the acquittal of accused 1, 3 and 4 is that they did not conjointly act with accused 2 in committing the murder. If they did no act conjointly with them, the result in law would be the same. It would mean that they do not take part in an offence. [687F H] Mohan Singh vs State of Punjab, ; , referred to.

The petitioner, a manufacturer of iron wire Indus tries, filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order dated 11th May, 1983 issued by the Central Government under section 132(1) of the Income Tax Act, 1961. The petitioner contended that the goods were supplied to M/s Industrial Cable India Ltd., Singapore for the supply of MSCR defective sheets or coils on 30th May 1984 and that the said goods were delivered in April, 1984. The goods were weighed on 7th August, 1984 and the goods arrived at Bombay Port per S.S.C. On 21st May, 1984, the Income tax Authorities issued a necessary no objection certificate lifting the ban. The writ petition was filed under Article 32 of the Constitution on 16th April, 1988 and on 22nd April, 1989 this Court passed an order directing that the petitioner be paid duty at the time of clearance of the goods. On 30th March, 1988 this Court directed the goods to appear before the Customs Authorities for clearance of goods. The petitioners ' request was rejected by the customs authorities on the ground that they had not been ready and willing to get the material on payment of duty on the date when the petitioner was actualling expressed willingness to remove the goods, and that it would be possible for them to clear the goods on payment. On 22nd May, 1988, this Court dismissed the writ petition. In the special leave petition under Article 136 of the Constitu tion, it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that in view of the language used in section 15(1)(b) of Income Tax 1961, it would not be possible to clear any goods imported without payment at that rate or without having the matter determined by the procedure envisaged and enjoined by the law for that determination. Dismissing the special Leave Petition, this court, HELD: 1. The relief under Article32 of the Consti tution is wholly inappropriate in the facts and circumstances of the case. [626C] 2.1 In the instant case, the petitioner as such has no fundamental right to clear goods imported except in due process of law. It is not permissible to move this Court on the theoretical basis that there is breach of the fundamental rights. Whenever a person complains and claims that there was a violation of law, it does not automatically involve breach of fundamental right for the enforcement of which alone Article 32 is attracted. [625D E] 2:2 In the facts of this case, such clear ance can only be made on payment Of duty as enjoined by Section 49 and importer may apply to the Assistant Collector of Customs for permission to store the imported goods in a warehouse pending their clearance and he may be permitted to do so. Section 68 provides that an importer of any warehoused goods may clear them if the import duty leviable on them has been paid. In that case, it is found that as the goods have been cleared pursuant to that order, the goods are cleared from a warehouse under section 68, on the dates when the petitioners were actu ings of being cleared, but could not be cleared because of the prohibitory orders of the income tax Department under section 102 of the . [627F G] 2 :3. The facts of the instant cases show that the peti tioner as such had no fundamental rights to clear their goods imported, except in a proper condition, are satisfied.

The appellant was the karta of a Hindu undivided family. He had two sons, one of whom was a minor and the other a son who died in 1942. The father died in 1943 leaving behind his widow, the appellant and his wife. The sons filed a suit for partition of their joint family properties and separate possession of their share. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the debt was not liable to be attached as it was not supported by any consideration or gift but was a debt for a debt incurred in execution of his decree. On appeal, the High Court reversed the decision of the trial court and held that the liability of the sons to pay the debts of their father under Hindu law was not dependent upon the father 's power to alienate the share of his sons but on the principle of pious obligation imposed on the sons under the Mitakshara law. The question for determination in this appeal was whether the debt of the father was assessable as an accretion to the estate of the deceased son, and whether it was a liability to pay off the debts. Held, that the appellant was entitled to defend his title to the properties of his father which were not tainted with immorality or illegality. The right of the son to alienate for payment of personal debt is ended by the partition of the joint family property. The pious obligation created in favour of a widow under the Hindu law would be sufficient to sustain the sale and defeat the sons ' suit in the same way and on the same grounds as in the case of execution proceedings. Held further, that in the present case the liability was not based upon the pious obligation of the appellants but on principle of joint family system of law. Held also, that a Hindu father who is a managing director and who draws a salary or remuneration for his illegal purpose cannot be held to have an absolute right under the personal law governing him as regards what he has to do in appropriate proceedings taken by them. The liability of a father who was a managing Director and who drew a salary for the son, though the successor was not brought on record would not be sufficient for sustaining the sale of his share. Held accordingly, that on the facts of the case it could not be held that a sale of the property which was not tainted by immorancy or illegality was based on the pious obligations of the two sons which continued to exist in the life time and after the death of the husband and which did not come to an end as a result of partition of joint Hindu family property, and that the right of a son to make an application under section 53 of the Bombay Land Revenue Code was not available to him. Held therefore, further, the liability for the debt incurred by the father in execution proceedings as also on the basis of the personal decree passed against him could not arise under the provisions of section 155 of the Act. The legal position is that the obligation of a person to discharge debts of the family which are not tainted and which cannot be termed as repugnant to good morals, must be distinguished from the pious liability imposed on a third person who has executed the decree. Held per KANIA C.J., PATANJALI SASTRI J. (FAZL ALI J. dissenting) that the legal position in both cases is the same. The obligation of one of the heirs to discharge the debts incurred by an heir under section 155(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure, which has been imposed on him by the Hindu Law, would be a question of fact in each case depending upon what was the estate acquired and not whether it had been acquired by the sons or brought into existence in the lifetime of the adopted son. Held (FAFAR ALI J., FAZL ALl, PATANJAL SASTHAR DAS J. concurring) that on a proper construction of section 56(1), the liability to discharge a debts incurred under the decree remains unaffected and the liability cannot be treated as repugnant thereto. The words "dissolved" in section 155 (1)

The petitioners, a number of persons, were arrested by the Delhi Administration and were sent to the Delhi Administrations for trial. The Delhi Administration had to examine first all those persons as provided by Rule 5(5)(a) of the Commissions of Inquiry (Central) Rules, 1972 framed under the Act. But before the Committee could complete its work, the petitioners filed a writ petition in this Court challenging the validity of the aforesaid orders and also the criminal proceedings initiated against them before the committee. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petition holding that since the petitioners had not been given notice under section 8 B of the Act, they were dealt with by the Committee as provided under Rule 5 (5)(b) of Rules, the Committee should have sent a report recommending suspension of the D.C.P. (North) and Jinder Singh S.I. in view of the facts and circumstances of the case. Allowing the writ petition, ^ HELD: 1. The petitioners were persons who fall under section8 B of Delhi Administration Act and have to be dealt with accordingly. [521D] 2. The Committee should not have in the circumstances of this case directed the filing of a complaint against either of the petitioners for an offence punishable under section 178 I.P.(N) P.C., in view to that no notice was given to them under section 9 8 B. [525E F] 3. The action of the Committee in asking them to be cross examined at the end of the inquiry is discriminatory. Mere non issue of notices to them, under section 7B ought not to make any difference if they otherwise satisfy the conditions mentioned in section 8B. The issue of such a notice is not contemplated under section eight B of Act. It is enough if at any stage the Commission considers it necessary to inquire into the conduct of any person. Such person would thereafter be governed by section 8(B) of Delhi Adminis tration and the Committee would have then asked them to give evidence along with others who were similarly placed at the conclusion of the enquiry. [421F G] 4. The committee should have considered whether the petitioners were entitled to be treated as persons governed by Section 8 B, before asking them for a reasonable opportunity of being heard in view thereof.

The Rajasthan Passengers and Goods Taxation Rules, 1959, were framed under section 3 of the Rajasthan Passengers & Goods Taxation Act, 1959. The petitioners challenged the validity of the said rules on the ground that they infringed their fundamental rights under articles 301 and 304 of the Constitution. Held: (i) The levy of tax cannot be said to offend articles 301 or 304 of Part 1 of the Constitu tion. The levy is justified on the assumption of a return in the shape of conveniences. If the tax were laid on passengers and goods, though what it was to be is deter mined by the amount of fare or freights attributable to the territory of another State when the route passes through such territory, even though the journey starts and ends in Rajasthan, there is no tax on fares and freights attributed to routes outside the State except in one instance which is contemplated by the proviso to sub section (3) of section 3 and to which reference will be made separately. The expression "shall" used both in Rules 8 and 8 A and the notification issued thereunder must be read harmoniously, and reading them so as to give effect to the word "shall". If the Act creates an option, it cannot be negatived by the Rules. (ii) The words "may accept" in r. 8 A are enabling and thereby authorise the State Government to accept a lump sum payment in lieu of tax actually chargeable. The word "may" is ordinarily mandatory but it is sometimes not so interpreted if the context or the intention otherwise demands. In re Rustom, C.J., and Cooverjee, , referred to. (iii) The expression 'shall ' in rs. 8 and 9A and the notifications are not void and contradictory of the Act. It is only when the tax was laid on persons who were comparable, and there may be days when the business done might result in tax in excess of the lump sum payable. The words 'may accept ' in rr.

The appellant company was engaged in the manufacture of a textile industry. The raw material for its manufacturing process was tin plates. The appellant served notice of retrenchment on 43 workmen and the workmen were asked to show cause why their wages should not be paid back wages from 1st August, 1974 with full back wages, permitting the appellant to deduct any amount paid as retrenchment compensation from the amount payable to the workmen as back wages. The workmen demanded a revision of the wage scales and the appellant pleaded that the workmen who were retrenched were entitled to the relief of reinstatement effective from that date. The Labour Court held that the reasons stated in the notice dated 1st July, 1974, Ext. E2, viz., heavy loss caused by non availability of tin plates, persistent power curbs and mounting cost of production were not the real reason for affecting retrenchment but the real ground was the annoyance felt by the management consequent upon the refusal of the workmen to agree to the terms of settlement contained in the draft dated 5th April, 1974 and therefore the retrenchment was illegal. The High Court also awarded full back Wages to the appellant. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the workmen concerned did not have any opportunity of explaining why their services should not he terminated and (2) the real reasons being the annoyance of the employer, there was no justification for not awarding them full back wage. Dismissing the Appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The scope and ambit of this wide constitutional discretionary power cannot be exhaustively defined. It cannot obviously be so construed as to confer a right to a party which he has none under the law. The Court will entertain a petition for special leave in which a question of general public importance is involved or when the decision would shock the conscience of this Court. [571C D] 2.1 In the instant case, from being a factor of production, the labour is a common venture, the participants being the capital and the labour. Gone are the days when labour was considered a factor which would help the workmen in breach of the principles of natural justice causing substantial and grave injustice to parties or raises an important principle of industrial law requiring elucidation and final decision by this Court or disclose such other exceptional or special circumstances which merit consideration of this court. [572F G] 2:2 The scope of the wide constitutional discretion cannot be broadly defined. The wide constitutional power cannot obviously not be so interpreted as to empower a court to grant special leave to appeal, inter alia, against the award of any Tribunal in the territory of India. The limited right to appeal is what should be the guiding considerations for awarding full backwages. All relevant considerations will enter the verdict. More or less, it would be a motion addressed to the discretion of the Supreme Court. Full back wages would be the normal rule and the party objecting to it must establish the circumstances necessitating departure. At that stage the Tribunal will exercise its discretion keeping in view all the relevant circumstances. But the discretion must be exercised in a judicial and judicious manner. [573F G; 571A] 2 :3 The scope for exercising discretion must depend on the facts peculiar to each case and the discretion should be exercised with full care and not appear on the face of it or the record. When it is said that something is to be done within the discretion, of the authority, that something was to be performed according to the rules of reason and justice, according to law and not humor. [574B C] 4:4 The question whether the workmen should be awarded full backwages or some sacrifice is expected of him depends on the circumstances peculiar to the case and it would depend upon the facts of each case reinstatement being accorded to the workman. That is the normal rules. Any other view would be discriminatory. Ordinarily, therefore, a workman whose service has been illegally terminated would be entitled to full back benefits except to the extent he was gainfully employed during the enforcement of the undertaking.

The accused was charged with murder and sentenced to death. The prosecution case was that on the night of September 16, 1969, at about 10 p.m., when the deceased was sleeping in a house in Shingara, he was found dead by the police. He was informed by one of his friends that the deceased had been murdered and that he had killed him. The accused were charged with having committed murder by jumping into nulla and the death was caused by a sharp edged weapon. The trial court convicted the accused under section 302 Indian Penal Code and sentenced him to death, but the High Court confirmed the conviction of the accused relying on the confessional statement made by him to the police regarding the crime. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the confessional statements were inadmissible in evidence and no oral evidence was produced in defence. HELD : (i) The confession was recorded during the investigation of a case by a second class magistrate, and as such admissible in evidence. [436 B] (ii) The High Court had rightly held that it was the accused and none else who caused injuries to Churi deceased as a result of which she died. [ 436 C D] (iii) The statement made to the Police Officer by the accused was not inadmissible in any way. [441 E] (iv) The evidence on record establishes beyond any manner of doubt that the dead body of the deceased, was recovered after the accused had visited the house of Shri Mahajan. It is well established that the discovery and arrest of the suspected offender are admissible in proof of an offence under section 164 Indian Penal code. [442 G] (v) The fact that the accused suspected the fidelity of Churi did not necessarily mean that he was not aware of the murder of Chriokhri. [443 A B] Nazir Ahmed vs King Emperor, L.R. 63 I.A. 372 and Inder Singh vs State of Delhi, ; , referred to. (vi) The mere fact that a person is charged with an offence in respect of some property may not be conclusive as to the guilt of the offence under s. 164 Indian Evidence Act. [444 A B]. (vii) The accused was rightly convicted by the High court. [44 C] (viii) The conviction of an accused under s, 302 I.P.C. is set aside and he is sentenced to imprisonment for life.

The plaintiff sued the defendant for a declaration that the properties in suit were joint family properties and that he was entitled to receive the balance of the mortgage debt. The defendants pleaded that the property was joint family property, that the plaintiff had no right to claim any share in it as the shares of the defendants stood in the name of the plaintiff and that the defendant was not liable for a half share in the mortgaged property; that the suit was barred by section 43 of the Contract Act. The trial court decreed the suit but on appeal the High Court held that the agreement was proved, that there was no contract to the contrary and that it was not proved that the parties were on good faith. Held, that under section 43 Of the Contract act a person is entitled to claim compensation for any loss caused by him in consequence of the contract. The words "the contract" in section 43 are wide enough to cover all transactions which may be entered into between the same parties and are capable of being induced to agree to accept ance which is its due. In the present case, the plaintiff was entitled only to a half of the amount claimed by him as a share in his property. The suit was therefore decreed. The plaintiff had not established that he had made any contract with the defendants for the payment of the entire amount and the balance due on the date of the decree. The agreement was not genuine, nor was it proved that there were negotiations between the parties. The fact that the claim was inartistically worded did not affect the validity of the agreement.

The appellants applied for the post of Asstt. Engineers (Civil) and (Mech.) in the Public Works Department, Government of Karnataka. The Selection Committee recommended for recruitment of Asstts. Engineers. However, the first appellant secured only 29.50 marks out of 50. The second appellant secured 66.40 marks out from 150. The 2nd appellant secured 67.70 marks out Of 100. The 3rd appellant secured 68.40 votes in the interview and 66.39 marks in the qualifying examination. The 1st appellant secured 69.96 marks out off 50. In the interview, the respondents No. 1 to 4 were not selected in merit as the last candidate selected for the above posts secured higher marks than the appellants. The appellants filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the Rules on the ground that the percentage of marks for viva voce as 33.3% was excessive and in violation of the decisions of this Court in Ashok Kumar Yadav & Ors. vs State of Haryana & Ors., [1988] Suppl. S.C.R. 657, and Mohinder Sain Garg vs State Of Punjab & Ors, , J.T. On a direction given by this Court on 4th September, 1991, the record of the Selection Committee was produced before this Court at the time of hearing. From a perusal of the marks awarded to the selected candidates it is clear that a large number of candidates have been selected though they had secured much lesser marks than those appellants in the examination but had secured very high marks in their viva voce out of 100. [495E F] Ashok Kumar & Ors vs State, ; , Jt. Commissioner, Haryana & Anr., J. T. On: a direction issued by this court on 4 th September,1991, the records of the selection committee were produced before the Court at that time.

The prosecution alleged that the deceased was a member of the Indian Administrative Service and was posted as Collec tor at the relevant time. On the 11th April, 1983, he started giving reli giction to Sadanand in jail. The deceased was taken out a bomb from the bag which he held and threw it at the Collector. The appellant who was one of the accused persons, was charged under section 302 read with section 120B of the I.P.C. and was convicted under section 3 of the Explosive Substance Act and sentenced to ten years rigorous imprisonment. On appeal by the appellant, the High Court confirmed his conviction and sentence. In the appeals before this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the prosecution had established by circumstantial evidence that the appellant was a Member of the India Administrative Service; (ii) the entire structure of the Ashram was demolished under the direct supervision of the Collector; and (iii) the appellant had been convicted under Section 302 readwith section 120 B of I. P.C., and sentenced for life imprisonment. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The confession of a co accused is not substantive evidence against other co accused persons in the same trial. As this Court pointed out in Kashmira Singh vs State of Madhya Pradesh, ; , the confes sion of a Co accused is neither substantive evidence nor substantive evidence and therefore would not be admissible against the other accused persons at the trial but could only be used for lending reassurance if there by any other substantive evidence to be utilised or acted upon. [408B C] 2. The prosecution has established by direct evidence that appellant was regularly visiting Sadanand at the jail. It is difficult to support the charge of conspiracy with direct evidence in every case but if the prosecution relies upon circumstantial evidence, a clear link has to be established and the chain has to he completed, otherwise it would indeed be hazardous to accept a part of the link as a complete one and on the basis of such incomplete evidence, the allegation of conspiracy cannot be accepted. [413D E] 3. The conviction of the co accused person is not sustainable. His appeal has to fail. He is acquitted and directed to be set at liber ty forthwith.

The appellant company was a manufacturing concern of a manufacturing concerns known as Crompton Parkinson Private Limited and its main business is distribution of the products of a manufacturer known as, Cromicon Parkin Ltd. The last of these companies was governed by the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, which came into force on April 1, 1959. In the year 1958 there were two references to the Industrial Tribunal in respect of wages and dearness allowance. The Tribunal held that the workmen were entitled to dearness allowance at a certain percentage depending upon length of service between 1950 and 1959. On appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant company that the Tribunal had gone wrong in applying the industry cum region formula which is the basis for fixing wage scales and dearness allowances. It was further contended that the Industrial Tribunals should have followed the method of fixing wages and Dearness allowance together with dearness allowance and that the tribunal erred in not following the industry ' cum region principle. HELD: (i) The Tribunal was right in holding that the appellant was entitled to one increment depending upon the length of services between 1950 & 1959. [368 E] (ii) The Industrial Tribunal was wrong in putting the subordinate staff in the same scale of dearness allowance as clerical and subordinate staff. It had made a comparison with the concerns which were earlier in the region. The main object of the industry is to fix wage scales for subordinate staff and factory workmen as in the case of clerical and sub staff. So far as subordinate employees are concerned, it was not necessary that the total wage packet should be fixed on the basis of the comparable industries. [369 E F] (iii) The tribunal had relied on a number of cases in which the maximum was higher than the highest but more than the lowest. In those circumstances it could not be said that the entire matter was left to the Tribunal and it may follow such method as it thinks best so long as it arrives at a fair conclusion after making the necessary comparison. [370 E F; 371 A] (iv) The award relating to wages and neutralise the rise in prices is set aside and the matter remanded to the tribunal for fixing the wage structure including basic wage and dearness Allowance. [372 B C] (v) The question whether adjustment should be granted or not is always a question depending upon facts and circumstances of each case. It is well settled that in considering the question of adjustment, the Tribunal has begun to give a higher ceiling and in one concern, namely Mackinnon Mackenzie, the ceiling has been fixed even so high as thirty moths by agreement, but this has to be done sparingly taking into account the total wages packet in fixing wages. [373 E F]. (vi) The dispute in these cases is not between a company and its workmen but between the designation and the class in which they are being placed. It cannot be said, therefore, that the whole of the employees of the same kind in a particular region are small in a different area in the particular region. [374 A B] (vii) The fact that there is no question of want of financial capacity and that Greaves Cotton & Co. which is not the concern of the unskilled class, is irrelevant because it is practically from the date of the first reference in the present case.

The appellants filed a suit against the mortgagees for redemption of certain mortgaged property. The mortgagees resisted the suit on the ground that the mortgage was not binding on them and that the mortgagees were not the heirs of the deceased mortgagor. The trial court held that the Rajinama executed by the mortgagors did not extinguish the title of the mortgagors in the mortgaged property but only created a complete relinquishment of his interest, but as regards the other defendants it held that they were entitled to redeem the mortgage. On appeal the District Court confirmed the decree. In second appeal the High Court held that under section 74 of the Bombay Land Revenue Code, as Shiddappa did not purport to file the same on behalf of annappa nor had he any right to do so; and that in view of the provisions of section 74 the Raj in question was a complete relinquish of his interests. Held, that the High court was wrong in holding that the appellants were entitled under section 73 of the Act to redeeminama. The mere assertion of an adverse title on the part of the appellants cannot affect the subsisting equity of redemption of the mortgages or operate to shorten the period of limitation prescribed for a suit for redemption. Khiarajmal vs Daim (1904) L. R. 32 Ind. App. Cas. 22 and Lalchand Sakharam Marwadi vs Khendu Kedu Ughade, , referred to. Held further, that on a correct interpretation of section 73 the RajInama passed by Shiddppa did not affect the right of an heir as he had no inherent or independent title to give any such notice so as to effect their interest in the occupancy.

The respondent, a company incor porated under the Indian Companies Act, 1948, was assessed to sales tax on carbon paper for the period commencing from July 1, 1966 to June 30, 1966. The Sales Tax Officer held that carbon paper not being paper falling within the purview of Entry 2 of the Schedule to the Act, but a specialised article used for copying purposes, its turnover had to be assessed at the rate of 2 per cent prescribed under the Notification and that the respondent was liable to sales Tax at the point and at the time of March 1967 at 6% and that of ribbon at 10%. The respondent challenged the levy on the ground that carbon papers did not lose its character as paper even after being subjected to chemical processes and that ribbon was a part of the typewriter. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that carbon Paper is an accessory or a part thereof and that it is not an accessory but an essen tial part of a typewriter, and therefore, will not come within Entry 2. The respondent contended before this Court that carbon is an integral part of typewriter and its turnover could not be subjected to salestax at the rates of 10% prescribed in the Notification. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) It is well settled that a word which is not defined in an enactment has to be understood in its popular and commer cial sense with reference to the context in which it occurs. In Attorney General vs Winstanley, , referred to. (2) The mere fact that the word 'paper ' forms part of denomination of a specialised Article is not decisive of the question whether the article is paper as generally understood. [840 C] (3) It an accessory and not a part or diesel is a part and diesel is not a component of a commercial sense. [850 E] (4) The word ' Paper ' in the common parlance or in the com plaint in order to reproduce on the lower sheet that which is written or typed on the upper sheet i.e. making replica tions, must be construed in its ordinary popular and distinc tion to these words by people usually conver sant with and dealing in such goods. [851 D] (5) The fact that a typewritor forms part o the denomination of the specialised article is not conclusive of the matter whether the Article is paper or not.

The respondents were employed by the appellant as seasonal workmen in the State of Nainital. The appellant was a partnership concern and the respondents were their employees. On January 19, 1955, the General Manager, the appellant ordered transfer of the respondents 1 to 4 from the appellant Mills at Bulandshahr. The respondents challenged the order of transfer on the ground that it contravened the provisions of Standing Order No. L(a) of the U. P. Industrial Disputes (Appellate Tribunal) Act, 1950, and that as the respondents had disobeyed the order they were properly dismissed by the management. Held, that the appellant was not a condition of service of the respondent No. 1 in the present case, that he had no such right to transfer him to a new concern stared by him subsequent to the date of his employment. The employer in the instant case has no such rights and it is well within the powers of the Labour Appellate Tribunal to entertain the appeal. Mary (Anamalai Plantation) Workers Union vs Seliparai Estate, ; , followed. Mary, Anamalai plantation Workers ' Union vs seliparani estate, , distinguished. The question whether a person employed in a factory can be transferred to another is essentially one of fact and the Tribunal has no jurisdiction to set aside that finding under section 7(1) of Industrial Disputes Act. Mary. (Anamaly Bouzourou vs The Ottoman Bank, ; and Mary (A.T.R. 119), referred to.

The appellant company which was formed in 1965 and went into production, the same year, was exempted from the provisions of Chapter V A of the . The Special Officer of the respondent company, who was also a member of the Employees State Insurance Scheme, made an application under section 73 of the to the effect that the employees ' contribution should be made by the employer under the or other similar payment or benefit under various other social welfare legislations. The appellant company challenged its liability to pay special contribution under Chapter VA of the Act before the High Court which dismissed it. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the contribution payable under Chapter IV A was a fee and its levy was illegal as the Act did not contemplate the rendering of any service or the conferment of any benefit to the appellant company or its employees as quid pro quo for the payment. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The object of the amendment was to make an equitable distribution of contributions by all employers. It was not considered fair that only employers of these regions to which the benefit provisions were extended should alone make contributions and thereby help to set up a corporation. [1094C] 2.1 The object is confined to a few areas and though special contribution is levied from all employers wherever they be, in the case of employers who straightaway receive the benefits of the insurance scheme, their rate of contribution is higher while in the cases of employers, who do not yet receive the benefit of the scheme, the rate of contributions is lower. So far as the latter are concerned, the scheme is analogous to a deferred insurance policy which parents often take out on the lives of their children, but which are to be effective only from a future date after the children attain a certain age, though premium is liable to be paid right from the start. Merely because the benefits to be received are postponed, it cannot be said that there is no quid pro viso for the delayed benefit from the point of view of time, but with reference to the very benefit itself and its connection with the levy.

The management of the National Mineral Development Corporation Ltd. had throughout denied the petitioners claim and alleged that they were discharging their duties as regular workers. The management contended that in fact, the petitioners were continued on humanitarian grounds for several years even though there was no work for them; that the petitioners had been continuously working on rolls on humanitarian ground for several year, even though the petitioners have been paid wages as regular workmen. Dismissing the writ petition, HELD: 1. The principle of regularisation of a daily rated workman and payment to him of the pay equal to that of a regular workman arises only when the daily rated workmen is doing the same work as the regular workman and there being a vacancy available for him, he is not absorbed against it or not even paid the equal pay for the period during which the same worked is taken from him. [620C D] 2. The principles of regularisation are not the position. This Court cannot interfere under Article 136 of the Constitution in view of clear findings supported by evidence that there are no vacancies or work available in the establishment for absorption of the petitioners and that for quite some time they have been continued on rolls and paid in spite of there being no work. [625E F] 3. The question of directing their absorption and regu larisation does not arise. The Court cannot, therefore, fail to interfere with the High Court 's decision in view the clear findings of this Court that there were no vacancies nor work available for absorption on the rolls.

The appellants were the owners of a piece of land in Calcutta. The property was acquired under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 by the State Government and the compensation payable to them was fixed at Rs. 12,000/ per annum on the footing that they had been in possession of the same for more than one year as their share in the estate. The appellants claimed that the said sum was not liable to be paid to them as the property was a joint family property and that the entire interest which represented the interest of the appellants in the land acquired was unaffected by the decision of this Court in Raja Ram vs Jagannath Singh, [1959] Supp. 1 S.C.R. 869. The claim was based on the basis that the lands were purchased by the appellants as they were joint family properties and that their share had been partitioned between them and the appellants. Held, that the suit was not barred by section 41 of the Transfer of Property Act, because (1) the transfer of property was not a joint Hindu family property but was for legal necessity; (2) the sale in favour of the co sharers was not binding on them as they had not been put in possession; and (3) the appellants were entitled to a decree for partition. The suit was maintainable under section 41(1)(c) of the Act, which provided that no person shall be entitled to any further compensation for his property except to the extent of 2 1/2 years as entered in the revenue records. The fact that the appellants had not put up their claim did not make out a case of possession and the suit must fail. The mere fact that they were co sharer would not necessarily mean that they could be entitled only to a further compensation, that is, if the transaction was real and intended to pass title to Pir Baksh, the plaintiffs would be entitled in addition to the amount claimed by them as in their plaint. The question whether the suit in such a case was substantially barred by limitation was not raised before the trial court or the High Court. The word "plaintiff" in section 41 (1)(a) of that Act must be given its ordinary meaning and it is only when the transaction is real and intention of the parties that the bar under section 21(2) would apply. The test adopted by the courts below was whether the plaintiff had been put on a real and effective title to the suit property or not, and if so, what was the nature of the claim as to the possession and dispossession in the present case. Held further, that even though the suit under section 11 of the West Bengal Land Acquisition (Amendment) Act, 1932, was barred by time, the bar created by it would be effectively effective only if the suit is dismissed for default or non compliance with any order passed by the trial Court.

The appellant was tried by the Sessions judge for offences under section 302 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code, and convicted and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence but reduced the sentences to imprisonment for life. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the omission in the charge to mention the names of the accused persons did not amount to an irregularity in the prosecution case and that the failure to give particulars of the offences under sections 173(4) and 207A(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure had caused prejudice to the appellant. Held, that the defect was curable by reference to section 537 of the code of Criminal procedure. The omission complained of in the instant case should not have a more serious effect than the omission to carry out the provisions of section 162 or section 360 of the Criminal Procedure Code. Abdul Rahman vs The King Emperor (1929) L.R. 55 I.A. 96, referred to. Held further, that there was no error in the High Court 's judgment in reversing the findings of the trial court and that it had failed to take into consideration the omission on the part of the investigating police officer to supply the necessary copies. The failure to mention all the documents contemplated by section 537(3), Cr. P.C., did not affect the validity of the prosecution unless the accused succeeded in showing that they were prejudiced in their defence. Abdul Rauf vs The Queen Emperor, (1928) L,R. 74 I. A.

The appellant, a chemical works discharged from the respondent 's factory in the surrounding area of Cuttack, was prosecuted under sections 153A and 153B of the Bombay District Municipal Act, 1901 for violation of article 19(1)(C) of the Constitution. The trial court convicted him but the High Court acquitted him on appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the provisions of section 153A were ultra vires the Constitution; (ii) the special officer had wrongly restricted the scope of the enquiry by taking an erroneous view as to the scope and effect of the inquiry before him and thus had refused to exercise jurisdiction which was vested in him under the Act. HELD : (i). The procedure laid down in section 153 A is to permit the Municipality, if it is satisfied that a nuisance in the terms of sub section (1) exists and on finding that it does exist to proceed further and to do something more, then the fact in question is not collateral but is a part of the very issue which the Municipality has to enquire into and decide whether the nuisance in question existed. [398 D] (ii). The scheme under section 153B is to leave it to the subjective satisfaction of the Municipality as to its existence. It is not a part or part of that very issue, which the municipality has to inquire into and determine whether a nuisance exists. If a nuisance exist it should be removed without delay in order to preserve the health of the community and the fertility of the soil. The special officer has wrongly decided that he could not go into the question whether the water of the effluent should be discharged. [399 E F] (iii). The Special Officer had wrongly decided on the ground that lie could not look into the entire matter where a party objects absolutely to the notice and the requisition contained therein as in the present case. There would have been no need for the appointment of a special officer to hold an enquiry into the matter.

The appellant was found to be in possession of railway stores. He failed to offer any satisfactory explanation of his possession of the goods. On the strength of information received on 28th July 1964 that some stolen railway property was being sent out of Lucknow through a motor transport agency, a Sub Inspector attached to the Railway Protection Force along with another Sub Inspector of Police visited the premises of the appellant and recovered from him certain articles which were in his possession. The appellant contended that the articles seized were railway stores within the meaning of section 2(b) of the Act and as such the question of punishment under section 3 did not arise. Held, that the prosecution must prove that the goods belonged to any particular railway administration and that the article was property of a railway administration but only those which are used or intended to be used in the construction, operation or maintenance of a Railway. The prosecution must also prove that articles were being actually used by a railway administrate and that they were not intended to use in the constructions, operation, or maintenance thereof. In most cases the burden of proof in this respect may be discharged by leading evidence about the identifying marks on the goods or some peculiarity of the articles not to be found in cases of non railway property. The mere description of the article as new would not fulfil the requirements of section2(b). The mere fact that the appellant had purchased the property in open market where goods of this kind were usually sold or that he had bought them from someone bona fide in the belief that the vendor had lawfully obtained the sale, did not by itself prove that it was in possession or was intended to have been used for the construction or operation of a rail. The evidence in the case did not establish that the gold belonged to the particular railway administrations.

The appellants are the tenants of a demised premises. The respondent landlord terminated the lease by notice under section 106 of Transfer of Property Act on the ground that the tenant had no right to continue in occupation of the demised premises, and the appellant was not entitled to the protection of the amended provisions of the Act. The Trial Court dismissed the suit holding that the appellants had not carried on the business with her as family business in the demised prem ises and that they were entitled to continue to be in possession of the premises. On appeal, the Appellate Court confirmed the decree of the trial court. In second appeal, it was contended for the appellant that the lease hold right was an heritable estate and on death of the tenant in September 1966, the appellants became trespassers. The High Court held that as the appellants were not carrying on business with their own business in tho demised premises they were not enti tled to the benefit of amended provisions. In this appeal by special leave it was submitted for the appellants that the tenancy rights of the tenanted premises for commercial or business purposes governed by the Act are heritable and the heirs of the deceased tenant under the 1956 Act, and therefore, the appellant is entitled to remain in possession even after determination of the contractual tenancy and no order or decree for eviction would be passed against him unless any ground was established to the satisfaction of the Court that the surviving spouse, son or daughter and other heir, in case of residential purposes, he/she ordinarily had been residing in the premises along with the tenant and continued to do so till date of death of his tenant. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The legal representatives of the original landlord and the tenant are entitled to enjoy the protection afforded by the Rent Acts at the relevant time. [18E] 1.2 In case of commercial premises governed by Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, the Legislature has not thought it fit in the light of the situation at Delhi to place any kind of restriction on the ordinary law of inheritance with regard to succession. It may also be borne in mind that in case where a tenant continues to remain In possession even before his death, he ordinarily had to be evicted from the premises as members of his/her family upto his/ her death.

The appellant Board, which was a statutory commercial concern, had its own factories in the State of Bihar. The Board had electricity including the generation, transmission and distribution thereof, and the maintenance of those lines of transmission and distribu tive distribution were spread all over the State and probably far out numbers those working in establishments which were factories. The appellant Board was willing to extend that scheme to all the workers except the Government servants who were on deputation and those to whom the Employees Provident Fund Act applies. The employees claimed that all workmen of the Board should have the same and similar benefits and that therefore there should be no distinction between the Board 's Contributory Provident Fund Scheme and the scheme under the Employees ' Provident Fund and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1948. The Industrial Tribunal held that the employees had the same rights as those of the generation and distribution of electricity and accordingly directed the contribution to be 6.25 per cent but not on the basic wages but on the total wages. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant Board that the State Government is the financier of the Electricity Board which charges interest now at the rate of 6. 25 per cent as against the previous 4 per cent per annum. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The Tribunal had dealt with the matter in a perfunctory way. It should be directed to dispose of the matter afresh in the light of the observations made in this judgment. [47 D] The Tribunal has dealt with matters in a very perfunctory manner. It is open to an ordinary commercial concern to credit any amount to the depreciation reserve. These and other matters cannot be properly decided in the absence of a detailed examination of the finances of the board. That is why the Tribunal has dealing with the matters in the present case in a dominant provident fund scheme. [46 E F] The Board ' maintains a Contributory Provident Scheme for its employees. It can be applied to establishments which are not factories if the Central Government by notification in the official Gazette specifies in this behalf. The industry in question is in a stable condition and the Board and employees contribute equally. The workmen claim that all workers of the Boards should have their wages at the rates they were covered by the Act.

The appellant wife filed a petition under section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 for grant of maintenance against the respondent husband. The respondent wife alleged that she was impotent and unable to perform her marital obligations. She further alleged that the husband had refused to live with her husband and hence the husband has not been able to persuade her marital relations to live in the husband 's family. The appellant wife denied the allegations and asserted that she is impotently and unable even to discharge her marital obligation, that the respondent was impeccable and unable for all purposes to refuse to live at the husband as the husband refused to cohabit with her. She also asserted that the appellant had not discharged his marital obligations, that she had failed to perform his marital duties, that there was no direct decision on the point taking a contrary view of the matter and that the High Court erred in holding that the wife has been impotaged and is not entitled to maintenance under section 488 of the Criminal Procedure Code. The High Court held that the mere ground that the consent of the husband was not given by him did not constitute an offence of cruelty within the meaning of section 488, Cr. P.C., 1973. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The High Courts have consistently taken a contrary decision and have not noticed this important principle of law. [707D] 1.2 In order to get justice into the facts of the case, it is legitimate for it to take into account the relations between the husband and wife and the husband, who is unable to discharge his marital obligation. This Court has taken a view that where it is proved to the satisfaction of the court that a husband is impo sed or compelled to live a life of celibacy while in law, such a proposition would be unreasonable and necessary under the proviso. Similarly, where the wife had a reasonable apprehension arising from the conduct of the wife that she may be physically harmed due to persistent demands of dowry from her husband 'and the wife would be entitled to maintain an order of maintenance, this Court would not make any difference in law whether the husband is guilty of cruelty to her husband according to his means.

The appellant was the owner of a plot in the city of Bhavnagar. The respondent State issued a notification under section 40(1) of the Bombay Municipal Corporation Act, 1948, declaring that the said land was to be handed over to the appellant on 7th January, 1964 for use by the State Government and it was given to the Saurashtra Government on 7.7.1952 for use free by the Government. The appellant claimed possession of the plot on the basis of a notification dated 19.1.1948 issued under section 80 C.P.C. The suit property was described in the plaint as plot No. 1, Part A, and part B 's house. The trial court held that the plaintiff had proved its title to the suit land and that they were in possession in the suit property till 7th July 1952 when physical possession was handed over by the military engineers of the Government of Saurashtra to the State Public Works Department of the State of Saurashtra. The High Court dismissed the appeal filed by the appellant. In this appeal it was contended for the appellant that the suit was not barred under section 65 C. P.C., because the suit lands were in their possession in a part of the city planning department on a federal basis and that the acquisition of such land was never recognised by the Union of India or the State Govern ment and that since the suit properties were in the possession of a municipal corporation, the appellant had no title to it. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The title itself should have been vested in the Municipality may now be noticed. The subsequent correspondance and orders of the government also show that the Government was only a right or an authority to sell the land as representing the Government but not a vesting of the title itself in the municipality. [231D] 2.1 In the present case, possession of lands were handed over on 7 7 1952 and therefore, these letters cannot be of any help to the appel lant. However, it may be pointed out that the document was evidence against the Municipality in so far as it treated the properties as belonging to the Defence Department of Government of India and that at the same time it may he pointed that the documents were in fact long before 1948 and that therefore the land alone could not have been acquired by the Municipality. [232E F] 2:2 The document was admissible under section 7(1)(a) of Bombay Municipal Act, 1949 as it was a copy of the proceedings of the Board of Officers of Defence Department in which they had described detailed inventory of Defence department assets, accommodations, installations, furniture, fitting and connected stores pertaining to Saurashtra state forces in Bhavnagar and the Government had treated those orders only as authorisation or transferring of power to execute sale deeds and collect rent in respect of Government lands situated within the Municipality, which should normally have been done by the state Government. [234G H] 2(a) The document is evidence against a municipality and not a vested interest in the Municipali ties under Resolution 37 dated 19th January 1948.

The appellant was a class III servant employed as a metal examiner in the Railway Carriage Workshops at Ajmer. He was charged under section 161 of the Indian Penal Code and section 5(1)(d) of Act II of 1947 for having accepted from one Nanak Singh a sum of Rs. 150 as illegal gratification as a motive for securing a job for one Kallu. The appellant contended that he was an officer in the service or pay of Government and was performing public duty and therefore fell within the definition of public servant contained in section 21(9) of the Act. Held, that the appellant was not an officer within the meaning of section 21 (9) Of the Indian penal Code and as such was not a public servant within the terms of section 2 of the Prevention of Corruption Act II Of 1947. The offence under section 5 (1)(a) of that Act is one which is committed in service and the appellant is, therefore, an officer of the Government within the term of section 6(9). Ram Krishan vs Delhi State, A.I.R. 1918 Lah. H.C.R 1, referred to. Held further, that as the appellant had been convicted under section 3 Of the Prevention Of Corruption Act 11 of 1947 and was also charged with having accepted a bribe from one of the officers of the Railway Service, his conviction and sentence were quite in order and he was liable to be acquitted. The appeal must accordingly fail. The question whether a person is an officer or not has to be decided on the facts of each particular case, cl. 9 of section 1 of the Penal Code of 1947 which provides that "for the purposes of this Act " public servant shall include any Government servant within tho meaning of that term.

The Respondent filed a suit in the Court of Sub Judge, Patiala for permanent injunction restraining the State and the Collector cum Deputy Excise and Taxation Commissioner from auctioning his half share in an immovable property consisting of a plot of land bearing Khewat No. 374, Khatuni NO. 374 and Khasra No. 39710 19 situate in village Ghagga, with a building constructed thereon. The auction was prohibited by the Punjab Land Revenue Act, 1887. The Respondent filed an appeal to the District Judge, which was dismissed on the ground that the portion of the building standing on the said plot of the land was being used by him for his residence and he had no other residential house and, therefore, his said half share was exempt from attachment under clause (ccc) of the proviso to sub section (1) of Section 60 of the Code of Civil Procedure 1908. The District Judge dismissed the suit with costs. The High Court in second appeal held that the conclusion arrived at by the trial court on facts was per verse and set aside the decree passed by the Sub Judge. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High Court had no jurisdiction to entertain the second appeal, because (i) the provisions of Section 6 of the Act which made the provisions in section 60 applicable to attachment and sale for recovery of revenue under the said Act were not exempt from being attached and sale under clause(ccc), of the Proviso to sub s.(1) was not exempted from attachment and sales; and (ii) that the provisions relating to the assessment and disposal of the portion in which the liquor shop was situated were exempt from attach ment. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. Section 60 is clear that section 60 of Code of Criminal Procedure does not apply to an attachment and Sale under any of her statute made expressly applicable thereto. So far as the said act is concerned, it contains a complete code providing for the modes and machinery for recovery, the attachment and the sale for realisation of revenue. The attachment in a question was levied under the provisions Of the Act and the sales which were exempt were exempted from attached to the said section 60. [848F G] 2. Section 6(1) has no application to an attach ment and sale in any proceedings other than in execution of a decree of a civil court. The provisions of section 60 are not applicable to an attached and Sale in any proceeding other than the decree of the Civil Court. [884G H] 3. Section 59 of the code does not make the provisions, of section 6(l) of that Act applicable to the attachment. In view of the said provision section 60 is not attracted to an arrest and sale. [881A B] 4. Section 61 of the Criminal Procedure Code provides for the mode and machinery by which the decrees of civil courts are to be attached and sold in execution. The opening words of sub section(I) of section60 are "the following property is liable to attachment, and sale" in sub section 2 of section 2, therefore. [851C D] 5. Section 62 of the Cr. P.C. provides that the following properties shall be attached to and sold, in execution thereof, (a) the property which is liable for attachment and (b) the proceeds of sale. The two sections are not exempt under any other provisions of the law.

The appellant, a widow of the deceased husband of the Indian State, filed a petition under section 18 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 before the Special Deputy Collector for acquiring certain lands belonging to one Rashid and his wife. The Special Deputy Collec tor, by his order dated November 14, 1969, determined the value of the properties passing on the death of Rashid in 1963 and fixed the compensation at Rs. 20,000/ per annum. On appeal, the High Court held that the value adopted by the Special officer was not a 'sales ' within the meaning of section 11 of the Act and their pendency in the Civil Court was not disclosed by the account books. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the accountable person had only a claim to get an extra compensation which was an inchoate right which could not be called 'property ' and (2) since the deceased Rashid had merely been acquired by the appellant, the compensation awarded by the special Deputy Collector was not liable to be set aside. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was wrong in holding that there were no two separate rights one a right to receive compensation and other a right of receiving compensation. [327C] 2.1 The High court was right in holding on the basis of the provisions of section 18 that the right to received compensation survived and it was not possible to accept the contention that no sooner the Collector had made his award under section 11, the right of receive compensation became property only when the claim would be accepted 'as at all. [328D] 2(a) The High Courts have rightly held that there are no two distinct rights but inferential facts and non disclosure thereof would not amount to failure or omission on the part of the accountable persons to disclose full particulars leading to escapement of assessment to duty. [330F] (b) The expression "anything" in section 11 is a right which can be acquired by an owner of the lands as soon as the lands are acquired by him. It is immaterial that the Civil Judge has made his awards on the assumption that there had been escapement from the record and that this reassessment has to be done within the period of three years from the date of the original assessment under section 73 A of the Income Tax Act. [332G] (c) The Collector, in the instant case, was not justified in holding the acquisition proceedings and passing the award on the ground that the estate duty had been assessed at Rs,.18,000 per annum on the dates of the relevant notifications. [333H] 2.(d) The order under section 59 and the rectification order passed by the High court are quashed. [33B] (e) The Revenue will pay the costs of the appeal in the Supreme Court.

The appellant 's election to the State Cooperative Bank was not called in question by the respondent. The appellant 'c dispute arose as to whether the appellant had borrowed a loan of total Rs. 10,000 (Rs. 7,000) from the Bank and he kept the loan constanty in arrears till 21.10.1986. The Deputy Registrar of Cooperative Societies, Nagpur, on 8.1.1987, removed the appellant from the Committee of Directors of the Bank holding that appellant was defaulter on 31.1 .86. On 8.12.87, the District Deputy Registrar, Nagpur passed an order removing the appellant 'from the Committee. The respondent challenged the said order by filing a writ petition in the High Court which was dismissed. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the disqualification as defaulter continued after the election of the Board of Directors is without jurisdiction inasmuch as the Act prescribes a separate procedure for calling in question the appellant "s election as a Director of the bank and that procedure having not been followed, the Assistant Registrar could not have acted under section 78(1) of the Act which did not envisage the setting aside of an election as has been done by the impugned order; (ii) the appellant having repaid the entire loan before the notice was issued, he was surely not a defaulter in presenti on the date of the notice and the provisions of section 78 (1) were not attracted; and (iii) even assuming that the disqualification on account of his being defaulter which continued after his election was imposed and the fact that he repaid the loan before 21. 10.1986, was no longer subsisting. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Court has rightly held that the appellant could be said to have made default on the day he contested the election and since the notice of the Deputy Registrar was in effect to say that the appel lant had already ceased to be a defaulter, his election had not been called in ques tion. [683F] 2. The fact that the disqualifications on account o f his being a defaulter are common both for election and for continuation as a director or Executive Committee member under section 73FF of the Maharashtra State Co operative Societies Act, 1960 and about ceasing too be a Director by committing default is not decisive. [684G] 3. The result is that this notice of election has to be interpreted harmoniously with other provisions of the Bombay Act. [682B] 4. The notice of Deputy Registrar is in effect a defaulter and so long that default continued he must be taken to have been disqualified and thereby ceased to he a member of the committee and his seat deemed to have fallen vacant. In this view of the matter, there could not be any infirmity either in the notice or in the impugned Order of removal. [685D] 5.

The respondent was in the service of the State Government as Supply Inspector and he retired from service on attaining the age of superannuation on September 1, 1977. After his retirement, the respondent was served with a charge sheet on October 16, 1978 containing allegations of misconduct against him for the period he was in service. Enquiry into those charges was held and the respondent 's services were terminated by giving full opportunity to defend himself. On the conclusion of the enquiry, the State Govt. issued orders on December 4, 1982 reducing the pension payable to the respondent by 50 per cent permanently under Rule 188 of the Bombay Civil Services Rules. The respondent challenged the validity of the Government 's order by means of a writ petition before the High Court which quashed the order reducing the amount of pension payable by 50% permanently under rule 188 of Bombay Civil Service Rules. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the State government had no authority in law to take any disciplinary proceedings against the respondent as he had already retired from serv ice and that the reduction of pension by 50 percent permanently under r. 189 of the Rules was disproportionate to the misconduct proved against him. Allowing the appeal partly, ^ HELD: 1. The Government 'Save Inspector and the State of Gujarat, the appellant 's power to reduce or withhold pension by taking proceedings against a Government servant even after his retirement is expressly preserved by the aforesaid Rules. [35G] 2.1 The validity of Rule 184 of Bombay civil Services Rules (which contemplates withholding or withdrawing of a pension or any part of it if the pensioner is found guilty of grave misconduct while he was In service or after completion of his service, has no application to the instant case as in the present case the purpose of the inquiry was not to inflict any punishment; instead the proceedings were initiated for determining the respondent "s pension". The proceedings were taken in accordance with Rules 188 and 189 of Bombay C.P. Services Conduct, Discipline and Appeal Rules. Rule 184 contemplates withholding of pension or withdrawing a pension, or any Part of it, if the pensioners is found innocent of grave offence while he is in service or After completion of the service. Grant of pension and its continuance to a Government Servant depend upon the good conduct of the government servant. Rendering satisfactory service maintaining good conduct is a necessary condition for the grant and continuance of pension. Rule 189 expressly confers power on the Government to withhold or withdraw any part thereof during the period of his serv ice. Granting of pension, and its continuation to a government servant depend upon his good conduct, the Government must be given opportunity of defence in accordance to the procedure specified in Note 1 to Rule 33 of the said Bombay Civil services Conduct, discipline and Appeal rules. [36A B] 2:2 The validity or otherwise of the rules was not challenged either before the Court or before this Court. In this view, the government had power to reducing the amounts of pension to the extent of Re. 1 per month be made applicable to Government servant who is borne on its establishment. Rule 188 expressly confers powers on the government to withhold, or withdraw a part of the pension, payable to a Govern servant for misconduct which he may have committed while in service and after completion thereof. Grant ingly, the reduction in pension by50% was too harsh and disproportionate to his misconduct proved. [37B C] 3.

The appellant was the landlord of a shop. He filed an application under section 3(1) of the West Bengal (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, for permission to sue his tenant in ejectment against the respondent on the ground that he had applied for permission under section 2(3) of that Act to institute a suit against him. The Commissioner rejected the request and the High Court dismissed the appellant 's writ petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the jurisdiction conferred on the Commissioner by section 3 (3) was not ousted by the provisions of the Act, because, the jurisdiction of the civil courts was barred in view of the provisions contained in section 3 of the said Act and section 16(4) of Act. HELD : The High Court was in error in coming to the conclusion that the permission granted by the Commissioner was invalid in law. [560 C] Under section 3 the Commissioner can pass such orders as appear to it to be necessary in a given case, if the subordinate court whose order is brought before the High court under section 115 "appears to have exercised a jurisdiction not vested in it by law or with material irregularity". The words used in section 2 (3), are clear and unambiguous. There are three categories of cases in which the Commissioner could interfere with the order passed by the District Magistrate. If the District Magis trate has acted illegally, the Commissioner cannot be justified in applying for an appropriate writ to the High Courts or adopt some other suitable remedy in law; but a revision in such a case does not appear to be competent under section 33(4). [560 E F] The power conferred on him by section 7 F is very wide.

The appellant, a member of the Punjab Public Service Commission, physically assaulted his wife and daughter on the night intervening 11th and 12th November, 1982. The respondent filed a complaint against her husband alleging that he had assaulted her. The trial court convicted him under section 302 I.P.C. and sentenced him to death. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the evidence of the witnesses should be allowed to be led only on the ground of misbehaviour; (2) the procedure adopted by the Supreme Court in dealing with a reference under article 317(1) is not mandatory but directory and (3) the High Courts have erred in holding that the evidence recorded by the trial court will automatically decide the fate of a prosecution or of a civil suit for damages. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The object of article 317 (1), is to ensure the independence of members of the Public Service Commissions and to give them protection in the matter of their tenure. The Judges of the Supreme Courts can be removed from their office only in accordance with the procedure prescribed by that Article. [646C] 2. It is impossible to accept that the Supreme court in one case and the Parliament in the case of those others are entrusted by the Constitution with the limited power of determining whether the facts found by some other body establish guilty of misconduct and whether the misbehaviour is of such a nature as to warrant the removal of the person from his office. [643D] 3. The Supreme Court has the power to summon witnesses and record their evidence. A procedural issue which was debated before it is whether the complainant should make a false allegation that she was slapped, courting trouble and involving her own status and respectability. [641C] 4. The evidence in this case will be recorded by a Magistrate itself. [651D] 5. The High Court has power to examine the witnesses as to the charge of misbehaviour or incapacity, as the case may be. [631E] 6. The procedure which is usually held in Delhi Courts is not specifically incorporated in Order XXXVIII of the Code of Civil Procedure. It will not be conducive to justice to decide the Reference on a consideration of the affidavits only. [661G] 7. The Court has no unfair advantage to either side if the questions of fact are decided by this Court straightaway. If the essential safeguards of a fair adjudication are observed, no grievance can legitimately be made that the facts which establish the charge are found by the highest court of the land and not by the lowest. [671A B] 8. The question whether the complaint against the respondent is false or motivated is irrelevant for the purpose of deciding whether the allegations against him are proved at all. [682C D] 9. The jurisdiction of the High court under article 318(1), Code of Criminal Procedure, is not affected by reading into it the facts themselves and facts also so as to enable this Court to pronounce upon the question whether a charge is false and motivated. [693D E] 10. It would be impossible to hold that the High courts in one particular case and those allegations cannot be adjudicated upon on a considera tion of affidavits only because they are made by the learned Judges of Delhi High Court. No useful purpose will be served by expending our own time in recording the evidence. [703G] 11. The observations made by this court in the earlier case that the affidavits filed in this Court will be treated as the examination in chief of witnesses cannot be accepted. [714A B; 71B] 12. It was not necessary to consider whether the allegation made against the appellant is false, inspired and motivated by interested parties to involve him in a false charge out of personal malice and hostility. [721C D].

The appellants are the deity installed in the temple. The temple was a public trust and the endowment was held to be of a public nature and the dedication was for a public purpose. The endowment was found to be a family deity in the suit temple. In the suit filed by the plaintiffs, the appellants defendants claimed that the deity was a family idol of the deity and the endowments were not of a private nature and therefore the provisions of the Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1939 (the Act) applied only to public temples and not to the members of the public or the descendants of the temple or their descendants. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the temple was an "public endowment" within the meaning of section 2(1)(f) of the Act and the respondent deity was also fully entitled to pass orders for its management. On appeal, the High Court reversed the decision of the Subordinate Judge and held that the endowment being a public endowment, it was of a Public nature and was not one of a "public nature" within section 2 (1)(g) of that Act. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that there was no "public" endowment or a private trust of a Private Trust of a purely private character and the intention of the founder was merely to instal the idol in the Temple by way of a declaration of the members. [835B] 2.1 The essential distinction between a private and a public endowments is that whereas in the former the beneficiaries are entitled to worship as of right, there is no specific mention of any contribution being called for from members of public or of the brotherhood or the Government could have taken over the management. In fact, both the public and the founder did not hold the endowment as of a trust or endowed all his properties. [881F] 2:2 The High court was in error in holding the endowment to be "public one" but it erred in holding otherwise. [888B] 3.1 It is well settled that the mere fact that members of a Hindu family are allowed to worship by itself would not make an endowment of a 'private trust ' only because they belong to a particular community which also shows that even if the family was to become extinct, the private nature of the endowment would be of no consequence.

The appellant Bank originally known as Bharat Bank Ltd. agreed to finance the contracts and to advance monies to Malhotra against his bills for supplies under the contracts. The power of attorney recited: "Whereas we are working as contractors to the Government in its various departments and have entered into certain contracts and will in future enter into other contracts and would in future entering into other contract and will, in future, enter into any officer or authority of the Government Departments concerned; to obtain cheques for sums payable to us under the contract directly in their own name or in our names in payment of such bills or other amounts and to pay appropriate such receipts towards and in repayment of the advances made or to be made hereafter and all other monies due from you to the attorneys in any account what soever. " The appellant Bank then filed objections to the execution proceedings on the ground that the appellant was the assignee of the bill and decreed the suit. The High Court allowed the appeal and dismissed the suit, but granted a certificate of fitness under article 133(1)(c) of the Constitution. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant Bank that the power of Attorney coupled with the endorsement on the bill dated July 19, 1948 amounted to an equitable assignment of the monies due under the bill in favour of the appellant and that the said document was a pay order. HELD: (i) The endorsement on bill dated June 19,1948 created an interest in a specific fund and was irrevocable. There was thus a sufficient equitable assignment.

The respondent was the manager of a Tea Estate under the managing agency of M/s. Gillanders Arbuthnot & Co. Ltd., and had a Provident Fund Scheme for its employees. The appellant, who was the Manager of a tea estate under the management of a company, was assessed to income tax on the ground that the said amount was his salary as defined in section 17 of the Income tax Act, 1961. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the receipt in question being profits in lieu of salary had to be considered as salary and that the same having not been assessed as his salary, the assessment order relating to that item of receipt was not legal. On further appeal by the respondent, the Tribunal came to the conclusion that the receipts in question were profits in the nature of salary under section 17 and therefore the same had to he brought to tax under section 56. The High Court answered the reference against the appellant. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the receipt of Rs. 27,948/ by the assessee with which we are concerned is exempt from payment of tax in view of section 17(3)(ii); and (ii) the said income is not exempt under what head the same has to be brought to taxable under section 12.
