Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The receipt of an interest on any investment is a gain made by the investor and therefore it is "income". The receipt is undoubtedly an income. [439C] (i)(ii) The receipt in the relevant accounting year cannot be considered to be salary though undoubtedly that is an income; and therefore brought to taxation under section 7 of the Act. Section 17(1)(iv) provides that income of every kind which is not to be excluded from the total income under the Act shall be chargeable to income Tax under the head "income from other sources" if it is not chargeable to Income tax under any of the heads specified in section 1.4 items 'A ' to 'E '. In computing the income relating to this item of receipts, the amount of interest on the amount received by the asses see from a investment is deductible from the income from other source 's income. The words "profits in lieu" in section 2(24) are not employed in the definition of "Profits in lieu Of salary". [440E F] (ii)(iii) The receipts in the instant case cannot be treated as salary though it is an Income. Commissioner for purposes of income tax.

The petitioners, who were the owners of a cow and female buffaloes, challenged the constitutional validity of the Bihar Act on the ground that it violated articles 19 (1) (g), 19 (5) and 31 of the Constitution. The petitioners contended that the impugned Act was void as it contravened article 14 Of the Constitution inasmuch as it imposed unreasonable restrictions on the slaughter of the cow and her buffaloes, which were not within the protection afforded by article 19(6) Of the Constitu tion. Held, that the provisions of the impugned Acts were valid in so far as they prohibited the slaughter Of the cows, buffaloes and calves of the petitioners, and the Act was constitutionally valid. The Act did not contravene articles 14 or 19 (i)(g), (ii) and (iii). The Act was not discriminatory and violated article 14 of the constitution. The provisions of section 3(1) of the Act were reasonable restrictions within the meaning of article 19 (6) and were therefore void. The impugned Acts infringed their fundamental rights under articles 19(1)(g) and 19(5) of our Constitution. Section 3(2) of that Act was valid in respect of the same prohibition as section 3 (1). The provisions Of section 3 of the said Act were not unreasonable, and could not be challenged on the grounds, inter alia, (i) that it contravened articles 14 and 19 (ii), (iii) and 30 (iv) of Part III of the Constitu tional Constitution. It was also contended that a total ban on the cattle of the petitioner 's cattle was justified as the Act did no more than provide for the maximum ban on slaughter of cows, sheep and calis of buffaloes, and that the restrictions imposed were not reasonable within the contemplation of article 48 Of the constitution; (ii). that the Act contravened articles 19 and 31 (1), (2) and 32 of the Consti tution. The State of West Bengal vs Subodh Gopal Bose, ; , referred to.

The respondent was a clerk in the appellant company. He was dismissed from service on the ground that he had been receiving a basic salary of Rs. 245 per month. The respondent filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution in the High Court challenging the order of dismissal and contended that the Standing Orders did not apply to him as he had no right to move the High Courts for appropriate orders under articles 226 and 227 of the constitution. The single judge held that the standing orders applied to the respondent, but the Division Bench allowed the appeal holding that the respondent was not an employee within the meaning of the Standing Order No. 2(a) of the local Act and as such could not be said to have a right to prefer a writ petition under articles 32 and 226 of that Constitution. The Division Bench also held that even if the Standing orders applied, they were valid in law and that the termination of the respondent 's service was without jurisdiction. Held: (i) The Standing Orders apply to the employees only to whom tickets had been issued will make employees synonymous with workmen a result negatived by two separate definitions given in Standing Order 2(b). The expression " employee" denotes a larger group namely, all persons male or females who are employed in the office, Mains Department, Stores Department, etc. and such a person is an employee. (ii) The word "employee" means any person employed in any industrial establishment to do any skilled or unskilled manual or clerical work for contract or hire or reward in any industry. The Standing Order does not require the issue of a ticket to a probationer; it only requires the person or persons who are found to have entered service as a result of the departmental musters ' strike and they are not intended to exclude employees who do not possess tickets or to whom a ticket has been issued. Perumal Goundan vs The Thirumalarayapuram Jananukachala Dhanasekhara Sangha Nidhi (A.I.R. , referred to. (iii) The words " whose names and ticket numbers are included in the departmental requirement" in Standing Orders 2(d), do not lay down any essential characteristic of an employee and are applicable only in cases where tickets have been issued to an employee, and that is, necessary declaration by the company which would entitle him to a ticket under Standing Order NO. 4. The words ' whose names, and ticket number are included, in the depart mental musters " occurring in Standing order No.2(a), donot lay down an essential characteristic for an employee '.

The appellant company was incorporated in the year 1961 and it went into production in 1964 65. The workmen claimed bonus at the minimum rate prescribed under the Payment of Bonus Act, 1965. The claim was resisted by the Company on the ground that the Alloy Steel Project was a separate establishment in respect of which separate balance sheets and profit and loss accounts were maintained for each unit, except that for the Head Office, though a separate balance sheet was prepared, the profit and Loss account were maintained only for the purpose of computation of bonus under the Act. The Tribunal held that alloy steel project could not be treated as a separate Establishment because under the provisions of section 16(1) of the Act, an establishment in a private sector would be one which is owned, controlled or managed by a person or body other than a Government company or a corporation owned by a corporation of the nature described in that clause. The High Court also held that the Tribunal was wrong in holding that merely because Alloy steel Project was owned, it could not treat the establishment as separate establishment under the proviso to section 3(1). In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The Tribunal went wrong in ignoring the fact that separate balance Sheets and profit & loss accounts are kept for each separate undertaking. [633 B] (ii) The only exception has been in the case of workmen of the Head office where no separate profit and losses were worked out and the bonus was paid on the basis of consolidated profits of all such units. The only exceptions have been in this case, of workmen, of the head office where there is no separate accounts maintained for one single establishment for purposes of section 3 of the Payment Act. [625 C] (iii) The proviso to sub section (2) of section16 also does not stand in the way of this claim because there is a clear evidence that though the Company, Hindustan Steel Ltd., has a number of undertakings, undertakings or branches of the establishment of a company, it may not be possible to make a deduction at all.

The respondent assessee, a sugar factory manufacturing rayon grade pulp, was engaged in the manufacture of sugar cane. The water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1977 was enacted by Parliament under Article 252 of the Constitution with a view to control the pollution of rivers and streams which had assumed considerable importance and urgency in recent years as a result of increasing industrialisation and urbanization. The Act provides for levy of cess on water consumed by persons carrying on any specified industry and every local authority and is calculated on the basis of water consumed. The Cess Act was intended to ensure that the industrial affluence and control pollution did not come within Entry 15 of Schedule I to the Act. The cess was levied on the person carrying on the specified industry. The respondent assessee challenged the levy before the High Court by filing writ petitions in the High Courts, which were dismissed. In appeal to this Court it was contended that sugar manufacturing industry would fall under Entry 15 and a Writ Petition filed by the assessee challenging the levy could not be said to be an industry within Entry. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The levy and collection of cess provided under the Cess Act is on water consumption and not in the form of processing of goods. [532C] 2. The term 'vegetable products ' means any industry as mentioned in Schedule I. The word 'veg etable ' has been used in Entry 15 'vege gorpen to indicate that sense which people conversant with the subject matter with Schedule I like Paper Industry and Textile Industry and even chemical industry which are covered by other entries could also be brought within Entry, 15. [525D] 3. The expression 'veetable products of or made of or out of vegetable. 'Vegetables ' as understood in common parlance are not products of manufacture unless we say that agriculture is an industry for certain purposes and vegetables are products of that industry. In order to bring an industry under any of the entires in Schedule 1 it has to be seen what is the end product produced by that industry.[526F] 4. The 've gor pate ' means ' product of or make of orout of vegetable, '. [54H; 54A] 5. 'Ten fruit ' as defined in the Act means any Industry as mentioned therein. The dictionary meaning of vegetable as understood is not products or made off or out side the processing for dinner purposes and it has a wider amplitude. It was also of the view that in manufacture some thing is brought into existence which is different from that originally existed in the sense that the thing produced is by itself a commercially different commodity whereas in the case of processing it is not necessary to produce a commer cially different article. processing essentially effectuates a change in form, contour, physical appearance or chemical combination or otherwise by artificial or natural means and in its more complicated form involves progressive action in performing, producing or making something. [53H; 53A B] 6. The definition given to the same word occurring in a social security measure or a regulating enactment may not be apt or appropriate when the same words are used in a raw state into marketable form. It would be inappropriate to refer to the dictionary meaning which is used in common sense and to the fitness of the matter to the statute. [55H; 56A] 7. The expressions 'vegaable ' have been defined in Entry No.

The respondent, an Advocate, filed an application before the Rent Controller seeking eviction of the appellant 's tenant from the premises in question on the ground that he required the premises for the purpose of carrying on his profession as an advocate. The application was contested by the appellant who contended that the practice of the profession of an advocate was not business within the meaning of Section 10(3) (a)(iii) and, therefore, the respondent could not seek the eviction of his tenant on the grounds that he requires the premises bona fide for the purposes of carrying out his profession. The Rent Controller held that the respondent bona fide required the suit premises for carrying on the profession as a an advocate and that the tenancy was not such as could be split up. The Appellate Authority confirmed the order of eviction. In revision, the High Court affirmed the decision of the Rent Control Tribunal. Dismissing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: 1. The expression business occurring in Section 10 (3)(a)(ii) is used in a wide sense so as to include the practice or profession of any person. [15E] 2.1 The word 'business ' has not been defined in the Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960. It is a common expression which is sometimes used by itself and sometimes in a collocation of words as in "business, trade or profession". It is anamolous to hold that all the provisions of the Act including Section 4 which provides for the determination of fair rent and section 10(1) which bars the eviction on specified grounds. The word must be interpreted in the context of the statute in which it occurs and not in the sense in which the term has been understood in the several statutes. [16G H; 17A] 2:2 In the instant case, the expression business is given a narrow meaning which the appellant wants to give to that expression. It would indeed be anampluses to hold the time attention and labour of men for the pur pose of lndia. The definition of 'business" in Section 2(a) (iii) is not used in any other statute or in a manner alien to the context in which such term has be understood generally. [17C D] 3.1 In the context, the word must mean everything that occupies the time back and labour is not the carrying on of a trade or business. The dictionary meaning of the word 'may have when it occurs in other statutory provisions. The words used in one Act with reference to their use in another Act are not cognate Acts. Neither the meaning nor the definition of the term in one statute affords a guide to the construction of the same term in another statute and the sense In which the terms has been interpreted in several statutes does not necessarily throw any light on the manner in which that term should be understood in its context.

The respondent filed a suit against the appellant for the recovery of certain amount due from him on the ground that it was a case of deposit of Rs. 4,00,000 with the appellant under an agreement dated September 1, 1942. The trial court decreed the suit in favour of the respondent but the High Court reversed the decree holding that the respondent deposited the sum of Rs 4 lakhs with the appel lant and consequently the suit was barred by limitation. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the use of the word " deposit" in cl. (ii) of the agreement showed that the words "depositY" were not intended for the purpose of having the use, but were only a mere loan of money and therefore the deposit was not an immediate obligation on the depositee to seek out the depositor and repay him; (ii). The respondent had no ordinary loan of Rs, 4 lakhs and as such could not deposit with the appellants any more. HELD: (i ) The words " deposit in the year 1943" in el. (iii) of cl. 5 showed that if a bank was the creditor of the firm of the appellants it would be more consistent with the case of a loan. [578 D] Nawab Major Sir Mohammad Akbar Khan vs Attar Singh & Ors., ; , followed. (2) The words ' deposit in an agreement to pay ' in cl.(ii) showed that there were mutual dealings between the parties and the appellant was giving oral evidence. The mere fact that money in specie was not paid would not be destructive of deposit. [577 F] Nawab, Major Sir Mohammed Akbar Khan & Ors.

The petitioner was detained by an order of the Additional Secretary to the Government of India, Ministry of Finance, Department of Revenue dated February 28, 1986 under section 3(1) of the , with a view to preventing him from dealing in smuggled goods. The grounds of detention were served on the detenu on September 27, 1985 and he was informed that his case for release on parole had been rejected by the Additional Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Delhi. On March 20, 1987, the petitioner made an application before the Additional chief Metropolitan Magistrate praying for revocation of the parole. The Additional Chief Magis trate passed an order dated February 29, 1986, rejecting the said application on the ground that the period of parole had expired and the detenu was in custody at the time the order of detention was served and since the detenu had been released from jail on September 30, 1985, he was not entitled to be released. The petitioner filed a writ petition in this Court challenging the order dated March 20. 1987, which was dismissed by a Single Judge of the High Court on February 22, 1987. In the appeal before this Court it was contended that the detenu 's detention was illegal inasmuch as he had been prejudiced in making an effective representation to the Board against his detention in the absence of the summons issued under section 108 of the Customs Act to him. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The fact that the petitioner is in custody when the order was made, yet he was satisfied that his preventive detention was necessary. [849C] 2. Section 3(i)(a) does not preclude the authority from passing an order prejudicial to the security of the State. What is necessary in a case of that type is to satisfy the court when detention is challenged on that ground thatthe detaining authority was aware of the fact that, the detenu is already in custody and yet he is sub jectly satisfied that the order is necessary. In this case there is suffi cient material to show that the detaining authority is aware of his fact that he was already in detention when the impugned order was passed, yet, he is satisfied that such an order is neces sary. [850D E] 3. The mere service of the detention order on the petitioner in jail would not take away the jurisdiction of the detaining author ity in making the order.

The petitioners were working as casual labourers in the Posts and Telegraphs Department. They were not paid wages for the work done by them, but were being exploited by the Union of India. The petitioners filed writ petitions before this Court challenging the constitutional validity of the provisions of the Inter State Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946 and the Rules for making regular appointments to the posts and pay scales applicable to casual labour in the Telecommunication Wing of the Department. The respondents contended that since the petitioners belong to the category of casual labourers they were not being regularly employed, they are entitled to the same salary and allowances as are being paid to them by the regular employees of the Posts. Dismissing the petitions, this Court, HELD: 1. The scheme of the Act is violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution. It is also opposed to the spirit of Article 7 of the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, 1966 which exhorts all States parties to ensure fair wages and equal wages for equal work. If a person does not have the feeling that he belongs to an organization engaged in production he will not put forward his best effort to produce more. That sense of belonging arises only when he feels that he will be turned out of employment the next day at the whim of the management. It was for this reason it is being repeatedly observed by those who are in charge of economic affairs of the countries in different parts of the world that as far as possible security of work should be assured to the employees so that they may contribute to the maximisation of production. [606C D] 2. The Government cannot take advantage of its dominant position, and compel any worker to work even as a casual labourer on starving wages. It may be that the casual labourers have driven him to that State. The government should be a model employer. [706D E] 3. In the instant case, the classification of employees into regularly recruited employees and casual employees for the purpose of paying less than the minimum pay payable to employees in the corresponding regular cadres particularly in the lowest rungs of the department where the pay scales are the lowest is not tenable. The further classification of casual labourer into three categories namely (i) those who have not completed 720 days of service; (ii) those, who have completed more than 1200 days of serv ice and not completed 1200 days ' service and (iii) those in whose case they have completed eight or ten years of service. [064E F] 4. The arrears of wages payable to the casual labour are directed to be paid within four months from today. These petitioners are accordingly disposed of. [076G H; 609A] 5. The State cannot deny at least the minimum wage in the pay scale of regularly employed workers even though the Government may not be compelled to extend all the benefits enjoyed by regularly recruited employes. It would be for this Court to decide on the facts and circumstances of each case whether in such cases of security of labour, the question of security is of utmost importance.

The appellant was a partner in a firm. The Income tax Officer, while assessing the income of the firm, included the total net income of Rs. 1,935. He added a footnote to the return filed by the assessee under section 22(3) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, showing that he had no business in the previous year exceeded the maximum amount which was not chargeable to income tax. The appellant contended that the notice issued under section 34 of the Act was invalid as it was beyond time and that the assessment proceedings commenced on February 26, 1951, was invalid because the return in question was filed within the time fixed by the notice. Held, that the Income tax officer could have avoided the result by issuing a notice under section 23(2) of Act, but he chose to ignore the return and served on the assessee a notice tinder section 34(1). The notice under s. 22(1) required in a general way what a notice was required of an individual. If a return of income below the taxable limit is a good return in answer to a notice unders. 22 (2), there is no reason to think that a return must be non existent. In the present case, the Income Tax Officer could have refused to issue a notice and with a view to issuing a best judgment assessment, he chose not to ignore it and served a notice on the appellant a notice. The notice was improper because with the return already filed there was neither an omission nor failure on the part of the assessee, nor was there any question of assessment escaping.

The first petitioner, a registered Central Trade Union, filed writ petitions in this Court challenging the circular dated 23.8.1982 (Annexure A) issued by the Joint Secretary to the Government of India, Ministry of Finance, Department of Economic Affairs (Banking Division), New Delhi. The petitioners contended that the Circular was ultra vires section 9 of the Act unless it was so read as to be in harmony with the provisions of the Central Government 's Act and repugnant to constitutional principles enshrined in Article 19(1)(c) and Article 43A of the Constitution. It was further contended that clause 3 of the Scheme in terms of which the circular was purported to have been issued is ultra vires Section 9 of Act unless the said clause is so read, as to restrict or interfere with the principle of election. The writ petitions were contested by the first petitioner contending that the impugned Circular was violative of the provisions contained in Article 14 of the Constitu tion and was not binding on the petitioners. It further contended for the first respondent that the circular is ultra vivi ly and contrary to the letter and spirit of the statute and repugnant thereto. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions. Hence these appeals by special leave. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The object of the Circular is to neutralise and dis crimination amongst the officers and to keep the directorship above union affiliation, and thus encourage the growth of a management culture. [857C] 1.2 In the instant case, the first Petitioner Company was appointed by the Central Govern ment from amongst the employees of the nationalised bank who are not workmen, and hence, the Director of each of the Nationalised Banks is appointed by Central Government from amongst them. The discretion as to the mode of appointment is, of course, left to the Central Gov ernment to specify by a scheme the manner in which the election or nomination is to be conducted bearing in mind the true intent of the legislature as to composition of the Board of Directors. [862E F] 1:3. The object is to give the Board a truly representative character so as to reflect the genuine interests of the various persons manning or dealing with the bank as an industry and a commercial enterprise. The objects of leaving the choice to the central Government as to how the employees from out of a panel of three names furnished by the representative Union of workmen or Association of non workmen as the case may be, would not be a perfect representation in keeping with the principles of election [862F G] 1 :4. In the circumstances, it is open to the National Govern ment to amend the Scheme to improve on the machinery for the conduct of an appropriate election, it was incumbent upon it, until any such amendment is made, to work the present Scheme in such a way as to give it the maximum scope for the concerned employees to exer cise their choice in the selection of their representatives. That means, it would be perfectly in order for the Central Govt. to continue the practice followed by it prior to the circular in question or to hold election of the repre sentatives of the concerned employee, and if necessary, to amend it suitably for that purpose. [861C D] 2.1 It is open for the National Government to amend its Scheme to improving on the machin ery for the conducting of an appropri ate election, It is incumbent upon the Central government to make a scheme in consultation with the Reserve Bank of India. Any amendment or variation of the scheme also requires consulta tion with the National Policy and objectives.

The appellant was imposed penalties under section 271(1)(c) read with section 274(2) of the Income tax Act, 1961 for concealment of certain income and furnishing inaccurate particulars. The assessee preferred appeals to the Appellate Tribunal which declined to order any stay holding that it had no power to grant such relief to an assessee. The Tribunal refused to grant stay on the ground that the assessee was not in default. In appeal to this Court by special leave, HELD: (1) The power of stay under section 254(1) with widest possible amplitude must carry with it the duty in proper cases to make such orders for staying proceedings as will prevent the appeal if successful from being rendered nugatory. [67D] (2) The powers which have been conferred by section 254 on the Appellate Tribunals are of the widest amplitude and have in some cases been held similar to and identical with those of the powers of an appellate court under the Civil Procedure Code. In the present case, the Tribunal had the power to impose the penalty as incidental or ancillary to its appellate jurisdiction. [69F] (3) The High Court was right in holding that the Appellate Assistant Commissioner could not even move an application when an appeal is pending before the Appellate Tribu nal under section 220(6) and it is only at the earlier stage of appeal before the Tribunal that the statute provides for such a matter being dealt with by the Income Tax Officer. It is a well established rule that an express grant of statutory power carries with it, by necessary implication the authority to use all reasonable means to make the order for staying the proceedings as would prevent the Appeal if successful. [70G H] (4) The Appellate Tribunal must be held to have the power under section 151 of the Civil procedure Code to grant interim relief to a person who has preferred an appeal to the appellate forum and not to the Tribunal. [71A B] (5) The right of appeal is a substantive right and the questions of fact and law are at large and are open to review by the Appellate Authority.

The respondent was appointed a constable in U.P. Police Force and on December 1, 1945 he was promoted to the rank of Head Constable and in May 1952 he was posted as officer incharge of Police Station, District Gonda. On December 17, 1952, the Superintendent of Police made an endorsement on the report that the Sub Divisional Magistrate had found substantial complaints against the integrity of the respondent. The respondent filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution challenging the order of dismissal passed by the High Court. The High Court held that the respondent was not covered by the first proviso to sub section (1) of section 4 of the Police Act and therefore his case was not governed by the second proviso to section 4(1)(a). On appeal by special leave, Held: (i) The order of the High court must be set aside. The State Government had no power to dismiss a member of the police force unless he has been tried judicially judicially; (ii) The departmental trial was validly held in respect of the charge of an offence and not of a mere irregularity and therefore the departmental trial is validly held by a Police Officer senior in rank to a Superintendent; (iii) the High Courts were wrong in holding that the departmental enquiry was only a further step in respect Of the misconduct of the appellant. The Punjab Government vs Babu Ram Upadhya, ; , referred to. (iv) The State of U. P. vs Baburam Upadhya, [1962] Supp. 1 S.C.R. 886, applied.

The appellant was appointed as Chief Ophthalmologist cum Associate Professor of Ophthaology in Himachal Pradesh. He was promoted to supertime grade II on a certain date and his appointment was later confirmed by promotion. The promotion of the respondents to super time grade II was made on a different footing from 19th July, 1966. In the seniority list prepared by the Selection Board the appellant was shown as senior to Dr. P.C. Sen. On the basis of merit in the service, he was promoted as Chief Engineer cum Associate professor in Himachal State. The respondents filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the promotion of Dr.P.C., Dr. Sharma and Dr. D.P.(M) on the ground that they were not qualified for the post. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the promotion was in contravention of rule 8(3)(a) of the U.P State Service Rules, 1965. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the appointment of Dr, P. C. Sen as Chief Enginhoster was made by way of transfer from the post of Assistant Engineer grade II and therefore he was not qualified; (ii) the promotion to super Time Scale II was in violation of rule 7(3) of Rules 8(1) of Central Service Rules; (iii) the appellant had no right to claim promotion as Dr. S.C, grade II had put in more than eight years of service and (iv) the officers who were eligible for being promoted to Supertime grade 11 were not entitled to be considered for promotion because they belonged to a different speciality and therefore the appellant could not have been promoted to that post. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The word 'category ' in rule 8 (3)(b) has to be understood to mean the post included in that category and consequently service in that categories would mean service in a post included therein. [68D] 2.1 Rule 8(2) of U. P State Service Code, 1961 requires every member of the service to be appointed to such service in accordance with the rules and that no appointment is made in favour of a person who qualifies for being appointed to that cadreing service under rule 9(3). [69F] 2:2 The word `category ` has been designated as a " unspent ' or an additional qualification. But it is difficult to accept the submission that the post must be included in the category and therefore, service in such category would mean a service in which specified posts in that class may be filled up by promotion of persons belonging to categories (a) and (b). [70G] 2(3), Rule 8 (4) of C.P .S. Rules, 1961 is not unconstitutional as it has been found that the appellant 's service was created in a certain grade, though not needed wherein some individuals were promoted or Assistant Professor in Ophtakmology speciality. The post was not a unspred one and therefore fell outside the purview of Rule 8. [71A B] 2.(4) The word "category" used in rule 7 (3) (a), has to mean a post which is timei nately connected with the promotion or in the ratio of the number of posts and the manner of filling them.

The appellants were owners of certain lands in the State of Punjab. They sought to stow away some of their lands from the land owned by them and for that purpose they sought to lay out a considerable portion of the land falling outside the scope of the Act. The Collector, however, did not accept the request. He, therefore, initiated proceedings under section 19B of the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953, for determining an area of 117 bighas as surplus in his hands. He also passed orders declaring an area as surplus. He then proceeded to determine the surplus area by adding a portion thereof to the total permissible area as set out in section 2(3) of the said Act. In appeal, the Commissioner upheld the Collector 's order. The High Court dismissed the appellants ' writ petition and held that section 19 B read with section 10A did not affect the appellant 's transfers. Dismissing the appeals by special leave, the Court ^ HELD: (1) The object of the Land Reforms Act is to preserve the surplus stock in an urban area which is owner and has to be decided on a regular basis. [633 A] (2) Section 19 B provides that even if the source of the excess area is inheritance, bequest of gift, the capacity to own is conditioned by the permissible limit. Section 10A does not militate against this mandate of section 19. The Act is wide in its terms and encompasses all surplus areas, howsoever obtained. Even section 10 A(b) strikes at these tactics. [733 B C] (3) The scheme of the Ceiling Act, according to the learned Judges, was to see that no one held in excess of the permissible area and since by the gift to the son or wife the latter had only lands within permissible limits, there was no frustration of the policy of the law. [32 D E] Amar Singh vs State of Haryana, ; , followed. (4) The Act does not offend against the provisions of section 10 B. It follows that the appeals have to be allowed. [33 F G] Amar singh vs State, ; and Corocraft Ltd. vs Pan American Airways Inc., ; , referred to.

The appellants were the tenants of Dhanora, the predecessor in interest of the respondent. The estate was impartible and de facto possession of Dhangar was given to the predecessor on December 3, 1950. On the death of the predecessor the estate devolved upon his widow, the appellants who claimed to be the adopted son of the deceased. The respondent filed a suit against the appellants for possession of the property and mesne profits. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the respondent had no right to succeed to those lands or compensation payable in respect thereof. On appeal by the respondents, the High Court held that the appellants were entitled to receive compensation in respect of the Malguzari lands and compensation in lieu of the decision of the Compensation Officer. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the respondent was not entitled to any compensation because the Maharaja of the erstwhile State of Madhya Pradesh had no authority to determine inheritance; (ii) the order of the Governor declaring the estate as a "estate" in his favour was not binding on the appellants and (iii) the decree of the trial court was not barred by the decision given by the Compensation officer. HELD: The appeal must be dismissed. (i)(a) The expression "nearest male relative" in section 14(1) of the Act means a person who disloyal or does not manage his estate properly or does anything to improve cultivation or is otherwise of unhealthy behaviour or guilty of bad administration, and (b) under the terms of the Chanda Patent the Zamindar is entitled to decide what he should be substituted. [316 B] (a) Under section 14 of the , the expression "one person in the State" has been defined as a Hindu widow, divested of proprietary rights. The word "heir ' has been used in the sense of an absolute rule for the selection of a single heir when there are several heirs of the same class who would be entitled to succeed in the property if it were partible under the general Hindu law; and in the absence of a special custom, the rule of primogeniture furnishes a ground of preference. [333 C D] (b). The word 'heir" is recognised by the Revenue authorities as final from ancient times and has its own connotation. Therefore, the rules of lineal primogenity governing an impartible estate which are well established in HinduEstates, have little evidentiary value when it is founded on a material piece of evidence which was untrue. [332 E] (c) The word `heir in section 3 of the Abolition Act does not invest the Compensation Officers with jurisdiction to determine competing claims of persons claiming proprietary rights to the property vesting in the Government by the operation of section 3. Section 14 is intended to determine only the proprietary rights in the land, qua the State. [336 E] The word has been interpreted in a wide sense and it cannot be intended by an Order under section 14 to determine complicated questions of title by the adjudication of a revenue officer in a summary inquiry without even a right of appeal and to make his adjudication conclusive unless a suit is filed within two months from the date of the order. That is also clear from the terms Of section 35(7) which provides that the payment of compensation under this Act to the creditors of a proprietor or to the proprietor in accordance with the prescribed manner shall be a full discharge of the State Government from all liability to pay compensation for the divesting of proprietary right, but shall not prejudice any rights in respect Of the said rights to which any other person may be entitled by due process of law to enforce against the person to whom compensation has been paid as aforesaid. [340 G H] (d) The order of Compensation Officer under section 3 is final and conclusive. Section 15 provides for assessment of compensation payable to the claimants in case of a Zamindar.

The respondent landlord filed a suit for recovery of possession of the premises on the ground that the appellants were in arrears of rent from 1st September, 1964 and also on the grounds that the appellant was in arrears. The appellants contended that they had been in arrears from 15th March, 1960 to 15th April, 1963, i.e., for over six months. In the written statement filed by the respondent landlord it was stated that the premises were in arrear of rent for more than six months and that the respondent bonafide required possession of it in view of section 12(3) (a) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947. The trial court held that the suit was within one month from the service of notice under section 12 (3) of Act and decreed the suit. On appeal the High Court confirmed the judgment of the trial court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the period of six months prescribed by section 12 of the Act did not apply to the suit, but that the suits were in continuation of the notice under the section and therefore there was a dispute as to rent within one year from the date of service of the said notice. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The expression "the tenant" in section 12 is wide enough to include a tenant only who is not entitled to the recovery of the possession of premises let for the purpose of the tenancy. [633 B] (2) In the present case the appellants had been given notice on 21st April, 1966 and the respondent filed the suit on 15th September, 1965. The notice terminating the tenancy was dated 5th April 1963. The suit was filed on 15 3 1957. The period of one month mentioned in section 11(3)(a) was a must of the first month from 1.9.1964. The High Court had held that to limit raising a dispute within one months from the receipt of notice, the second condition in section 13(3), namely, that there was no dispute regarding the amount of standard rent or permitted increases at the date when the notice was issued and since there was admittedly no dispute in regard to standard rent, the suit must be deemed to have been filed on 30th May, 1955. [ 634 C D] (3)(i) The High Courts nullifies the provisions contained in section 2(a) (b) of Bombay Rents. Hotel and lodging House Rates control Act, and are not entitled under section 11 (4) (c) of that Act to raise a dispute on the question of standard or permitted increase. [ 635 C D]. Ambalal vs Badaldas, ; , followed. (ii) The notice dated 17th November 1966 terminating the lease was not in accordance with the provisions of section 11 of the Rent Act and therefore the suit is barred by limitation.

The respondent company was incorporated in India with the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. It had a controlling interest in it as contemplated by section 2(21) of the Excess Profits Tax Act, 1940. The Aluminium Ltd., which was then British India having a capital of Rs. 3,600, divided into 360,000 shares of Rs 10 each and in exercise of the power given to it by article 105 of the articles of association of the respondent company appointed three permanent directors on the board of directors of the company. Two of these directors later retired and only one was then left out of those three remaining shares. The question for determination in this appeal was whether the directors of a company had a control over its affairs at general meetings and as such could control the affairs of the Company and in computing the standard profits of the appellant company, the statutory percentage should be taken at 10 per cent. per annum. Held, that the directors who held the majority of shares as trustees were not holding any beneficial interest in the respondent Company and as they cast their votes according to directions of his principals, the shares being always subject to his will and ordering and, therefore, they cannot apply either of them or to exercise the same power on behalf of the shareholders. Commissioners of Inland Revenue vs J. Bibby & Sons Ltd., , applied. Commissioner of Income tax vs Bipin Silk Mills Ltd., ; , followed. Commissioners for Excess Profits tax vs Jamed Hodgkinson, and Commissioners of Income Tax vs Bipin silk Mills Ltd. , referred to.

The respondent was serving as an Accountant, Grade II in the Electricity Department of the former State of Mysore. On 1st November, 1956 he was allotted to the new State of Karnataka with effect from 1st Nov., 1956. The post which he held came to be equated with that of I Division Clerk in the former state of Mysore, was abolished by the Indian Electricity (Supply) Act, 1948. On 30th December 1966, some persons junior to him were promoted on their having passed Part I and II of the S.A.S. examination while promotion was denied to them as he had not passed the examination. The respondent filed a writ petition before the High Court which allowed the same holding that the respondent was exempted from passing the Departmental Examination before qualifying for the promotion. The Division Bench held that the writ petition could not be thrown out on the ground of inordinate delay and laches on the part of the respondent and also on the grounds that in view of the later Resolution of the Board dated 5th January, 1970 it was no longer open to the respondent to rely on the resolution dated 19th May, 1969. In appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: The High Court rightly held that there was nothing to indicate that the allottees were exempted from pass ing the Departmental examination before qualifying the examination and therefore allowed the writ of mandamus to the appellant to consider the case of the respond ent for promotion as an Accounts Superin tendent. [512 D] (1) The resolution dated 5. January,1970 was not intended to cover the case where the rules do not specifically require the passing of the examinations and the language test. These G.O.s do not apply in the present case as the Regulations framed by the Board under section 79(c) specifically prescribe the passing offi cation. [511 E F] (2) The High Courts found that the later resolution did not affect the earlier Resolu tion on the basis of the subsequent Resolution dated 19.5.1969, and that the resolution was passed by the respondent in pursuance of certain proceedings of the Government referred to in the Resolution itself. Paragraph 2 of the Resolution clearly indicates that unless in the Recruitment Rules relating to the service concerned Depart mental Examination had been incorporated and prescribed and unless it is clearly specified for what purpose the tests are prescribed viz., whether for increments or promotions, the passing Of the Departmental examina tion would be necessary to be insisted in future also.

The petitioner, a retired Railway employee, was detained under the provisions of the Orissa Police Act, 1962. The grounds of detention were served on him in jail and his case was that he was running a train on the railway track and by doing so, had killed his wife and daughter in law. He was arrested and released from custody on September 19, 1973. On the basis of these allegations, the petitioner filed a writ petition before the High Court praying for the issue of a writ of habeas corpus directing the State to release him from custody. The High Court held that it was a case of custodial death and directed the State Government to pay compensation to the petitioner for the loss suffered by her husband. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that (i) the State had no locus standi to file the writ petition; (ii) the order of the District Magistrate directing payment of compensation did not amount to enforcement of fundamental rights under Articles 21 and 226 of the Constitution; (iii) the High Courts should have awarded compensation to a person who was in actual possession of his property by way of compensation for deprivation of life and personal liberty, and (iv) the petitioner could not be allowed to suffer any hardship. Dismissing the writ petitions, ^ HELD: 1. The State has the right to be indemnified by and take such action as may be appropriate under the law for the wrong done factually or in addition to the remedy in private law for damages for the tortuous act of the State. [603B] 2.1 The State is responsible if the person in custody of a police officer is deprived of his life, which he has so long as he exercises his right to seek redress through civil and criminal proceedings or can it go further and grant redress to the aggrieved person except by punishment of imprisonment for life. [600D E] 2:2 The State cannot be allowed any relief under Article 32 of the Constitu tion in a writ proceeding against an officer who has been found guilty of negligence, which is not denuded of his fundamental rights. [599F] 2.(i) The right to compensation is guaranteed by Article 21 of the Consti tution and the right is independent and distinct from the State 's liability for contravention of any law or order of a competent jurisdiction. It is an obligation of the state, to ensure that there is no infringement of the indefeasible rights of a citizen to life, except in accordance with law, while the citizen is in its custody. [501G] (ii). The right of the citizen to compensation for violation of fundamental right under Article 21 cannot be denied to convicts under trials or other prisoners in custody, except according to procedure established by law. There is a great responsibility on the police or prison authorities to ensure the safety of their persons and to prevent them from being prosecuted for the offence committed thereby. [500B] (iii). The State should pay compensation for contraventions of fundamental freedoms guaranteed under Article 22(4) of the Con stitution, if it is established that there has been an infringement of a fundamental right conferred in the Constitution, which enables the award of compensation in appropriate cases, where that right is denied to the injured or the victim whose fundamental rights are infringed. [525C] 2(iv). The obligation to pay the compensation under Article 19 police Act and not under the criminal law is distinct and independent of the rights available to the victims under the Criminal Procedure Code, 1973, which enable the award by way or in lieu of compensation to be awarded against the wrong doer for the resulting offence, and recovery of damages under private law by the ordinary process.

The petitioner was convicted by the Chief Reporter of the Hindustan Times, Smt. Prabha Dutt, for committing an offence under section 302 Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. The High Court dismissed his petition for commutation of sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that if the Supreme Court had decided to allow the petitioner to interview two convicts Billa and Ranga who were under a sentence of death, the interviews could be permitted only subject to the rules and regulations contained in the Jail Manual. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The constitutional right to freedom of speech and expression conferred by article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution which includes the freedom of the press is not an absolute right nor indeed does it confer any right on the Press unless in the first instance, the person sought to be interviewed is willing to be interview. [1187B C] 2. The Press is entitled to exercise its freedom of expression and if it is thought necessary that such a search should be taken, a person who desires to interview a prisoner may have to subject himself or herself to the search in accordance with the rules, and regulations governing the interviews. There is a provision in the rules that if a person sought inter alia to be invited by a convict is a female, she can be searched only by a matron or a female warden. Taking an overall view of the matter, it cannot be said that the two prisoners are ready and willing to he interviewed. [1108C D] 3. The petitioner has been asking for permission to interview the prisoners right since the President of India rejected his petitions for commutation. He is not entitled to any other appropriate writ or direction directing the respondents to allow him to interview them. While it may be thought necessary, that such an application should be made, a persons who desires the condemned prisoner to be heard must appear before the Court and in accordance therewith, and in accord with law, the Court cannot ignore that issue. [1087E F] 4. The right claimed by the petitioner is not the right to express any particular view or opinion but the right of means of information through the medium of an interview of the two convicts who are sentenced to life imprisonment. No data has been made available to us on the basis of which it would be possible for the Court to say that the petitioners should be allowed to interview their petitions.

The respondent mortgaged a tea garden called the "Ishanchandrapar Tea Estate" to M/s. Das Bank Ltd., on January 19, 1950. On January 20, 1950 the appellant entered into a surety bond in respect of the estate on February 10, 1950 for the purpose of the particular proceedings which were pending before the District Judge and was created under the order of 1 950. C The application filed by the respondent on February 28, 1950 was heard along with the mortgage suit. On August 26, 1950, the appellant applied to the Sub judge for damages from the Receiver and the Sub Judge ordered that the Receiver should pay the amount within two months failing which the amount should be recovered from the security of Rs. 50,000. The appellant filed an appeal against this order but the same was dismissed by the Judicial Commissioner on June 29, 1970. On October 4, 1961, the respondent moved an application requesting for damages to the extent of Rs 32,525. He also prayed that the receiver should pay him the amount. The Sub judge allowed the respondent 's application and directed that the appellant should pay to the Receiver a sum of Rs .32,525 as costs. On appeal by special leave, Held: (i) Under the terms of the bond, the appel lant rendered itself liable as a surety for the fulfilment of the conditions imposed on the Receiver under the orders passed by the Court. Therefore, the order for the recovery of damages obtained by the respon dent against the Receiver could be executed against the appellant to the amount which was rendered itself personally liable under the terms thereof. (ii) Under section 150 of the Code of Civil Procedure, save as otherwise provided, where the business of any court is transferred to any other Court, the transferee Court has the same powers and is entitled to perform the same duties as those respectively conferred and imposed by the Code upon the transferor Court. The surety bond was a part of the proceedings pending before tho District Judge, and on the transfer of the suit the entire proceedings including the bond stood validly transferred to the Court of the Subordinate Judge. (iii) Under Section 150 of Code of Criminal Procedure, except under certain circumstances, no other order could be passed in respect to any loss caused to the tea garden by fire. The words "as aforesaid" which qualify the words "in relation to his duties" mean "in respect of his duties". He was put in possession of the tea gardens in his capacity as a Receiver and indeed parties had made contentions from time to time as to whether the tea estate was managed by the Receiver economically and efficiently. The sureties bond was executed both be the Receiver 's responsibility and the appellant was put incharge of the Tea garden in his place as the Receiver. (iv) Under clause 12 of the surety bond, if the appellant is neither the successor nor the successor in office of the District judge, he has to enforce the suretyship by enforcing the bond. Therefore the order made by the surety for recovery of the damages obtained on the lease hold of the mortgaged property including the tea Garden was given retrospective operation with effect from January 22, 1950 being the date on which the Receiver had taken possession of it including the Tea Garden.

The appellants who were dealers in food grains, supplied wheat to the Regional Food Controller diverse quantities of wheat in compliance with the provisions of the U.P. Essential Commodities (Levy) Order, 1959. The Sales Tax Officer levied tax under the U P. Essential Supplies Dealers Licensing Order, 1960 on the aggregate of the price of wheat by the appellants and assessed them to sales tax. The appellants challenged the validity of the levy on the ground that the wheat supplied was not sold by them to the Controller. The High Court held that the turnover resulting from supplies of wheat was not taxable under the Act as it was not a sale within the meaning of the Act. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The expression "sale" in the U .P. Sales Tax Act means a transfer of property in goods for cash, deferred payment or other valuable consideration but not including a mortgage, hypothecation, charge or pledge. [678 F] (2) The definition of "sale " in section 2(d) of the Uttar Pradesh Essential Commodities Dealers Licensing order, 1959, is wide enough to include a contract of sale between persons competent to contract for a price paid or promised and a transaction in which an obligation to supply goods is imposed, and which does not involve an obligation on the Central Government to refuse to comply with the amount to acceptance of an offer or to make of an offers. [679 G H] (3) The High Courts were right in holding that the sales made by the appellant could be regarded as for sale within section 2 (d) Of the Act and not for sale under section 2 of the Indian Contract Act. [680 D] (4) The transaction was a sale of goods and was not liable to tax under section 7 of the Sales Tax Acts. The sales were therefore taxable under section 3(a) of U. P. Sales tax Act, 1948. [681 G] (5) The State Government could not by agreement provide for any consensual arrangement between the parties. The agreement was enforceable only in respect of matters not covered by the Act but also the transaction relating to goods sold within the contemplation of section 2. [682 A B] (6) The transactions were enforceable by law and were regarded as contracts of sale as defined in section 4 of the , and the sales tax authorities were bound to take action under section 6 of the . [681 E F] M/s New India Sugar Mills Ltd. vs State of Madras, ; , followed. (7) The Sales tax Officer was not competent to assess the appellant under the provisions Of the U Pradesh Act. The order passed by the High Court is set aside and the question referred to it is answered in favour of the assessee.

The appellant was detained under the provisions of the Gujarat Prevention of Anti Social Activities Act, 1985. The grounds of detention were served on him and he was informed that he had been arrested and sentenced to prison. He challenged his second order of detention in a writ petition before the High Court which dismissed the same. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 If the report of the Advisory Board is not made within three months of the date of detention, the detention becomes illegal notwithstanding that it is within three month from the date on which the report is made. The period of three weeks stipulated by section 11 of the Act expired on July 14, 1986. The petitioner was entitled to be released on July and the order of his detention dated June 23, 1986 had been revoked and a fresh order of deten tion was made on the same day. [206C D] 1.2 In a habeas corpus proceeding it is not a sufficient answer to say that the procedural requirements of the Constitution and the statute have been complied with before the date when the earlier order is revoked and the subsequent order is made.[207D E] Shibapada Mukherjee vs State of West Bengal, ; , referred to. 1.3 The procedural requirements are the only safeguards available to a detenu since the Court is not expected to go behind the subjective satisfaction of the detaining authority. The procedural requirement are the most safeguards available lo a detenu though the court is not expect to go beyond the subjective satis faction of the detain ing authority.

The petitioner, a father of the respondent, filed an application for filing the award and sought to file it in terms of the award under section 17 of the . The application was converted into Special Civil Suit No. 84 of 1977. The petitioner contended that the notice issued by the arbitrator was already given to him and he had also informed him that the entire responsibility of solving the dispute was entrusted to him, and that he had taken the responsibility. He also alleged that the time for making an application to set aside the award had expired and no such application was made. The trial Judge rejected the objections filed by the petitioner but did not pass any order confirming the acceptance of the deposit. The High Court dismissed the revision application. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that there was no written agreement signed by both the parties to refer the dispute to arbitration, and therefore, the notice was already issued to the party concerned about the filing of the Award. Dismissing the special leave petition, ^ HELD: 1. The conduct of the parties that there is an arbitration agreement and by signing the award it could be said that the parties had agreed to refer their disputes in writing to the arbitration of the named arbitrator. This agreement was done twice, firstly by signing an endorsement below the award, secondly by entering into an agreement in the form of a letter dated 14th August, 1978 (Exhibit 40). In that view of the matter, it cannot be said to be a proper arbitration agreement in terms thereof. [538C D] 2. The contention that there had been no written consent by both parties to reference is not correct. The Civil Court had jurisdiction to take cognizance of the said award under sections 14 and 17 of Act. This question had come up for consideration before the Judicial Committee in Rajah Amir Hassan Khan vs Sheo Baksh Singh, 11 I.A. 237. In that case, the Judicial committee held that they had perfect jurisdiction to decide the question which was before them (i) whether the suit was barred as res judicata; and (ii) whether it did decide it rightly or wrongly. The judicial Committee held that both of them had re affirmed the acceptance by the Civil Court and that the award was not set aside under section 30 and (iii) that the High Court had recorded a decree in terms Of the award. In the light of the facts and circumstances of the case, it was held that the revision before the High court suffered from res judicata. [540D E] 3. The civil court had jurisdiction under section 9 of the Civil Procedure Code to take cognisance of the order under sections 15 and 17. This view is not in consonance with the law laid down by this Court in several cases. [541F G] 4. In view of all these factors, the High Courts were right in holding that the civil court has jurisdiction to taken cognizance of an award under Sections 14 and17 of the Act. [542G H] 5. The Judicial Committee held in Rajah Hasan Khan vs Ram Baksh singh, 11 1.A 237 that the conduct of parties that the there was an arbitration clause and by entering the award in form of the letter dated April 7, 1978, it could not be said, that the proceedings under the Act had become highly technical accompanied by unending prolixity, at every stage providing a legal trap to the unwary. [543A B] 6. The practice of the Court in making an arbitration award is that the Court shall (subject to the provisions herein contained) have jurisdiction to try all suits of a civil nature excepting suits of which their cognizance is either expressly or impliedly barred.

The appellant mortgaged his properties to the respondent. The respondent 's father died in 1939 and the appellant filed a suit for recovery of the mortgage debt due from him on account of arrears of rent, and the trial court decreed the suit holding that the appellant was not entitled to an equitablebora tion under section 36(1) proviso (ii) of the Transfer of Property Act. The High Court in appeal reversed the decree and held that the respondent 'different dates from which he had obtained a mortgage were different from those when he instituted the suit for possession of the properties to which the Act applied. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The appellant was entitled to recover his debt under section 35(5) of Act XIV of 1940 as if it were arrears of land revenue and not as an usufructuary mortgage. [587 C] (ii).The expression "any decree other than a decree in a suit to which this Act applies" is used in the widest possible terms of a decree, and so long as it subsists, the proceeding in execution can well be regarded as pending on the 1st day of January 1939, and there was no question of any inconsistency between the appellant 's title and the respondent (the mortgagee) as the transaction took place long before that date. [588 E F] (iii).The words "unless the Court shall make an order to the contrary" in section 36 (5) are wide enough to include a limitation on the power of the court to pass a decree. The words "if the court is satisfied that the assignment was bona fide and that he had not received the notice referred to in cl. (a) of sub section (1) of section 28, as the transactions took place before the Act came into force. [589 E F; 590 A] Ram Kinkar Banerjee vs Satyadhan Mukhopadhya, L.R. , referred to. (iv).The word "dissolved" in cl.(a) means "any suit or proceeding instituted or filed on or after that date and includes a proceeding in the execution of a mortgage decree which is not fully satisfied by the first day of the January 1939". The words 'unless the court shall make order to that contrary ' mean that the proceedings which had resulted in the attachment were kept alive. [591 F] Ramkinkar Banerji vs Satya Charan Singh, L R. , distinguished. (v)The word 'dissatisfied ' occurring in cl(a) must be given its ordinary meaning and must be construed in a wider sense than that of an expression which may be used to denote the existence of an attachment. The word 'determine ' is not defined in the Act, but it has been understood by the legislature as meaning "anything done or thing done". [591 E] (vi)The words 'in any suit or proceedings ' occurring under cl. 2(22) of a. 2 of the Act are wide and comprehensive. The definition of 'property ' contained in section 2(23) of that Act is not exhaustive but only illustrative. It does not mean that an assignee of a debt is within the meaning of the expression in cl, (a), or (b) of cl. 28 of the deed. [592 E F]. Ram Kimkar Banerjee & Anr.

The appellant was the karta of a joint family consisting of himself and his four sons. The properties were divided by metes and bounds in 1947 after the execution of exhibit A 1 and A 2 there was a disruption of the joint family. In 1954, he transferred to the appellant certain properties belonging to the joint Hindu Family. In 1947, he transposed to the family of his wife and sons. In 1950, he sold the properties to the respondents. The appellant filed suits for recovery of possession of the properties alleging that the documents were executed without consideration or for immoral purposes and were void. The trial court dis missed the suits. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the decree in favour of the respondents and decreed them. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) future illicit cohabitation was not the object or the consideration for the transfers under exhibit A I and A2. [46 C] Balo vs Parbati, I.L.R. , referred to. (2) The conduct of the appellant in an illegal transaction is the motive and not the consideration. In the instant case, the transfer was without consideration and was therefore void. [47 D E] Balos vs Parbathod Zipru Bhate, I,.L. R. , approved. (3) The transfers were without consideration, and were by way of gifts. The gifts were made in consideration of past illicit cohabitations and were not hit by section 6(h).

The appellant, a private limited company, had taken on lease certain policies of the year 1975 75 with the respondent company for a period of 5 years from 1.7.1975 to 31.12.75. The first policy was that the company should pay interest on the policy which remained in force upto 31.3.76 and thereafter at 6% per annum on the amount paid by it. In view of this, the appellant had to pay interest upto 30.4.77. On 4.4 77, the respondent issued a notice under section 226(3) of the Income Tax Act, 1961 calling upon the appellant to pay the said sum within 15 days from the date of receipt of the notice. The appellant challenged the validity of the said notice by filing a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court held that the last two policies having lapsed on 14.9.72 and 28.3 .72, the interest payable under the first policy could not be paid in terms thereof. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the liability for payment of interest on policies arose only at a later stage; (ii) the notice issued by the I.T.O. was invalid as it did not disclose any basis for such liability; and (iii) the policy having been issued on oath under section 22(3)(vi), the appellant could not claim that the said policy had been wrongly taken away by the company. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The policy having expressly provided the mode of raising such an objection in the form of a statement on oath specified in clause (vi) of sub section (3) thereof, the I .T.C. could not have made the payment only of interest. [109B] 2.1 The liability arising after making the requisite statement on behalf by the L.I.C., did not amount to discharge of the statutory obligation under section 21(3). The liability arose from the failure of the Ll.C to pay any sum to the I,T.I., in obedience to the notice under sub section(3), and the appellant was entitled to recover it by way of interest from the IL.C.[109E F] 2:2.1. The liability arises when the I C.I./O.C./D.C.(N.S.) is required to make a statement in writing under section 23(3); and the person who makes the statement on an oath that the sum demanded or any part thereof is not due to the assessee or that he does not hold any money for or on account of the assessee. [110F G] 2.(a) The liability of the I/O.T., 1961, in respect of the 1st respondent Corporation, was that of the C.l.O., and its officers making the necessary statement on the oath under Section 226(2)(vi) and (vii). The I.I .C. did not have the effect of investi gation of the assignment nor did it have the consequence of any risk of personal liability. [111B] (b) The L.lO.E.C 's order dated 1.4,77 was not a valid and legal notice under Section 22(1)(vi). The appellant could make the payment even according to the stand taken by the l.I C.T./October 31, 1975. [112B] 3. The LlOE 's conduct in making the statement of the respondent 's son on oath was after inordinate delay and therefore it was not possible for the respondent to obtain revocation of the latter notice under clause (vii) thereof within a reasonable time. [114C D] 4. The respondent 'could not claim the benefit of the order dated April 1,77 in the instant case. [115E F; 116A] 5.

The appellant was the owner of a suit property. He filed an application under section 29(2) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, for setting aside the order of the Tribunal and for directing that the appeal be heard by a Single Judge of the High Court. The Single Judge held that the order passed by the Tribunal was not appealable under section 116A of the Act as it had no jurisdiction to hear the appeal. On appeal by special leave, Held: (1) that the expression "a period of limitation different from that prescribed therefor by the First Schedule to the Limitation Act" in section 29 (2) must be given a wider meaning and not extended to the other words in the First schedule. The word " period of Limitation" in the said clause is used in the context of the Limitation act, which relates to procedure, and does not ordinarily deal with substantive rights; but it is only so much of it as is expressly made applicable by the Act. In the present case the first part of section 29 of the , was intended to apply only when a special or local law prescribes a period of time for an appeal and not under section 537 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The second part of the said section, which was in force at that time, did not apply to an appeal under the Act because it had been made provision for a period more than one year from the date of the decree or order appealed against. (2)(a) The word 'prescribed ' in the first limb of sub section (2), could not be construed as meaning that schedule I must also positively prescribe the period of the limitation. (b) The expression "any" in sub section(2)(b) of section 12, would mean that a right of appeal is conferred by section 116 A(1). (c) The words "a time limit for any suit, appeal or application a period not exceeding three years from the commencement of the civil proceedings" occurring in the second part only meant that the period during which an appeal was expressly excluded by the first clause. (d) The second clause of sub s.(2) would apply even to cases where a special statute prescribes a time limit and the second clause does not require that the schedule should be amended for any period of delay prescribed for any such suit, appeals or applications by any special or special law. (e) The first part only mentioned that the limitation of one year prescribed for an application for appeal would be deemed to be an appeal from an original decree passed by a civil court in respect of which a period is prescribed in the Second Schedule. (f) The third clause of section 30(2), which was not expressly made inapplicable, could not apply as it did not provide that the first portion of the second proviso must be strictly complied with. (g) The question whether a suit, Appeal or application under the Code would fall within the first paragraph of the fourth proviso to s.30(2). (h) The High Court was right in holding that the second para of section 28(2); did not require any period for an appellate order etc., and that the third para of the third clause must be read as one part of it and the words "any", clearly indicated that the appellant was entitled to a decree, appeal and application under sub s (3) of s.29. (i) The last portion of section 5(2): of the Indian Limitation Act, 1908, which is in pari materia with the first para of sub sec tion (2). The second para only provided for a time period of one month from the execution or decree passed under the said provision.

The appellant, a person providing transport service in the District of Mathura, challenged the order dated May 22, 1986 passed by the District Magistrate, Mathura under Section 76 of the (Act) on the ground that the District Magis trate had no power to appoint any area as a bus stand under section 76 of Act. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that section 76 was not applicable to a permanent bus stand which was a sort of radi ty and therefore the order made under Section 77 was unassailable. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 Section 76(2)(r) of the Act has nothing to do with the fixation or alteration of a bus stands and the power to issue a notification fixing a bus Stand is implied in section 68(2) (r). [717B] 1.2 The High Courts were not justified in upholding the impugned order passed by District Magistrate. [718C D] 1:3. Section 76 is also in Chapter VI dealing with 'control of traffic ' and section 76 is in Chapter VII dealing with "control of transport vehicles". It is not disputed that in the instant case no order has been passed by Regional Transport Authority, Mathura to determine the area in question as a Bus stand and the District magistrate cannot be equated with the Regional Transport Author ity constituted under the Act. [700D E] 1 :4. The Town Area Committee can derive any assistance from this rule. It only authorises the District Commis sioner to exercise the powers under section 77 which is confined to the question of determination of parking places and halting places which are not the same as bus stands which can only be notified by the Regional Authority as held by this Court in T.B. Ibrahim 's case.

The appellants were convicted by the trial court under section 7 of the . The High Court dismissed their appeal. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) There was no attempt on the part of the appellants to commit the offence of export. It was merely a preparation on the parts of the appellant and as a matter of law a preparation for committing an offence is different from attempt to commit it. The preparation consists in devising or arranging the means or measures necessary for the commission of the offence. On the other hand, an attempt to committing the offence is a direct movement towards the commission after preparations are made. In order that a person may be convicted of an attempt under section 3 of the , it must be shown first to have had an intention to commit an offence after preparation were made. [666 D F] (ii) The preparation consisted in devizing or arranging, the means and measures necessary to the commission Of the offence; on the other band, an attempts to commit a crime, he must be proved first to having had an intended object to commit that offence and secondly to have done an act which constitutes the actus reus of a criminal attempt. [667 E F] In order to attract section 7, it must not only have been intended to have an intention in the preparation after preparations were made, but also depends upon the circumstances of each particular case. The test for determining whether the act of the accused constituted an attempt or preparation is whether the overt acts already done are such that if the offender changes his mind and does not proceed further in its progress, the acts already do not be completely harmless.

The Sassoons of the respondent company, who was a partner in a firm carrying on business as Managing Agency agents, entered into an agreement with the Sassoon and Company for the purchase of their shares. The managing agency agreements provided that the transferees would be entitled to receive from the company the amounts due to them. The transferors were to be paid the remuneration specified in cl. 2(d) of the agreement which was a commission of 10% on the net profits of the Managing Agency and transfer of 10 per cent on the gross profits of each year. Clause 3 provided that "the Company shall not be liable to pay any commission or remuneration for the year payable under the managing agency Agreement except as provided in cls. 2 (d) and 3 (e). " The respondent company was assessed to income tax by the Income Tax Officer, who held that the Managing Agent had no debt due from the respondent and directed the company to pay tax only on the amount of commission paid to it. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed this order but the Tribunal held that as the managing agent had created a liability on the company under the agreement to pay to the Managing Agents the liability was not liable to be taxed. On reference, the High Court held that though the managing Agency Agreement provided for the transfer of the entire remuneration for each year and not for a portion thereof and therefore no commission could be claimed by the respondent from the appellant company as it was not a debt due to the Sassoon and that the transaction amounted to a capital receipt. On appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The managing Agency agreement was the source of income and was the joint income of both the assignor and the assignee. It could be said that the remuneration for a part thereof accrued on the completion of the year and was not by itself enough to vest in the assignee a beneficial right to the remuneration of the company. [361 E F] (ii) The mere ownership of the managing Agent did not vest in it a beneficial interest to the respondent, and the transaction could not be said to have acquired any share in commission for the broken periods. The liability was the creation of income bearing asset which carried with it a right to receive the entire income. [362 G] (iii) The transfer of a present right to collect the entire profits of a remuneration did not depend on any specific contract to the contrary between the persons who contributed to the work or business, the fruit of such work or of such business and on the construction of the agreements the Sasomans disclaimed the income. The mere fact that the ownership of Managing Agency could not as a matter of law be treated as the source or the property of the assessee would not make it an asset of the remuneration. [365 G H] (iv) The right of the assignee to receive a part of the income from the managing company and his liability to pay the income accrues on the date of the assignment.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed both the conviction and sentence.
