In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The evidence on record can be accepted as a whole and no other reasonable hypothesis was or could be suggested. [90 C] (2) There is a clear distinction between the admissibility of an admission or confession and the weight to be attached to it. A confessional soliloquy is a direct piece of evidence. It may be an expression of conflict of emotion; a conscious effort to stifle the pricked conscience; an argument to find excuse or justification for his act; or a penitent or remorseful act of exaggeration of his part in the crime. The tone may be soft and low; the words may be confused; they may be capable of conflicting interpretations depending on witnesses, whether they are biased or honest, intelligent or ignorant, imaginative or prosaic, as the case may be. [91 D E] Pakala Narayana vs R. , referred to. (3) The High Courts have consistently accepted the circumstantial evidence adduced in the case and the circumstances found by the High Court, which lead to only conclusion that the accused must have committed the murder. No other reasonable conclusion was or was possible on a consideration of the relevant provisions of the Evidence Act. [92 E] (4) In the instant case, the High Courts had accepted the evidence adduced by the prosecution and convicted the appellant under section 307 of the Penal Code. The appeal fails and is dismissed.

The appellant was working as Divisional Manager at Delhi. He was appointed by the Central Government under General Insurance (Emergency Provisions) Ordinance, 1971 replaced by Act 57 of 1972. The appellant was kept under suspension from August 9, 1973 pending investigation into the embezzlement, Explanation was called for on October 16, 1973. During dropping of the proceeding, the appellant was served with termination order dated April 17, 1975 issued by the respondent. The said order was challenged in a writ petition in Delhi High Court which was dismissed by a Single Judge holding that the invalidity of the termination order as it was passed without an enquiry or giving an opportunity, the termination was not void and therefore the impugned order terminating the services of the appellant is illegal. In appeal to this Court, on behalf of the respondent it was contended that (i) Rule 5 of the Rules of Delhi Transport Corporation Service Regulation gives naked power to terminate the services by giving one month 's notice or pay in lieu thereof; (ii) the rule is ultra vires article 14 of the Constitution; and (iii) the impugned termination order is illegal as void. Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1. Rule 5 does not become arbitrary. unreasonable or void offending Article 14. [226D] 2. The word "in the event of the Society not having any further need of any employee 's service whether permanent or temporary which should be decided by the Board" is susceptible of two interpretations. The one interpretation put up by Sri Ramamurty is that the Board may unilaterally and arbitrarily decide that there is no need for the services, of a particular employee, in given facts and circumstances, though the post which the officer or the employee is occupying no longer is in need. Thereby, the post would be abolished. This would be a policy decision depending on the exigencies. [227E F] 3. The words "in this event ofthe Society not being having any other need" are susceptible to two interpretations and the one interpretation placed by Sri jagurty was that the respondent 's action may form an objective opinion, on the basis of the material, that the post is owned no longer was in need of the employee '. [228F G] 4. The expression "in his event not having no further need" of any employees ' service whether temporary or temporary, which should he decided by Board, the Principal Officer shall give 30 days ' notice in writing for termination of his service or in lieu of notice in lieu thereto, pay one month"s salary including allowances upto the period of termination. [229F G; 228A] 5.

The appellants were the unsuccessful bidders in a writ petition filed by them before the High Court. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the State Government had no power to grant an exclusive privilege under section 22 of the Bihar and Orissa Excise Act, 1915, and it was not open to the Collector to follow the process of auction under the directions of the State Govern ment. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the High Courts had no authority to issue a writ in respect of the licences granted for the retail sale of country liquor; and (ii) the State Legislature was not competent to issue such a notification under section 29 of the Act as the power of the Government to reject a bid was vested in it. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: (1) The High Courts have held that the appellants were entitled to the exclusive privilege of manufacturing and selling liquor under the outstill system within the meaning of section 22(1) of the Orissa Excise (Second Amendment) Act, 1971. [830 D] (2) The power to accept or reject a tender without assigning any reason cannot be said to be arbitrary as section 29(2)(b) which has been amended with retrospective effect from 1st May, 1972 by the Bihar & Orissa Excise Laws (Amendment) Act of 1970 is not valid. [823 E F] (3) The expression "fee" in the rule is not defined in the Act and it has been used in section 2(a) to mean a fee which is in substance a tax or a fee under Entry 51 of List II of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution. [824 G H] (4) The word "fee ' in the Rule means a fee payable by an applicant for a licence on payment of consideration with such conditions and restrictions as may be necessary in the public interest. It is not possible to say that either the Government or any of its officers abused the power by acting either unreasonably or in a mala fide manner, and that it has no fixed or fixed remuneration. [825 G H; 826 A] (5) The use of the expression "fees" in rule 103 of the Rules makes it clear that the Government retained the power to reject or refuse a tender for any licence on the payment of considerations with such condition and restrictions for its regulation as may he necessary in public interest, and the fact that the fee was not an ordinary auction where binding agreement could be deemed to have been concluded at the fall of the hammer, creating mutually enforceable obligations. [826 A B] (6) The rule is a self contained code and does not require any specific provision for the exercise of such power. It has been made clear in this regard by this Court in Amba Prasad Saha vs State of Orissa & Ors., ; , that the power can be exercised only in the interest of public revenue, and not in a colourable exercise of legislative power. [827 C D] The Bihar Government Order dated August 19, 1970 was issued under section 5(1)(d) of Act 17 of 1970 and it had been made effective from April 16, 1970. The order was made on May 15, 1971 and the appellant was given notice to show cause why he should not be evicted from the land in question. The Collector passed an order on August 19. 1970 holding that no fee was payable under section 23(2) of 'the Act. The appellant filed a writ application before the Patna High Court challenging the validity of the order and the High court dismissed the petition.

The appellant was charged with murder and murder of his grandson. The prosecution case was that the deceased was a man of unsound mind and accused No. 3 was his classmate and through Dinkar, accused No 2 and his wife were also members of a family. The deceased was living in a house where he used to visit his cousin brother 's place. On the day of occurrence when the deceased went to the house of accused No 1, the appellant came there with a view to frightening him and that he would look after the deceased 's wife. The appellant was tried for an offence under section 302 read with section 120B I.P.C. and section 201 read with sections 109 and 302 I. P.C., and convicted and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence of accused 2 and 3 but acquitted him on the ground that there was no corroboration of the actual participation in the murder. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that there were no corroboration in regard to the crime; that there had been corroboration of evidence which connected accused No 3 with the crime and that the High Court erred in holding that there Was sufficient corroboration of his evidence. HELD: (i) The conviction of accused 1 and 2 under section 120 B read with s.120B I P. C., was not sustainable. [620 D] (ii) There was no corroborative evidence to connect accused No, 3 with murder. The evidence must confirm that part of the testimony which suggests that the crime was committed by the accused. If a witness says that the accused and he stole the sheep and he put the skins in a certain place, the discovery of the skins is not sufficient. [625 E] (iii) There is no corroboration to the evidence of the witness as regards the crime. The nature of corroboration is that it is confirmatory evidence and it may consist of the evidence, of second witness or of circumstances like the conduct of the person against whom it is required. Corroboration must connect or tend to connect the accused with the time. When it is said that the corroborative evidence must implicate the accused in material particulars it means that it was not enough that a piece of evidence tends to confirm the truth of a part of it to be corroborated.

The appellant was the owner of a Hindu undivided family. He was granted sanction to the draft scheme under section 22 of the Bombay Town Planning Act, 1954 (Bombay Act No. XLIII of 1954) for the purpose of development of land and payment of compensation for the land taken. The Town Planning Officer awarded compensation to the appellant at the rate of Rs. 2.40 p.m. On appeal by the appellant the Additional Commissioner held that the appeal was not maintainable as the Act did not provide an appeal against a decision of the Town Planning officer on matters dealt with by him in his order dated November 4, 1971. The appellant preferred an appeal to the Board of Revenue which dismissed the same holding that the Appeal was incompetent. The High Court also rejected the appellant 's revision petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) in view of section 32(1) of the Act the enactment of a rule determining compensation payable to an owner for loss of land had to be determined on the basis of market value of the land at the date on which declaration of intention to make a scheme was made; and (ii) in the absence of any specific provision in section 32 (1) or section 73 of the , the effect of the final scheme coming into force has been outlined by Shah J. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Act contains the necessary provisions for estimating compensation payable in respect of any property acquired under that Act. It is made clear in clause (xiii) of section 23 (1), which requires the court to take into consideration in determining the amount of compensation to be awarded for land acquired under the Act, the damage sustained by the "person interested" must be read as a matter of language and having regard to the scheme of the . Act. [94C D] 2. The object of the Land Acquisition Act is to consolidate and amend the law for the making and execution of a town planning scheme. It contains provisions regarding the principles on which compensation payable under section 64 (1)(f) of that Act is determined. On the making of a Town Planning Scheme, the value of land at such declaration is to be fixed; but the amount by which the owner is deprived of his land whether in whole or in part, has amenities, including the cost of working and works thereon of such person shall be deducted from or added to as the case may be, the contributions leviable from such person. [95F G] 3. The purpose of section 22(1)(iii) is that the size and shape of every reconstituted plot shall be determined; and the amount payable to the owner in respect thereof, the net amount of loss shall be payable to him by "the local authority in cash or in such other way as may be agreed upon by the parties". The principle for determining compensation is the same whether an owner of land is given a reconstituted plot or not. [96G H] 4. Section 73 provides that the owner 's right which is injuriously affected by the making, of a city planning scheme shall be entitled to obtain compensation from the local authority or from any person benefited or partly from the Local Authority and partly from such persons as the Town planning Officer may in each case determine. It would be the value by which an owner is given the reconstituted plot to persons in ownership in common, the shares of such persons; and section 73 provides for a case where the amount determined under the scheme has not been specifically indicated therein. [97H] 5. The principle laid down in State of Gujarat vs Shantilal Mangaldas & Ors., ; , applied. In the instant case the High Court was right in holding that enactment of the Punjab Land Improvement Act, 1953 was applicable to the State of Bombay.

The appellant was the brother of his wife. He had a brother, who died in 1934 leaving behind him three sons and two daughters. The widow sold her share to the appellant on the ground that she was entitled to the property taking into account the lands of her father. The appellant did not accept this right of selection as he chose to select the nearest heir to make the selection. The question for decision was whether the legatees had a right to choose in such circumstances. Held, that the testator intended his brother to select and give him certain land as he would take it out of the vattam lands and not for the daughters to make selection. It is only when the uncertainty is so great that there is no way of resolving it and finding out the intention of the testator that section 89 comes into play. The words "he shall give to the female children " in section 89 are not intended to cover the selection of the legatee but they must be construed as an artificial rule of construction. Held further, that where a testator save one of similar properties from his own self and uses them for purposes of his own use it is not possible to say on the construction of a will that the legatee himself indicated the selection or appointed a third person to make it. The test of benevolent construction in cases where the testator has not made or intended to make a selection himself or has not nominated a third persons to make an selection, is whether he should make the selec tion himself or give him a share in the property bequeathed to them. Held also, that if the intention was to make such a gift it would be necessary to have it certain. The rule of benevolent construc tion laid down by English Courts in England that in such cases the testator 's heir cannot make the Selection and appoint a third party to select for himself the shares of the deceased.

The appellant was the widow of one B, whose husband 's brother 's widow had inherited the property in dispute from his brother 'S '. The respondents filed a suit for joint possession over the share of the appellant and her husband 'S" on the ground that they were in separate occupation of the land or plots in dispute and the appellant had absolutely no concern with them. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the respondents were in joint possession of the lands and off and on the basis of the settlement, separate plots were carved out and she was never informed about any proceedings by the defendants and was under the Impression that her share would be properly looked after. The District Judge decreed the appellant 's suit for a joint possession. On appeal, the District judge held that some sort of fraud must have been committed by the respondents and that the appellant lost her title by operation of law. In second appeal, however, the High Court set aside the decision of the District Judge on the grounds that there was nothing to show that any fraud was practised upon the consolidation authorities so as to make the order a nullity. The High Court also held that the finding of the High court regarding fraud having been committed in the consolidation proceedings was not legally sound. In this appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellant that after the chakbandi was completed under the U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, the suit was barred by section 49 of the said Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.

The petitioner, a Deputy Prime Minister of India, was elected as Deputy Prime Minis ters in the State of Haryana. The first respondent filed an affidavit stating that he was the Chief Minister of Haryana when the oath of office of his new assignment was administered to him and that the Chief Ministers were not the oath in accordance with the prescrip tion of the Constitution. In the affidavit it was stated that the petitioner was still functioning as the Chief Minis ter, and that describing Shri Devi Lal as Deputy Chief Minister was descriptive only and for all purposes he was a Minister. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. Dismissing the appeal by special leave, HELD: 1.1 The oath register is by the incumbent signed as Prime Minister and all other ministers sign as Ministers. He further indi cates that describing him as Deputy Minister does not confer on him any powers of the Prime Minister along with his other submis sions. [2] 1.2 In view of the clear statement made by the learned Attorney General that respondent No. 1 is just a Minister like other members of the Council of Ministers though he has been described as Deputy Ministers, the petitioner cannot press it. [3] 1:4 The practice which has been followed by this Court in the case of Virji Ram Sutaria vs Nathalal Premji Bhavadia & Ors., , is referred to. In view thereof, no further constitutional sanction for the post of Deputy Prime Ministers along with the petitioner is upheld.

The appellant, a company which was carrying on the business of "strike" in its factory, had expressed its willingness to comply with the request of the workers to declare the forenoon of 1st November, 1948 as a holiday for solar eclipse. On the 3rd November, the management put up a notice that the stoppage of work on 1st Nov., 1948 was illegal and that the management had decided that the workers who had participated in such strike would not be entitled to holidays with pay as provided by the Act. The workmen were refused permission to declare their forenoon. On appeal the Labour Appellate Tribunal held that the continuity of service of the workmen was broken by the interruption caused by the illegal strike and that as a consequence the workers would be deprived of only half their holidays with wages under section 49 B(1) of the Factories Act. Held, that the action of the management in awarding punishment to the workmen for not complying with the provisions of Ch. IV A of the Industrial Disputes Act was not justified on the ground that the strike was not a lock out and was not illegal. The fact that the closure of the factory did not amount to a strike does not affect the legality of the action taken by the management on the night of 1th November, 1949, but only amounts to an illegal strike. The provisions of section 49 A(2) of Factories Act do not apply to the case of the Carnatic Mills in view of the notification dated 23rd August, 1946, issued under Ch. V A of 1947, which was in accordance with the provi sions of Ch IV A, of the Act, and the decision of the Labour Court on this point depends on the construction of the rules and this in volves a substantial question of law.

The appellant, actor, was convicted under section 292 I.P.C., for having been duly certified for public show by the Board of Censors. The High Court dismissed his petition challenging the order of conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended that once a certificate sanctioning public exhibition of a film has been granted by the competent authority under the Act, there is a justification for its display thereafter and by virtue of the antidotal provisions in section 79 I. P.C. the public exhibition, circulation or distribution or the production of the film, even if it be obscene, lascivious or tending to deprave or corrupt public morals are liberally certifi cates, the legislation meant by Parliament to protect people 's good morals and make powerful mental impact so much so the treatment of this form of art on a different footing with pre censorship may well be regarded as a valid classification, as was held in K. A. Abbas vs The State of Maharashtra, ; , referred to. In the instant case, the prosecution is unsustainable because section 79 is exculpatory when read with section 5A of the Act and the certificate issued thereunder. Therefore, the trial court when it convicted the appellant under section 293 I.p.C.; did not consider the film as a obscene or not, or at any rate, does it generate a belief induced by a mistake of fact that the certificate is offensive. The Board of Civil Proce dure was therefore justified in displaying public exhibition.

The petitioner, a Government Pleader for the Patna District, was appointed as an advocate by the State of Bihar. He filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the power of the Government to appoint any other lawyer except under him and never by excluding him. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the Government Pleader was only an agent of the government pleader and his duties were only to the Government who were his clients, and that he owes no duty to the public at all and that for that reason he would not be the holder of a lawyer 's office. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that (i) the Government pleader is only an advocate for the litigant; (ii) his duties are only to his client who has a crowd of cases to be conducted, and (iii) the Advocate General is not bound to encourage monopoly within the profession. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The Government Pleader is only a lawyer for a litigant. He holds a public office. It is heartening to notice that the Bihar Government Pleader has been appointed according to administrative rules of the State. Each one is a Government pleader and may depute other lawyers and exercise control over such surrogates. In this view, ordering about a Government Counsel is not in the interests of justice. [766D E] 2. The practice of legal remuneration has no distributive bias nor socially sober ceiling. Some States have already adopted such a policy. Indeed, the State must evolve a policy in regard to its Law Officers which admits of lawyers convenience becomes a bane when it is used only for augmentation of counsel 's income, resisting democratisation and distributive justice within the professional profession. These principles make poor appeal to those who count, which is a pity. [764E F] 3. The State, appreciating this need and with a view to help the court liquidate the docket explosion, appointed more than one government pleader for every District, depending on the case flow. Thus, the Government Pleaders and Assistant Government Pleader are expected to assist the Court in arriving at a second economic look. [765G H] 4. The very purpose of a Government lawyer is to act on the advice of the District Judge regarding the choice of Government pleaders. When there were several thousand cases in which Government finds itself entangled flows from land acquisition, the Court should engage competent lawyers without hunting for political partisans regardless of capability. Public offices and Government Pleadership are one shall not succumb to Tammany Hall or subtler spoils system if purity in public office is a desideratum. [763C D] 5. The judicial journey vindicates the short High Court order dismissing the petition which is main merit. [761G H; 770A] 6. The time has come to examine the quality of the product or service, control the price, floor to ceiling, enforce commitment to the people who are the third world clients and practice internal distributive Justice within the professions from the liabilities of other occupations. [762C D].

The appellants held out of a total issue of 800 shares of the Bank of India Ltd. The Mills purchased 5,000 shares of their Bank of Indian Company at the rate of Rs. 100 per share for every three shares held by them in the proportion of one new share for each share held by the shareholders. The shares were issued at a premium of Rs 50 and the appellants agreed to the allotment of these shares and ultimately transferred them to a private company Jesing with the direction that the right to apply for the shares of that company should be distributed amongst its nominees. On receiving the circular letter, the Directors of the Mills passed an order on May 25, 1948, increasing the share capital of the Company to Rs. 50 per share and also increasing the amount of the right of the appellants to the remaining 1,600 shares of a company of India. The appellants agreed that the shares should be allotted to their nominees. The Board of Directors passed a resolution on May 5, 1948 reducing the share holding of the company from Rs. 500 to Rs 100 per shares and it was resolved that the said company should pay 1,000 preference to the existing shareholders in the ratio of one old share for all the shares held. The said resolution was confirmed by the Board of directors on May 26, 1948 and the Directors were informed that this company was entitled to get 1,6662 more ordinary shares on payment of Rs 100 as capital and Rs 50 as premium per each share. The company challenged the action of the Income tax Officer in re assessment for the years 1946 47 and 1949 49 by filing a writ petition under article 226 of the Constitution. The High Court held that the distribution of the rights to apply was not a distribution of dividend within the meaning of section 2(6A) of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922, but was still dividend within its ordinary meaning and that the definition of "dividend" in section 2 (6A), as inclusive of various items and exclusive of certain other categories of receipts which may not otherwise be included therein, did not constitute distribution of dividends. The appeal to this Court was filed on a certificate granted by the High Court. Held:(i) The High Courts were right in holding that the distributed of the share holders amounted to distribution of "Dividend". (ii) The resolution passed by the Legislature by section 2 of the Act sought to define the expression "different shares" in its ordinary sense is a distributive share of the profits or income of a Company given to its shareholders. When the Legislature, by section2(6 A), sought to defined the word "daccend", it added to the normal meaning of the expression several other categories and not an exhaustive definition. The resolution was therefore not called upon to advise on the question whether the receipts by the appellants amounted to a distribution or dividend within that meaning. (iii) The view taken by the Bombay High Court in nominating its shareholders to exercise the option to purchase the new issue of the bank of India, amounted to "dispute" within the extended meaning of that expression in section2 (6 A).

The appellant was defeated. The election petitioner filed an election petition challenging the election of the first respondent, a defeated candidate, on the ground that the returned candidate had not been given notice of his or any of them and that he would keep the witnesses present in Court a list of witnesses submitted by him under Rule 1A of Order XVI of the Code of Civil Procedure 1908. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that except Bahre son of Sher Singh, no other witness could be examined and that as soon as the evidence of the election petitioner was recorded, the Court would proceed to record the evidence on behalf of the returned candidates; and thereafter the matter will be set down for hearing oral arguments of the parties. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf the appellant that (1) the High Court had no jurisdiction to decline to examine the witness produced by the returned party, (2) the provisions of Order XV of the Civil Procedure Code were not attracted in the present case; and (3) the Court must ascertain how far sub rule (3), would carve out an exception to the enabling provision contained in Rule 1 A. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1(a) The scheme of Rules 1, XVI and Rule 22 of the High Courts Rules is that after the court framed issues which give notice to the parties what facts they have to prove for succeeding in the matter which notice would enable the parties to determine what evidence oral and documentary it would like to lead, the party should file a list Of witnesses with the gist of evidence of each witness whose name is entered in the list has to be carried out in respect of those witnesses for procuring their presence. [532B C] (b) The consequence is that where the witness summoned either to give evidence or to produce documents fails to attend or to have been authorised to do so, such witness may not be permitted to be examined, Rule 1B would have given a clear legislative exposition in that behalf and the marginal note of Rule 1. [525C D] (c) The result of the legal consequence ensuing from the issuance of a summons by the Court and failure to comply with the same, the scheme of rules 1, XVIII and 22 of Order XVII of the C.P.C.

The appellant, a non government aided school, was appointed as Principal on one year probation in the scale of 550 1200 at initial pay of Rs. 2000 1200. The appointment order stated that he was permitted to take charge of the post of Principal on the basis of the prohibition imposed by the Uttar Pradesh Secondary Education Act, 1921. The appellant was required to present himself before the Manager of the College and take over charge within 10 days of receipt of the order of appointment failing which the appointment would be void. On receipt of this letter, the manager of the college sent a copy of it to the Principal of the institution who advised him that the appellant 's appointment may be terminated. The Manager thereupon issued an order dated April 27, 1981 directing the appellant to hand over charge to him. The order was challenged by the appellant in a writ petition before the High Court which dismissed the same. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1. The power and authority enjoyed by private managements of educational institutions was left untouched. But there was no power of appointment, including the appointment of a Head of an institution and of teachers. Sub section (10) of section 9 of the Act is not attracted in this case and the appellant was appointed in contravention of any provision of the said Act. Therefore sub sec. (10), is not applicable to the present case. [975G H; 976A] 1.2. The provisions of the Uttar Bihar Secondary Education Service Commission Act, 1922 are not attracted. The Director of Education, U.P., is a highly qualified person. There was nothing hanky panky in his appointment. If the power to make appointment was riot suspended it would have no difficulty in upholding the appointment. [977B C] 1:3. The State Government promulgated the U. P. Secondary Education Services Commission and Selection Board ordinance, 1981 (8 of 1981) which was replaced by the act bearing the identical name.

The respondent, a textile mill, was assessed to sales tax on the ground that it had wrongly escaped assessment. The Sales Tax Officer rejected the claim of the respondent and levied sales tax. On appeal by the respondent, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the goods were exempt from taxation. The High Court in reference, however, did not go into the merits of the case. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The taxing authorities have the jurisdiction to decide the question whether the "tyre cord fabric" is more correctly capable of being described as a fabric or as merely cord pretending to pass off as ar textile fabric This is really a technical question. [503 D] (2) It requires careful consideration of the technical processes of manufacturing, of the composition of the "semiwine" and an evaluation of opinion of experts on the subject, to be able to decide whether the product under consideration rightly or wrongly has been described as "fabric". The mere fact that the tyre cord fabric may be so well established a category of rayon "f Fabric" does not appear to give the exact meaning of the term "textile", as used in the relevant entries entitled to exemption. [500 E F] (3) For some reason, entry No. 22 does not enumerate rayons and silk fabrics in the same fashion as the cotton fabrics are specified by name in item 19. In answer to this argument, the respondent contended that the High Court should have interfered with the decision of the Commercial Tax Officer.

The appellant company was engaged in construction of coal. The management moved the High Court by way of a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution to quash the order dated August 8, 1988 passed by the Labour Court, Dhanbad for not giving an opportunity to the appellant to represent its case before transferring it from the labour court, Patna to Labour Court Patna. The High Court did not agree with the contention of the management that no reasons were stated for passing the order. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Courts of Calcutta, Andhra Pradesh and allahavi sion Tribunal, Calcutta, have taken a contrary view. [302G] 1.2 In work men of Punjab, there is a turning point in development of doctrine of natural justice as applicable to administrative bodies. Both the authorities laid down that for application of rules of natural justi fication, the classification of functions as 'judi cial ' or 'administrative ' is not necessary. The authority is under legal obligation to record reasons in making the order of transfer after affording a reasonable opportunity of being heard to the assessee in the matter. [303H; 304A] 1:3. In work man of Punjab Chheharta vs State of Punjab & Ors., ; this Court held that the power to transfer pending case under section 33 B is not a mere administrative but quasi judicial power and the appropriate Government cannot transfer a case on the basis of allegations of one party without giving reasonable opportunity to other party to represent his point of view. This was also the view recognised by the Madras High Court in Management of Sri Rani Lakshmi Ginning & Weaving Mills Ltd. vs State Of Madras, [1985] (Suppl.) 2 SCR 13. 1.4 In the instant case, the State has withdrawn and transferred the case from the Labour court to another Labour Court at Patna on the representation of the workman without getting it veri fied from the management. The State in fairness ought to have got it verified by giving an opportuni ty to the management which is a party to the pending reference. Denial of that opportunity is a fatal flaw to the decision of the Government. [304B C] 1/3. The principle of natural Justice being presumptive, it should be followed by the authorities unless it is excluded by express words of statute or by necessary implication. [305E F] 2.1 In workman of Punjab Chaibasa vs State, ; this court held that there was a re quirement that justice must not only be done but be seen to be done" is the essence of fairness equally applicable to judicial power. It has no set form or procedure. It depends upon the facts of each case. As Lord Pearson said in Ridge vs Baldwin, ; , it would be difficult to appreciate how a party can possibly have any question decided by a partic ular court. [306G H] 2:2. The principles of natural natu rity are fundamental in the consti tutional set up of this country. No man or body 's right should be affected without an opportunity of hearing to ventilate his views. The justice is a psycho logical yearning, in which men seek acceptance of their view point by having an opportunity before the forum or authority enjoined or obliged to take a decision affecting their rights. It may be noted that the terms 'fairness of procedure ', 'fair play in action ', `duty to act fairly ' are perhaps used as alternatives to "natural justice" without drawing any distinction. But Prof. Paul Jackson vs Varty, ; ; Pearlberg vs Varties, , referred to.

The appellant was the manager of a hotel. The respondents were the Chief Commissioner, Delhi, the Additional Industrial Tribunal and the Hotel Workers ' Union, whose names had been mentioned as its workmen. The appellant challenged the order of reference on the ground that the reference was incompetent and two grounds had been urged in support of it namely (1) that the union could not be made a party to the reference under the , and (2) that even if the union was entitled to be represented by an officer of a trade union of which he is a member, the reference in this case did not mention any officer of the trade union but mentioned only the union itself. Held, that the dispute raised by the appellant was one relating to the terms of employment or conditions of labour of a body of workmen and its employees were not concerned with the dispute as it was between the management of the hotel and its workmen and therefore the reference did not fall within the purview of the , but only mentioned the union alone. The large number of references under the Act which were made in this form, did not indicate how many of the workers of thirty different categories working in the hotel were involved in the dispute. The nature of the dispute was also specified in the terms Of reference. State of Madras vs C. P. Sarathy (A.I.R. referred to. Held further, that there is no force in the contention that the references were bad simply because they did not specify how many workmen of thirty one categories working therein mentioned as their workmen.

The appellant imported a part of the engines mentioned in Heading No. 8406, and claimed benefit of Notification No. 281 Cus/76 dated 2 8 1976, which exempted parts of the engine from payment of customs duty in respect of articles specified in column (2) of the Table annexed to the Notification. The Assistant Collector and the Collector of Customs rejected the claim on the ground that the appellant was entitled to the benefit of exemption under the Notification No, 281 Cft/76. The Customs, Excise and Gold (Control) Appellate Tribunal dismissed the appeal of the appellant. In the appeal before this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the bushings and bearings are the same and identical articles as held by the Appellate Tribunal and, therefore, the question of any exemption under Notification No., 281 C. Ex. or Notification No . 224 dated 2 7 1976 could not arise. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Notification grants exemption in part from payment to internal combustion piston engines, but only to "parts thereof" and not a few parts thereof. [225B] 1.2 In the instant case, the Notification exempts also parts of engines mentioned under Heading No 8406.06. [226C D] 1:3. The Notification does not mention 'parts ' of such engines. Non mention of 'part ' in Heading 84.06 has given rise to a controversy between the parties. It may be that two articles have the same functions but nonetheless they are distinct and separate. As the functions of bushing in imported in a knocked down condition, are the identical, even though they perform the same function. [227D E] 1 :4. The intention of the Notification is clear enough to provide that the parts of these engines, mentioned under heading No.84.06, will get the exemption under notification and in the absence of any provision to the contrary, it is necessary that the Customs authorities should embark upon the question and decide whether the bushes, imported by the appellant, are really parts of such engine. [228E F] 1 5. The Notifications are not only intended to grant exemption to internal fire pistons but also to 'part parts thereof". [229F] 6. The words "part" in Heading Nos.

The right of management was divided between the two sons each taking six months ' time from 1st July, 1970 and 10th November each and to 6th December each year. The plaintiffs claimed that they were entitled to be in management of the Dargah for 27 days in all in the month of February, March, June and October and that the said 27 days shall be Febru ary 1 to 6 and October 1st to 6 respectively. The defendants contested the suit on the ground that the plaintiffs had been entitled to manage the Dargah as they were female members. According to the defendants, the plaintiffs claimed through their mother that after the death of their mother the right and management of their Dargah was recognised for 9 days in a year during the months of Februar, March and October November each year and that even if they were enti tled to any right or claim in the offerings in the Dargah, they would be barred by limitation. The Trial Court decreed the suit and in appeal the High Court held that the Courts below proceeded upon an erroneous assumption as if it was duty of the defendants to prove by what hostile assertions of title and possession ouster has been established. In this view of the matter the High court set aside the judgments and decrees of the courts below. The High Court took the view that the courts had proceeded on an erroneous basis as if the plaintiffs right of Fathima Bee had become barred by their not exercising the rights, the Plaintiffs themselves could have no independent right to claim. It was further held that after decree in Civil Suit No. 116 of 1909, it was only male heirs who were exercising their rights. The appellants and their counsel contended before this Court that they had lost their right by ouster and that they would not be entitled to any share in the management or share in their offerings. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1.

The respondent was a gangman in the employ of the Central Railway. He was charged with house rent allowance for 10 months and dearness allowance. The Railway Board under the Ministry of Railways, issued a scheme of grant of compensatory (city) allowance to all employees of the railway who were paid dearness allowance by an employer to his employee for services rendered according to the terms of the contract between them. The respondent claimed that he was entitled to the house rent allowances as part of his wages. The claim was rejected on the ground that the house rate allowance was not admissible to him under the rules framed under the Act. The Authority, however, allowed the claim on the basis of the scheme for payment of house rent and also the benefit of the rules. On appeal by special leave, Held, that the rule making power conferred on the Central Government by section 15(2) of the , is not ultra vires article 14 of the Constitution. Section 7 of the Act prohibits an employee from entering into such a contract as has the effect of depriving him of his vested rights in certain costlier cities for excessive rents paid by them over and above what they might normally be expected to pay; nor is such an allowance "intended to be a source of profit" or to be "an allowance in lieu of free quarters", as specifically stated in the preamble to the letter No. E47 CPC/14 dated 1st December, 1947 issued by the Railway Board. The house rent Allowance which may in certain circumstances as aforesaid be included in "wages" is not the same thing as the value of any house accommodation referred to in sections 7 and 11 of the . The definition of "wages " contained in section 2(vi) of that Act includes all remuneration capable of being expressed in terms of money, which would, if the terms are otherwise, be payable, whether he actually occupies or does not occupy the quarters offered to him.

The detenu was detained under the provisions of the . The grounds of detention were also served on him. He filed a petition before the High Court for the issue of a writ of habeas corpus. The High Court dismissed his petition holding that the order of detention purported to have been signed by the detaining authority on February 18, 1980 and that it was not necessary to furnish copies of the relevant documents. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) There is no force in the contention that the grounds of deten tion were as elaborate as possible, that the substance of the statements of the four persons, as they had been incorporated in those 'grounds ' which were served on them, and that the detenu had asked for copies of all the documents. The detaining authority, without applying its mind to the nature of the documents, the copies of which were asked for by the detenus mechanically refused as desired by the Collector, to supply the copies. [350 D E] (2) There was no evidence of smuggling in this case at all and the detaining authori ty had not made any such statement in his counter statement. The detenu had requested for copies on February, 18,1980, but it was only on March 27, 1980 that he made a representation to the detaining au thority which was rejected by an order dated April 23, 1980. [351 E F] (3) There were no evidence on record to show that the detaining Authority, in fact, had passed any order of detentiOn. The detention was therefore vitiated. [352 G] Khudiram Das vs The State of West Bengal & Ors., ; , followed.

The appellant State filed a joint appeal against acquittal of several accused persons, and the High Court held that the joint appeal was not maintainable. The appellant contended that r. 6 in Chapter XXVI of the Bombay High Court Appellate Side Rules (which are applicable to proceedings in Gujarat High Court) was inconsistent with Chapter XXXI of the Code of Criminal Procedure with the result that a joint appeals by the State against several accused were not maintainable and that the High court had no jurisdiction to entertain the appeal. Held, that the power to frame this rule is specifically conferred on the High Courts by section 554(2)(c) Cr. P.C., and r.6 does not seem to be inconsistent with any provisions of the said Code. The power to framing this rule was specifically conferred upon the High courts by section 209(2) (c) Criminal Procedure Code and r, 6 did not seem therefore to be consistent with any provision of the code. The powers to frame the rule are specifically conferred under section 554 Cr. It is well settled that a Joint appeal by the state against several persons acquitted at a joint trial has also to be held not to be contrary to any provision Of the Code and therefore not legally prohibited. The word "person aggrieved" in section 419 of the Criminal Procedure means an appeal in a case of acquittal by the court in respect of the joint trial. The plain reading of this sections makes it clear that the appellate Court hearing an appeal cannot admit it only on a question of sentence and that such a restricted order of admission being invalid, the appellant would be entitled to insist that his appeal should be heard on the merits.

The appellant, a firm carrying on business in India and in the former Federated Malaya States, was assessed under the Indian Income tax Act, 1918, to income tax for the year 1939 40. The income of the assessee from these years was not liable to be taxed by reason of section 25(3) of the 1922 Act. The question for determination was whether the income of a foreign firm which consisted of Meyyappa Chettiar and his two brothers carried on business as partners in a partnership firm, was assessable under the 1918 Act. Held, that the assessee was entitled to relief under section 25 (3) Of the 1922 Income tax, 1922 Act with regard to the rental income from house properties owned by the foreign firm. The High Court was in error in holding that the foreign business of the appellant was not charged under the provisions of the 1918 and the income for the said period was accordingly liable to tax. Commissioner of Income tax Madras vs section V.R.M. Palaniappa Chettiar and Others, , followed. Commissioner Of Income tax vs sectionV.RM Palanippa Chettiar, , distinguished. Commissioner, of Income Tax, Madras vs Section V. R. M. Palananiappa Chetty and Co., , referred to. Commissioner o/s. Indian Income Tax vs section P.M., Palaniappan and Others (A.I.R . referred to). Commissioner of income tax, Madras City vs Chugandas & Co.

The respondent assessee entered into a contract with the Public Works Department of the Government of Gujarat for manufacture and supply of kiln burnt bricks to the said department for construction of a capital project. The assessee made an application under section 52 of the Bombay Sales Tax Act, 1959, on November 19, 1967 to the Deputy Commissioner of Sales Tax, stating that the supplies of bricks by the assessee were not for works contract. The Deputy Commissioner held that the supply of bricks was not sales and that the materials supplied were not of the best quality and were not in strict accordance with the specification and price conditions agreed upon between the parties. The respondent preferred an appeal before the Tribunal against this order. The Tribunal following its ratio laid down in Chandra Bhan Gosain vs State of orissa, , held that supplies of brickbats, bricks, tiles and other mate rials were not sales within the meaning of section 2(a) of the Act and accordingly rejected the assessee 's appeal holding that the transaction envisaged by the contract entered into by the applicant with the public Works Department was a works contract and not a works contracts. The High Court held that there was no question of a contract of sale of goods and sale of work and labour. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the contract in this case was a contract for sale and not as works contract, and that it was a "works contract" and not "works contracts". Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The contract in the instant case is a contract which is a " works contract" whose main object is the transfer of the property in and the delivery of possession of a chattel as a chatte to the buyer. [165G] Chandra Bhan Pandya vs State Of orissa & Ors., ; , referred to. 2. The question whether in making the contract to brick produced was transferred as a "Supply of materials" for consideration and whether it was " works contracts" depends upon the intention of the parties executing the contract. [166H; 167A] Chandra Mohan Gosain V.

The petitioner, a member of the Lok Sabha and Chairman of the Rajya Sabha, filed a petition under Article 32 of the Constitution challenging the validity of the Emergency Ordinance passed by Parliament on July 21, 1971. The President of India issued a proclamation under Article 352 of the Consti tution declaring that a grave emergency existed whereby the security of India was threatened by external aggression. The petitioner challenged the validity and legality of the said proclamation on the ground that it violated the fundamental right guaranteed to him under Articles 14 and 19(1)(a) of the Constitu tion. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the proclamation did not amount to a Proclamation as contemplated by Article 352(2) of Constitution. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the President 's Emergency was required to be communicated to each and every member of Parliament before the expiration of the period of two months from the date of issue of the proclamation, and that the Proclamation did not contain any provision for the resolution passed by both Houses of Parliament approving the proclamation. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The proclamation of emergency was not a valid law in force on August 3, 1971, and therefore it was not saved by Article 372(2). [455C] 2. The expression 'public order ' occurring in Article 352 (2) has been defined to mean any act or omission which is required to take place under the authority of law for the time being in force in a Province or in the State. It would be an offence if such act or proceeding was expressed to have been performed on a particular day then such mode of publica tion as may be specified by the Chairman of that Council is one such mode. [456E] 3.

The appellant filed a suit for declaration that the property in dispute was private property and for an order setting aside the decision of the authorities. The Trial Court held that the premises were private property but set aside the order of the High Court holding that the properties were not private property. On appeal by special leave, Held: (i) The appellant 's case was that the subject matter of dispute in the suit was the private property of the family capable of alienation and the allegation of the plaintiff that it was a private or public temple could have no market value. The question whether the property was a public temple or a public trust was essentially one of claim for an ordinary title to the said family property. The appellant had claimed that the suit property belonged to the Thoguluva family and he was in management thereof for and on behalf of the members of the joint family. The suit was filed by him in the form of an application under section 84(2) of Madras Act 19 of 1951. Under that Act only a fixed court fee was payable. That being so, the appellant did not have to pay court fees as it would in the case of an ordinary suit on a valuation made by him therefor. (ii) The High Court was wrong in proceeding on the assumption that whether the properties belonged to Thoguva family or were private properties of the said families. The subject matter in the present case had to be ascertained with reference to the claim made by the plaintiff in his plaint and since according to the respondents the property is a private property, it was incapable of valuation. (iii) The question as to whether the suit properties belonged exclusively to Thotamyan and his undivided sons does not arise for decision.

The appellant, a non gazetted employee of the respondent company, was appointed as a clerk in an existing staff. On his retirement he was paid a consolidated salary of Rs. 250 without any dearness allowance. The respondent claimed that he should be given cash allowance in lieu of the tiffin arrangements at present made by the appellant and they urged that the practice started by the appel lant of re employing retired persons should be discontinued. The Tribunal held that the appellant was under an obligation to provide some cash allowance for tiffs, and that the system adopted by the company was not based solely on humanitarian considerations. On appeal by special leave, Held, that the decision of the Tribunal is erroneous in law. When it appeared to the appellant that some employees who had retired found it difficult to maintain themselves and their families, the appellant bonafide and generously considered their request for re employment and that is why the Tribunal thought it unnecessary to make any such direction. The fact that the respondent gave assurances to its employees that the re employed would not be resorted to on a liberal scale, could have no bearing in dealing with the point. It was not obligatory on the part of the appellant to make a provision for the tiffering any further facility to the employees by way of giving them a cash allowance. Nor was it obligatory on its part to make such a provision in that behalf. The result is, therefore, that there was no justification for the respondent 's grievance that the impugned decision was erroneous in Law.

The respondent was a subscriber to the State Bank of India 's Provident Fund. He elected to be governed by the Provident Fund Sterling Accounts Rules, whereunder payment of the provident fund credited in his account in rupees was on retirement to be made in sterling. The respondent applied for transfer of the money from the Reserve Bank of lndia to the Reserve bank. The Union of India claimed immunity from attachment of the cheques on the ground that they represented provident fund money which by section 3 of the , was immune from attachment. The High Court confirmed the order of attachment. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The respondent 's money in the hands of the Reserve Officer as the agent of the Railway Administration was attached to the Bank and he had undertaken to discharge its obligation by arranging to have the amount converted into sterling and to remit it to Browne. Under section 60(1)(k) of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 read with section 3, the compulsory deposit in any recognised Provident Fund Account is exempt from attachment in execution of a decree of a civil court. Section 3 (1 ) of the does not authorise the Reserve Banks to receive payment of money on their behalf nor has it authorised the Reserve Officers to receive the amount on his behalf. So long as the money remained under the control of the railway Administration as provident fund moneys, it was exempt from attached to Brownee. [32 E G] (ii) The Union 's claim that they were entitled to immunity from attach ment is not accepted by the High Court. The Bank was in respect of the Provident fund money in its hands and the Reserve Fund was exempt under section 3(1) of , which provides that the performance of any promise may be made, inter alia, in any manner or at any time which the promise prescribes or sanction. Browne had not authorised the reserve bank to receive payments of the amount by the Bank on his own behalf. [33 G H] (iii) The High court was in error in holding that the money in hand of the respondent 'S was immune under section 60 (1) (k) from attachment and that the order passed by the executing court was not liable to be attached.

The appellant was employed as a pump operator in the respondent 's factory. He was later transferred to another station where he worked. The management terminated his services by a simple notice on the ground that he had lost confidence in him and the Labour Court held that the termination was illegal and immune from interference. In appeal, this Court held : (1) that the appellant had lost faith in the employee; (2) that there was no evidence to show that he was an employee of the respondent; and (3) that his dismissal was bad as it was not established by any evidence that he bad confidence in the appellant. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1)(a) The Labour Court had the power to go behind the form of the order, look at the substance and set aside what may masquerade as termination simpliciter, if in reality it cloaked a dismissal for misconduct as a colourable exercise of power by the management. [494C] (b) The charge against the appellant was that he joined as a distributor in 1963 and that the suspicion of dislocation arose for the first time in 1968. This circumstance completely demolishes even the whimsical and tenuous stand taken by the employer. It was manifest therefore that loss of confidence is often a subjective feeling or individual reaction to an objective set facts and motivations. The Court is concerned with the latter and not with the former, although circumstances may exist which justify a genuine exercise of the power of simple termination. [498C D] (c) The appellant was given two extra increments in addition to his normal increments as stated already. In appreciation of his hard work, he has lost confidence and loss of trust has gained ground. The law is simply this. The Tribunal has the power land, indeed, the duty to X ray the order and discover its true nature if the attendant circumstances and the ulterior purpose be to dismiss the employee because he is an evil to be eliminated. But if the management, to cover up the inability to establish by an enquiry, illegitimately but ingeniously passes an innocent looking order of termination simpliciter such action is bad and is liable to be set aside. Loss of confidence in law will be the duty of this Court to interfere and set matters fight. [500E F] (d) The management has misled itself on the law land. It is manifest therefore, that loss has resulted in an ineffectiveness but ingenious terminations. The court is concerned about the constitutional mandate of Part IV of the Constitution. [501F G] (e) The Tribunal had the powers to go back to the workman for misconducts or on other ground valid in law. The appellant had not dis closed the grounds oil which this suspicion arose in 1968, and no doubt after 1968, the appellant came to know that the respondent was divulging secrets relating to his business. [525G H] (f) The labour court has misled himself on the Law land. He is given two more exceptional circumstances, namely, (i) that he could wilfully withhold faithful action against the respondent and (ii) that it was bona fide. It must rest on some tangible basis and the power has to be exercised by the appellant objectively in good faith which means honestly with due care and prudence.

The petitioner, a retired Government servant, filed a writ petition in the High Court of Uttar Pradesh challenging the notices issued by the Deputy Director (Eye Camps) under section 338 of the Indian Penal Code. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the victims of this medical mishap and lack of institutional post operative care contributed to the infection or the aggravation of its effects, and that the guidelines prescribed by the Government did not prima facie seem to encourage such compla nation in regard to the imperatives of post operative health. The petitioner filed a Writ Petition in this Court challenging the findings of the High Courts on the ground that the doctors who conducted eye camps were allowed to go back immediately after the operations, and the guidelines for conducting the medical miseries had been violated by the State Government. The respondents contested the petition contending that the patients were allowed by the doctors to go away immediately after operations. Allowing the Writ Petition, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The guidelines prescribed in the Indian Medical Council (Dental) Code of Conduct for conduct of eye camping are not sufficiently comprehensive to ensure the protection of the patients who are generally drawn from the poorer and less affluent section of society or whether any further guide lines would require to be evolved. [254B] 1.2 The guidelines issued by Union Government on 9.2.1988, with the suggested modifications, can be held to be satisfactory. [255C D] 1:3. The guidelines for conduct and management of eye camps are set out in the judgment of this Court dated 9.4.1988. They are: (a) that the prisoners should be performed by qualified doctors who have suffered? (b) that they have suffered irre versable damage of the eyes which has rendered them wholly incapacitated; (c) that a monitary relief by the state Government is no reason why they should not be afforded some monitary Relief by the respondent State Government.[255D E] 1(4) The guidelines are sent to all States for implementation. [253E F] 1.(5) The policy of the Union Government in the wake of reports of mishaps in 'Eye camps ' is quite comprehensive and expeditious. It implies that the eyes of the people would be impaired if such an eventuality occurs by prior tests and inspection. But, owing to a general air of cynical irreverence towards values that has, unfortunate ly, developed and to the mood of compla tion, the very concept of standards and the imperities of their observance tend to be impaired. This is a disturbing feature. The remedy lies in a ruthless adherence to the virtue of method and laying down practical procedures in the minutes of detail and by exacting not merely expecting strict adherence to these proce dure but also the full effect, and by preciseing not only expected strict observance to these provisions, but also, the standards of cleanliness and hygiene in public hospitals casualty. [251E F; 252A B] 2(a) The new guidelines issued on 9th February, 1988 have been followed after a careful study of all aspects of the problem. [252B C] (b). The guidelines have to be strictly construed and applied at the time of administration of interim relief. [250G H] (c ) The guidelines in the instant case are not only for the unfortunate air of the cynological deterioration, but really on the professional commit ment with which the prescriptions are implemented that the ultimate result rests. Government, States and Union, incur enormous expenditure of public money on health care, But, the standard of cleanliness or hygiene in the public hospitals unfortunately, leave greatly to be desired. The maintenance of the highest stand ards of a septic and sterile conditions at places where Ophthalmic Surgery or any surgery is conducted cannot be over emphasised.

The petitioner No. 1, a registered society under the provisions of the Bidhannagar Municipal Act, 1984, was elected as its Mantriphants in the year 1982 and elected to the State Legislative Assembly. The petitioner No 2, who was one of the members of the Samiti, challenged the election by filing a writ petition before the High Court on various grounds including that the management and control of the said Samiti had been taken over by the State Government under Section 16(Gha) of the Act and the Chief Minister of Assam was the ex officio President of the Committee appointed by the Government and all the members present in the meeting except one supported by the petitioner No 1. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the impugned Act had been passed after the passing of the impugned order and as such the Chief Minis ter, which was a public body constituted under Section 3 of the Assam Rashtrabhasha Prachar Samiti (taking over of Management and Control) Act,1984, was not competent to take over the management of the affairs of the Parishad. Hence this appeal by special leave.

The appellants were the reversioners of a Hindu widow. The respondents filed a suit for partition and separate possession of the properties in dispute on the ground that the family properties were not her stridhana property, that the gift was made by the father to her daughter in law, that there was no compelling reason for the High Court to differ from the appreciation of oral evidence by the courts below, that they had failed to prove that the appellants had made a verbal gift of the four houses in question at Asansol, and that such a gift was not supported by reliable evidence. The trial court held that the respondents were entitled to the properties as stridhanis and that the High 'Court erred in holding that the widow was competent to make a gift of her share in the properties. On appeal, the High court reversed this finding and held that there were no compelling reasons for the gift. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (1) the gift made by one of the sons of the husband was not bona fide; (2) the adoption of the widow in favour of her daughter was valid, (3) the High Courts had erred in law in holding the gift to be invalid and (4) the property was properly divided between the parties. HELD: (1)(a) The gift made in favour by the widow of a reasonable portion of the property for the benefit of the daughter and the son in law was valid and binding on the reversioners. [476 D] (b) The evidence showed that there had been an ex parte partition between the two families, and the gift deed was not a genuine one. It was open to a widow to make an alienation for religious acts which were not essential or obligatory but were still pious observances which conduce to the bliss of the deceased husband 's soul. [477 F] (c) The High Court erred in its view that there could be no valid gift as the property had been properly divided and that it was open for the widow to fulfil that promise. [478 G H] (d) The question whether a particular gift is reasonable or not will have to be decided on the facts of each case. It is well settled that in the case of essential or statutory promise, if the income of the donor has been paid in marriage to a suitable husband, it is a duty which must be fulfilled to prevent alienation and direct spiritual benefit is conferred upon the father by such a marriage. [479 G] (e) The fact that one of his sons had become indebted cannot take away the power of the father under section 14(1)(c). [479 B] (f) The object of section 123 is to get the property properties in the hands of the son itself, and it is not essential to make any gift at the time of marriage but only some time later. It would be a duty to spiritual benefit conferred upon a Hindu female by a widow of landed property to give a girl in marriage. The fact of the gift being made on the occasion of the marriage, the provision for maintenance under section 123(1) is mandatory and it must be complied with before the gift can be made.

The appellant was elected to the Punjab Legislative Assembly. The polling took place on May 31, 1980 and the counting was done on June 1, 1980. The margin between the votes secured by Tej Singh and Avtar Singh (appellant) was only 123 votes, but at the instance of Tej Singh, a few persons were also declared elected. The appellant challenged the election of Tej Kaur alleging corrupt practices in the statement of facts. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the allegations of corrupt practices indulged in by Tej Kaur had been clearly proved and that the posters said to have been printed and circulated were Annexures P 1 and P 2 which appear at page 42 of the second paper book and it may be necessary to extract certain portions thereof "Keeping in view the present conditions in the country it is imperative to defeat the dictatorial Congress in these elections. Therefore, I fervently appeal to all the voters of Baghapurana Constituency to vote and elect Shri Tej Singh the joint front candidate of the Akali Dal, because Shri Tej singh was the only candidate who can defeat the Congress. " Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The corrupt practice alleged by Tejinder Singh had been established by him as a strong presumption and possibility that the votes polled in favour of Rup Lal would have gone to Avtar Singh cannot be ruled out and that would have doubtless materially altered the result of the election. [419G H] 2. The result is that the irresistible inference and inescapable conclusion that can be arrived at is that Tej Singh had actually paid for the posters which were printed at his instance and Rup Lal was not collected with the printing of the posters. Tej Singh falsely represented to the voters that the poster was circulated by Ruplal. [416A B] 3. In view of the very narrow margin of votes (123) between Tej Singh & Avtar Singh, the appellant has proved beyond reasonable doubt that Tej Kaur was responsible for committing corrupt practices particularly when the printing is clearly admitted by him, as indicated above. It is also clear to us that in view of this very narrow trend of votes, the irresistible conclusion that could be arrived is that Shri Tej Kaur actually paid Rs. 16,000/as a result the votes would have go to Avtar Sing Singh cannot he ruled out.

The appellant, a Forest Officer in the Council of Ministers headed by Shri Bhajan Lal, was defeated in the legislative assembly election held in 1982. The Chief Minister of the State filed an application for contempt against the respondent, who was then the Chief Minister, alleging that one Shri Devinder Sharma, a forest officer, had been illegally detained and that the constitutional validity of the said Ordinance was challenged by him in the High Court. The Single Judge of the High court dismissed the application holding that there were circumstances to indicate that it was not a fit case in which the court should exercise its jurisdiction under the Act. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that as no punishment was imposed on the respondent by the High Courts in exercise of their jurisdiction to punish for contempt, section 19(1) of the Act only empowered the High 'Court to punish a person who has been punished for contempt of itself. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court exercises its jurisdiction or power as conferred on it by Article 215 of the Constitution when it imposes a punishment for contempt. When no punishment is imposed by the high court, it is difficult to say that the High. Court has exercised its jurisdiction, or power to punish any person who is not a party to the writ petition. [893C D] 2. The scope and ambit of this judgment will be confined to criminal contempt. In considering a question whether the alleged contemnor is guilty of contempt or not, the court may examine the materials produced before it and, if necessary, examines witnesses and, thereafter passes an order either acquitting or punishing him for contempt.[893D] 3. The jurisdiction of the ' High Court is to punish. When the High, Court does not impose any punishment on the alleged contemner, the High Curt cannot be said to be exercising its jurisdiction for contempt for such exercise will mean that the high Court should act in a particular manner, that is to say, by imposing punishment for Contempt. So long as no penalty is imposed, by the 'High Court, the same is difficult. [8893E F] 4. The power of the Supreme Court under Article 215 confers on the High ,Court the power to impose for contempt and not to dispose of it in the exercise of its jurisdiction to impose any sentence or dismiss the same. But when a court is conferred with the power or jurisdiction to act in the particular manner the exercise or power will involve the acting in that particular manner and in no other. Article 215 confer on the high 'Court the powers to punish ' for contempt '. [881F G] 5. The question whether there is a right of appeal or not will have to be considered on an interpretation of the provision of the statute and not on the ground of porosity or any other consideration.

The appellant was the owner of a house in Bombay. He had let out his house to one R on 13th September, 1943. The rent was paid by R on behalf of R and he was informed that it would be in arrears of rent. On the same day R filed a suit for ejectment against R on the ground that R was entitled to the whole of the property as he had become defaulter by reason of non payment of rent and that R had defaulted in paying rent. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court held that the lease was not executed prior to the coming into force of the Act, and that the appellant was entitled only to a relief against forfeiture for non payment. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf Of the appellant that (i) the statutory provisions of section 111(g) of the were not applicable to leases executed prior in time; (ii) the provisions of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947 were not based upon any principle of equity; (iii) the provision for notice under section 111 was not based on any principle or rule of law; and (iv) the appellant had failed to prove that R acted in excess of his statutory right. HELD: (i). The provisions of sections 109 and 110 of the are founded upon principles of reason and equity, and they apply equally to statutory leases. [1024 D] A statute has given a wide meaning of the term. It is not intended to give a wider meaning than it in other words, as it now stands. It does not mean that the legislature should be given an indication by some unequivocal expression of intention on his part of taking advantage of the breach from which he was not accustomed to exercise it in his favour. [1124 D E] (ii). The section is a rule of justice and does not require that the Court must and will always insist upon certain things when the Act does not requires them, and the facts of some unforeseen case may make the court wish it had kept a free hand. [1225 F G] (iii). The provision in section 111 (g) which recognises the validity of a contract is not based or enunciated on any principles of equity. It must be distinctly understood that there may be cases in which any or all of them may be disregarded. If, however, the delay, the conduct of the parties and the difficulties to which the landlord has been put, should be weighed against the tenant, this Court would be reluctant to take advantage of his own wrong and to plead relief against forfeited forfeiture on every occasion, particularly when he was warned by the court of appeal on a previous occasion. He bad already had relief three times on equitable grounds and it is time that the court withheld its hands and ordered his ejectment. [1526 F G; 1527 A B] (iv). The High Court was right in holding that the tenant should have been given relief against the forfeiture.

The appellant was a union called Kymore Quarry Karamchari Sangh. The Management passed an order on 13.9.1968, dismissing the workmen from service. The respondents were called upon to submit their explanation in respect of charges to the General Manager which they did on 24th October, 1968. A departmental enquiry was held against them by Shri H.S. Mathur who was a member of the union. The management served charge sheets dated 3rd November, 1968 and 7th February 1970 on the respondents in which four common charges were levelled against all of them. In addition to the three charges against the respondents, an inquiry officer was appointed who held the enquiry. The Enquiry Officer found that the two charges were fully proved and the fourth charge was partly proved against all the respondents while the additional charges against other employees were also proved. The appellant challenged the award in a writ petition before the High Court which dismissed the same on the ground that the Arbitrator had misconstrued Standing Order No. 17 and that no second opportunity was required to be given to the respondents and that in the alternative the interference with the punishment of dismissal in respect thereof would be detrimental to the appellant 's case. The High Court also held that there was a violation of Standing Order 17 and therefore, the findings were bad as they were not vitiated by any misconduct under Standing Order 16. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the concept of second opportunity being given to a delinquent which obtained under section 240(3) of the Government of India Act, 1935 or article 311 of the Constitution prior to the insertion of the proviso to Article 311(2) could not be invoked or applied to the instant case; and (ii) assuming that the enquiry was vitiated for the reason mentioned by the Arbitrator even though once serious mis conduct was proved by leading evidence before the Arbitrator it was not open to him to interfere with the penalty of dismissal inflicted upon Rama Shankar and Burma Pradhan. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The High court has rightly construed the Standing Order NO. 17 as requiring a second opportunity to offer explanation in regard to the alleged misconduct charged against him. [368C] 1.2 In view of the construction placed on Standing Order read as a whole, no second opportu nity of showing cause against the proposed punishment is contemplated either expressly or by necessary implication. [369E F] Hamdard Dawakhana vs Badri Das & Ors., ; and Meerut Light Railway Co.
