's Case (supra) referred to. 1.3 The High Courts have rightly construed Standing Order Nos. 17, 18 and 19 as requiring the second opportunity spoken of by para 3 OE S.O. 17 is the opportunity to be give an opportunity to a workman to offer his explanation. [370G] Hamad Dawakhan vs Badri Dass & Ors. ; , referred to 2.1 In the instant cases, the Arbitrator has undoubtedly taken the view that the second notice was vitiated because of some acts or omissions that constitute misconduct or efficiency and striking work either singly or with other workers without giving 14 days previous notice, inciting whilst on the premises and worker to strike work and indulging in a Gherao, which would amount to an 'act subversive of discipline or efficiency ' are obviously included therein.

The appellant was the owner of a portion of an area of Ac.0.D. in Malabar to which the provisions of the Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1963 were applicable on the 11th day of April 1955. The High Court took the view that the benefit of section 7D would apply only to persons whose occupa tion of the private forests or unsurveyed lands had a lawful origin and not to persons m unlawful occupation based on trespass or forcible and unlawful entry. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the said interpretation placed by the High Court on section 7A must be held to be correct. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: 1. The intention of the legisla ture was to grant protection only to person whose posses sion had a legal origin in the sense that they had either bona fide believed the lands to be Government 's lands of which they could later seek assignment or had taken the lands on lease from persons whom they bona fide believe to be competent to grant such leases or had come into possession with the intention of attorning to the lawful owners or on the basis of arrangements like varam etc. which were only in the nature of licences and fell short of a leasehold right. [114F G] 2. The expression "in occupation" occurring in section 7 D must be construed as meaning "in lawful occupation". In the present case the finding of fact entered by the trial court is that the appellant had come to possession of the lands by trespass.

The appellant was found in possession of certain goods. The police officers searched the room and recovered a portion of the room from which the goods were recovered. The appellant 's explanation that he had been in possession at the time when the raid was made, was not accepted by the trial court as well as by the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the presumption contained in Section 123(1) of the Act corresponding to section 128(A) of that Act was available only to goods seized under the Act and that the appellant had not given any evidence to show that his sub tenants had placed the boxes there, or that there was any reason why he should allow them to use the portion reserved by him for himself. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that the goods in respect of which the appellant was prosecuted were not seized under section 111(a) of Act. [541 C] 2. Section 123 (1) does not empower the prosecution to ask the court to presume that the accused knew that the, goods must have been smuggled or imported in contravention of the law. The fact that the person who has to prove that the must have taken part in the fraudulent evasion of duty does not enable the prosecution 'to apply section 106 of the Evidence Act when the appellant could not know where the goods came from or when they were imported or that duty, if leviable was not P d on them. [542 E F] 3. The mere possession by the accused of such goods could not enable him to obtain benefit of doubt. [543 G] 4. In the instant case, there is some evidence to enable the courts to come to the conclusion that the articles must have be known to the appellant to be smuggled even if he was not a party to a fraudulent evasion. The very appearance of the goods and the manner in which they were packed indicated that they were newly manufactured and brought into this country very recently from another country. [544 E F, 545 A] 5. The possession of the accused person of such articles could not be said to have been known to him to be imported even if the appellant 'was not a member of the same country of their assumed origin after a time when they had come to his house and that he may have sub let other portions of the partitioned room to other persons, but there is no reason to doubt that the appel lant was found at the scene of the offence.

The appellants were the Presidents of a registered association which was dissolved and the members of the Association were joined as proforma defendants. The Association was reconstituted in 1951. In April 1946, the appellants filed an application to be impleaded as plaintiffs. The trial court dismissed the suit on the ground that the suit was not maintainable because (1) the suit had been instituted by a President who was not registered and its formation was in contravention of section 4(2) of the Rewa State Companies Act, 1935, and (2) the appellants were not entitled to any share in the profits made on the sale of the goods. The High Court dismissed the appeal. Held, that the preliminary objection must be overruled. Section 4(1)(a) of a. 4 of the Madhya Pradesh General Clauses Act, 1937, being prohibitory in nature cannot be excluded from consideration even though the bar of that provision has been raised at this late stage. The provisions of section 2(2), (3) and (4) of that Act, being mandatory in character, must be held to have been waived by the appellants. The suit was therefore not one for accounts of a dissolved firm but for accounts. Surajmull Nargolkar vs Triton Insurance Co., Ltd., ; , referred to. The question whether a person is entitled to claim a share in a consignment of goods arose out of an illegal transaction or not, and the question must be decided on the basis of the provisions of the Act. The general objection that the appellants had a right to bring a suit for accounts was negatived by the trial court as well as by the High Court.

The respondents were charged with offences under sections 51(1) and 56 of the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972 read with section 51 of the said Act. The Magistrate took cognizance of the offence and ordered issue of process against the accused. The respondents challenged the order before the High Court by way of a Writ Petition. The High Court quashed the proceedings against them on the ground that the Magistrate had no jurisdiction to take cognisance of the offences under section 51(i) read with sec. 2(16) and 50(1). The High court observed that the investigation was in progress in relation to the same offence, the offence punishable under section 9(1), read with Sec.2(16), and 50 (1) of the Act, in its ingredients and content, is the same or substantially the same as Section 429 IPC and that after due investigation and police had filed a final report that no offence was made out and that initiation of any fresh proceedings against respondents would be impermissible. The appellants contended before this Court that the complaint did not spell out the existence of the cognizance of such an offence, but only once and, therefore, section 210(1)(a) of Cr. P.C., 1973 was attracted and that as an investigation by the police was in the nature of a criminal prosecution under section 500 IPC read with Section 2( 16), and that since no offence had been made out, the complaint envisaged by sec. 9( 1) read along with secs. 2 (16) was not maintainable. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Courts have taken a view that cognizance of an offence under section 499 IPC is barred. [468F] 1.2 In the instant case, the allegations in the complaint do not spell the ingredients of an alleged act of killing of an elephant, altox, which a man is an inter state inter alia part or that it should not be liable to be punished twice for the same offi cial offence. The proviso to section 56 has also a familiar ring and is a facet of the fundamental and salutory principles that permeate penalies and reflected in analogous provisions of sec. 26 of General Clauses Act, 1897. [467G H] 1:3. Section 2 (15) of Contempt of Courts Act, 1953 defines criminal contempt as meaning any act or omission which constitutes an offence u/s 4(1 ) in section 56 of that Act, merely imports the idea tat the same act or omitted might constitute an offence. It is trite juris diction under sec. 482 Cr.P.C. which saves the inherent power of the High Courts to make such orders as may be necessary to prevent abuse of the process of any court or otherwise to secure the ends of justice, has to be exercised sparingly and with circumspection. [466B C] 1 4. The same set of facts in conceivable cases can constitute offences under two different laws. An act or an omission can amount to and constitute an offi cer under another law and could be tried under such other law or laws also. The offence of read along the lord and vice versa. [470C D] Municipal Corporation of Delhi vs R.K. Rohtagi, ; , referred to. 1.5 In the present case, there is no prior conviction and sentence for an offence punishable u/S 56 of Act, 1973.

The petitioner, a member of the Tamil Nadu State Bar Association, was convicted for non bailable offences under section 10(1) (a), 10(2) and 14 of the . The High Court upheld his conviction. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the petitioner 's brother was not in a position to pay bail as he had been sentenced to imprisonment for a long period, while the State was still free to dispense with surety or to receive an Indian bailor across the district blair. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The law is being followed by the Courts in the country and the provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure disclose that the criminal courts are not onlygy but also a mockery. [346D] 2. The Constitution (Forty Second Amendment) Act, 1966 has stipulated inter alia that release on bail shall be granted in non capital cases where there is reasonable assurance that the individual will reappear when required; that the Courts should make use of a variety of release options depending on the circumstances; that information should be developed about the individual bond with or without sureties. [347E F] 3. The vice of the system is brought out in the Report of the Legal Aid Committee appointed by the Government of Gujarat and headed by the then Chief Justice of the State. It was enacted to protect the defendant 's poor, as well as the poor, from suffering from any language trespass in Bastar, Port Blair, or distantly criminal trespass in the district; but the Act does not provide for both the bond of the accused and the undertaking of the surety being conditioned in the manner mentioned in the sub section. To read 'bail ' as including only cases of release with sureties will stultify the sub sections; for then, an accused released on his own bond without sureties would be both exer cise and expensive means. [349G H] 4. The constitutional philosophy of bail is that the accused should ordinarily be released on order to appear before a Magistrate at the appointed place. The discretion to release the petitioner on his personal bond being demanded and what sum should be insisted on are dependent on variables. Even so, poor men Indians in monetary terms indigents young persons infirm individual and women are weak categories and courts should be liberal in releasing them on their own recognis tions put whatever reasonable condition you may. It Shocks one conscience to ask a mason like the petitioner to furnish sureties for Rs. 100,000/ . The magistrate must be given the benefit of doubt for not fully appreciating that our Constitution. enacted by 'The State ' is meant for butcher, the baker and the candle stick maker shall we add the bonded labour and pavement dweller. To add insult to injury, the Magistrate has demanded sureties from his own district. [344A B] 5. The petitioner ' s brother was convicted under section 3(1)(a) of the , and sentenced to a term of imprisonment for one year and a fine of Rs. 10,000. An appeal against the conviction was dismissed by the High Court. In this Court the petitioner contended that he had rich at least a vakalat in the Supreme Court and that the jailed defendant lost his liberty because of his community standing and past history or minority and distant dense cation. The State contended that it is not necessary that the Magistrate should always bear in mind that monetary bail is not a necessary element of the criminal process and even if risk of monetary loss is a deterrent against fleeing from justice, it is no ground to impose conditions on release. [345B C] 6. The High Courts have failed to appreciate that the Constitution (Seventh Amendment) Bill, 1966, was enacted in the United States and the Indian Constitution (Seventeenth Amendment) Article 2 protects all Indians qua Indians within the territory of India.

The assessee, a company, had at different places in India branches one of which was an industrial undertaking conducted in the name of Eldee Velvet and Silk Mills called for the sake of brevity. The Income tax Officer, Special Circle Amritsar, and the Appellate Assistant Commissioner rejected the claim of the assessee to include in the computation of capital invested by Eldees 'Castle ' in the taxable income of the company. The Appellate Tribunal modified the assessment and directed the Tribunal to state the case and refer it to the High Court. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The finding of the Tribunal that the business called 'Cantle ' at Bombay was a branch of the appellant was not conclusive. [429 A B] (ii) The Tribunal had considered evidence covering all the essential matters before arriving at its conclusion and it was not possible for the High court to discard the Tribunal 's finding of fact, if there is some evidence to support the finding of facts, if There is some material to support such a finding. [ 430 C D] (iii) The decision of the Appellate Tribunal that a question of law does not arise out of the order of the Income tax Tribunal is not conclusive and cannot be regarded as a finding not giving rise to a question liable to be referred to the Court. Non inclusion of the income of 'Chinnold Textiles ' in its assessment of the asses see may have been a relevant circumstance, but its effect had to be considered in the light of other circumstances on which the Appellate Assis tration was founded and overlooked other relevant matters.

The Minister concerned filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the notification dated January 29, 1974 fixing the seniority of the engineers n the Irrigation Department of the Punjab Government. During the course of hearing of the writ petition the Minister concerned was directed to file his affidavit. The Minister concerned thereafter heard the parties and made a speaking order on February 18, 1975 affirming the earlier seniority list. The High Court in its judgment dated January 28, 1975 held that the Minister was not impleaded as a party. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the State of Punjab that the Secretary of the Department should file his personal affidavit. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The Minister is concerned to decide in the light of the allegations made in the petition as to whether he should or should not file an affidavit. [972C] (2) The High court was in error in directing that the minister be impleaded as respondent. The other part of the order whereby the Minister had been called upon to file the personal affidavit is set aside. [963D] (3) The direction for impleading of the Minister as a necessary party was given by the High court with a view to apprise the Minister of the allegation made in his petition and thus to afford him an opportunity of controverting those allegations, if he so deemed proper. Taking the totality of facts and circumstances of the case it is not possible to interfere with the order of the High Courts adding the Minister to the allegations that he should be impleaded.

The respondent was a tenant of the appellant. The respondent filed a suit for recovery of rent on the ground that he had committed a breach of the provisions of the Cantonment Act, 1924 and in any case under section 259 of the Act. The trial court held that the appellant had no jurisdiction to recover the arrears of rent due under the lease. On appeal the High Court reversed this decision holding that the respondent was not entitled to claim rent for the period of rent as he had failed to prove his provisions under the Act and that the suit was barred by limitation. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the respondent that (1) the expression "recoverable by a Board" or "under the Act" in section 259 meant "claimable by the Board for recovery or damages for breach of contract, because, under the terms of any notice, order or requisition issued to any person under this Act or the rules made thereunder, requiring such person to execute any work or to do any act, it shall be lawful for the Board to recover from him the amount due from the owner under section 256; (2) the words "recoversable by" and "under this Act" used in section 258(1) meant "in any case, he was entitled as a person to recover or receive by way of punishment for occupation of a building or land belonging to the landlord. HELD: (i) The word 'rent ' in section 256 is not intended to include money payable by one person to another when they do not stand in the relationship of tenant and landlord. It is the duty of the Board, among other things, to maintain and develop the property vested in or entrusted to its management. [346 C D] (ii) The words "requisitioned" in the section are meant to govern "a Board". The word "rent" in Section 259 means a thing given under the provisions contained in the Act or under the Rules made thereunder. But if the expression is interpreted in the way suggested by the High Courts, that word would become purposeless and would be rendered otiose because there is no provision whatsoever in the statute which expressly makes rent claimable or recoverable by either of the two authorities specified therein.

The appellant was terminated from service on 12th July, 1973. The respondent company terminated the services of the appellant by an order dated 2nd January, 1973 under section 15(b) of the Industrial Disputes Act. The appellant challenged before the Labour Court the said termination on the ground that the termination itself was illegal and justified. The Labour Court held that the appellant could not be held to be a workman employed for manual, skilled, unskilled and/or clerical nature and that the provisions of the industrial Disputes Act were not applicable and the reference was incompetent. In appeal by the appellant company it was contended that the respondent company was required to supervise the work of the local salesmen appointed in the area of his operation as well but it was only incidental to his main function of canvassing and promoting the sale of the product of the Company. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The finding of the Tribunal on the nature of the work is a finding on a question of fact and it is also borne out by the document produced before the labour court. [475G] 2. The supervising work of other local sales men was part of his work considered by the Tribunal as only incidental. He was required for the purpose of canvassing, that is, to supervise and promote the sale, of the company 's product in his area. The Tribunal found that the appel lant was not a workman and that he was employed for casual, unskilled or clerical nature. [476D E] 3. The supervision work of another local salesman was part and incidental to the main work. He also required to suggest about the publicity in markets and melas, advertise ments including the need for posters, holders, cinema slides and suggest means to canvass the sale in this area. [477F G] 4. The management should pay some compensation to the respondent. This is a subsequent enactment and it was not applicable to him and in view of the fact that a long period of over 16 years had passed it would be unjust to leave the appellant without any remedy at this stage. [478G H; 478A] 5. The findings of the Labour court on the question whether the appellant is a workman are correct. [479B C] Burmah Shell Oil Storage and Distribution Company vs Burmah shell Management and Staff, ; , referred to.

The respondent Company was a company registered under the Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code, 1959. The Company was in terms of the lease granted by the State Government. The lease was extended for a further period of ten years in Samvat 2001. When proceedings were initiated against the Company for eviction of the Company, the Company filed Suit No. 14 of 1960 for declaration of title and perpetual injunction. The Civil Judge dismissed the suit holding that the land in question was held by the Company under lease from the Government after it had been acquired by the Government for a public purpose of the State. The High Court confirmed the order of the trial court. In appeal to this Court, on behalf of the appellant State it was contended that the Company was not a 'pakka ' tenant and did not enjoy the status of a ` Gair Maurusi ' tenant. Dismissing the Appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The finding of the High Court to the contrary was totally unjustified and opposed to law. [179F] 2. The order of eviction passed by the Additional Collector under section 182 of the Code is set aside. The findings of the Additional Collec tor are set aside and the order passed by him is restored. [180G] 3. The direction given by the High court that the company was not 'pankka ' tenants, is vacated. The State entered into an agreement with the Company to grant a fresh lease for a period of 10 years from 9.2.1971 subject to payment of enhanced rent as agreed upon between the parties. Since the Company failed to pay the agreed rents and thus contravened the conditions of the leases, proceedings were started by the Addl. Collector by his Order dated 1.10.1977 for eviction. [181B C] 4. The Additional Collector was well justified in having recourse to the proceeding prescribed under section 183 of the code. [182D] 5. The appeal by the respondent company is allowed with costs throughout.

The State of Orissa acquired certain lands belonging to the appellants under the Orissa Land Reforms Act, 1960. The State Government issued a notification under section 1(3) of the Act which provided for payment of compensation at a rate which was less than the market value of the land falling within the ceiling limit as originally fixed by the Act. By section 2(5) of that Act it was provided that "the interest of the person to whom the surplus lands relate and of all land holders mediately or immediately under whom the excess lands were being held shall stand extinguished and the said lands shall vest absolutely in the Government free from all encumbrances". The appellants challenged the validity of these provisions on the ground that they contravened article 31 B of the Constitution. Held, that section 47 of the Orissa Act which provides for payment to the land holders of landholders under any law for the time being in force was not ultra vires the authority conferred by it and as such was void. The right to compensation which is not less than tho market value under any laws providing for the acquisition by the State of any estate in an estate in the personal cultivation of a person is guaranteed by the second proviso only where the land is within the Ceiling limit applicable to him under any Law for the lime being in existence. The Act does not provide for the compulsory acquisition of land which may be laid only if the law provides for the transfer of ownership or right to possession of any property to the State or to a corporation owned or controlled by the Government. Held further, that the provisions of section 47 were not ultra rites and as they contravened articles 14 and 19(1)(f) of Part III of the Constitu tion, they could not be deemed to be law in force unless it was brought into operation by legislative enactment or by the exercise of authority by a delegate empowered to bring it into operation.

The widow of her husband, who had inherited the property from her husband 's widow, filed a suit for possession of the properties on the ground that the widow was not entitled to any share in them. The widow contended that the gift made by her husband to her husband was invalid and that the reversioners were entitled to succeed to the estate. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court reversed the decree holding that the plaintiffs proved that the widows had acquired a right of ownership in their favour, and that they could sue for possession at once. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (1) the widow had no interest in the property during her lifetime; (2) the gift by the widow to her daughter was not valid as she had acquired good title against the widow; and (3) the reversioners had acquired the right of a prior alienee from the widow 's estate which was an inter State property. HELD: The widow was entitled to sue for recovery of possession of her properties during her life time. [350 D] Per Subba Rao, J. The gift made in favour of the reversioner was not binding on the reversioners and no valid gift could be effected by the reversioner. [351 E] (1)(a) The widow 'different from the husband and if the widow died a natural death it would be binding upon her heirs. [352 F] (b) The right to the property vested in the reversioner under section 16 of the Hindu Succession Act, which operates only when a son is adopted by a widow subsequent to the death of her deceased husband. Such adopted son is given the rights of a posthumous son and the fiction is that he was in existence from before the father 's death and if he had any right to possession of his property, it would not be defeated by reason of the surrender made by the reversioners. [353 G] (c) The gift in favour by the widows was not a valid gift under Hindu law but was only an act of surrender as contemplated by section 16(2). [354 B C] (d) The effect of the gift is to destroy the widow property in the same way as if she suffered physical or civil death. [355 G] Per Sarkar, J: 1. The right of the reversioners to enforce it is no part of the widow estate at all and, therefore, could not be surrendered to the reversioner.[354 C] 2. The reversioners have enjoyed their property since 1925, and as the title which they had acquired is not available against the reversionary interest, there is no principle of law under which the acts of the widows could bind him. [354 D] 3. The fact that a surrender stands on a different footing from adoption by a Hindu widow does not make it clear that the reversioner has been deprived of his estate in favours of the grandsons. [356 G] 4. The question whether a surrender is valid or not depends upon the alienation as distinguished from an antecedent transaction which is not binding upon the reversioners, and if a surrender was made subsequently by the husband, the surrender must take it subject to such prior interest. [357 B C; 356 E F] 5. The effect is that in case of alienations by a female widow of his husband 'the widow ' is to be deemed to be severed from the inheritance and if such an alienation is made subsequently, the surrenders must take effect from her death or on the date may be specified as a person entitled to it. If the surrender is without any legal necessity, there would be no possibility of alienations being made by a reversioner. The widows ' right to challenge it is not part of their estate at the time of surrender but only of the heirs who have acquired interest in her husbands property without any justification. [358 E F; 358 A B] 6.

The appellant was a member of the Cotton Mills Company. The Cotton Mills company filed a petition under section 397(1) (a) of the U.P. Land Revenue Act, 1901, for the appointment of a Receiver to take possession of certain shares in the Polytex Company held by it. The Custodian of the erstwhile Mills Company appointed a Receiver in respect of the said shares. The appellant challenged the order of the Custodian on the ground that the appointment was without jurisdiction and that the requisition made by the Collector under section 169 of the Act required that the Chairman of the Board of Directors of the company shall, on the requisition of such a person or members of the Company as is specified in sub section (4) thereof forthwith proceed to call an extraordinary general meeting of the Mills. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the receiver appointed by the Commissioner was not competent to hold the shares and that he had no power to issue notice under section 170 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, and that if those shares were omitted from consideration then the shares held by the other requisitionists would not have been eligible for requisition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the extraordinary general meetings had not been validly called since the Cotton Mill Company had ceased to be a member; (ii) the requisition in question was without any authority and could not be treated as shareholder 's notice under s 169 of Act; and (iii) the Board had acted illegally in passing the orders under section 18AA(1)(a). HELD: (i ) The order of appointment of the Chairman was made on the making of an order of adjudication. [886 B] (ii). The High Courts have not much relevance to the case. It is well settled that a Receiver appointed by 3 court in respect to certain shares of a company without more cannot be treated to have any effect on them. [889 G] (iii). The power of the receiver to vote at the meetings of the companies is one of the modes of enforcement of a judgment or order for the payment of money to the creditor. Under section 176(1), the Court may, in its discretion, give directions regarding the property in any form of security or otherwise, movable or immovable belonging to a judgment debtor, as a result of the pledge or sale of a share.

The petitioners, who were the owners of a suit land in the State of Punjab, filed a suit for declaration that they were owners of the suit land along with some others. The Gram Panchayat contested the suit and raised preliminary objection that the Court before which the suit had been instituted had no jurisdiction to try it by virtue of section 13 of the Punjab Village Common Lands (Regulation) Act, 1961. The trial court framed an issue relating to its jurisdiction and tried it as a preliminary issue. It held that since the question involved in the suit was simply one of title to the suit property and it was not necessary to decide whether the suit lands were shamlat deh or not, and whether the land had validly vested in the Panchayat or not being shamlat ly, it had jurisdiction to entertain the suit. The petitioners filed revision petition before the High Court which allowed the same holding that the issues involved in a suit were not triable by a civil court by virtue Of section 11 read with section 13 C.P.C. and accordingly he held that the suit is not maintainable before the civil court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the land in question was shamlat ter and it had been vested in it, and therefore, the civil courts had jurisdiction under section 11 of the Act to try the suit; that the plaintiffs could not by drawing their plaint cleverly by not claiming a declaration that the disputed land was not shamlat or not sham ly shamlat. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The plaintiff who claimed to be the owners along with others of the Suit land had avoided to seek a declaration in his suit. [835D] 2. Section 13 C P.C., provides that no civil court shall have jurisdiction to adjudicate upon any question whether any property or any right to or interest in any property is or is not shamil d to have been vested or deemed to have vested in a Panchayat under the Act or to question the legality of any action taken by the Commissioner or the Collector or the Panchayat under this Act. The plaintiffs cannot by drawing the plaint cleftly by merely claiming that the plaintiff had right, title or interest therein. [883E] 3. Section 12 of the Haryana Village Common Land (Regulation), (Amendment) Act 1976 provides that any person claiming right, titles or interest may submit to the Collector within such time as may be prescribed, a statement of his claim in writing and verified in the prescribed manner and that the Collector shall have jurisdic tion to decide such claim in such manner as may he prescribed. Any person or a Panchayat aggrieved by an order of the Collector made under sub section (1) may, within sixty days from the date of the order, prefer an appeal to the Commissioner in such form as may prescribed and the Commissioner may after hearing the appeal, confirm, very or reverse the order appealed against and may pass such order as he deems fit. [853G H] 4. The suit had not been filed clever by the plaintiffs. They could not, by drawing his plaint cleffi narily claim that the lands in question belonged to it as shamlat land. They had, however, questioned the correctness of entries in the revenue records which showed that the Panchayat was entitled to the same. [864A] 5. The defendant No.

The Andhra Pradesh Electricity Board, which is a State Electricity Board under the Electricity Supply Act, 1948, has been constituted under section 49 of the Act. Section 59 provides for payment of interest at certain rates on the deposit made by the consumer in respect of consumption credit to the Board. The Board has also fixed the tariff rate of interest on the amount of energy consumed and other charges payable by it. The Electricity Board is entitled to adjust its tariffs for the purpose of Board 's finance. The State Electricity Boards, which are a State Government, have been conferred statutory powers under section 59(1) of the Supply Act to determine the conditions on the basis of which supply is to be made. Section 49 provides that the Board shall not pay interest on any security deposit or any other amount payable by him. The petitioners who were consumers of electricity in the State of Andhra Pradesh, filed writ petitions before the High Court challenging the levy of the Electricity Board 'S 1910 (Supply) Act, 1910 and the Interest Act, 1978. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the interest on security deposit was a condition of supply and not a deposit in the real sense for the consumers to claim the benefit of interest. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellants that the Electricity Boards are bound by the provisions of the 1910 Act and as such the Board is not entitled to recover interest on their security deposits. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The terms and conditions of supply of energy with reference to all the Boards are real and it is not in dispute that the electricity board is required to make a provision for payment to the consumers. This is not even a case of a constructive trust under section 90 of the Indian Electricity Act, since no advantage is gained by the Electricity board in derogation of the rights of the consumer. [252E F] 2. The consumption security deposit is not only to secure the interest of the Board for any such violation but should serve as a deterrent on the consumer to the extent and conditions as laid down in the regulations. It also requires that there should be some protection by way of security deposit if the consumer pays and consume electricity on credit ranging from 2 to 3 months depending upon the category of consumers. [253G H] 3. The supply is an integral part of the money which is payable to the Electricity Company with the Board to secure its Board against default in payment of its dues. The amount of security is not so unconscionable as to shock the conscience of the Court. [254A B] 4. The quality and conditions for supply of electricity are basically different from fixed deposit. It is not a case where the supply is provided like Andhra Pradesh and Bihar. In one sense, the consumption security deposits represents only a part of money which was payable to it on the bill being raised against the consumer credit. [255C D] 5. The demand for payment by the Board under section 50 of the is in terms of the agreement interpreted in the form of an additional security deposit with interest at the rate of 3 per cent from the date of default. [260E F]. 6.The consumption security deposited is not to be treated separately.

The petitioners in these petitions were working as officers in the Telecommunication Research Centre in the Department of the Ministry of Communications, Government of India. They were working in the said Telecommunication Institute from 1975 onwards. The posts of Scientific and Technical Officers Grade I (Telecommunications Re search Centre) were manned by transfer of Group A/Telecomputers Grade I. The Recruitment Rules provided for recruitment to the different cadres in the service and Telegraphs Department. In response to a notification issued by the President under Article 309 of the Constitution of India, the petitioners who were working on the said posts were recruited in four batches in 1965, 1967 and 1973. They challenged the said notifications before the Central Administrative Tribunal contending that they were not competent to recruit them as they were directly recruited to the Telecommunications Centre for a limited purpose. The Tribunal allowed their writ petitions holding that denial of promotional opportunities to them on account of irregular implementation of the rules of promotion contained in the Recruitment Rules and the second relating to violation of Article 14 and Article 16 of the Constitu tion was arbitrary, unreasonable and the effect of adding insult to injury. In these appeals by special leave it was contended for the petitioners that the said two officers were not given any Special Pay in these grades and they were given only the pay at the time of promotion. Dismissing the petitions, HELD: 1. The direct recruits (to which category the petitioners belonged) in the Telegraph Engineering Research Centre are entitled to the Special Pay of Rs. 300 Rs. 200 and Rs. 150 per month in addition to their scale of pay which is the same as the scale of Pay of direct recruits because the transferred officials had to perform in the telephone Research Centre duties which are not in their general line. [1013C D] 2. The Central Administrative Tribu nal has virtually admitted that all relevant things such as qualifi cations, functions, duties and responsibilities are the same. In other words, there is no justification to deny the Special pay at this rates to the direct recruits amounts to viola tion of Articles 14 and 16 of t he Constitution of lndia. [1094D E] Randhir Singh vs Union of India & Ors., ; , followed. The Indian Telecommuni cation Service Officers who are working in thority Research Centre for more than six years, cannot be treated as deputation allowance. It is paid for the arduous and special nature of the functions to be discharged in the telecommunications Research Centre. Denial of Special Pay will amount to vio lating Article 14 or Article 16. [1002E F] Randhir singh vs Union o India & Others, ; , referred to.

The appellant, a workman in the Bidi industry, was dismissed by an order of the Labour Court under section 42(1) of the Bombay Industrial Relations Act, 1946. The respondent filed an application before the Labour court under section 78(1), claiming that the charge sheet served on him was not proper and that the Head Office of the appellant had no authority to deal with his case under the Standing Orders. The Labour Court held that the findings of the enquiry officer were perverse and set aside the order of dismissal. On appeal by the State, the High Court held (i) that the Labour 'Court was competent to pass an order under section 79(1). Dismissing the appeal to this Court, HELD : (i)(a) The scheme of Chapter VIII is that in regard to any "change" in an matter there must be compliance with the provisions of that Chapter. In other words effort must first be made by the employer intending to effect any change in respect of matters covered by section 42 (1) or an employee desiring a change in the respect of any order passed by the employers under standing orders which would of necessity include an order, of dismissal to see whether it was possible to come to any agreement and an application to the labour court could only be resorted to after efforts had been made to settle the dispute and no agreement had been arrived at. The scheme is that a Labour Court is to have power to decide all the disputes covered by paragraph A.

The appellants filed an application under section 12 of the Bihar Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1947 before the Munsif Ranchi for eviction on the ground that they were the successors in interest of the lessor company. The respondents contested the application contending that the appellants were the successor in interest as a result of which a new month to month tenancy was created and the respondents had formed a partnership. The appellants filed a suit against the respondent for possession after the expiry of the period of one year, but the same was dismissed by the Munsif on appeal. The Additional District Judge affirmed the order of the Munsif. The High Court in revision set aside the order and restored the decree passed by the Munsiff Ranchi. In the appeal to this Court it was contended that the application under Section 12 of Act before the Civil Court was maintainable and the High Court was in error in holding otherwise. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The question is whether the petition which was filed by the appellants as an application for eviction under section 11 and extension of period of lease under section 13 of the Act can be treated as a plaint and the impugned proceeding as the one in a suit followed by an appeal and a second appeal. [975C] 2. The expression "any other good and sufficient cause" in section 12(bb) of the said Act, is such as would fall within section 47 and so the decision on it is appealable and a regular suit is barred. In view of the circumstances of the present case, the proceeding arising out of the appellant 's application before the Munsiff should be treated to be a suit and the judgment of the Subordinate Judge as a decree therein. [ 975D E] 3. The order passed by Munsif as a court of general jurisdiction under the Code of Civil Procedure is vested in the Controller. But as regards the question of dealing with the eviction of tenants under section11 and extension thereof, the civil court is the proper forum. In this case it is the Civil court, which is the appropriate forum for exercise of such power. [977E F] 4. The view taken by the High Courts that the scope in which the proceeding by the parties were addressed was the same as in a second suit, and the decision also was accordingly given, is not correct. [978F G] 5. In a case dealing with compulsory retire ment this Court in M.R. Singh vs The Chief ' Commissioner (Admn.) Manipur & Ors., AIR 1929 Patna 141, held that the exercise of a power will be referable to a jurisdiction which confers validity upon it and not to a jurisdic tion under which it will be nugatory, and there is no reason to exclude the application of this rule to judi cial proceedings. [979G H] 6. The scope in section 11(1) of Bihar BuildingsLease, Control Act refers to several authorities for decision of different issues, one of them being Control ler as defined in section 2(b) of that Act and another 'Court as the court of special jurisdiction under that Act as defined under section 2 (bb).

The appellant, a registered society, filed a suit for declaration of the immovable property through its then Secretary. The trial court allowed the suit and dismissed the suit. In appeal, the High Court held that the application under section 15 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure was not maintainable. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 A court has inherent power to correct its own proceedings when it is satisfied that in passing a particular order it was misled by one of the parties. The principle was correctly applied in Sadho Saran Rai and Others vs Anant Rai and Ors., AIR 1923 Patna 483; Vilakathala Raman vs Vayalil Kavalai Vayalikupowda Patil, AIR 1923 Pat 483; Basangowda Hanmantgowda Patil and Others v Churchigirigowda Yogangowda & Anr., AIR 1924 Patna 483, referred to. 1.2 The fact that the suit was instituted by a prayer purported to have been made on behalf of the plaintiff does not make it an application on behalf the appellant at all and the impugned order was passed as a result of the court being misled. Such an order cannot bind the appellant and has to be vacated. [236B C] Sadho Chaprala Raman & Ors. vs Anant Raj & Ors., ; , referred to 2. The High Court while confirming the order of the trial court, said that in the exercise of inherent power under section 151 Code of Criminal Procedure a court can vacate an order obtained by fraud on it. [237C D] Sadhukhannappa vs Anantraj and Others, AIR 1924 Pat 483, approved.

The appellant was the accused of an offence under section 7 read with section 4 of the Ordinance read with sections 109 and 110 of the Indian Penal Code. The prosecution alleged that on June 27, 1940, the appellant and his servant were found to have committed an offence punishable under section 73 read with s.4 of the ordinance read with the provisions of section 4 Of the Ordinance. On April 1, 1946, the Governor General of India promulgated the Prevention of Corruption (Amendment) Act, 1946 (Act No. XLIII of 1946), which came into force on January 12, 1946. The appellant was tried and convicted by the Additional Chief Presidency Magistrate under section seven read with SS. 4 and 5 Of the ordinance. On appeal the High Court confirmed the conviction but reduced the sentence to a fine of Rs. 1,000. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the Ordinance was not in operation as the Ordinance had ceased to exist on April 1. 1946, by virtue of section 7 of the Act and therefore the prosecution under the Ordinance could be continued in force only for a period of six months from its promulgation; (ii) the ordinance having been promulgated during the period specified in section 3 of the India and Burma (Emergency Provisions) Act 1940, it was not made retrospective in operation and (iii) the appellant was entitled to the benefit of the provisions Of section 7. Held:(i) The Ordinance was validly promulgated on January 13, 1946 and the Ordinance having been passed by the Indian Legislature without any limitation on its duration was to continue in force until it was repealed. The Ordinance having ceased to be in operation on July 11, 1953, the date on which the offence in question was committed by the appellant, and the appellant being rightly convicted by both the courts below, the period of his duration had to be determined having regard to the provisions contained in section 72 of the Government of India Act, 1935. (ii)(a) The words " for the space of not more than six months" in section 7(2) of the said Act were omitted from section 72 during the currency of the period mentioned in section 4 and the effect of such omission was that Ordinances promulgated under that sub section during the periods specified in s.3 of the Constitution were subject to no time limit as regards their existence and validity unless imposed by the Ordinance themselves or other amending or repealing legislation, whether by Ordinance or otherwise. The appellants were convicted under section 302 I.P.C. and sentenced to death by the Additional Sessions Judge, Jabalpur. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence of death passed on them. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the death penalty imposed upon the appellants was not justified as the prosecution had failed to make out a legally valid ground for awarding the lesser sentence; (ii) the prosecution must make out by special circumstances, why the sentence of imprisonment should be reduced to one of life imprisonment and (iii) the High Court erred in confirming the death sentence passed on the appellants. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The judgment under appeal is set aside and that of the High court confirmed. [1073G] 2.1 The legal position is what the Supreme Court has to do in this case. It is neither feasible nor desirable to define or describe every case. The only thing in a Judge decision binding party is the principle upon which the case is decided and for this reason it is important to analyse a decision and isolate from it the ratio decidendi. [ 1073B] 2:2 In the instant case, the death of the deceased was not proper or uncalled for. The crime may be shocking and yet the criminal may not deserve death penalty. The crimes in question are quite unmerited. The cases where the accused have been sentenced to life imprisonment are very unsettled and the law and that they should not intrude into the field of policy making. [1173G H] 3.1 In the present case, there is no reason why the High Courts should choose between a sentence of life sentence in the instant cases. The Sessions Judge has committed an error in human beings and the High COurt erred in upholding the death sentences passed under section 368(a) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973. [1273H; 1274A] 3:2.1 There is no need to define nor legally permissible for this Court to limit or circumscribe the connotation of "special reasons" mentioned in section 354(3). The judgment if not binding on the Supreme Courts under article 141 of the Constitution on the question of sentence must depend upon the facts and circumstances obtaining in such case. [ 1274B] 3 2:3.2 In a minority opinion, I.L.R. referred to. (i)(a) The death penalty is neither easy nor 'law declared by this Court under article 142 of the constitution so as to bind all Courts within the territory of India. [1375C D] (b) The sentence of capital punishment is not morally unacceptable to the contemporary society and found it shocking to their conscience and sense of justice. [1476D E] 3(i) In the case of a minority community, the legal obligation to pay capital penalty must relate not to the crime as such but to the criminal. The offence may be lesser superstitious or brutal in the absence of any specific indication in that behalf '. [1575E F] (ii)(a). The sentence imposed on the appellant was neither "erroneous in principle" nor was "arbitrary or excessive", or "indicative of an improper exercise of discretion". [1576G H; 1577A] (iii)(b) In a majority judgment, it is not every thing said by a Judge when giving judgment that constitutes a precedent. The judge is not bound to draw the same inference as drawn in the earlier case.

The appellant was appointed as a Lower Division Clerk in the Indian Railway. He was promoted to the post of Income tax Inspector in 1942. He filed a suit challenging the validity of departmental proceedings on the ground that he had entered into partnership with others under the name of Gautam Cycle Mart, Meerut and that he was confirmed early in 1952 as an Income Tax Officer. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the order passed by the Commissioner of Income Tax was void and inoperative. On appeal the High Court held that the appellant had been subjected to trial on allegations which had been the subject matter of previous enquiries and that the evidence did not support the charges levelled against him. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The question whether the appellant was given a reasonable opportunity to lead evidence and to be heard or not is essentially a question of fact. It is only when an opportunity denied is of such a nature that the denial contravenes a mandatory provision of law or a rule of natural justice that it could vitiate the whole departmental trial. [583 E] The doctrine of prejudice is based on no principle of law which is applicable to criminal trials and not on abstract principles of justice. [584 F] In the instant case, the State Government had issued a preliminary enquiry into the same charges against the appellant. The witnesses who were examined under the charge of conspiracy in contravention of the Government Servants ' Conduct Rules did not state that they had been disallowed by the punishing authority. They could have been given a further opportunity to meet a new case.

The appellants were the last purchasers of manganese ore from mines and minerals. The appellants contended that their sales of manga nesses to the Mines and Minerals Trading Corporation in short called the M.M.T.C. were complete within the State of Andhra Pradesh. The High Court held that there existed a bond between the contracts of sale entered into by the appellants with the M/s. T.C., and the actual exportation of the goods. The contract between the appellants and the M,T. C. was integrally connected with the contract entered into between the appellant and the foreign buyers on the one hand and the respondent on the other. The contracts between the parties were two separate and independent transactions of sale. The respondent contended that the contracts were different and there should be examination of five other contracts. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: 1.1 The contracts in question were different contracts and it was the S.T.,C. which entered into direct contract with their foreign buyers for export. The directions given by the Corporations to the merchants to place the goods on board the ship are pursuant to the contracts. These directions are not in the course of export, because the export sale is an independent one between the Corporation and its foreign buyers. [444E F] 1.2 In the instant case, the contracts between M/S. T.,C., & the ST.c. were two different and independent agreements of sale, that is, the seller 's duty was to place them on board. The export sale was an unconditional appropriation which passes the property. This is not because of any peculiarity of F.O.B. contracts but because in this type of contract the seller "s duty is to deliver the goods F.o.B., once they are on board, the buyer normally obtains a mate 's receipt which he transmits to the buyer and the buyer exchanges this for the proper bill of lading. In this sort of F .O. B. contract the almost univer sal rule is that property and risk both pass on shipment as soon as the goods are over the ship 's rail and if it should be material, the property and risks in each part of the cargo will pass as it crosses the (the course at the same moment when delivery is made to the steamer. [445C D] 2.1 In the case of a contract between a merchant and the S .T.P., the seller and shipper are the only authorities allowed to export out of our country. These corporations enter into direct contracts with their other foreign buyers who were the importers and the s.T."C. would not be in the progress or process of export. There is no room for two or more sales in the instant cases. The only sale which can be said to cause the export is the sale which itself results in the movement of the ' goods from the export er to the importer. [441E F; 445A] 2:2 In view of the decision of this Court in Serajuddin 's case, there cannot be two views possible. The appellant was employed as a salesman in the Delhi Cloth and General Mills, on a salary of Rs. 520 per month from 8th December 1973. The respondent terminated his services with effect from 19th October, 1974 on the ground that he had been appointed as a probationary period for six months and subsequently extended period of probation for one year. The appellant challenged the termination order by filing an application before the Labour Court under section 25F(1)(b) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. The Labour Court held that the termination was neither illegal nor improper but only on the basis of a notice dated 12th October 1974 issued by the respondent and as such the service of the appellant was terminated during the period of his probation on account of his unsatisfactory work which did not improve in spite of repeated warnings. The High Court dismissed the writ petition filed by the appellant under Article 226 of the Constitution. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The termination of service of a workman is ab initio void and inoperative. [532C] 1.2 In order to invoke the fiction enacted in sub section (2) of Section 25B the workman must be shown to be in continuous service for not less than one year under that employer who has retrenched him from service. Section 25F provides for a fiction to treat a workman in continuous Service for a period of one year despite the fact that he has not rendered uninterrupted service for a specified period. [525D E] 1:3 The termination would constitute retrenchment and by a mere declaration follows that he continues to be In service with all consequential benefits.

The appellant was appointed an Inspector of Consolidation by the Settlement Commissioner of Patiala and East Punjab States Union. He was served with a charge sheet setting out his mis conduct in respect of dereliction of duty, as illegal gratification from one Ude Singh and bad demanded Rs. 150/ as illegal remuneration from one N. The Settlement Officer submitted his report to the Deputy Commissioner, Bhatinda that he had received Rs.150/ as illegally gratification from another person and had demanded Rs 30/ as bribe from one S.I. The appellant was called upon to show cause why disciplinary action should not be taken against him if the allegations in the charge sheet were proved. The Deputy Commissioner by his order dated March 17, 1955 ordered that the services of the appellant be terminated forthwith and in lieu thereof he was asked to showcause why disciplinary proceedings should not he taken against the appellant if the allegation in the report had been proved. On February 22, 1955, the Settlement Officer reported that the chage relating to handcuffs had been found out and that the appellant had demanded a bribe from another officer. The order of dismissal was confirmed by the Deputy Commissioner on March 17. 1955. In appeal under article 226 of the Constitution the High Court held that the order of termination of employment was in contravention of article 311(2) of the Constitu tion as no reasonable opportunity to show ' cause against the order was given and dismissed the appellant 's writ petition challenging the order. The State appealed to this Court by special leave. HELD : (i) The protection of article 31(2), which is a temporary measure, cannot be invoked in cases where the stigma affecting his future career is appropriately described as one by way of punishment. But an order discharging a probationer following upon an enquiry to ascertain whether he should be confirmed, is not of that nature. The third proposition in the present case was whether the order is by way 'of punishment in the light of the tests laid down in Parshotam Lal Dhingra case. [719 D E] (ii) The appellant had been given no such opportunity and article 311 was therefore not complied with. [ 719 B C] State of Orissa vs Gopi Kishore Prasad, A.I R. 1960 S.C. 689; Ram Narayan Das vs State of Punjab, ; , followed.

The appellant State Government issued a notification dated July 25, 1969 for selection of Professors in supersession of the claims of the writ petitioners who were senior and more qualified persons. The Commission was consulted by the Commission and a member of the Commission was appointed. The appellant challenged the appointment of respondents Nos. 1 to 46 and others as Professors in the colleges. The High Court allowed the petition and quashed the State Government 's Order No. 643 dated July, 25,1969. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the Commission had been consulted in regard to the principles to be followed in making appointments to civil services and posts and in making promotions and transfers from one service to another and that the selection was invalid for that reason. HELD: The Commission had not discharged its function as a consultant either in regard t0 the principles set out in section 133(2) (b) of the Constitution of Jammu and Kashmir, nor was it necessary for the Commission to entrust the selection to a committee consisting of only one of its members so long as the Commission reserved to itself the right to approve or disapprove the Committee 's report. No argument to the contrary had been urged in this Court that what clause (b), of sub section (2) of section 133 required was that the commission shall be consulted; (i) on the principles, to be adopted in making appointment to civil service and posts; and (ii) on t0 its own motion.

The petitioner, a citizen of India, was convicted and sentenced to imprisonment for six months. The conviction and sentence were confirmed by the High Court in appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the privilege of the House of Commons under article 194(3) of the Constitution had not been infringed as the privilege, privileges and immunities of the Houses of Parliament and the members and committees thereof had not become subject to the provisions of the Constitu tion. Held, (per Sinha, C. J., Gajendragadkar, Wanchoo and Ayyangar, jj.), that the privileges, privileges, immunities and immunities enjoyed by the House were not of a kind like those enjoyed by it as a citizen under article 19(1)(a) of our Constitution; but they could be no longer subject to such restrictions as might be imposed on the fundamental right guaranteed by article 19 (1) (a). The privilege of Parliament under article 105(3), which is a part of the fundamental freedom, was not absolute and unfettered. It was not subject to any limitation or restriction imposed upon the Legislature in respect of its powers, privileges or immunities. The privileges enjoyed by members of the Legislative Assembly of Bihar were not such as could be claimed by them as they had been granted by the Speaker of the Assembly. The privilege which a member of the Legislature of a State was entitled to claim under article 197(3)(a), was subject to reasonable restrictions within the ambit of article 19, and the privileges enjoyed in respect thereof were not protected by article 194 (3) Of the Constitution. The right conferred on the Legislature by article 105 (3), read with article 194, was subject only to such limitations as might have been imposed under clause (2) of article 194. The fundamental right conferred by article 197 (1)(c) was not an absolute right and could not be restricted to a privilege granted by it. The Constitution did not provide for any limitation on the power of the legislature to make laws, but only provided for certain restrictions which were imposed upon its powers under clause 2(3). The privileges and privileges enjoyed and conferred by the members of a House of Parliament were subject to those of the United Kingdom and the United States of America. The provisions of clauses (1), (2), (3)(c), (4) and (5) of Article 194 were not intended to be exhaustive, so as to cover all matters which were not covered by the Constitution and could be extended to other parts of the country. The expression "the Legislative Assembly" in article 194 was wide enough to include a House in the United State of America within the meaning of article 195(3); it did not mean that the Legislature had the power to make, amend or repeal any law made by Parliament or the State Legislatures; it could not have intended that the House might be "the House of People" and therefore, the Legislative Council of the State was competent to enact a law relating to the procedure of the Executive. The powers, duties and immunities conferred on members of Parliament by article I36 (1).

The appellant State Government took over the management of a College on and from March 9, 1971. The college was taken over by the Govern ment in pursuance of the resolution of the managing committee of February 18, 1970. The Government prescribed qualifica tion for appointment as Reader and thereafter a formal agreement was executed between the Managing Committee of the College and the Governor of the State. The appellant 's writ petitions challenging the validity of the said clause were dismissed by the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that since they had all the requisite qualifications for appointment, as Reader, they were not entitled to be considered by the Public Service Commission for appointment and hence these respondents were not eligible to be consid ered by the State Government for appointment. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: 1. The condition of draw ing of Rs.600/ or more on the date of taking over, which has been laid down in the said circular as a particular qualification for eligibility for appointment is arbitrary and discriminatory. This condition has no nexus, whatev er, with the object underlying the qualification test in an educational institution having regard to quality, efficiency and progress in all respects. It is not unknown that private institutions generally have great handicaps in the matter of finance and oftener the teaching staff in a private college has not the same scales of pay and sometimes even has much lower scales than that of the Government colleges. It was one thing to lay down appropriate educational and invariable qualification for certain posts in a college and also teaching experience of a specified duration but com pletely different from those requisite for eligibility, and experience of teachers. [778C D] 2. The requirement of draw up a separate circular had no nexus with the objects underlying the qualifications test in the instant case. It has no relation, what is relating to qualification, whether prior or subsequent to the employment and also include promotion, (See The General Manager, South ern Railway vs Rangachari, ; , referred to. In the present case, the Respondents were not able to join the new service under the Government for the first time, and so could be in that sense fresh entrants. [777E F] 3. It cannot be said that the Respondents had been denied equal opportunity under Article 16 of the Constitution in the matters of appointment as Readers on the ground that they would be entitled to appoint ment as Readers. Their names shall be referred to the Commission, accordingly. Whether they will be suitable for appointment or Reader will depend upon the plea of absence of teaching experience in Government service, for consideration for appointment of a Reader under Article16. [779G H; 780A] 4. The Respondents are entitled to have considered for the post of Reader only on the plea that they will he suitable for selection for the Post of Reader. Their name shall be refer ted to the commission accordingly. [780C D].

The appellants applied for temporary permits under section 68 F(1 C) of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1939. The State Transport Authority rejected their application on the ground that once a scheme has been published in view of the provision contained in section 68F(1 A) the Corporation alone could grant temporary permit and if such an application is made by the Corporation and granted no one else was entitled to obtain a temporary permit. On appeal, the High Court held that since a scheme had been published for preparing and publication under section 69C of Chapter IV A of the Act, the Corporation only could not grant temporary permits and if the State Transport Undertaking wanted to operate vehicles on the route, it would be entitled to all the temporary permits to the exclusion of any other operator. In appeal to this Court, HELD: The correct approach would be that keeping in view the strength of the vehicles fixed by the competent authority, the authority should first examine the application for number of temporary permits made by a route. If the Corporation is unable to provide service by obtaining all requisite temporary permits, the State transport Authority or the Regional Transport Authority as the case may be, in exercise of power conferred specifically upon it by section 68(1) C) can grant temporary rights till the approved scheme is published yet if the Corporation has made application for temporary permit covering all the vacancies the matter ends there. But if the corporation does not apply for all the permits but only for some, the inescapable conclusion is that for the remaining strength the Corporation had made no application for the temporary permit, and section 68 G(1 D) would be squarely attracted. [985C E] In interpreting the provisions of Chapter V A of it, the competing claims between the Corporation as well as the other private operators may be examined with reference to the provisions Of the Act. But the overall consideration namely the service is for the benefit of the travelling public should never be overlooked for a moment. Reverting to the facts of this case if the approach of the High court was accepted it would lead to a startling result.

The appellant was the son of a Hindu undivided family governed by the customary law prevailing in the Punjab. The custom prevailing in Punjab was that the property in suit was ancestral property and he was entitled to challenge his alienation on the ground that it was not ancestral property as defined in the customary laws of the Punjab, but as regards the mortgage of the lands in question. Held, that the appellant had no right to bring the present suit. The doctrine of stare decisis is based on the principle of stare finality which is recognised by the Courts and has been applied consistently with the practice of the courts of Punjab. It is well settled that a decision which has been followed for a long period of time and which should be followed in similar cases, must be determined in each case by the discretion of the court, and previous decisions should not be followed to the extent that error may be perpetuated and grievous wrong may result. The principle of law is that the doctrine of prospective overruling is in applicable and should present no obstacle in holding that the earlier cases of the Full Bench decision were not correctly decided. Attar Singh vs Thakar Singh, (1937) L.R. 64 I.A. 250, distinguished. Held further, that in view of the fact that the Privy Council had laid down the law on the question of the applicability of the doctrine, the doctrine was applicable and the principle applied by the High Court to the case was correct. The rule of staresettled is that a principle of binding precedent should not apply where the law as it stood before the amendment of the Act came into force in the State.

The appellants were tried by the Additional Sessions Judge, Birbhum for offences under sections 449 and 307/34 of the Indian Penal Code. The prosecution case was that on the night of the 14th November, 1950 when Ebrar Ali was sleeping on the Verandah of his hut, these two appellants entered Ebir with the common intention of killing him and caused injuries to him. Ebber Ali died on the same day in furtherance of the common object of all of them to kill him and some of them held him down. Febbar Ali succumbed to his knees ' death and Habibullah was convicted under section 449 and section 307/ 34 of the Code. On appeal, the High Court acquitted Ebrrar Ali but convicted him under section 302 read with section 34 of Indian Penal code. The appellants contended that there could be no conviction under section 450 of the Penal Code unless murder had actually been committed "in order to the committing of an offence punishable with death" and that as the offence was not committed "with the purpose of .which the house trespass was committed", the offence of house trespass should have been committed. Held, that the words "in Order to ' have been used by the legislature not only in section 449 Of the Indian penal Code but also in the two succeeding sections, 450 and 457 of the Criminal Procedure Code, and section 456 of the I.P.C., clearly showed that the offence under section 307 read with s. 34 of I. P. C. was not sustainable in law.

The appellant was the nearest male holder of a property in Gurdaspur district. He died leaving behind his widow Musammat Melo and a daughter Musammee Devi. The respondent filed a suit for declaration that he was entitled to the lands mentioned in the plaint as well as to the sum of Rs. 1,539 7 0 as the daughter of the last male holder excluded the daughter from succession to the self acquired property of her father. The trial court decreed the suit but on appeal the High Court reversed the decree holding that the appellant was entitled only to succeed to non ancestral property in preference to collaterals of the deceased father and that the respondent had failed to discharge the onus that was cast on him by producing a Riwaj i am of the Gurdaspur District prepared by the revenue authorities. Held, that the High Courts were right in holding that as the appellant had failed in proving that the property in dispute was ancestral or self acquired it was sufficient for her to prove that she had discharged the onus which lay heavily on her. The evidence showed that the collaterals were not excluded from succession and that there was no evidence to show that the properties left by the deceased belonged to the appellant as a result of the production by him of the Riwj i am and that it was only the daughter who could have succeeded in preference. Held further, that even if the presumption as to correctness of the entry in the Rivi am of 1951 that the father had inherited property of his father has been rebutted by the evidence on record, the appellant must succeed to displace the initial presumption which if accepted would be weaker still and only a few instances would be sufficient to rebut it. Held also, further, the High court was right in its view that the evidence as to succession to self acquired properties of the respondent was reliable and trustworthy documents.

The appellant was the Managing Director of a company which was incorporated in India on April 1, 1948. He applied to the Collector of Calcutta under section 31 of the Indian Stamp Act for adjudication of duty payable on a power of attorney marked as exhibit A in respect of certain properties allotted to his share in favour of another member of the company. The Collector referred the matter under section 56(2) Of the Indian stamp Act to the decision of the Chief Controlling Revenue Authority who, by his order dated April 1. 1948, held that the Stamp duty was payable on the power "for as many as three years" as the proper duty payable had been paid in respect thereof as the appropriate duty. The appellant applied to Collector of Customs under section 30 of the Act for determination of duty and the Collector referred it under section 57(2). The Collector, however, held against him. On appeal by the Board of Revenue, the Board held that (1) the different capacities of the executant were distinct matters and must be construed as distinct matters; (2) the instrument in question was a power which was chargeable with a higher duty as on an instrument of partition; (3) the proper stamp payable on exhibit A was not one on those transactions but on those which were of the description mentioned in the Schedule to the Stamp Act, and (4) the instruments in question did not constitute distinct matters within section 5. Held, that the Board 's order was correct and must prevail. The words "distinct matters" used in section 5 Of the Act meant only different categories of instruments which could be executed by persons jointly and severally with others and that is specifically provided for in article 48(d). The question whether a power to attorney marked difference in respect to each of those capacities was one that will have to be decided on a consideration of the terms of the instrument, to comprise distinct matters, must depend on the nature and extent of the authority conferred thereby. The matter being not dealt with separately for purposes of section 5, it is not necessary to refer to the words of section 6 which are intended to cover distinct matters but must be understood in the light of the generally accepted notion of what are distinct matters. The question as to whether a Power of attorney relates to distinct matters or not will depend on a number of factors such as who are parties thereto, which is the subject matter on which it operates and so forth. The test is whether the instrument proposed to be executed must consist wholly or in part of the instruments. In the present case the instrument was executed by one person, who was acting as an executor or administrator of a deceased person. It was within the very nature of the general power of Attorney by the donor in favour Of the donees constituting the donee and there was delegation of power by him in both those capacities. The transaction was not a single transaction which could have been executed in different capacities but was one of several donors who were acting in his own individual capacity, and the position in law was exactly the same as if different persons join in executing a power in respect Of matters which are unrelated. The instrument in the present ease cannot be split up into separate instruments each comprising or relating to a distinct matter in so far as the different duties of the donor are concerned.

The appellant assessee was a Part B State. In 1948, the Saurashtra Income tax Ordinance, 1949, was passed which provided that "the provisions of the Act shall not be applicable to any depreciation allowance under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, if it had been in force before the previous year. " The assessee contended that no deduction should have been made on the strength of the words "any law relating to tax on profits of business" in paragraph 2 of the Removal of Difficulties Order, 1949. The High Court held that the expression "or any law relating thereto" in para 2 of that order meant "any laws or rules relating to income tax and super tax". In appeal to this Court it was contended that the words used in para. 2 of an order under section 12(1) of the Finance Act, 1950, were intended to qualify the phrase "anylaw relating to business" as they were intended and that the word "of a Part ' State" was not intended and must be given its ordinary meaning and should have reference to the provisions of that Order. HELD: (i) The words "of any law" in Paragraph 2 of this Removal of difficulties Order must be applied according to its terms. It is only when a difficulty arises in giving effect to the provision of the Indian Incometax Act, that the provision in the said paragraph would come into operation in a particular case. [227 D] (ii) The expression "of such Part B States" in Para 2 of article 31 must be read as including "any Law relating to taxes on profits" of business".

The appellant entered into a contract with the Mysore Construction Co.
