(M.C.) for the construction of a Main Station, Building and Industrial complex, for a public building of a power plant at an estimated cost of Rs.1,8.94 crores. The agreement provided that the intending tenderers would satisfy the tender documents within ten days from the date of receipt of the requisite clarifications from the M.C.C., and that the appellant would furnish the following information: (i) the intending tenderer should furnish the required information with requisite clarification in respect of the contract furnished in this regard, and if the K.P.C was not available to him, he would perform to the best of his ability and to the requirement of the person who wants to have the contract. If the KP.c. furnished a certificate that they had executed works including insulation in a power Plant, the certificate should be irrevocable. (ii) The appellant was required to furnish the requisite clarification within ten weeks from the commencement of the Contract. On receipt of this information, the appellant 's tender was accepted and he was given a certificate for the purpose of the M .C.A. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the said contract. The High Court held that the conditions required by the terms of the tender notice were only the three conditions set out in para I of the agreement, and that it was not necessary to give any details as to how the requirements had been fulfilled. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant: (1) The M.P., Construction Co., being a juristic entity, could be said to have been denied altogether the right to tender for the contract consequent on the delay in subordination; (2) The conditions and stipulations in para IV were not complied with; (3) The terms and conditions of the Tender Notice were not supplied along with the application for the tender; (4) The documents in question were not furnished with the request for extension of time, and (5) The contract was unlikely to be terminated by supplying such of the documents called for in para V. The Court held: (a) that the M C.A., had adequate opportunity to all the parties to make a representation against the proposed termination; (b) that it would not be proper to deviate from this established procedure; and (c) that there was no justification for interfering with the decision of the Government accepting the tender of the 4th respondent, even though they did not satisfy the requirements of para V, and the only thing required was that the applicant should supply information to show that he had experienced in insulation work and that he could carry out the contract; (d) that para V should also be treated as part of the prequalifying conditions for the supply of forms; (e) that if a party comes to court saying that the person issuing the tender has the right, it would be stopped from doing so, the Court will decline relief. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The requirement of para IV of the Agreement was not complied in all respects and the appellant was much better qualified for the time. [240E] 2.1 The conditions of para I were not fulfilled in this case. The clause and stipulations were not a minimum qualifyinge eligibility condition. It was not known on what grounds that application was rejected nor had that party come to Court with any such grievance. The question whether the course adopted by the KC. was justified or not, did not arise in this situation but that any deviation, if made, should not result in arbitrariness or discrimination. [241H; 242A] 2:2. The conditions, and stipulations of para II were not so in the instant case, a matter for the K C.E.C.(s) to consider whether the applicant fulfilled the pre qualification requirements set out therein.

The appellant was a evacuee. He filed an application under section 5A of the East Punjab Evacuees ' (Administration of Property) Act, 1947, for confirmation of certain transactions relating to evacuee property. The Custodian rejected the application on the ground that the transaction was not bona fide and that he had no intention to take action with regard to evacuee properties. He also refused to confirm the order of confirmation. The appellant then filed a suit in the High Court for confirmation under article 226 of the Constitution. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the Custodian bad no power to cancel the transfer by an order dated May 3, 1947. On appeal the High court held that the order was not open to appeal or revision but became final and conclusive. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the application for confirmation was not made within the time prescribed under section 27(3) Of the Act; (2) the order dated April 3, 1948, confirming the transfer was invalid as it did not comply with the provisions of section 5 A and (3) the High Courts had no jurisdiction to interfere with the orders of the Custodian. HELD: (1)(a) The application for the confirmation under section 25A of East Punjab Act XIV of 1947 was not barred by article 226. [1134 B] (b) The order of the High courts is such that it does not call in aid of the principle of merger or merger or con tention. Under section 5B of the Act, the Custodian has the power to exempt from any provision of the law of India if he considers that the legality or propriety of any order of any authority of the Government is affected by such order. [1105 C] (c) The words "previous operation of the repealed law" in section 58(3), which are new sections 5A and 5B, mean that this was subject to the repeal of an earlier law. The effect of the repeal is that all orders passed under the repealed laws shall be deemed to have been done or taken in the exercise of the powers conferred by or under this Act as if this Act were in force on the day on which such thing was done or action was taken. [111 F G] (d) The fact that the provisions in section 5 B of East India Act XIV Of 1947, which purports to indicate the effect of repeal of certain existing laws, are not relevant for deciding whether they apply to evacuee lands would have to be determined as if the repealing Act had not been passed. Section 6(b) of the General Clauses Act is a new provision and it cannot be construed as being subject to any such limitation. [112 G H] (e) The effect is that section 5(3)(a), which purports "to indicate the intention of the legislature followed by a fresh legislation" is not restricted to cases where the earlier Act has been repealed or replaced by a new legislation. It would have borrowed from out of some portions of the remaining sub sections (c), (d), (e), (f) and (g) of section 6 of the general powers conferred on the Central Government under section 8(3). [112 F H] The fact, however, that the appellant had no kind of interest in the land which could be taken into consideration by the Custodian General was not relevant. [114 G H; 115 A B] In the present case, the appellant did not have any kind of interests in the lands which were evacuee properties and the respondents had no means to get a declaration that they were evacuee property within the meaning of section 58 (3). The appellant could not call for a certificate under article 32 of the Constitu tion.

The appellant company was a registered trade union where the workmen employed in the tiny mills of the respondent company were getting their wages for the years 1965 and 1969. The dispute between the parties related to the practice or custom prevailing in the establishments before 1965. The reference was answered by the Tribunal in favour of the workers. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the bonus Act was a complete code, and as such the Act did not bar claims to customary bonus. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The Bonus Act speaks of payment of bonus on the basis of profits or gains and does not govern customary, traditional or contractual bonus. [605 D] (2) The definition of "profit" in section 2(g) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, includes a term of the employment itself. It is well settled that the word "profit", as used in the Act, means an expenditure on capital and not on revenue. [507 E F] (3) The dictionary meaning of the word 'profit ' is to take in every kind of bonus or one which may be paid by way of remuneration or other customary bonus, but it is quite conceivable that the codification may be of everything relating to profit bonus in which case other types of bonus are left untouched. [065 F G] (4) The term "profit ' as used by section 10(1)(d) of Bonus Act means a term which is defined as a term or term of service not sounding in or conditioned by profits. The definition does not include any kind of profit. It does not require calculation of profits, available surplus, because it is a payment founded on long usage and justified often by spending on festivals and the Act gives no guidance to fix the quantum of festival bonus; nor does it expressly wish such a practice. [076 G H] (5) The word " profit" as used under section 10 of the Bonus Act, although wide in its amplitude, includes bonus which is one specific kind of claim and perhaps the most common sense of the law is the soul of the statute. The dictionary clause in Ch. IV of the Act refers to a profit bonus and matters connected therewith and doesnot mean that there cannot be contractual bonus or other species of bonus. There is no categorical provision in the Bonus act, because, it deals with and only with profit based bonus as has been explained at some length earlier. [086 G] The definition given by section 2 (g) includes a "mere" bonus which was hitherto unwareted by mere implication from a statute unless there are compulsive provisions creating an industrial dispute. [096 A B] (6) The Industrial Tribunal had no jurisdiction to try the dispute referred to it.

The Punjab Superior Judicial Service Rules, 1963 were framed by the Governor of Haryana in consultation with the High Court. Rule 12 provided that seniority of members of the service shall be determined with reference to the dates of confirmation. The High Court held that the rules did not provide for inter se seniority of the members of service and that the direct recruits appointed directly from a particular source were entitled to claim seniority strictly in accordance with the provisions of rule 12. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High Courts had no power to interfere with the exercise of their administrative functions, and that (i) the power to confirm a District Judge was vested in the Governor and not in the High court; (ii) the High courts were not competent to frame rules regulating the recruitment and conditions of service of persons appointed to services and posts in connection with the affairs of the State as provided by rule 8(2); (iii) the direct recruit could be treated as confirmed only when a substantive vacancy was available; (iv) the seniority of promotees was rightly fixed by the length of continuous service on a post in the service irrespective of the date of confirmation; and (v) the rules were not ultra vires. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The power to regulate the recruitment, conditions of Service of persons employed to serve in the State, and to make rules for the purposes of that service is vested in a Governor and cannot be exercised in a manner which will affect or be detrimental to the control vested in him by article 235. [1056C] 2. The rule of rotation cannot be read into the rule of quota prescribed by rule 12 of the Punjab Superior judicial Second Amendment Rules, 1976 for the mere reason that on principle it is unconstitutional for reasons similar to those for which it was held by this Court in Haryana State vs State of Haryana, [1977] 1 S.C.R. 869, followed. 3.

The respondent State issued a notification dated February 18, 1986 under clause (5) of Article 371 D of the Constitution declaring that the local cadres in the State local cadres comprising of Revenue districts of Adilabad and Karimnagar may be treated as one division and Warangal. The appellant State Government issued another notification on April 29, 1988 amending cl. (5)(a) of article 371 D by substituting clause (2) of the said order with a new clause (3). The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the amended cl. The High Court allowed the petition holding that the zonal seniority is the criteria and not the basis for promotion, as envisaged under para 3(7)(ii) of Order dated April 29. 1988. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The phrase "or constituted otherwise" engrafted in the definition of local cadre in paragraph 2(e) read with paragraph 3(1) of order dated April 1, 1982 is only relatable to the power given by the Presi dent to the State Government to organise local cadres at its will tending to defeat the object of article 37 I D. The phrase 'or constituted other ' engrafted in para 2(a) is of wide amplitude but is only referable to the powers given by this Court to the state notwithstanding the expiry of the period of twelve months prescribed in sub paragraph (1). [574E F] 1.2 In exercise of the power under cl.

The mortgagor in possession of Gadi Sirampur and his father, who was the manager of a joint Hindu family, granted a permanent lease of four villages to one Hiraman Ram for a term of ten years. The lessee executed a mortgage of Gatuari in favour of the Manager of the Court of Wards in charge of the plaintiff 's estate during his minority. The mortgagor and the mortgagee were put in possession in execution of the decree. The mortgagee purchased Gadi Surait from the Court and sold it to the appellant who was one of the sons of the mortgagee. The appellant contended that the patta granted by the mortgagor was a mere mortgage and not a lease and that the mortgagee had no right to redeem the mortgaged property. Held, that the question whether the mortgagor in Possession has power to grant a permanent leases of the mortgaged properties depends upon the facts and circumstances of each case. It is for the lessee if he wants to resist the claim of the mortgagor to establish that the lease in his favour was granted the usual terms in the ordinary course of management. Such a plea if established and it must not be overlooked that the burden of proof in this matter is upon him. The true position has been stated in the following terms by the mortgagee: "The mortgagor, after he has granted the mortgage, does not take any interest whatever in the property demised to him. " The question whether an assignee from the mortgagor acquires no interest in the mortgaged land or from month to month in the case of agricultural lands or from months to month is a mixed question of law and fact. It has nothing to do with the mortgagor 's power to lease the mortgaged Property.

The petitioner, a company incorporated in 1978, was appointed as an arbitrator to execute the work within 9 months. The respondent filed an arbitration suit in the Calcutta High Court under sections 5, 12 and 33 of the for short the Act. The learned Single Judge held that the claim was hopelessly barred by limitation and dismissed the arbitration petition. On appeal, the Division Bench set aside the order of the Single Judge and restored the award. In the special leave petitions to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that (i) Clause 68 of the Contract provides for appointment of an arbitrator and when the petitioner has legally invoked clause 68 and issued notice to the respondent to refer the dispute for arbitration, the respondent is duty bound to appoint an arbitrator; (ii) Section 5(2)(b) of the Act contemplates that there must be an order of appointing an arbitrator or umpire and thereafter the same cannot be revoked except with the leave of the Court unless a contrary intention is expressed in the agreement. Dismissing the special Leave Petitions, ^ HELD: 1. The Court has power to enlarge the time so agreed upon just as they would now be applied in a court of law. [368C] 2. Clause 68 provides that when any disputes or differences have arisen, he should approach the Engineer in the first instance seeking reference of it to an arbitrator. In given circumstances and the factual background the Court may be justified to exercise the power under sections5 and 12(2) (b). The question whether the court would be justified in interfering with the authority to refer a dispute or differences arises only when the party defending the arbitration may voluntarily determine among themselves the procedure to be followed including the constitution of the arbitral tribunal to adjudicate the dispute or difference. [369D E] 3.

The property mortgaged by the appellants in favour of the respondent was an Estate within the meaning of section 2(1) of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950. The mortgagee filed a petition for passing a final decree on September 19, 1955. The estate mortgaged vested in the State of Bihar on January 1, 1956 as a result of a notification issued under section 3(1). A final decree was passed in the mortgage suit on October 1,1956. Thereafter the mortgagees applied to execute the mortgage decree against the respondent on the ground that the decree could not be executed in view of the provisions of the Act. The executing court held that the objection raised by the judgment debtors was barred under section 4(d) of Act. On appeal the High Court set aside the order and directed the execution of the mortgage debt against the appellants. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (1) the objection as regards the executability of the decree pleaded in the suit was barred by the principles of res judicata; (2) the bar of resjudicata was not applicable because the objection in question was barred because the objections were barred by principles of Res Judicata and (3) the mortgage was only a part of the mortgaged property which formed part of a mortgaged property had vested in it. HELD: The contention must be negatived. The decision of the executing court was affirmed by the appellate court but reversed by the High Courts. [913 B] The question whether the objection was barred was one relating to execution proceedings in which the decree holder sought to proceed against the estate of the debtor. In order to find out the implication of the clause extracted above it is necessary to bear in mind the object and purpose of the enactment. It is not correct to say that what vested in a State are only those interests not coming within section 6. Section 4(a) provides that no suit shall lie in any Civil Court 'for the recovery of any money due from such proprietor (proprietor whose estate has vested in him) or tenure holder the payment of which is secured by a mortgage of, or is a charge on such estate or tenure and all suits and proceedings for the recovery thereof shall be dropped. [936 D E] The true effect of the decisions of this Court in the case of Rana Sheo Ambar Singh vs Ram Saroop Singh, ; , is that where the whole of the property mortgaged is an estate there can be no doubt that the procedure prescribed by Chapter IV has to be followed in order that the amount due to the creditor should be determined by the claims officer and the decision of claims officer or the Board has been made final by the Act; but that section proceeds on an erroneous impression that another object which the Act wanted to achieve was to give some redress to the debtors whose estates have been taken away from them by the notifications issued under s.3. Therefore, in construing section 4 (d) it is not right to assume that the interests of the debtors affected by the provisions Of the Act do not fall within the protection of the , and again at page 578 " Having regard to the said scheme, it is difficult to confine the application of section 4 to execution proceeding in which a decree holder seeks to proceed with the estate. [ 914 F H] Ramnarain vs Basudeo, A.I.R. 1962 Cal. 272, approved.

The appellants, who were candidates for the post of Assistant Engineer (Civil) in the Central Public Works Department, applied to the Indian Administrative Service Commission for appointment to the I.P.S. Group 'A ' posts. The Selection Committee recommended that a candidate should not be less than 21 years of age and not more than 26 years as the case may be. The appellants were selected by the UPSC in accordance with the procedure laid down in Rule 4 of the C.S.(Main) Rules, 1987. The respondents filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the second proviso to Rule 4 on the ground that it was violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the second Proviso to Rule4 of the Civil Services Examination Rules,1987 did not violate Article 14 of the Constitu tion as it made a discrimination between candidates who had appeared for the IPSC examination and those who had been allocated to the service. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The second proviso is not ultra vires article 14 of lndia Constitution as it does not violate Articles 14 or 16 of ly. [92F] 1.2 The proviso to rule 4 of C.P S.S., Civil Services (Main) Rule 1987, which insists that a candidates who have appeared for an examination in the I PSC Examination shall be eligible three attempts at the examination. If the number of attempts are covered by any of the exception that may from time to time be notified by the Central Government in this behalf, every candidate normally can appear for all the permitted attempts at this examination but if he fails to join duty, the next Civil Service Examination will be notified. [94H; 95A] 1:3 The proviso carves out an exception to Rule 3 of CP SS, Civil Services Rules, which states that a person who has been allocated for the service shall not be eligible to appear again in the main examination unless he first resigns from the service and applies to him for appointment. [95E F] 1.(a) The proviso does not travel beyond the intent of the main rule putting any unreasonable restriction on the right to resigning a person or to I.A.S, or Central Services Group ' A ' to sit at the next civil Service Examination but it does so in the interests of efficiency and justice. [96F G] (b) The second Proviso is not unconstitutional as it has been enacted with the object of preventing the manner in which the right of a candidate in appearing for the competitive examination is to be exercised and, therefore, the restriction imposed in the second provisos cannot be said to be unreasonable. [97G H; 97A B] (c) The first proviso to r.

The appellant was detained under section 3(1)(i) of the . The detaining authority, as appears from the counter affidavit filed by the respondent, stated that the detaining authority was represented by customs officers of the rank of Deputy Collector of Customs and Superintendent of Central Excise. In the grounds of detention sent to the Government, it was stated that he had no statutory right to be represented by a retired Assistant Collector of Central excise. The appellant 's representation against the order of detention was rejected. The respondent filed a writ petition before the High Court which dismissed the same. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The detaining authorities have the assistance of the Deputy Collector and a Superintendent of central Excise. [790B] 1.2 The Advisory Board has no justification to refuse assistance of a friend in order to ensure due observance of the policy of law that a detenu is not entitled to representation through a lawyer. As has been indicated by this Court what cannot be permitted directly should not be allowed to be done in an indirect way. [789D] 1:3 The Advisory Boards have no justification for refusing assistance of an Assistant Collector as a friend was bad and continued detention of the appellant became vitiated. [788E F] 2.1 In the instant case, the detaining authorities had the assistance with the legal provisions and the procedure adopted by them. It is not for this Court to examine and assess what prejudice has been caused to the appellant on account of such denial. This Court has reiterated the position that matters relating to preventive detention are strict proceedings and warrant full compliance with the requirements of law. [ 791F] 2:2 The order of refusal by the Advisory Board to permit the appellant to be assisted by a lawyer was bad, because, it had been for the request of the detaining author ity or a lawyer to be appointed by him. It did not preclude the Board from granting assistance of such assistance to the appel lant in such circumstances.

The Government of India issued a notification under section 4(1) of the Defence of India Act, 1939, directing that the goods requisitioned and acquired by it shall be deemed to have been delivered at the disposal of the Government. The appellants who were the managing agents of the mills in respect of certain goods, were served with notices of acquisition on the managing agent of the Mills under r. 75 A(2) of Defence of lndia Rules, 1939. The notice stated that the managing agency was to be brought to the knowledge of the persons whose interests were being affected by it and that this was done in pursuance of the orders of requisition made by the Government of the United Provinces under r., 75 A (2). The appellants contended that the notices of requisition were invalid as they had been served on the owners of the goods and not on the mills as required by r. 77(1)(b) of Rules, but the same were issued in contravention of the provisions of the rule. Held, that the orders terminating the services of the managing Agents were valid and binding on them. The orders of requisitioning were properly and validly made and binding upon the respective defendants. The words "other principal officer" occurring in r. 2(a) of Order XXIX, r.2(b), do not mean that in law the title passed to the holder of the pucca delivery order as soon as it was issued even though it is not disputed that there was no actual delivery and the delivery was made absolutely representing the goods to which they related. The service of the notices on the appellants did not cease to be service on the same day as the managingors of the textile mills were served. Held further, that in view of the decision of this Court in Anglo Indian Jute Mills Co. Ltd. vs Owen, Cal. 838, the orders passed by requisition and notices of acquisi tion were valid.

The assessee company was a Private Limited Company. The assessment year concerned was 1963 64. The Income Tax Officer did not agree and the matter was ultimately taken up for hearing. The appeal filed by the assessee against the order of the Tribunal was allowed by the High Court. In the appeals to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that inasmuch as no order levying additional tax under Section 23A was made on or before the date relevant to the assessment year 1963 64, the said amount cannot be treated as a provision and not a reserve. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The assessee itself called it a provision. It did not call it a reserve nor was it set apart or appropriated as a reserve for profits, profits and, therefore, to be taken into account against gross receipts in the P & L. accounts and the balance sheet. On the other hand reserves are appropriations of profits, the assets by which they are repre sented being retained to form part of the capital employed in the business. Provisions are usually shown in the balance sheets by way of deductions from the assets in respect of which they were made whereas general reserves and reserve funds are shown as part of proprietor 's interest. [113E F] Metal Box Company of India Limited vs Their Workmen, ; , referred to. In Vazir Sultan Tobacco Co. Ltd. etc. vs Commissioner of Income Tax, Andhra Pradesh etc., , the distinction between provision and reserve is stated in the following words: "The distinction between provisions and reserve are charges against profits and therefore to be treated separately as reserve". [113F] In VIr Sultan Tobacco Company Ltd. vs Their Workman, ; this Court held that the distinction is between provision of a provision made towards a liability which had attached on account of the issuance of a notice was a provision, and not merely a reserve; it did not calls it a Reserve nor was set apart nor appropriated as an reserve. [114F] Vazir Qasim Sultan Tobacco Cooperative Ltd. & Ors. vs C.I.T., Andhra Pradesh, etc.

The petitioners who were appointed as Assistant Engineers in the State Service of Engineers (Class I) were subjected to competitive written and personality tests and in the nature of things only the very best could emerge out successfully. The respondents challenged the validity of the classification of personnel into those that were recruited on the basis of the competitive examinations and those that are recruited by selection, but both by Union Public Service Commission as well as by the President of India, the petitioners contended that they were recruited in Class I service and supported their claim on diverse grounds so as to obtain the result of the recruitment so adopted. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions holding that the classification was not challenged by the respondents across the list of competitive examinations but only a virtual review of the selection so adopted, and that the object of recruitment being different from the Indian Railway Establishment Board, there was no question of their entitlement to equal rights arose until and unless the temporary Assistant Engineers got absorbed into the Indian Railways Service of engineers Class I. Allowing the writ petition, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The distinction between the two services was well marked in Katyani Dayal 's case (supra) and the important question of equality was once for all settled. To find fault with it, at this juncture again on the touch stone of equality dimension would be to unsettle a settled position. That venture is neither in the interest of justice nor in the interests of service. When there has been complete absorption of the personnel of one service into the other and the seniority of the absorbers is to be reckoned from their date of absorption as stipulated in their appointment matters and as held by this Court with weightage of half the length of service as temporary Assistant Officers subject to a maximum of five years, it would otherwise be imprest, if the same has been earlier decided by a competent court by a judgment which became final. [1025C D] 1.2 The distinction is once for some people did get impleaded as parties in that case to project their. point of view and due to the nature or status of their absorption into the service. No doubt, the distinction and classification of temporary Assistant officers and members of the Indian railway Service of Engineer Class I fell within the same line as of Katyni Dayal ' Dayal '. [ 1026D E] 1:3. The distinction and the classification between the petitioners in a representative capacity and Engineers across also in a representa tion elsewhere, still it was a dispute raised before this Court which has been decided finally. A dispute now sought to be raised under Article 32 of the Constitution must be held to be barred by principles of res judicata as also in the rule of constructive res judicata. [1126F G] Katyabhai Dayal 'S case (Supra) distinguished.

The appellant was tried by the Special judge for offences under sections 302, 307 and 392 of the Indian Penal Code read with section 34 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The prosecution case was that on a particular day the appellant along with two others were found guilty of murder and sentenced to death. On appeal the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence but reduced the sentences to imprisonment for life. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (1) the provisions of section 11 of the West Bengal Special Courts Act, 1950, which authorises the State Government to direct any class of cases or offences to be tried by a special tribunal, were invalid as being violative of article 14 Of the Constitution; and (2) the restrictions imposed on the fundamental right under article 19(1)(f) of the Constitution are not reasonable within the meaning of article 19. Held: (i) that the provisions in section 11 are valid and do not violate article 14 of the Constitu tion. The power conferred by section 11 is subject to the limitations contained in article 14. It is not a law made by Parliament but by the State Legislature or system of administration. The restrictions imposed by the impugned Act on the exercise of such powers are reasonable within that meaning. The provisions of the Act do not contravene article 14 and therefore they violate articles 14 and 19(i)(f). (ii)The expression "acts done in pursuance of an order made under clause (a) of sub section (1), of section 3 of the said Act, is wide enough to include all acts done or things done by a person who may be charged before an ordinary court with similar offences. The word " act" in section II of the Ordinance means a thing done in execution and not done in the course of official discharge of the official duty. The words "classes of offences" in article 19 (1)(d) do not mean merely that the classifi cation must be rounded on an intelligible differentia which distinguishes persons or things that are grouped together from others left out of the group, and that differentia must have a rational relation to the object sought to be achieved by the Act. The State of West Bengal vs Anwari Ali Sarkar, [1954] S.C.R. 435, referred to. (iii)The word "act" in the section means something done on an objective basis and not on any reasonable basis having a relation to its object. The impugned Ordinance was therefore valid.

The appellants were convicted under section 302 I.P.C. and sentenced to death by the Sessions Judge, who was of the opinion that they had been falsely implicated in a case which was pending before the police at about 2 p.m. on the night between 16th and 17th February 1968. The High Court accepted their evidence and convicted them under section 396 I. P.C., and sentenced each to death. On appeal by special leave, it was contended that (1) the F.I.R. was lodged at the Police Station within the meaning of section 157 Cr. P C; (2) the delay in lodging the Fard regarding the occurrence had not been explained and (3) the evidence of P.W. 2 was corroborated by the medical evidence, and that the High Court erred in holding that the FI.P.,C. should have been relied on for basing its conviction. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1(a) The F.S.I., the investigating officer and the Sessions judge were of the view that a formal F. I.R., was recorded to the effect that the information given by P.Ws. 2 and 3 had been lodged at about 6 p. m. on 17th Feb. 1968. [577F] (b) The evidence of the doctor who conducted the postmortem examination was not corroborated by any other evidence. It is not possible to agree with the Sessions Court that no reliance could be placed on the evidence given by the doctor for holding that P. Ws. 2, 7 and 8 were in fact recovered from any of the appellants. [578F] In the instant case, the F I.I,R. shows that the first information report was lodged within a short time after the occurrence. The FI R.I 's evidence is not corroborated on any material particulars. It has been deposed by P W. 2 that he had recorded the FL1 in the Fi dence of the eastern kotha of the house of the deceased and that it was in working condition. The presence of the lantern in the eastern Kotha at the time of occurrence could not be doubted. [580D E] (c) There is no reason whatsoever for rejecting the evidence on record as there is no other circumstance to show convincingly that the appellants had entered the house and assaulted her husband fatally and that some of them caused injuries to her and committed dacoity by looting properties worth about Rs. 2.700/ from her house. [581G H] (d) The High court was in error in holding the FIII. R. to have been lodged with the police. [583A B] (e) There was no reason for rejecting evidence of PW. 2 who had seen the appellants and the villagers at the scene of occurrence left the place. It could not therefore be said that there was any motive for concocting a false story so as to attract section 34 I.p.C.[581F G] (f) The prosecution has proved the case against the appellants beyond all reasonable doubt and that their conviction under section 201 I.PC. and the sentence awarded to them by the trial court and confirmed by the High Courts are correct.

The appellant employer took a contract for the purpose of discharging its employees. The employer terminated the employment of some of the employees during the initial period of probation and of some others during the extended period on the ground of unsatisfactory service. Thereupon an industrial dispute was raised by the workmen in respect of their termination and the Labour Court held that section 25F of the had no application to the effect that the discharge was invalid. The appellant employer came up before the High Court challenging the award. A single Judge dismissed the writ petition holding that the order of discharge amounted to retrenchment as defined in section 2(oo) of the and those orders were bad for noncompliance with section 25 F. The Division Bench upheld the decision of the Single Judge. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant employer that (i) the services of the employee were probationers at the time of discharge from service; (ii) the order terminating the services was bad for non compliance with section 2 (oo); and (iii) those orders being bad for comply with section25F. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The expression 'retrenchment ' in section2(oo), and as used in section 25FF of the has no wider meaning than the ordinary accepted connotation of the word. It means the discharge of surplus labour or staff by the employer for any reason whatsoever otherwise than as a punishment inflicted by way of disciplinary action. [790B] 2. The effect of non compliance of section 25E is that every case of termination of service except those not expressly included in section25 F or not expressly provided for by other provisions of the Act such as sections 25FF and 25FFF. It is not necessary to dilate on the point nor to refer to the earlier decisions of this Court in Hariprasad Shivshanker Shukla vs A. D. Divikar, [1971] 1 SCR 591; Santosh Gupta vs State Bank of Patiala ; and Mohan Lal vs Management of M/s Bharat Electronics Ltd., Desai, J.T. 1987 (2) S.C.R. 592, referred to. 3. The stage has come when the view indicated in Money 's case has been "break down" and there is no scope for putting the clock back or for an anti clockwise operation. Once the conclusion is reached that retrenchment as contemplated under section 2 of the covers every case, of termination, except those which have been embodied in the definition, discharge from employment or termination of services of a probationer would also amount to retrenchment. [789D E] 4. The question whether the discharge is invalid or not depends on the language used by this Court and there can be no scope of putting theOA back or to consider the earlier conclusion. [ 791E] 5. The High Court has rightly come to the conclusion that in these cases the order is bad and consequently it upheld the Award of the Labour court which set aside those orders and gave appropriate relief. These appeals are dismissed.

The assessee, a dealer in unclaimed and unconnected goods for money consideration, filed returns of sales effected by it of unclaimed and unrelated goods year after year and paid sales tax pursu ant to the assessment made by the Sales Tax Department. The Commercial Tax Officer assessed the assessee as "dealer" under the Bengal Finance (Sales Tax) Act, 1941. The assessee applied for registration as a dealer under the Act. The commercial Tax Officer examined the case and did not accept the contention that the assessee was not a "dealer". On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the disposal of unclaimed goods for valuable consideration was a regular feature of the assessee 's activities and that therefore the assessee fell within the scope of the Act and accordingly directed registration of the firm under the provisions of the Bengal Act. In second appeal, by the assessee, the Tribunal held that since the disposal was not carried out in the course of business, it could not be treated as a " dealer" within the meaning of section 2(c) of the West Bengal Finance Act, 1940. The High Court answered the question in favour of the Revenue and against the assessee. Dismissing the appeals by the Revenue, this Court, HELD: 1. The activity of so disposing of the goods was adjunctive to the principal activity of the carriage of goods by the Railway. It is an activity which may be regarded as necessarily incidental or ancillary to its business as carrier of the good. It seems to South Eastern Railway was a "manufacturer" for the purposes of the Calcutta Finance ( Sales Tax) Amendment Act, 1942. In the other case, the assessee Eastern Railway disposed of scrap and unserviceable material lying with it. The case is covered directly by the decision of this Court in the District Controller of Stores, Northern Railway, Jodhpur vs The Assistant Commercial Taxation Officer and Another, [1976] 37 S.T.C. 423. [781 D E] 2. In a case where the good came into possession of the asses see it acquired rights over the goods under section 56 of the Railways Act enabling it tO sell the goods. The question is covered by the decisions of this court in the case of the District Magistrate, Jodhpur v. Assistant Commercial Taxes Officer and Anr., [1976]. 37 S C.R. 423, except that the assesseee is the Eastern Railway and it is engaged in selling scrap and inefficient material lying within the definition of "dealer", under the West Benga ly Act. [780 E F] 3. The Tribunal was right in holding that the High Court was right on the view that the disposed of the case did not indicate that the Railway concerned was carrying on business as a 'dealer ' under the Assam Finance (Sale Tax)Act, 1941 and therefore the Controller of stores, Eastern Railway is a dealer for the purpose of as sessment under the said Act. It was an activity that of so disposed of goods which could be regarded necessarily incidental to its commercial business as carriers of the same.

The appellant company was incorporated in 18th and 19th of the Indian National Bank. The respondent, a Director of the said company, was appointed as the General Manager of the Insurance Company in 1938. In 1953, the appellant filed a complaint against the respondent for offences under section 409 I.P.C., and section 409 read with section 120B I. P. C. alleging that the respondent had committed breach of trust by transferring funds to the Union Agencies through its branches and that the amount received from the Bank was not in the nature of capital expenditure within the meaning of section 409, I.p.C. The appellant contended that the transactions were not entered into with the Bank and that they were not authorised by the respondent to deal with and sell securities. The trial court held that the transaction amounted to a breach of the trust and dismissed the complaint. On appeal, the High Court held that it was not proved that the securities were in fact sold or pledged and that even if the transactions had been entered into under section 239 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the respondent could be said to have acted in contravention of the provisions of section 120 B, I P C. The High Court also held that as the appellant did not know about the transaction it was entitled to take action under section 408 Of the Indian Penal Code. On further appeal by special leave, Held: (i) The mere fact that the appellant had entered into a contract with the respondent Agencies for the purchase of the securities or for payment of money without transferring the same to the Bank did not make him liable for the sale price which had to be credited to the account of the Bank. (ii)The transaction was not one of agency within section 409 Of the Code, as it was in respect of a contract relating to the purchase or sale of securities or to any other dealing with the same matter. The fact that a person who held the post office of the Union Government had been asked for the transfer of the shares and could have known that the said temporary loans were being given by him on behalf of the appellant, did not mean that he was being informed for the first time that the temporary loans arranged by him for the Union agencies Ltd., in the name of the Imperial Bank of India. (iii)The mere fact of coincide with the original diversion of the funds of the respondent Bank to the appellant 's branch did not necessarily mean that Gurha had been informed for a long period of liquid funds to be utilised in the fictitious purchase of securities. In the present case, the transactions amounted to the first sale and were therefore illegal. (iv)The fact that there was no question of any loss to the respondent by reason of the information supplied by him did not affect the appellant company 's control over the respondent agencies. The accounts of the bank were kept in a separate building and being looked after by Gurha, the account books were maintained by the appellant with the Chartered Bank at Delhi. (v)The conduct of the parties showed that the money was received by them on September 22, 1955 and that it had been paid to the Imperial bank on September 17, 1955. The mere circumstance that the accounts of a particular company were not alleged to be fictitious did not lead to any inference that the funds were being sold or borrowed for the Bank in the ordinary course of business of the company. (vi)The appellant was guilty of breach of contracts and had no control over its affairs.

The appellants were holding permanent posts in the ministerial service of the Secretariat Service of the State of Gujarat. The State Government issued a notification dated August 19, 1966 under article 309 of the Constitution directing that the posts of clerks in the Secretariat service of a Secretariat Service should be deemed to have been allotted to serve in connection with the affairs of the said Secretariat and that they should be treated to have continued to be regularly appointed in the posts shown against their names in column 4 of the statement. The appellants were not absorbed in the Ministerial staff of the secretariats of the Part B State of Saurashtra and Kutch. By a notification issued on August 19 1966, the Government of Bombay sanctioned certain rules called "The Allocated Government Servants (Absorption, Seniority, Pay & Allowances) Rules 1957". The appellants challenged the validity of the order by filing a petition in the High Court. The High Court held that the order violated r. 138 of the Recruitment Rules framed by the Government and quashed it. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The High Courts were right in holding that the rules violated r, 138 of Recruitment Rules. [519 D] The State has the authority to transfer subject to the Constitution and the rules made under article 310 any public servant to render service which by his training and aptitude he was competent to do. Transfer of the personnel from the States of Saurashtra to the Secretariat in the State is not affected on account of absorption and integration of service under the or the Allocating Government Servants Rules, 1957. [525 E] N. Raghavendra Rao vs Deputy Commissioner South Kanara, Mangalore, ; , followed.

The Punjab General Sales Tax (Amendment and Validation) Act, 1967 was passed by the Punjab Legislature in 1948. The petitioners challenged the validity of the Punjab General sales Tax (Amend ment and Validation and Validation ) Act, 1968 on the ground that they were violative of articles 14 and 19(1)(f) of the Constitution. They contended that the provisions of the Act were ultra vires and void as they contravened article 14 and were also unconstitutional being in violation of Articles 14 and19(1) (f). The High Court dismissed their petitions. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the Act did not suffer from any of the defects in the Act and was, therefore, valid. HELD: (i) The Act does not sufferfrom any of its defects. It is well settled that the legislature of one of the States seeks to amend a law passed by a composite State. This is what the legislature has done and there is nothing that can be said against such amendment. In regard to Haryana, the rate of tax was also subject to the legislative competence of the Legislature in that area. The Act has been amended in the new States in relation to the area of that State and it is inconceivable that this could not be within the competence of Parliament. If the argument were accepted then the Act would remain unhampered unless the composite State came into existence once more. [555 E F] (ii) The scheme of the State Reorganization Acts makes the laws applicable to the new areas until superseded, amended or altered by the appropriate legislature in the old States. This was what the Legislature has done. It was not within the competency of the legislature to pass such an Act retrospectively. The defect pointed out is the self same defect which was noticed in Bhawani Mills case. [557 B C] (iii) The new Act applies now as an independent Act to each of the areas and is subject to its legislative competence in that Area.

The appellants were the mortgagors of a joint family business. The mortgage bond was executed by them in favour of defendant No. 2 and defendants 3 to 7 who were interested in a joint Hindu family business, but they did not pay the amount due under the decree as scaled down by the High Court. The question for determination in this appeal was whether the debt due to the appellants was a debt scaled up by the judgment debtors or not. Held, that the contention must fail. The fact that in a mortgage debt when the loan has been advanced to more than one person, if one of the debtors happens to be an agriculturist while others are not, the agriculturist debtor would certainly be entitled to have his debts scaled under the provisions of the Agriculturists ' Relief Act, 1922, but this is inherent in and arises out of the proposition established by the decisions already given. The Madras Agriculturists ' relief Act is a special statute which aims at giving relief not to debtors in general but only to a specified class of debtors viz., those who are agriculturists as defined in the Act. It is to be noted that in case of a mortgage decree when the loans have been advanced, to more persons than one, if the one of them happens to he an agriculturist, while others arc not,the agriculturist debtor, would certainly he enti tled to have their debts sched down under the Act in spite of the provision of general law which prevents a mortgagor from denying the liability of the interest which he owns in the mortgaged property to satisfy the entire mortgage debt. The judgment debtors are the mortgagors themselves and according to the plain provisions of section 8 of the Madras Agriculturists Relief Act they were entitled to get the benefit of the scaling down of the decree in favour them, though their rights remained indivisible.

The appellants filed a suit against the respondents for recovery of rent and arrears of hotels and lodging houses. The respondents contended that they were trespassers and had no right to be on the premises. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court in appeal reversed the decree holding that the City Civil Court had no jurisdiction to entertain the suit. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The suit was not one between a landlord and a tenant. The suit did not cease to be a suit between a lessor and a lessee. The plaint in the suit disclosed no cause of action. [374 D] (ii) The High Court rightly decided that the suit filed by the appellants could not be determined by the City civil court. [376 E] (iii) The suits were essentially a suit for possession of premises within the meaning of section 28 and the City of Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, was by a landlord. Eviction of the tenant and those to whom he had sublet the premises were sought on the ground that they had been wrongfully sub let. [375 G] (iv) The City Civil court could not decree the suit for eviction unless its claim to remain in possession was established under the Act or any of its provisions. [373 A B] (v) The Bombay Rents. Hotel and lodging House Rates (Control) Act, 1944, did not apply to the present case because the suit was one relating to possession of the premises which did not arise out of the Act.

The appellant was appointed managing director of a private company in the same name. The appointment of the appellant was made after the commencement of the Act and his appointment was confirmed by the appointment of another director. On the question whether the appointment was void under section 312 Of the , HELD : (i) The word "assignment" does not mean merely "appointment". The word 'assignment" in section 312 means "appointments". The words "assign" and "dissenting" are used to denote the putting in of someone in a vacancy. The word is not used as meaning "appointment", but it has to be given by the articles, such as "perpetual management". It does not include appointment. [334 C D] (ii)The word "asignment ' does not refer only to appointment but also to appointment. The words are not intended to mean appointment. In section 312 of the new Act a power is given to an officer appointed after a term of his office, by a company in his place and this power is not an appointment at all. [336 E] (iii)The appellant Govind had been lawfully appointed as managing director in his places. He was not appointed as such but only to the extent the articles permit him to be appointed otherwise than by the company. The Act did not intend that he should appoint any person to be the managing director. Such a director is not the chosen representative of the shareholders and the shareholders cannot claim to have a say in the appointment. Such an appointment does not involve any appointment. Therefore, section 312 was not concerned with such an appointment. It would therefore be an improper exercise of the power under that section to hold that all appointments of their successors by directors would be assignments within the main part of section 86B of the old Act. [333 G H] (iv)The proviso to section 86 B does not indicate that it was intended that the word "appointing" in the main Part of section 87B should include appointment". The proviso is intended to exclude appointment but for the proviso, it would be an unwarranted extension of this principle to hold, that all appoint ment of directors would he assignments within its main part. [332 B C] (v)The words "as respects" in sub section (2) of section 83 of the , are wide enough to include "appointment" and thus exclude appointment.

The appellants are the partnership firm and are the partners of the respondent firm. The respondent filed an eviction petition being H.R.C. No. 641/75 against the appellants and one other partnership firm, carrying on business in the name and style of M/s Adeshwar Glass Mart on the ground that they were unlawful sub tenants. The Trial Court held that the appellants had unlawfully and without the consent of the Respondent sublet the shop let out to the said M/ s. Adeshwar glass Mart and were liable to be evicted for contravening the provisions of Section 10(2)(ii)(a) of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960. The Appellate Authority dismissed the appeal upholding the finding of unlawful subletting by the appellants. The High Court in second appeal held that it was only by virtue of the provisions under order 30 of the Code of Civil Procedure 1908 that a firm can sue and be sued in its own name without the partners being impleaded as respondents or serving them as partners and hence, the eviction petition was not maintainable at all. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The appellants are entitled to have their claim for eviction set out in the eviction proceedings either and hence the ratio laid down in Chhotelal Pyarelal case is directly applicable to the case before this Court. [420B] 2.1 In the instant case, no such objection has been raised at all till the stage of Special Leave and it is surely not open to the appellants to raise such an objection at this stage at all.[420C D] Chhotelial Pyarelal, the partnership Firm and others vs Shikharchand, [1969] 1 S.C R. 156, relied upon by Mr. Nayar, are cases where the partnership firms and others were also joined as respondents in the suit on the grounds that they had unlawfully, and without their consent, sublet the said shop to the appellant firm. [426D E] Chh landlady Sohanlal, vs Shikhachand, ; , referred to.

The Andhra Pradesh Land Reforms (Ceiling on Holdings) Act, 1976 was passed by the Andhra Pradesh Legislature in exercise of its power under Article 246(1) of the Constitution. The Andhra Pradesh Act was enacted with retrospective effect from 1st January 1975 and by this amending Act certain provisions were made which included inter alia the introduction of section 41A into the Land Reforms Act. Section 3(f) created an artificial unit called "family unit" by defining it as "family units". The term "family" in section 2(n)(ii) was defined to mean a family unit consisting of more than five members and a family within the meaning of section 2 (m) which includes a family consisting of a family member. Section 4 provided that the ceiling area in the case of an individual who is not a member of a Hindu family unit shall be deemed to belong to category D in that Schedule. The appellant, a Hindu undivided family, was sought to defeat an agrarian reform enacted by the State or the benefit of weaker sections of community of community. It was contended on behalf of the appellants that the Andhra Act was ultra vires and void as being outside the legislative competence of the Andhra State Legislature. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The definition of "family", in section 3(j) is materially in the same terms as the definition of family unit in the Andhra pradesh (Ceilingon Holdings) Amendment Act, 1977. [1155E] 2.1 The Andhra Act is an agrarian reforms legislation and it is protected against challenge on the ground of infraction of Articles 14, 19 and 31 by the protective umbrella of Article 31A. [1102F] 1.2 In order to fall within the exclusion, the land must be entered in the revenue or land record before the appointed day as for the purpose of agriculture and must also not have been specified in the master plan for a purpose other than agriculture. The expression "family area" in Section 2(o) is defined in section (2)(a) to mean any land within the limits of an urban agglomeration and includes land deemed to be agricultural land under this Act. [1056F G] 1:3. In order that a divided minor son would clearly be included in the family unit and by reason of section 4 his land whether self acquired or obtained on partition would be liable to be clubbed with the land held by the other members of the family Unit. The land obtained by the divided minor sons on partition will be liable for assessment under the ceiling Act. No sooner such area is notified to be an urban land, the Central Act would apply in relation to land situate within such area. [1015G H] 1 :4. In the instant case, the Andhra Pra Pradesh Act came into force on 1st of January 1975. The Act was not enacted by Parliament and therefore it could not have legislative competence to provide for imposition of ceiling on land situate outside the State except as provided in section 4 which provides for inclusion of such lands in the holding of an undivided family. [1005A B] 1 5. The term 'land ' is defined under section 2.(o) to include inter alia an individual and a Hindu Undivided Family. The word 'person ' is used in section 42(a)(ii). Section 4 defines 'family unit ' to mean the urban agglomerations for the acquisition of such land in excess of the ceiling limit, to regulate the construction of buildings on such land and for matters connected therewith or ancillary thereto in such manner as may be prescribed by the Rules. [1000B C] 1 6. The Central Act imposes a ceiling on holding of land in urban agglomerated areas other than land which is mainly used for the purposes of agriculture, in an urban area.

The appellant company was a private limited company and its workmen were dismissed for misconduct. The company terminated the services of all other workers on the ground that they had failed to produce satisfactory evidence in support of their action. The workmen contended that the workmen were entitled to be reinstated with effect from August 24, 1953, when the place of employment was closed. The Industrial Tribunal held that the appellant was justified in keeping the workmen in a position and that the company should not have interfered with the decision of the Company unless it found that the decision was mala fide or amounted to victimisation. On appeal by special leave: Held, (i) that the finding of the Industrial Tribunal that the charge against the workmen was completely baseless was based on no evidence and the Industrial Tribu nal had misdirect ed itself as to the true scope and effect of the reference. The findings of the Tribunal were erroneous and must be set aside. (ii)The Labour Appellate Tribunal had not committed any error in holding that the respondent company was justified by the finding that it had held a regular and proper enquiry in which the appellant did not give an opportunity to the workmen to explain their conduct. The Tribunal had also misdirected itself as regards the appellant 's misconduct. (iii)The findings of fact recorded by the Industrial Court on this point were erroneous. The evidence showed that the workers were found guilty of unauthorised absence and that they were not in a fit case for reinstatement. The finding of fact was based upon the evidence of the workmen and it was not possible to hold that the Tribunal had committed any misdirect ment with regard to their conduct prior to August 24.

The University of Rajas than invited applications for the post of Professor in Botany. The Selection Committee constituted under section 5 of the Rajasthan University Teachers and Offi cers (Selection for appointment) Act, 1974 recommended the names of Dr. G.S. Nathawat for the said post. The name of Dr, G. S. Natany was mentioned in the reserve list by the Selection Committee. The appellant Dr. Urea Kant was selected on 20th June, 1989 and he was appointed as Professor in the department of Bot any year. The respondent No. 1 filed a writ petition in the High Court initially challenging the appointment of Dr Urea Koshy on the ground that the selection committee was properly constituted. The Single Judge held that the constitution of the Selection Commit tee was valid but as regards the appointment, it was held that once a person selected by the Committee had joined, that post was filled and some vacancy was caused thereafter a fresh Selection Committee should have been constituted. Aggrieved against the order of the Single Judge, the appellant preferred special appeal before the Division Bench which dismissed the same. Hence these appeals by special leave. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Court committed an error in restricting the scope of reserve list only against the post for which the selection was made and which according to the High court could only be available to the incumbent in the reserved list if the person recommended in the main list did not join such post. Such interpretation is not borne out from any of the provisions of Section 3(1) of the Act of 1974. The very purpose of preparing a reserve list would be defeated if the view taken by the High Courts is accepted that once the person selected for appointment has joined that post then selection made by the committee is exhausted and the reserve lists are being prepared from the reserve List against future vacancies arising on account of resignation, retirement, promotion or otherwise. This is done in view of the fact that it takes a long time in con stitutional meeting which has a cumbersome procedure and in order to avoid ad hoc appointments keeping in view the interest of the student community. The selection committee in the present case was constituted for the selection of Professor. In the absence of any other university or universities, the Selection committee had approved and recommended the name of the appellant Dr Uran Kant as a Professor in a University. [422B C] 1.2 The High court committed an apparent error in taking the view that a regular vacancy of Professor having arisen on the retirement of Dr (Urea Kant) and such Selection Committee had approved, and recommended his name for appointment on the post. [420C D] 2.1 A reading of Section 5 with section 6(4) makes it quite clear that the Selection Committees constituted shall recom mend not only the candidates selected by it in order of merit but shall further prepare a reserve List to the extent of 50% of the vacancies and persons kept in the Reserve list will be considered as having been selected for the concerned post and shall also be entitled for appointment if any vacancy is caused during the validity period of the reserve panel.

The petitioners challenged the constitutional validity of the Bombay Municipal Corporation Act, 1888 (Bom. III of 1888) and the provisions of sections 9 and 10 of the Act on the ground that they infringed their fundamental rights under articles 14, 19(1)(f), 21 and 31 of the Constitution. The petitioners contended that section 19(3) of the said Act was ultra vires the State Legislature because it gave a retrospective operation to the provisions contained in sections 4 to 16 of the impugned Act which provided for extension of the period of four years from time to time by a notification issued under section 6 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894. The respondents contended that the petitioners had no right to acquire any land designated for public purposes under section 7 of the aforesaid Act and that the power conferred on them was arbitrary and uncontrolled and unguided and uncanalised power in that they exercised arbitrarily and without any notice to the public. Held: (i) The power given by section 19 of the City of Bombay Municipal Act, 1949, to declare a town planning scheme as for the purpose of carrying out the purposes of the city within the meaning of section 7 was not arbitrary and unguided. It was not reasonable to say that in view of the immensity of the task of the local authorities to find funds for the acquisition of lands for public purpose, a period of ten years was not too long. The power conferred by section 9(3), therefore, vested in the Town Planning Officer only after giving notice to all the applicants whose interest might be affected by such modification and no opportunity could be given to them to make representations without any opportunity to them. (ii)The petitioners had failed to establish that the Town planning scheme was sanctioned under section 22(1) of Act and the power exercisable under sections 9, 10, 11, 1.2 and 2 of the Town Plan were unguided, uncontrolled and uncanalised. The provisions of the section did not in any way affect the validity of sections 4 and 11(3). (iii)The scheme was a valid enactment and was not one which offended article 14 of the constitution. The scheme as framed by the Town Development Officer was a reasonable one in the circumstances obtaining at the time when the statute was enacted. The legislature was aware that a good deal of time might elapse before the development plan was finally sanctioned and that is why provision was made for extension or extension of time to make other provisions for affording the slum dwellers better living conditions. (iv)The power conferred under sections 4, 5 and 11 (3)of the Act was neither uncanalised nor arbitrary. It may be that the reason at first given was not adhered to later but that was because by then the plan had undergone a modification. The Town Planning Act was enacted in respect of certain areas which included some lands of the petitioners. After considering the scheme, the second respondent forwarded the draft development plan to the State Government for approval under section 10 of Act. The State Government approved the draft Development plan and published it in the Official Gazette. The first respondent forwarded a copy of the draft scheme to the Government for publication in the official gazette. The Government approved of the scheme and published the same in the Gazette. In pursuance of the directions given by the Government, the first respondent sent a notice to both the petitioners calling upon them to submit their objections. The second respondent submitted his objections. Thereafter the State issued a notification under section 9 of the for acquisition of the lands belonging to the appellants. The appellants challenged the validity and the High Court quashed the notifications on the grounds that sections 9(1), 10,11, 12 and 13 of the were invalid and unconstitutional as they contravened article 14 Of the Constitution and were not valid. It also held that section 17 of the was invalid and ultra vires.

The appellant State of Gujarat filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the proposed transfer of certain territories from Sind to Pakistan. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the boundaries of the territory of India were administered by the British Government and that the dispute was one relating to the boundary between the States of Kutch and Gujarat. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The dispute related to the location of the State of Saurashtra in the State and the dispute involved a question of cession of territory. The dispute was referred to the High Courts under article 143(1)(a) of the Constitution and the decision of the Tribunal was binding on the parties. [152 E] (ii) The disputes related to two Governments, namely, the British India and Pakistan. Both the Government of India and the State were governed by the provisions of the agreement between the two States. The territory in question was comprised in the Union Territory of Sind. The agreement provided that the territory should be administered as if it was a Chief Commissioner 's Province. The Union of India had exercised its powers under section 290A of the Government Regulation, and the Central Government had also exercised its power under section 288A of that Regulation. [154 G H] (iii) The High Courts were not competent to go into the question whether the dispute related only to the boundaries between the State, but to the Dominion of India. [155 B C] (iv) The jurisdiction of the High courts was not ousted by article 143 (1)(b). The dispute relating to boundary between Sind and Pakistan was a matter which could be decided by the Supreme Court under article 136 of the constitution. [156 E F] (v) The decision of this Court in Attorney General for Canada vs Attorney General of New South Wales, ; , relied on. (vi) The award did not purport to nor did it operate as giving rise to an obligation to cede Indian territory. [157 B C]. (vii) The Union Government was competent to make a reference under article 144 of the Consti tution.

The mortgagor executed a mortgage deed in favour of the mortgagee and on October 2, 1927 he assigned his interest in Mauza Bahaldih to one Mahendra Nath Rai who was then a mortgagor. The mortgagor 's right to transfer encumber or sell the whole property included within the said Tauzi No. 16 of Collectorate of Dhanbad. On August 27, 1922, the mortgagor executed another mortgage deed whereby he agreed that the mortgagees were to receive the amount payable in two equal instalments and also agreed that in default of payment, the mortgagee would be liable to pay the amount due on the date of mortgage. The mortgagors ' claim was that the mortgagee did not have his interest therein and therefore the suit filed by the mortgagor for enforcement of the two mortgages was barred by limitation. The trial court rejected the defence raised by the defendants and held that the suit in respect of the first mortgage was not barred by the law of limitation because the mortgage "was partly simple and partly usufructuary" and even though the plaintiff could not rely upon any other part payment of principal or interest to extend the period of limitation for the suit, he could still maintain the suit relying on the dispossession of the mortgagor from the property in dispute. The High Court also held that as the plaintiff had not relied upon any sale deed of 1937 and the mortgage deeds executed by him in favour Of the mortgagee were not binding on the mortgagors under either of the mortgages, the suit was within time. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that: (1) the mortgagor 'S was entitled to transfer or sell his interest as security for realising the principal amount and (2) the mortgage deed dated June 14, 1922 was not binding upon the mortgagee under either section 20 of the Limitation Act. HELD : (i) The suit filed on July 12, 1946, was barred because the mortgagor had parted with his interest during the period April 14, 1925 to August 27. The mortgage deeds were placed in the possession of the right to recover royalty in respect thereof. [642 C] (ii) The question whether a mortgagor who has lost all his interest by payment of interest in the mortgaged property at the date when the money sued for becomes due is governed by article 120 of the Indian Limitation Act, 1908 and has to be decided in the light of finding that the mortgagor was placed in possession of such property. [643 D] (iii) The right conferred by section 68 is again not a right to enforce the mortgage but a right which arises when the mortgagee is deprived of his security. But the mortgagor has parted with the interest in one way or the other and the mortgagor is not a "person liable to payment" of the mortgage debt. [641 D] In the present case, the appellant had not produced any other document showing that he could have been given notice of the suit under either Of the two deeds. The suit was therefore barred by section 20. [651 F G] (iv) The period of Limitation for filing a suit to enforce payment of money charged upon immoveable property may be extended by part performance of the contract, but the mortgagor bad parted with possession of that asset in satisfaction of his mortgage claim unless it was mortgaged to him. The intention appearing from this covenant is clearly to encumber the mortgagee 's interest in immovable property and does not extend the time for a suit for recovery of the money.

The appellants employ as many as 7000 workmen in those factories. In order to provide transport facilities to their employees, the appellants provided transport which would pick up passengers from Pune or Khed or Vadgaon or Vadig or Dharchvad and back. For this journey a nominal charge of Rs. 10 per month was realised by the appellants from the employees. Similarly, for the transport facilities provided to the employees from Chinchvad Village to TELCO factory at Pimpri or Chinchwad and back, the appellant also undertook transport which was to be used in the case of the appellants. The appellants were charged with the transport charges. The question before this Court was whether the transport vehicles provided to them by the company would be a public service vehicle within the meaning of section 3(1) of the Bombay Motor Vehicles Act, 1958. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The word "public" has got a well known connotation and means a carriage to which any member of the public can have free access on payment of the usual charges. It cannot by any process of reasoning or stretch of imagination be deemed to include employees of a private company who are given facilities not as members of the Public even if he wanted to pay full charges could be carried on the said vehicle. [361 E F] 2. The words "public as contemplated by rule 2(i) of Bombay Motor Vehicle Rules, 1940, are wide and academic. The Commissioner, appears to have dismissed the appeals of the company and holding that the transport provided to its employees by the appellant could be a "public service vehicle" in any sense of the term. [362 G] 3. The definition of "stage carriage" has not been defined either by the Act or by the Rules but that however does not create any difficulty because having regard to the Preamble of the Act it is of the opinion that the tax can be levied only on passengers who are carried by road, and (a) that such passengers must be carried in stage carriages. [363 A B] 4. The term "public services vehicle" has been defined as follows: "stages carriage" means a motor vehicle carrying or adapted to carry more than six persons excluding the driver, which carries passengers for hire or reward at separate fares paid by or for individual passengers either for the whole journey or for stages of the journey. Rule 2(1)(a) of Gujarat Motor Vehicles Rules 1959 defines "passenger" as follows; "Private service vehicle means a road vehicle carrying not more than nine persons excluding tho driver, but as holding a special status, namely, the employees of that company." Thus, qua public the employees form a separate class and cannot be said to be public as contemplated under rule 2 (i). [362 B C] 5. The Bombay Motor vehicles Rules 1959 define "private service vehicle". It has been amended several times right from the year 1960 to 1975. Before analysing the relevant provisions of the Motor Vehicles, 1958, it may be necessary to extract the Preamble to the Act which runs thus: "Under section 2(7) of this Act, "stay carriage" includes a motor car carrying or intended to carry less than six passengers and also a motor cab or other omnibus when used as a contract carriage within the meanings of the . Rule 2 (1). The word 'public ' has got wide a wellknown connotation and mean a carriage by which any members of tho public can be free access to on payment off the usual charge. It could not by any processes of reasoning, or stretch the imagination be considered to include employee of a Private company who were given facilities, not as member of public but as held by the Bombay High Court in the instant case.

The appellant, a statutory cinema licence holder, was granted a "no objection certificate" by the State Government under the M.P. Cinemas (Regulation) Rules, 1972. The respondent No. 3, who had objected to the grant of a no objection certificate, filed a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court challenging the validity of the said order of the State government conceding that they were the residents of the locality and that they had objected only to the renewal of licence on the ground that there was a mosque, a "madarsa" and a temple in the vicinity of the place where the proposed cinema house was to be constructed.
