The High Court allowed the petition holding that the District Magistrate was not influenced by the fact that there were no objection certificates granted by him and therefore the order granting the no objection Certificate was perfectly justified. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that if before the grant or renewal of a licence the State Govt. had accepted the objections and rejected them, the District Collector as well as the High court were in error in granting the licence. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order granting a "No objection" certificate is without prejudice to the right of the licensing authority to refuse a cinema licence under Rule 102. [899E] 2.1 A perusal of Rules 3 to 6 envisage issuance of a license for a permanent cinema and quasi permanent cinema as well, and a mere executive necessity to be taken into consideration, cannot depend on proof of an interest which is bound to be injured by not hearing the party claiming to be entitled to a notice and nor are they entitled to be heard. [800G] 2:2 The right to object is at the initial stage when a no objections certificate is applied for by the intending applicant for such a certificate. But there is nothing in the Act or Rules which requires the licensing authori ty to invite objections before grant of licence. This scheme emerges from the combined reading of rules 3, 5 and 6. Chapter III in the Rules prescribes rules in respect of the building to be used as a cinema house. But before one proceeds to construct the cinema, obtaining of a No objection certificate relevant to the site on which cinema house is to be built, etc., the licence was renewed twice over upto and inclusive of 30th September 1976. The appellants did not file any objection at that stage "no objections" certificate was granted by order dated 10 February 1976.

The respondent executed a contract in respect of the mining lease. The appellant entered into an agreement with the respondent for the grant of specific performance of the contract. The respondent wrote to the appellant that the contract was concluded on September 2, 1957 and that the appellant had not agreed to purchase the mining leases. The respondents filed an appeal against this decree. The High Court allowed the appeal and dismissed the suit. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the respondent was entitled to remain in possession of the lease for specific performance because the contract being a concluded contract, the respondent could not get a possessory right before execution of a conveyance of the mine. HELD: (i) The plea that the rule can apply under our practice and procedure is not sufficient. In the peculiar facts of the case a contract to take shares was concluded by an oral application for shares followed by allotment though no notice of allotment was given to the applicant. Ordinarily there is no contract unless there is an acceptance of the application for share and the acceptance is communicated to the respondent, see Boys vs Ayerst (1893) 1822 6 Madd. 316, referred to. (ii) The appellant 's case that the respondents accepted the offer was not sufficient as the service of a copy of the plaint along with the writ of summons was a communication of the acceptance. [585 E F] Bloxam vs Akerst (I.L.R. 1822) approved. Bloxmull vs Aierst (1) 1823 6 Mad. 316 and Pellatt 's Case, referred by the High Court to.

The appellants were office bearers of a company. A complaint was filed against them under section 3(1) of the Essential Commodities Act, 1955 alleging that they had failed to pay to the sellers the price of sugarcane purchased by them within the time prescribed. The Magistrate took cognizance of the offence and issued process. The appellants challenged the legality of the investigation in a writ petition before the High Court which was dismissed. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that section 3 (1) cannot be used for controlling the payment of price of food crops, it can only deal with foodstuffs; food crops are outside its scope and that the power conferred on the Government under section 4(2)(b) of Act is not unguided or uncanalised. HELD: The power conferred by section 3 of the Act cannot be challenged as invalid. There is no substance in the contention that the impugned order contravened the fundamental right guaranteed to the citizens under article 19 (1). [677 D] Ch. Tika Ramji and Ors. vs The State of U.P., ; , referred to. Section 2(a) of that Act defines essential commodity. Sub section (2)(d) provides that any person who is a producer not to pay the price thereof, shall be liable to pay a price of the sugarcane purchased within 14 days from the date of delivery of the sugar. This is a specific mandate. If the Bihar Act provides anything to the contrary the same must be held to have been altered in view of article 372 of the Constitution which provides that all laws in force in the territory of India immediately before the commencement of this Constitution shall continue in force therein until altered or repealed or amended by a competent legislature or other competent authority. [677 E F] Chic Tika Ram and Ors vs The Stale Government, ; , followed.

The Government of Karnataka decided to adopt a policy to encourage rapid industrialisation. An Order No. CI 58 FM 69 dated 30th June, 1969 was issued which recited that the Government had on 30th November 1966 issued directions indicating the incentives that would be given to entrepreneurs starting new industries in Mysore State. The Government also stated that the concessions granted under the orders referred to earlier were of no legal effect as there was no statutory provision under which such concessions could be granted and the order dated 12th January, 1977 would undoubtedly apply to industries started after that date. On 12th December, 1981, the Government issued another Order which recited the incentives given by the earlier order dated 30st June 1969 to the entrepreneurs starting existing industries in the Mysore State, but subsequently it was clarified that the benefits of the said orders were being misused and undue advantage was being taken of the same. The appellant company filed writ petitions before the High Court claiming that the industrial undertakings started between 30th July 1969 when the order was passed and before 949 the Order dated 12.1.1977 was issued could not be deprived of the concessions given to them by the former order as the said grant of concession constituted a promissory estoppel against the Government on the basis of which they had acted by starting new industrial units requiring investment of considerable funds and the Government was not entitled to go back or that promise as it had sought to do by the Order No 949 dated 30.6.1969 was beyond the powers of the State or how the State can say so either. The High Court allowed the writ petitions and granted relief on the ground that the doctrine of Promissory Estoppel was not applicable in the present case because it was found by the Government of the Karnataka that the concession granted under this order dated 31st June,1969 had given room for many types of misuse but such a recital by itself cannot establish that the facilities were in fact misused. The State appealed to this Court by special leave. Allowing the appeals and setting aside the judgment of the High Courts, ^ HELD: 1.1 The doctrine of promissory Estoppel is not applicable to the present cases because it is found by Government that the incentive granted was beyond its powers of State or what the State could say so both on merits as well as on merits. [950 F] 1.2 In order to test the validity of the order of the Government one has to see the substance of the concession granting under the Order and not merely certain words used out of context. Although the benefit regarding sales tax granted to the new industries is by way of refund of sales tax paid to the extent provided in the Order, it is clear that, in effect, the benefit granted is in the nature of an exemption from the payment of the sales tax or reduction in the sales Tax liability to the amount stated in the order. In view of this, there is no substance whatever in the contention that the State Government had no authority to provide for the grant of refund. [951 G H; 953 A] 1:3 The mere fact that the order passed by the High court did not specify the power under which it was issued will make no difference because such a power is clearly there in Section 8A and where the source of power underwhich it is issued is not stated in an order but can be found on the examination of the relevant Act, the exercise of the power must be attributed to that source. The second submission of the learned counsel for the appellants must also fail.

The appellants were charged with offences under Sections 147, 148 and 302 read with Section 149 I.P.C. for causing the death of one of the persons. The Trial Court acquitted A 1 and A 2 but convicted them under Sections 148 and 307 read with section 149 I P.C., and sentenced them to imprisonment for life. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence of A 1 to A 3. In appeal by special leave, it was contended that after the acquittal of four accused persons by the courts below the conviction of the appellants under Section 302 readwith Section 34 I. P. C. could not be sustained. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The appellants being only three in number, there was no question of their forming an unlawful assembly within the meaning of Section 141 I.p.C.[1D] 2. It is not the prosecution case that apart from the seven accused persons there were some other unidentified persons who were involved in the crime. The High Court clearly fell into error in confirming the conviction. [2E F] 3. The evidence of P.W.3 to the extent it is corroborated by the evidence 6 of the eye witnesses and the number and nature of injuries, is sufficient to bring the accused under Section 149 and on applying 149 I .P. C.[3F G] 4. The conviction of A 2 to A 7 under Sections 302 read alongwith 34 I P C. and keep them sentenced to imprisonment is set aside.

The assessee, a house owner, was carrying on business in an urban area. He sold the house to his daughter in law and five children of his children. The assessee sold the property for Rs. 16,500. The Income tax officer assessed the assessee 's income for the assessment year 1966 67 under section 148 of the Act and levied a capital gains tax on the sale of the house by the assessee. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of reassessment but the Tribunal held that the fair market value of the property as on the date of transfer exceeded the limit of Rs. 45,500 and that it was not possible to say that the transfer was effected with the object of avoidance or reduction of the liability of the assessee under section 45. The High Court in reference held that under section 52(2) of the Income tax Act, 1922, the only condition for attracting the applicability of that provision is that the assessee should have discharged the burden which lies upon him by showing that there was no extent of the under valuation or in other words, the actual extent of concealment and the full value of consideration received for the transfer. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that (1) the High Court had no jurisdiction to interfere with the order made by the Income Tax officer; (2) the assessee had not discharged the onus of proving that there is under statement of consideration in respect of the transfer and the transaction was undervalued as the assessee did not show understatement of consideration but it was only a device to evade tax; and (3) the income of the family by reason of the sale having been genuinely refunded to the assessees, they had actually received more than what is declared or disclosed by him. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order of re assessment made by Income Tax Officer pursuant to the notice issued under section 34(2)(b) of Income tax, 1961 was without jurisdiction and the majority judges of the Full Bench were in error in refusing to quash it. [655D] 2.1 Section 52(1) of Act is a self contained provision which provides that where the consideration for the transferred capital asset as on date of the Transfer exceeds the full amount of the consideration declared by the assesses, the difference between the fair value of such consideration and the total consideration received in respect thereof shall be computed in the manner provided in sub section (2). The net effect of this provision is to save the assessee from the rigour of sub section(2), that it is not possible for the Revenue to show and hence sub section 3 provides the statutory measure for determining the consideration actually received by the asses see. [651C D] 2:2 In the present case, the assessee was entitled to have the notice under section 149 of the Code of Civil Procedure issued by the I.T.O. pursuant to its notice issued in respect to the transfer made by it. The assessment order pursuant to which the notice was issued did not contain any provision for attracting section 52 of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1961. [641D] 3. The expression "for the purpose of determining the value" occurring in sub sections (2), (3), and (4) of section 52 is a wide term and includes all transactions which are taken out of the purview of sub sections to avoid hardship to the assessee, and therefore, the Income 'tax officer could not ask the Court to presume that the second condition was satisfied. [566D] 4. The object of imposing the condition of difference of 15% or more between the market value and the amount of consideration which is chargeable as gift could not be intended to be charged also as capital gains. [678E] 5. The proviso to sub section 2(2).

The appellant was charged with offences under section 16(1)(a)(1) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954. The prosecution case was that the appellant had gone to "a shop to make purchases" without giving either the name or the name of the shop or approximate date or time of his visit. He was found in possession of a large quantity of Til seeds and he was selling it for sale. The appellant was convicted under section 7(1) (a)(i) of that Act and sentenced to pay a fine of Rs. 1,35,000/ . On appeal the High Court acquitted him but convicted him under section 3(i)(a) (1) Of the Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the whole object of the Act was to prevent adulteration of "food" meant for human consumption and that the use of the article sold was not entirely irrelevant. HELD : The High Court was right in holding that the prosecution had to prove beyond reasonable doubt that what was stored or sold was `food ' within the meaning of section 7 of the . [357 B] (i) It is enough if an article of adultered food is either manufactured for sale, or stored, or sold or distributed in contravention of any provision of the , Act or of any rule made there under. The charge was that it was "fruit" and not "foods". The charge did not fall within section 7 (i)(b) because it was a matter of common knowledge that black Til seeds were not used as food. [337 C D] Bhagwan Das vs Delhi Administration, ; , applied. (ii) It was not correct to say that the High Courts had no doubt that the evidence led by the prosecution was not sufficient to prove an offence defined by section 7. The use of article of food in the course of pooja with which we are concerned was not altogether irrelevant.

The appellant was dismissed from service by the Collector on 13.1.1966. He filed a suit for declaration that the order of dismissal was inoperative and he continued to be in service. The suit was decreed in his favour on 30.9.1969. On appeal, the Divisional Commissioner confirmed the decree in his first appeal. In second appeal, he held that the suit was barred by limitation. The High Court in second appeal upheld the dismissal of the second appeal. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The cause of action shall be taken to arise not from the date of the original adverse order but on the date when the order is passed. [514C] 1.2 In every such case only when the appeal or representation provided by law is disposed of, cause of actions shall first accrue and where such order is not made, on the expiry of six months from the order when the Appeal was filed or representation was made, the right to sue shall first accrued. submission of just a memorial or representation to the Head of the establishment shall not be taken into consideration in the matter of fixing limitation. In all these three cases after the appellate authority has disposed of the appeal the operative order is the order passed by the appellate authori ty whether it has reversed the original order or modified it or confirmed it. [52F G] 1:3. The cause for action first arises when the remedies available to the public servant under the relevant service Rules as to re instate are disposed of. The question for consideration is whether it should be disposal of one appeal or the entire hierarchy of reliefs as may have been provided. Statutory guidance is available from the provisions of sub sections (2) and (3) of section 20 of the . [52G H] 1 :4. In every case only if the appeal has been disposed of not from a date of original adverse orders but on tho date when order of the higher authority where a statutory remedy is provided entertaining the appeal against the public servants. The law is soon going to get crystallised on the line laid down under section 20. In this background, if the original orders of punishment are taken as the date which power of condonation of delay has been set up for Government servants of the Centre and sever al States have already set up such Tribunals under the Act for the employees of respective States. The Law is soon gov erned. [53H; 54A B] 1 5. In a case where the remedies availed of has not been provided by the law, the cause of the action first arose when the remedy available to it under the rele vant service rules as to redressal of grievances, (a) if a final order has been made by the Government or other competent authority or offi cer, and (b) where no such order was made. [54E] 1 6. The legal position is not at all referred to or examined. It is appropriate that the position in such cases should be uniform.

The appellant filed a suit against the respondent for recovery of certain amounts due from him. The trial court decreed the suit and the High Court affirmed the decree. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The question whether an appellate decree passed by the trial court was one of affirmance or not must be determined in the light of the provisions of section 110 of the Code of Civil Procedure. If the judgment or decree is set aside by the High court and the decree appealed against is set in accordance with law, it would be unreasonable to limit the scope of that order on a case where different causes of action are involved. [465 B C] (ii) The expression "judgment" occurring in section 110(3) of the Civil Procedure Code means judgment or order passed by a court in appeal and not an order of affirmation. A judgment or an order may be either in terms of a decree or in any representative capacity, and it is open to the court to modify that decision. [466 D] (iii) The words "judgment " in section 2(3), "decree" in section 3(1)(a) are clear and unambiguous and have no meaning in such cases. The words used are wide enough to include a formal expression of an adjudication which conclusively determines the rights of parties with regard to all or any of the matters in controversy in suit, and they must be construed as including the words "the decree is of affirmence and this is not affected by the extent of the variation made or by the fact that the variation is made in favour of the intending appellant and not against him. [467 E F] (iv) The word "decree " in article 133(1) (a) means a formal adjudication which determines the right of parties, and does not include an appeal as a matter of law. An order passed under section 35 of the Act is made to be final and conclusive. It is open for the court in revision to modify it by ordering a variation of the decision of the trial Court but merely makes a variation in regard to the order as to costs such a variation would not confer a right of appeal as regards matters unconnected with the matter in respect of which there has been a variation. [468 E F; 469 A B] (v) The use of the word "judgment ' in article 136 does not justify the imposition of a strained meaning on the relevant words used in that Article. If an appellate court had considered the question of construction afresh, it did not follow that the said principle can be legitimately invoked in construing a statute and that the matter should be referred to a Full Bench. [470 E F]. (vi) The contention that the High Courts should have granted special leave to appeal must fail. The word 'judgment ' is used in article 134(1), and it cannot be restricted by an application of the principles of natural justice. It has been held by this Court that if a judgment or a decree is passed on the basis of a variation, the appeal would not be open to challenge as a result of the appellate decree but only to the extent that the court had acted upon the words used therein and the meaning of the words 'the variation in question ' would not necessarily mean the decision. The fact that if the judgment was one which was cause of action would not make the difference in the case would not justify an order as a revision under section 115 C.P.C., as the matter had been concluded by the decision in the present case. [473 E F, H; 474 A B]. (vii) The High Court erred in holding that the appellate court was justified in setting aside the decree of the Trial Court on the ground that the Appellate Court had not fully satisfied itself with the correctness of the test of substance which was then applied by some of the High courts.

The provisions of section 115, Code of Civil Procedure, read with the relevant sections of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, are in pari materia with those of the original section 115. The High Court has exclusive jurisdiction under section 115 in cases arising out of original suits of a value less than Rs. 20,000 and above, and in other cases the revisional jurisdiction was concurrently shared between the High Court and the District Court. Section 25, in its application to the State of Uttar Pradesh continues to be governed by section 115 as it stood before that date. The language of the successive amendments introduced in the bifurcation of revisional jurisdiction into the High Courts is clear from the provisions of the Act which are in identical terms. The legislative history of revisional power with regard to a revisional order reducing the number of revision petitions filed in the High court would be frustrated if the legislature while enacting the Amending Act intended to confer revisional powers on the highest court in the State, and when it decided to interfere in making an appropriate order, the High Commissioner was not competent to exercise revisional power under section 25, which had been admitted, after preliminary hearing. The scheme of bifurcation of the revisional jurisdic tion with effect from 1st February, 1977 and the subsequent amendments made in 1972 show that it is a self sufficient code so far as the present enquiry is concerned. [38 C D] In the instant case, the Central principle continues to hold, notwithstanding the amendment effected in section 25 that the hierarchy of remedies enacted in the Provincial Small Cause Courts Act represents a complete and final order of remedies, and it is not possible to proceed outside the Act to avail of a superior remedy provided by another statute.

The respondent State Government issued a notification under section 52(1) of the Rajasthan Urban Improvement Act, 1959 for acquisition of certain lands belonging to them. The appellant challenged the said notification before the High Court by way of writ petition. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the notice issued under section 51(2) of Act was not sufficient and the authority had no jurisdiction to issue a rule nisi on the petition filed by the respondents under article 226 of the Constitution. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the petition could not be issued till February 8, 1984 because the Government were primarily thinking of making the land available for construction of residential houses before making provisions for construction. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The entire cause of action culminating in the acquisition of the land under section52(1), on the respondents at their registered office at 18 B , Brabourne Road, Calcutta, is within the territorial jurisdiction of the State of Rajasthan at the Jaipur Bench. [606C] 2. The notification dated February 8th 1984 issued by the State Government under section 49(1 ) of the Act became effective the moment it was published in the official Gazette as thereupon the notified land became vested in the State free from all encumbrances. It was not necessary for the respondents to plead the service of notice on them by the Special Officer, Town Planning Department, Jaipur under section 54(2). [605D] 3. The word " cause of Action" is tersely defined in Mulla 's Code of Civil Procedure: "The 'cause of action ' means every fact which if traversed it would be necessary for a plaintiff to prove in order to support his right to a judgment of the Court". In other words, it is a bundle of facts which taken with the law applicable to them gives the plaintiff a right to relief against the defendant. The mere service of the notice under section 53(2), on tho respondents at its registered office, at 18B , Bra bourne road, Calcutta i.e., within the geographical limits of the state of West Bengal could not give rise to a cause of ' action within that territory unless the service is an integral part of the cause of the action. [065E F] 4. The whole cause of actions culminating in acquisition of land under Section 52( 1) on the respondent at their Registered office at18 B , brabourna Road, and within the jurisdiction of State of WestBengal could not given rise to the cause 'of action within the territory unless tho service of such notice was an integral parts of the ' cause of a action. The Court had no territorial jurisdiction to entertain a petition under Article 226 of tile Constitution or to make the ad interim ex parte prohibitory order restraining the appellants from taking any steps to take possession of the acquired land. [ 606F G] 5. The expression "cause of actions" is conse quently defined in the Mulla ' s Code of civil Procedure: 'The ' cause ' of action is ter sely defined under Mulla ' 's code of Civil procedure: 'the ' cause thereof, if not present part of cause arose within the territories of the Union of India. The term of the causes of action within its meaning includes a bundle and therefore there is always the need to use such extensive powers with due circumspection. There has to be in the larger public interest an cleav ing restraint. [ 607H; 606A] 6. The power of the High Courts under article 227 of the Constitu tion are far and wide and the Judges must ever be vigilant to protect the citizen against arbitrary executive action, nonetheless, the judges have a constructive role and therefore, there is never been always the necessity to use the such extensive power with due surprise.

The respondent landlord filed a suit for eviction of the appellant tenant from the premises in question on the ground that the appellant was inducted as a tenant of the premises by a co operative society and that the building was not covered by the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972. The Trial Court dismissed the suit holding that the buildings were exempted from the operation of the new Rent Act on two grounds: (i) that the landlord had purchased it from the society and, therefore, the view taken by the Judge that the premises were not ten years old was erroneous; and (ii) that since the building in question had been constructed by a cooperative society and the landlord was not a tenant under the U P Urban Buildings Act, the suit was barred by section 20 of the Act. The Additional District Judge dismissed the appeal holding that (i). the building being exempted from operation of Act, on two ground, namely, (a) that it was not ten year old on the date of suit and (b) that there was no default in payment of rent. In second appeal, the High Court held that the construction of a building by the society was not 10 years old on that date and therefore, it could not be said to have been completed on 1st October, 1971, the date when the building came into effect. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: (1) The building in dispute had become more than ten years of age on the day of suit. But during the pendency of the litigation it completed ten years. Then the question arises whether by seeking the benefit of section 39 of the old Act there is a change in the cause of action. In A.K. Gupta & Sons vs Damodar, 342 Valley Corporation Ltd., this Court held: (2) The expression "cause of action" in the new rent Act, will be given to the tenant if the conditions com mitted in those sections are satisfied. [340D] (3) The question in the present case is whether by seek ing the benefit under section 39, the building had been exempted from its operation. [341E] (4) The appellant in the instant case only seeks the protection of the newly added new Rent Acts which became applicable to the premises after the date on which the first assessment thereof came into force. The Act has not therefore, application to the building. [342F G] (5) The High Court was right in holding that by seeking benefit of s.39 of the amended Act there was a change of the cause 'of action. [343G H] (6) The fact that the new Act had been brought into force by new facts also did not detain this Court as it is covered by decision of this Court in Pasupati Venkateswrlu vs Motor and General Traders, ; , referred to.

The appellant entered into three contracts with the respondent for construction of aerodrome, hangarettes, buildings, stores and other works at Ranchi. The first contract was to be executed on November 5, 1942, and the other two were contracts Nos. 6 and 8 dated April 5, 1943. The second contract was made by one Y. K. Lall, Executive Engineer, Ranchi Division, and by the respondents who were the appellant 's agents. On February 6, 1948, the appellant filed a petition under sections 17 and 20 of the Indian , for a decree in terms of the award. The respondents contended that the agreement to refer to arbitration was not one relating to execution of works as that had been completed and signed by both the parties. Held, that the contract was executed by a person who was authorised to do so by the Governor and in consequence there was a valid reference to arbitration. It was not necessary for an arbitrator to enter into this contract founded on the basis of the misconception that the appellant had been authorised or authorised to execute the agreement in question. The fact that Y.K. Lall was authorised by the Government acting through his Secretary to execute it did not make any difference in the position because the Secretary undoubtedly did intend that Y, K. Lal should execute the contract and that is all that he could do under section 175(3). The appellant had the Executive Engineer 's office at Ranchi and he did so on behalf of the Government and did so as he was authorised or authorise by the said Governor.

The appellant was working as Executive Engineer in Public Works Department in the State of Punjab. On various dates in 1980 some complaints were received against him pertaining to the purchase of sign boards which were required by the Department to avoid accidents on roads and for traffic safety. The First Information Report was lodged on August 27, 1985. In the meantime, the respondent had retired from service as Executive Engineers with effect from October 31, 1982. The appellant filed a Writ Petition in the High Court challenging the First Information report on account of which challan could not be filed and it was only when the challenge to the First information Report was repelled by the High court that a challan was filed on August 28, 1985 in the court of the Chief Judicial Magistrate. The High Court allowed the Writ Petition holding that the said Rule placed an embargo on initiating judicial proceedings for prosecution of a government servant on the expiry of four years from the date of cause of action or event mentioned therein. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that since the Government had the power to make suitable amendments even retrospectively in Rule 2.2, the said rule cannot be interpreted to mean a rule placing an embargo upon prosecution of public servants on the expiration of their term by a statutory rule; and that the High Courts should not have intended to regulate the conditions of service of such a person. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The intention of framing the said rules was not to grant immunity from prosecution to a government employee if the conditions mentioned therein are satisfied. [923D] 1.2 In the instant case, the Government servants cannot constitute a class by themselves so as to bring their cases within the purview of reasonable classification, if the purpose of granting immunity from criminal liability on the ground that they are not specified in the rules is to bring an embargoon of prosecution of government servant after his retirement for grave misconduct or negligence during the period of his service, including service rendered upon re employment after retirement. [936E] 1:3 The expression "conditions of service" means all those conditions which regulate the holding of a post by a person right from the time of his appointment till his retirement and even beyond it, in matters like pension etc.

The respondent company was a public limited company under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. It had its registered office in the trade name of a company which was known as a public Limited Company. In September 1936 the respondent company sold its shares to the appellant company. The preference shareholders were under the Articles of Association entitled to vote at the meeting of the company each shareholder being entitled to exercise one vote for each share. In the course of assessment proceedings for the year ending March 31, 1948, the Income tax Officer found that for three years ending March31, 1948 and March 31 1949 the respondent had declared each year a total dividend of Rs. 38,750/ . The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed this order. On further appeal the Tribunal held that the respondent was one in which the public were substantially interested and there fore the income tax officer could not pass an order under section 23A of the Income Tax Act for any of the three years and on that footing answered the question in the negative. In reference, the High Court held that (1) the respondent Company was one of fact to be in which public were substantial interested; (2) the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to pass an assessment under section 3A of Income tax Act for the reason that it was a company in which it was substantially interested; and (3) the income Tax officer could have no jurisdiction. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The High Court was right in holding that the Tribunal was authorised by the Income T tax Act to pass the order under which the income was deemed to be distributed among the shareholders entitled thereto. [17 E] (1)(a) The distinction between the controlling group and the public is not along the line which distinguishes directors from the remaining members of the 16th company. If a director does not belong to the controlling Group, he will be regarded as a member of the public for the purposes of the third proviso and the Explanation to section 23 A even though such director was directly entrusted with the management of the affairs of the Company. The Commissioner cannot therefore be said to have jurisdiction under section 22(2) of the Act. [18 E F] (b) The expression "thirty five per cent of the voting power" in section 23(1) is not synonymous with "compulsory notional income which was not in fact received by the shareholders as a result of the terms of the proviso to section 3 A even if such director were directly entrusted to the management. [19 F G] (c) The words "thirty 5 per cent. of the shares are held by persons other than the controlling groups" in the proviso, and the expression "twenty five per centum of the total voting right is not linked to or acquired unconditionally by or beneficially held by the public.

The appellants were the sole selling agents of the respondent Mills. The goods were delivered to them by a firm called "Sangri Moolji" and they were the only selling agents for the respondents. The delivery was not on record but it was made clear that the goods were in the possession of the appellants at all material times and were in fact delivered to Dharsi Moolji. The respondent filed a suit against the appellants for recovery of the amount paid by them as price of the goods specified in the " ready sale note" and for damages. The trial court decreed the suits but the High Court on appeal held that the godown belonged to the first appellant, but was not the agent of the quota holder. On appeal by special leave: Held, that the appellants were guilty of an unauthorised way over a period of years and as such liable to pay the amount claimed. Dwarkadas Khetan could in the circumstances be described without any straining of language as the person to whom the goods had been delivered. The words "possession in the popular sense" in section 2(c) of the Essential Supplies Act, 1946, meant actual delivery or possession in fact and not actual physical possession. The word "consumption" in a broad and liberal sense means a state of fact of exclusive physical control. Haradhan Kuwarji vs Tirkaram Sheolal, A.I.R. 1938 Nag. (2) 835, considered. Kalyanji Kuwar vs Tirkalingam Shelolal ; , distinguished.

The appellant was a public servant. He was charged with offences under section 161 of the Indian Penal Code and section 5(2) read with section 5 (1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The Special Judge convicted him under section 165A of the Penal Code, and sentenced him to pay a fine of Rs. 500/ . On appeal by the State, the High Court held that the prosecution case was proved against both the accused. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the words "by any of the fees or commission for the performance of any public duty" in section 5 of the Act were not wide enough to cover cases of corruption and therefore the provisions of the Criminal Procedure Code should be applied to cases of a Government servant who commits an act punishable under the said provision even though when the act is committed by him he is holding a different position which is not that of a government servant; (ii) the use of the word "officer" in sub clause (a) of section 5, in the context of the words immediately preceding the last part would indicate that the remuneration contemplated was remuneration by the Government and therefore, if the public servant used corrupt or illegal means for obtaining a valuable thing, or pecuniary advantage he commits an offence as contemplated by section 5; and (iii) the word 'other wise ' refers to corrupt or illegality which is capable of being obtained by corrupt or illegally means or otherwise than those means. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The use of word "other wise" in clause (d) in sub cl. (a), (b) and (c) of sub section (1) of Section 5 of Prevention of Corrupt Practices Act, 1949, shows that the expression "public servant" must be given a wide meaning. If the meaning to be given to the word is to be employed it is abuse by corrupt, or illegal or may be of such a nature as would savour of a dishonest act. But the abuse of position as a public officer which has been understood and employed in the Ninth clause does not constitute remuneration by him. [334 C D] 2.

The petitioners, who were casual labour engaged on terms of casual labour for periods varying between 10 and 16 years in the construction Department of the Signal Unit in the Northern Railway, filed writ petitions before this Court praying for a direction to treat them as temporary servants and to declare that they are entitled to equal pay for equal work and have asked for their absorption in regular cadre in the permanent category as per the circulars issued by the respondents. The petitioners also prayed for a direc tions to treat the petitioners at par with maintenance workers and to treat their services as temporary employees and to consider them for regularisation of their service. Disposing of the writ petitions, this Court, HELD: 1.1. It is the stand of the Additional Solicitor General that no pensionary benefits are admissible even to temporary railway servants and, therefore, that retiral benefit is not available to casual labour acquiring temporary status. [143G] 1.2. The respondents shall consider the claims of each of the petitioners promptly and make appropriate orders for their regularisation. For over ten years, litigations of this type have been coming before this court. about three years back, this court directed a scheme for absorption in Yadav 's case which has been framed and is operative. Casual labour seems to be the requirement of the Railway Administration and cannot be avoided. The Railway Establishment Manual has made provisions for their protection but implementation is not pub lished by the Railway Establishment manual. [144H; 144A] 1:3. There is no break in such continuity, the previous service is also taken into account.

The appellants were the agents of a Forward Markets Commission. The commission was to act under section 12(1) of the , and the provisions of the Act were made applicable to it by the Central Government. Section 11 of the said Act provided that the Central Govern ment may, either on a request in writing received by it from any other body or authority, make bye laws for the regulation and control of forward contracts. The appellants challenged the validity of the notification issued under section 11 of Act on the ground that the Forward Markets Act was ultra vires the Government as it had no power to issue such a notification. Held, that the notification dated January 21, 1956, by which the appellants were authorised to make bye law with retrospective effect was not invalid and could not be challenged in view of the provisions contained in section 4(f) of Act 19 of 1956. The power conferred on the Central government by section 12 (1) Of the Act is not a delegated one and must necessarily imply a power to make a bye law retrospectively. The notification issued by the Forward Market Commission was illegal and could be challenged only if it contravened any provision of the Constitution or the provisions thereof. The Government had no administrative functions or powers of management or control over the agents, and hence the notification was not ultra vires. The Act did not confer any such power on the State Government. The Central Government had the authority to issue a bye laws under section 18 of the . The power of the Central Govt. under section 13 (1 ) of the was not limited by the provisions Of section 11 and could only be exercised by the Board of Directors or their nominee, if in its opinion it was expedient so to do. The words "under the Act" in section 11(a) were intended for the purpose of bringing within the body of the bye laws the word "regulate" must mean "to make a provision of law". The power to frame bye laws is not conferred on an authority by statute but by statute. The word "may" in the context means "to do so". If a rule was not expressly made by the legislature, it could be said that it was intended to operate retrospectively and not to direct the same. The expression "underthe Act" would include a rule made in exercise of the power conferred under section 1 (a) of section 11. The rules framed under the Act in so far as they purported to operate prospectively are wholly inapplicable to a byelaw made by an authority in exercise or purported to be made under a statute.

The assessee company was a shareholder of a company styled the Ukhara Estate Zamindaries Ltd. The Ukharai Bank, which was a share holder, held shares in a company which comprised salami or premia received by it as consideration for grant of long term leases. In respect of which they were paid compensation for compulsory acquisition of lands for public purposes, the assessee claimed that out of the amounts set out in the table only Rs. 8669/ for the year 1357 B.S., Rs. 20,469/ for 1951 51 and Rs. 21822/ for 1952 53, he was entitled to a long term lease as dividend but as income of other sources. The Income tax Officer brought the entire amount to tax declared as dividend for each of the three years in question and grossed up the amounts under section 16(2) of the Indian Income tax Act 1922. In appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that part of the amount distributed which was attributable to salami received by the company for the grant of short term leases was not taxable as dividend, but as the compensation for the compulsory acquisition was not exempt from liability to tax under section 12 as dividend income liable to tax. The Appellate Tribunal held that the entire sum was income in the hands of the assessee and that it was not liable to pay dividend but only a part of it being dividend within the meaning of section 2(6A) of Income tax, 1922. On reference, the High Court held that it could not be said that distribution of dividend out of capital gains was taxable as dividends but as incometax which is statutorily payable on compensation is income and is not capital gain. In the appeal to this Court, HELD : The order passed by the High court is set aside and the case remanded to the High Tribunal for disposal according to law.

The respondents were charged with offences under the Kerala Forest Act, 1961 for short the Act. The prosecution case was that Sandalwood oil was not a wood oil as defined in section 2(f) (1) of the Act and therefore it was not an 'wood oil ' as defined by section 2 (k) (i). The Trial Court found that the Sandal Wood Oil is not 'wood Oil ' as understood under section 2.2(k) of Act. On appeal, the High Court held that Sandals were not ' wood oil ' and hence the conviction was unsustainable. Hence these appeals by special leave. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The word 'wood ' used in section2 (f) would show that it did not intensify the intention of the law giver '. [502C] 1.2 In the instant case, the Karnataka Forest Act 1963 incorporated in its definition of forest produce Sandal wood oil after the word ' wood ' and the legislature in Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu Acts has rightly construed the meaning of the word as used in the Act, because it did. The dictionary meaning is not meant to prevent the word receiving its ordinary, popular and natural sense whenever that word was used in commercial parlance. [506D] 1:3. In the context of the explanation given to Entry 22, the word includes 'is technical and part of inclusive definition has to be construed in its technical sense but in an exhaustive manner it cannot be restricted in such a manner so as to defeat the object and purpose of the statute. The process by which the oil is extracted is not decisive as oil may be extracted by natural process of exudation or it may be derived by subjecting to chemical or mechanical process and Sandal timber (Santalum Album) are cut into pieces. Its heart wood and roots of drums are also included as forest produce.

The appellant was tried by the Sessions Judge for an offence under section 302 of the Indian Penal Code but acquitted. The High Court set aside his acquittal and convicted him under section302 read with section 34 and sentenced him to transportation for life. On appeal by special leave, Held, that the conviction of the appellant was not vitiated on account of material contradictions in his statement made before the trial court which had been rejected by it. It was not proved that the opinion of the doctor as to the innocence of the accused was disregarded as it must be disregarded in this case because ordinarily a dying declaration of the kind which the prosecution has relied upon is by itself insufficient for sustaining a conviction on a charge of murder. The evidence in the present case was of such quality and no legitimate inference of guilt could properly be drawn from the evidence of the two eye witnesses, who had been examined as eye witnesses. The Sessions Judge was therefore right in holding that the evidence was not free from suspicion and he was of the opinion that the appellant had made a dying declarations to three persons. The recovery of the kassi is a wholly neutral circumstance because it has not been proved that it belonged to Bhagwandas. The fact that the katta was recovered from the appellant 's body was also not in accord with the opinion expressed in books on Medical Jurisprudence by authors like Modi and Lyon. The circumstances relied upon were such as could reasonably infer from them that the accused had made the dying declarations. The medical evidence showed that the deceased had not been subjected to any weight and value to the statement of a person who was present on the spot by using the statement.

The appellant company was a registered establishment under the Bihar Shops and Establishments Act, 1948. The workmen employed in the factory were paid dearness allowance at double the ordinary rate for overtime work exceeding 39 hours but not exceeding 48 hours per week. The appellant company claimed that the workmen of the factory should be given special leave to attend the meetings of its executive committee and that the union 's representatives should be allowed to attend meetings of the executive committee or any other meeting called by the union except mass meetings and the said statement was accepted by the Government on the basis of the agreement between the management and the workmen. The Tribunal held that the appellant company had been allowed without loss of pay, and dismissed the demand for special leave with pay. On appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Tribunal was in error in making its award operative not only to the said workmen at its Jamshedpur factory but also to workmen at their other establishments and that in doing so it acted beyond jurisdiction. HELD: (i) The agreement between a company and its employees is not binding on the workmen and the employer in fairness would be expected to pay him compensation for such overtime work. [560 F] (ii) The Tribunal was not justified in obliging the appellant to grant special leave demanded by the Union. The result is that except for the overtime rate allowed by the Tribunal which is confirmed, the rest of the appeal has to be allowed and the Tribunal 's award set aside. [559 G] (iii) The award is operative in respect of the workmen in the appellant Company 's factory at Jamshedpur and not the workmen thereof.

The assessee firm carried on business in the name of M/s. Hakam Mal Tani Mal Tai Mal Tami, and its business was taken over by two partners of the firm Gajjan Mal and Jodha Mal Kuthiala. The timber business of the assessee firm was taken up by two partner of the partnership firm. An instrument of partnership recording the terms of the said partnership and reciting the dissolution of the earlier partnership was executed on June 29, 1939. The assessee was dissolved in March 1943. In assessment proceedings for 1943 44 the assessee contended that the firm M/S. Hakham Mal Toni Mal Tni Mal Kthiala Abdullapur Depot, Simla had been dissolved on March 31, 1939 and the firm alone was entitled to relief under section 25(4) of the Indian Income tax Act 1922. The Income tax Officer completed the assessment without giving to the assessee the benefit of sub sections (3) or (4) Of section 25 of the Act. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order holding that succession to the family firm M 's. Jodhi Mal Thani Mal Tiani Mal had fallen to his share to run which business after April 1, 1939 was taken by the assessee. The High Court in reference held that the assessee was not entitled to the benefit provided in section 25 (4). In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the income tax authorities were right in holding that the appellant firm was not liable to be assessed under section 5(3) of Indian Income Tax Act, 1922. HELD : The assessee had no right to claim the benefit under section 26(4). The assessee commenced doing business immediately after the dissolution and before the Income tax (Amendment) Act 7 of 1939 had come into force.

The appellant was granted stage carriage permit under section 48 of the , for the route Devenagere to Shimoga via Honnali by the Regional Transport Authority, Shimog, by its order dated May 3/4 1963. The Secretary to the Regional Authority, respondent No. 1, in exercise of his powers under Rule 119 of the Mysore Motor Vehicles Rules, 1963, granted a stage carriage permits to the appellant on the same day. The appellant challenged the grant of the permit before the High Court which dismissed it. In appeal to this Court, HELD : Section 64(1)(a) of the Act is the only section creating rights of appeal against the grant o. the permit and other matters with which we are not concerned here. There is no dispute that section 64(11) is theonly section creating right of appeal in favour of the appellant. [189 D] The appeals before the State Transport Appellate Tribunal and the further appeal to the Mysore Revenue Appellate Tribunal are, therefore, not competent under section 64 of the . [189 E F] Section 64 has to be read with rule 178 of the Rules which prescribes the procedure for appeal to various authorities Appeal is a creature of the statute. There was no dispute about old rule 151 of the old Rules and rule 119 of Mysore Motor vehicles Rules 1963. Therefore, the order granting the permit to the appel lant stands restored. [190 G H] The High Court was therefore not right in dismissing the writ application of the appell ant.

The appellant was elected to the Lok Sabha. The respondent filed an election petition challenging the election on the ground that the appellant 's witnesses were not present at the meeting of the Republican Party and that there was no public meeting held in support of the allegation that the respondent had demanded and received Rs. 5,000 as charges towards use of electricity. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the evidence of the witness was not corroborated by any other evidence and that the witnesses were interested in protecting the appellant and that they were not allowed to cast their votes. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that there were no discussion of the entire evidence and the High Court erred in holding that there had been a contract between the parties and it was alleged that the supporters of the respondent would not be allowed to vote and the denial of the same by the respondent was not justified. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The election petition was liable to be dismissed because (a) the pamphlet was an incident of corrupt practice within the meaning of section 123(3A) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951; (b) the speeches were made with the consent of the candidate or his election agent and (c) the newspaper publication said that the differences between Hindus and Harijans were being spread by the supporters. [903 D E] (2) The evidence in the case showed that the speeches did not amount to communal propaganda against the appellant. The statements in question had to be first a false statement bearing on the personal character and conduct of the candidates and secondly, the statement complained of must be one which is reasonably calculated to prejudice the prospects of the election of the person.

The appellants filed an application under Order XXI Rule 90 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the sale of the property auctioned by the auction purchaser. The learned District Judge held that in view of Article 134(1) of the Constitution, a purchaser of property at a sale in execution of a decree would be deemed to be a party to the suit in which the decree was passed and all questions relating to the delivery of possession of the properties to such purchaser of immovable property would be decided by the executing court. The District Judge also held that since the application for setting it aside was not barred by limitation, the sale was not liable to be set aside. The High Court dismissed the revision petition filed by the appellants against the order of the District Judge confirming the sale. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that: (1) Article 134 of the Limitation Act would apply to an application for delivery of posses sion under Order 21 Rule 90, and (2) since the applications were filed more than one year after the confirmation of the sale, it was barred by time. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The application for set aside the sales made by the 4th judgment debtor auction purchaser against the post & Telegraph Department for setting the sale in question was admitted out of due time on the ground of fraud. [368C] 2.1 Article 134 will apply to a case where there is an appeal from an order dismissing an application to set aside an sale, and where such an application is made and disallowed, the court shall make an order confirming the sales, and thereupon the sale shall become absolute. It is inconceivable that even though no appeal has been filed against an order rejecting an application of the 4 th judgment debtor 's claim for setting at naught such an order passed by the Executing Court under Order XX Rule 90 cannot be equated with an application made to a court in which decree was executed, as provided in clause (a) of Explanation II to section 47 of the Civil Procedure Code. [369D E] 2:2 In view of the provisions of Section 47 of C.P.C., it is not possible to accept the contention that the sale becomes absolute only under the circumstances as mentioned in Rule 89, and that apart from the provisions contained in Rules 89, 90 and 91 of Order XXI of the C. P.C. there can be no doubt that limitation under Article 134 would apply only to an applica tion for setting out the application to be made and may be passed under Order XXII Rule or Rule 91 where such application is filed and disallowed.

The appellant, a candidate for election to the Kerala Legislative Assembly from the State of Kerala, filed an election petition challenging the election of the Kerala Congress Party. The first respondent alleged that there were corrupt practices on the part of the appellant in connection with his election campaign and that he was entitled to be declared duly elected from the said constituency. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the evidence was reasonably calculated to prejudice the prospects of the election. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the first respondent that (i) the words "the candidate or his agent" in the poster were not defamatory and therefore the appellant had no reasonable cause for non compliance with the provisions of section 83(1) of the Act; (ii) the appellant having failed to prove the extrinsic facts to show that he had not taken the extrusions from the voters and that the appellant was guilty of corrupt practice within the meaning of section 123(4) of Act, and (iii) the High Court erred in holding that there was no evidence to show the allegations contained in annexures 1 and 2. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The High court has rightly held that the statement of the second respondent was not a true one. [760C] (2) The appellant had nowhere stated that he or his agents were present at the time of the meeting. It is also not clear from the evidence as to how the allegations in annexures I and 2 were related to the third respondent. [764D E] (3) The evidence on record clearly showed that the wall poster was a part of two corrupt practices committed by the appellant. [774G] (4) The first Respondent had not stated that the election petition or the appeal was false. It was also not stated in the petition that he did not give particulars of the acts done by him. [753A B] (5) The second respondent had not produced any documentary evidence to prove that the poster was defec tively stamped and distributed with a view to create an impression that the candidate or the agent was the holder of the legislative, election work. [754C D] (6) The corrupt practice alleged is committed not by the first Respondent but by his workers with a deliberate intention to defeat the prospects in the elections. It may be that the first respond ent had not shown as to what the appellant did or which he was interested in going to his place of business, because, he had followed as a witness for the pasting of the poster. [758E F] (7) The mere fact that the respondent had complained that the work was done by the workers was not known to him and that it was not necessary to prove this allegation. It could not be said that the corrupt practice was committed in the two election petitions. [759F G] (8) The allegations of corrupt practices were not proved. There is no evidence on which the High court can come to a conclusion that the statements made by the respondent in his election petition were false or that they were calculated to cause any harm to him. It cannot be said, therefore, that the High Courts have insisted upon the personal character of the candidate as well as his at any rate, that it must be held that he has reasonably calculated that the voters had been given a written statement of their intention to show them even though they were not aware of the contents of the statement. [761G H] (9) The respondent 's election petition was liable to be dismissed on the ground that the extraternings in question were defamatory and that there could be no justification for holding that it would be a concise statement of facts on which he relies.

The respondent No. 5, a public limited company, was granted the land in question by the State Government under the Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1966. The land in dispute was purchased by the respondent No 5, an owner of the land. The respondent No 2 set aside the order of the Commissioner of the Municipal Corporation rejecting the plan submitted by the appellant for construction of a five star hotel on the ground that it was proposed to earmark the said land under reference as a recreational ground with suitable internal network of roads during the revision of the development plan which was in the offing. The appellant, therefore, issued a notice to the respondent Nos. 2 and 3, calling upon them to submit their objections, if any, within 15 days from the date of the notice. The appellants filed a writ petition challenging the legality of the order passed by the Commissioner on 25.7.1978. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petition holding that the land was proposed for keeping reserved for a green belt or recreational ground in the interest of the general public. The Municipal Corporation preferred an appeal to this Court against the judgment of the High Court. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The contention of the appellants against the validity of the resolution dated 14.3.1974 and Misc. Petition No. 463 of 1974 is no longer tenable, regard being had to the fact that the draft revised development plan has since been published and the plan was submitted by respondent No, 5 and conditioned by the respon on behalf of the respondent NO. 5. [928C D] 1.2 The contention that the respondent no. 2 has misunderstood the provisions of section 46 is without any substance and is rejected. The Respondent No. 2 had acted in public interest by imposing the conditions mentioned therein. The condition would show that considerable area out of the disputed land has been reserved for recreational ground or green belt. The plan, as sanctioned by the Respondent No 2 with the conditions imposed, has been shown in the draft revision plan. It was open to the Municipal Commissioner to accept the verdict of the appellate authority and it had done so by not challenging it in the High court or before this Court. [936E F] 1:3 The contention raised by the appellants that the order granting exemption should be quashed is without substance and the appellate authori ty was justified in allowing the appeal. It is, therefore. not correct to say that after the Municipal Corpora tion had decided to revise the development scheme, no appeal would lie under section 47 when the Municipal Commis sioner had decided the application for permission to set aside it. [830C D; 928D] 1 :4 The contention regarding the legality or otherwise of the exemption granted by the Government to the Respondent NO.5 has all been considered by the High Courts in its order disposing of the review applications. The contention is without merit and must be rejected. [981E F, 929A] Life Insurance Corporation of India & Anr. vs Municipal Corporation of Greater Bombay & Ors., Writ Petition No 2944 of 1932 disposed of on 6.31984; Life Insurance Corpn. of India and Another vs Municipal Corporatio n of GreaterBombay & Others, Writ Petition Nos. 1745 of 1932 and Others, W.P. No. 2944/ 1932 disposed o.f by the Division Bench of the Bombay High Court in Life Insurance Corpora tions of India vs Municipal Corpration of India, ; , referred to.

The employers contended that they had been guilty of imposing and continuing a lock out as provided in Item 6 of Schedule II of the Maharashtra Recognition of Trade Unions and Prevention of Unfair Labour Practices Act, 1971. The Industrial Court held that the employer had committed an unfair labour practice by imposing and continued a lockout as provided under Item 6. After hearing the parties, the Industrial Court passed an order directing the employers to depute its senior ministerial officer to visit the industrial undertakings of the employers and to satisfy itself that the old workmen were being re inducted in service and that as resumption of production was gradually expanded, the old workman would be re inducted into service. The employer filed two appeals before this Court. The first appeal was dismissed by a single Judge of the High Court holding that the employers had not committed an error apparent on the face of record. The Division Bench held that since the employers have accepted the findings of the Industrial court, the employers were not guilty of unfair labour practices and therefore, there was no error being repeated in future, the employer could not be said to have committed any error in accepting the complaints filed by the union. In the appeal before this court it was contended on behalf of the employer that there was a closure of the industrial undertaking and it was not a case of lock out and that the Industrial Courts were not precluded from declaring unfair labour Practice. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The correct approach ought to be that when it is claimed that the appellant has resorted to closure of industrial activity, the industrial court in order to determine whether the employer is guilty of victimisation must ascertain on evidence produced before it whether the closure was a device or pretence to terminate services of workmen or whether it is bonafide and for reasons beyond the control of the appellant employer. [661C D] 2.

The appellant company was incorporated in 1924 as an investment company. In 1947 the respondent company made a claim for a deduction of certain amounts paid to its shareholders, creditors and properties. The Income tax Officer rejected the claim on the ground that the company had not been registered as a dealer in investments and properties but only an investor. The Appellate Tribunal held that the assessee was a dealer within the meaning of section 2(b) of the Indian Income tax Act and therefore was not liable to be assessed to income tax. On appeal by certificate, Held: (i) The question whether on the facts and in the circumstances of the case the assessee could be treated as a 'dealer ' or an investor is itself a question of law. It is within these narrow limits that the conclusions of fact by the Appellate Tribunal can be challenged under section 66(1). Such conclusions can never be challenged on the grounds that they are based on misappreciation of evidence. There is, however, a third class of cases in which the assessee or the department may seek to challenge the correctness of the conclusion reached by the Tribunal on the question of mixed law and fact. The proper construction of statutory language is always a matter of law and therefore the claim of the assessee that the profits and losses arising from the sale of shares, securities etc. cannot be taxed as profits of a business involves the application of law to the facts found in the setting of the particular case. In dealing with such questions of mixed legal and factual fact the High Court must not enter into the final conclusion; and in that sense the scope of enquiry and the extent of the jurisdiction of the High court in dealing with those points is the same as in dealing in pure points of law, and this Court will not ordinarily interfere with the findings of fact drawn by the appellate Tribunal on such questions. The question as to what are the characteristics of the business in shares or interpretation of relevant provisions of a statute must be regarded as conclusive in a proceeding under section ' 66( 1). G. Venkataswami Naidu & Co. vs C.I.T., ; , referred to.

The appellant was appointed as a Subordinate Judge in the Madras Provincial Judicial Service and on June 19, 1950, he was posted as Subordinate Judge of Masulipatnam. On August 22, 1950 he was transferred to the Subordinate Court of Amalapuram. The appellant filed an application under article 226 of the Constitution for a writ quashing the order of suspension dated January 28, 1954, on the ground that under r. 4(1) (a) of the Madras Civil Services (Disciplinary Proceedings Tribunal) Rules, 1953, which had been published by the Andhra Government on October 22, 1953 with effect from October 1, 1953. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the enquiry was without jurisdiction and that the order in question was void as it was in contravention of article 311 of the Constitu tion. Held, that the rule is not ultra vires the Constitution and must be struck down as invalid. It is well settled that a Government servant has no jurisdiction to decide whether he should dismiss or remove him from service if he together with officers of higher ranks. The order passed by the High Court on January 28 1954 was merely one of suspension pending final orders by the Government and such an order was neither one of dismissal nor of removal from service within article 311 Of the Constitution. It was not a case of dismissal or discharge from service in the subordinate ranks of police forces of the rank of Sub Inspector and below but only sub rule (2) of r. 2 which provided that no cases relating to Government servants on a monthly salary of Rs. 150 and above shall be referred to the Tribunal.

The appellant was a registered holder of 2674 shares of a company which owned shares in the United Kingdom and in British India. The National Bank of India Ltd., obtained probate of the said letters of trust from the estate of a deceased person, who had died on May 13, 1945. In 1946, the National Bank Of India Ltd. obtained probate from the Court of Wards, Bombay, and appointed the respondent James Anderson as the respondent. On August 14, 1946, a notice under section 34(1)(b) of the Income tax Act, 1922, was issued to the estate in British Indian. The respondent thereupon filed an application for and obtained an order on March 26, 1953, under section 23A of the Act, stating that he had reason to believe that the said interest assessable to income tax for the year ending 31st March 1949 had escaped assessment and that he proposed to re assess the escaped income and for that purpose called upon the respondent to make a return of his total world income. The Income tax Officer included the dividends deemed to be distributed in respect of those shares and no question arose as to whether the dividend deemed to have been distributed under the order dated March 26. 1953, was taxable in the hands of the applicant. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner and the Tribunal held that the dividend declared by the estate to the Estate in British British India was not distributed within the meaning of section 24B of the Indian Income tax (Second Amendment) Act, 18 of 1933, but was only a limited application to the income received by a legal representative of the estate who had survived. The High Court on reference held that though after the expiry of the year of account receipts which if the person earning had not died would have been treated as his income, ceased to be liable to assessment as income of the deceased and therefore the dividend was assessable in respect thereof under section 24A of Act 18 of 1932. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that even if after the expiration of the period of one year receipts which, if the persons earning had, not died, would have be treated as their income, then the income deemed to he distributed must be regarded for the purpose of assessment as the personal income of a person who had become a director of the company in place of the person whose estate was vested in him but because the estate was not liable to tax in respect Of the dividend so deemed to remain exempt from tax under section 25B, it had to be followed by an order of assessment to make tax on such income eligible. HELD: (i) The expression "assessee" in section 2(2) as substituted by the Indian Incometax (Second amendment) Act 18 Of 1933, means a person by whom income tax or any other every person in respect o which any proceeding and this Act has been taken for the assessment of his income or of the loss sustained by him or of any amount of refund due to him. By section 3 where income tax is chargeable for any year at any rate or rates prescribed by the Act of the Central Legislature, tax at that rate shall be charged for that year in accordance with and subject to the provisions of the , in respect to the total income of such previous year of every individual, Hindu undivided family, company and local authority. [601 D E] (ii) The word "assessee ' in section 24 B of the Bombay City II vs Shakumtala & Ors., ; , referred to.

The appellant was the Ruler of a State. He entered into an agreement with the Government of India whereby he agreed to pay certain sums of money to the Government and also agreed to make provisions for other matters connected therewith. The agreements were registered under the Indian Independence Act, 1947, and in accordance with the provisions of the Act, the appellant was recognised as a Ruler by the Government. He was assessed to land revenue. On December 15, 1947 he entered into another agreement with Government of india whereby he undertook to pay to the State Government certain sums which were agreed to be paid out of the Consolidated Fund of his State. The appellant contended that the lands in question came within the definition of "proprietor" under section 2(j) of the Indian , and as such fell within the purview of the expression "mahal" given in article 366(22) of Constitution. Held, that the appellant could not claim to be a Ruler for purposes outside the Constitution. The definition of 'proprietor ' contained in section 2 (j) and it was applicable only to a grantee from a State or a Ruler of an Indian State. A maufidar could be a person who was the holder of land which was exempted from the payment of rent or tax. The word "maufidar" in section2(j), includes an ex Ruler, and therefore, the respondent was not a Ruler. The ordinary dictionary meaning of 'Maufi ' is "Ruler". In the definition it is mentioned that in the definition a Ruler means a Prince, Chief or other person by whom any such covenant or agreement as is referred to in cl. (1) of article 366 was entered into and who for the time being was recognised by the President as the successor of such Ruler.

The respondent was working in the office of the Scientist SE, Botanical Survey of India. He was transferred from Shillong to Pauri (Uttar Pradesh). As many as 19 persons were transferred under the said order including the respondent. The respondent filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the transfer order on the ground that his wife is also employed at Shillong in and off ice of the Central Government, that his children are studying there and also because his health had suffered from some mental infirmity. The High Court quashed the order of transfer on the following reasoning: "The transfer order No. DMlO 80/80/80 Estt. dated 29.1.1991 is not vitiated by mala fides on the part of the authority making the order, though the Tribunal does say so merely because certain guidelines issued by the Central Govern ment are not followed, with which finding we shall deal later." The Union of India preferred this appeal against the judgment of the High court. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The guidelines issued in Government of India O.M. dated 3.4.1986 have not been kept in mind while ordering his transfer. It cannot substitute its own judgment for that of the Authority competent to transfer. [431C] 1.2 In the matter of considering transfer of an individual officer, the Office Memorandum dated 3 4 1986 has no application nor can it be said that the Court or Tribunal can quash the order transferring the order if any of the administrative authorities do not consider it feasible. The only thing required is that the departmental authorities should consider this aspect along with the exigencies of administration and enable the two spouses to live together at one station, if it is possible without any detriment to the administrative needs and the claim of other employees. [ 430D E] 1:3. In the instant case, the Tribunal has clearly exceeded its jurisdiction in interfering with the order passed by the transfer. The order of the Tribunal is set aside. [ 431F] Bank of India vs Jagjit Singh Mehta ; , referred to.

The appellants were charged under Section 302 read with section 109 I.P.C. for intentionally causing the death of one Jawahar and they were convicted under Section 304 Part I read with Section 34, I. P.C., and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for five years. The High Court maintained their conviction and sentence.
