In appeal by special leave it was contended that the participation of the appellants in the occurrence which resulted in the death was proved beyond doubt. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The intention of the accused was to cause grievous hurt and as such the offence committed by them comes within the parameters of Section 325 read with 34 I.p.C.[635E] 2.1 In the instant case, the intention of appellants was to caused simple and grievous injuries to P.W. 3, who was also injured in the same day. The deceased had been charged under Sections 147 and 148 I.PC. for instigating A1 to 6 to commit the murder. The second charge related to rioting wherein A 1, A2, A4, A5 and A3 were tried under Sections 302 readwith Section 34 I P. C. and also for causing them to undergo imprisonment for life. [635F G] 2:2. In the event of none of the deceased accused being held guilty, they could have certainly killed him especially after carrying him into the cholam field and left him dead there instead of merely causing simple and simple injuries to him. Even with reference to the aspect whether the accused persons could have intended to cause such injuries as would be sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death, it is not possible to give a finding in favour of the prosecution. [35G H] 2 :3. The conviction and sentences passed against the appellants under Section 323, Part I, read with Sections 34, IPC and the sentence of imprisonment for 5 years respectively are set aside.

The appellant Bank filed a suit against the respondents for recovery of certain amounts due to it on account of loan together with interest. The respondent No. 3, the Managing Director of the respondent No 3 and the respondent Nos. 4 to 12 were also alienees of the mortgaged properties. The appellant bank was nationalised on July 7, 1969 under the Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Act V of 1970. The respondents Nos. 1 to 3 filed a counter claim against the Bank for a sum of Rs.34,48,799. It was contended that they were bona fide purchasers for valuable consideration and the Bank was bound by the alienations and transfers made in their favour under the cash credit account on 28 11 1967, 3 4 1968 and 17 2 1972 respectively. The suit was decreed by the Subordinate Judge holding that no equitable mortgage was created in favour of the Bank and accordingly dismissed the suit against respondents Nos 4 to 13 and refused to direct sale of the properties alleged to have been mortgaged to the Bank. The High Court held that the Bank being a nationalised bank, was not bound by it and as such the Bank could not be bound by alienations and transfer made in its favour of its branches for valuable considerations and the bank was entitled to recover the entire amount without the same being scaled down as provided under section 13 of the Act. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant Bank that (i) the words `any special Indian law ' in section 4(e) of the said Act refer and relate to a special law enacted by the Indian Parliament; (ii) the expression `special Indian law" has a clear and unambiguous meaning and there is no need for its interpretation. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The words `special ' law ' are placed after the words 'an Act of Parliament ' and before the words "in pursuance of an Act of the British Parliament of the United Kingdom or any special Indian Law or Royal Charter or Letters Patent" in section 2(a) of that Act. [970C] 2.1 The expression `Special Indian law` means a special Indian statute enacted by an Act, and not in pursuance of such a law. It will be highly unreasonable and illogical to think that as a corporation has been formed by or under a special I Indian law and not by the law itself in order to come within the purview of section 4 (e) it is not necessary for the legislature to look at the setting in which the words are used. [971D] 2:2 The expression 'special Indian Law ' means a Special Indian law enacted or by an enactment of the Indian Legislature. In this connection, it may be pointed out that in Krishna Murthy 's case, the question was whether the Banking companies Act by or has been enacted by Parliament as a piece of special legislation under the provisions of section 3(a), of the , would not apply to corporations formed or created by any special II law. [969E F] 2 :3 The expression "special Indian laws" in Section 4(c) refers and relates to a law made by the British parliament specially for India. It is not known what was the actual balance on the date of the bank being nationalised. It has been stated that the words, `any ' special Indian laws ' refer to a Special II.P.C.

The petitioners were dealers in sugar factories in Punjab, Uttar Pradesh and North Bihar. They did not join the petition. The Central Government promulgated Sugar (Control) Order 1955 under which the Central Government was given power to appoint an export agency for carrying out the work of buying sugar in the Indian market and exporting it to foreign markets and fixing the quantity of sugar for export. The petitioners challenged the validity of the impugned notification on the ground that it violated article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution inasmuch as it imposed unreasonable restrictions on their right to carry on trade under article 19 (1) (g). Held, that the impugned Notification was not an unreasonable restriction on the petitioners ' right to carrying on trade. The object of the Act is to secure essential commodities for the general public and to ensure equitable distribution and availability at fair prices. The control provided under cl. (c) of section 3(2) is control at any of the three stages mentioned therein. The power conferred on the Central Govern ment by section 3 is controlled by the circumstances of each case. In a case like the present, where the sugar factory was not compelled to sell at any price, whether it was fixed at an earlier stage or not, and there were no reasonable grounds for such restriction, the impugned notifications could not be said to have been discriminatory because they infringed article 19 of the constitution. The provisions of section 4(1) and (2) of Act IV of 1958 are intended to protect the essential commodities from being compelled to trade under Article 19(i)(g).

The Government of West Bengal by its order dated September 13, 1956, made an order transferring the dispute from the file of the Second Industrial Tribunal to that of the Fifth Industrial Tribunal. The appellant company challenged this order before the High Court on the ground that the order was bad in law and without jurisdiction as it had not been passed in accordance with the provisions of section 19(6) of the , and therefore, the reference was bad. It was contended by the Company that the award was invalid because it did not refer to the fluctuating rate in 1957 and that the Tribunal went wrong in taking the rise in the cost of living index between the years 1954 and 1957 instead of taking the fluctuations in the year 1954 as a result of which the workmen were settled at the intervention of Shri A. R. Ghosh, Asstt. Labour Commissioner, who was appointed by the Government to make an award on August 26, 1957. The Company contended that the Award did not terminate in accordance therewith and that it had no jurisdiction to refer the fluctuities in the index to the Industrial Tribunal under section 19 (6) Of the Act. Held:(i) The award of the Tribunal was binding on the appellant company and it was not open to it to make out a new case for the first time before it disposed of the appeal. The question whether there was a change in the circumstances which entitled the employees to claim an increase in dearness allowance was a matter within the jurisdiction of the Industrial Disputes (Amendment) Act, 1956. Pritam Singh vs The State of Punjab, ; , followed. (ii)The award of December 13, 1957, was not binding on it and could not be challenged under section 34 Of the Indian Arbitration Act. The award did not set out any particular point raised by the parties but only stated that the question whether the Tribunal had jurisdiction to entertain the claim before it or not was a new dispute which was referred under the agreement. Pritam singh vs The Union of India, ; and Pritam Singh v The State, A.I.R. 1954 S.C. 271, relied on. (iii)The Tribunal wrongly relied upon the correspondence between the parties and held that there was change in circumstances which could not have been permitted to be raised by it in this Court.

The appellant was the Matad Nyadar of a village in the district of Anantapur. He filed a suit challenging the validity of the scheme on the ground that it contravened his fundamental rights under article 19(1)(f) and (g). The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court allowed the appeal holding that the scheme having been framed as early as 1939, the appellant was not free to make a scheme in consonance with the provisions of the earlier Act which was valid when it was enacted. In appeal by certificate, Held:(i) The scheme is valid and the scheme as a whole will be deemed to have been made under the latter Act and will be effective from the 26th January 1950 under article 13(1) of the Constitution. (ii)The scheme as framed in 1939 was valid and it was not necessary to examine whether all the provisions Of the said schemes were necessarily justified by or consistent with the relevant provisions of this latter Act; and (iii)the scheme was validly continued by operation of section 103(d) of that Act and so it was open to the appellant to challenge the validity thereof on the grounds that it deprived him of his fundamental right under article19(1). East End Dwellings Co. Ltd. vs Finsbury Borough Council ([1952] A.C. 109), relied on. (iv)The High Court was in error in holding that since the scheme was framed and a challenge made by the appellant, it contravened the Mathadhip Act, 1947, and the appellant could not be allowed to challenge it.

The appellant was appointed as Hindi Teacher in Bani gochha, M.E. School (Orrisa) for a period of 89 days or till a candidate selected by the State Selection Board was made available. He joined the school on July 12, 1982 and continued to serve the school with repeated spells of 89 day appointments and one day break in between the spells, till May 25, 1986. He was not paid the salary for the period of summer vacations during all these years. The managing committee of the school considered his continuous appointment as Hindi teacher but no action was taken by the said authority. The appellant filed a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution before the Orissa High Court claiming regularisation as Hindi Teachers with effect from July 12 1982. The High Court rejected the prayer for regularisation and held that the appellant was not entitled to the benefit of the Validation Act on the ground that his initial appointment was conditioned by the stipulation that he would continue until replaced by a candidate from the select list. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The State Government is expected to function as a model employer. "We are of the view that the State is committed to secure right to education for all citizens. bulk of our population is yet illiterate. Till the time illiteracy is effaced from the country the resolution enshrined in the Preamble cannot be fulfilled. Education is the dire need of the country. There are neither enough schools nor teachers to teach. Insecurity is writ large on the face of the teaching community because of nebulous and unsatisfactory conditions of service. [995E F] Rattan Lal vs State of Haryana, A.I.R 1987 S.C. 478; Rattan Lal V. State of Punjab, AJ.R. 1987 S C. 478 and Rattan Lal v. State, A J.R., 1987 S .C. 477, referred to. 2. The law is enacted by the Orissa legislature with the obvious object of granting relief to those members of teaching community who are being exploited for years together by keeping them in short spell appointments like 89 day appointment as here with one day breaks and in the process denying them their rightful dues and other service benefits.

The appellant was a Chairman of a Panchayat Samiti. He was elected to the State Legislative Assembly and his election was challenged by the respondent, who was the Chairman of the Panchayat Samiti in an election petition filed under section 116A of the Representation of the People Act, 1951. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the allowances paid under rules 3 to 7 were not salary, remuneration or honorarium and therefore could not be deducted from his own pocket for purposes of payment of salary. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that : (i) the payment of travelling allowance and daily allowance under r. 3 to a Chairman, Panchayat Sanstha and Members of Panchayat Samitis and Zila Parishads were based on Rules 3 to7 of the Punjab Panchayat Samitis ' Rules, 1952; (ii) the rules did not convert the office of Chairman of Panchayat Samiti into an office of profit; and (iii) the appellant was entitled to draw travelling allowance. HELD : (1) The payment under rules 4 to 7 was in addition to the payment under r 3. [427 B] (2) The High Courts were right in holding that as the respondent was the Secretary of a Gram Panchayat performing a journey by Motor Vehicles, he could not spend money out of his own pockets for the discharge of his official duties. [426 C D] (3) The rules did indicate that the allowance paid is not salary or honorarium. It is clearly an allowance paid for the purpose of ensuring that the Chairman must undertake journeys within the district and must be incurring expenditure when attending meetings, supervising plans, projects, schemes and other works and also in connection with the discharge Of other lawful obligations and implementation of Government directives. No evidence has been led on behalf the appellant to show that out of the amount received as daily allowance the Chairman will in fact invariably make a saying, it cannot be held that this payment would result in gain so as to make the office an office an 'office of profit. [527 C D; 428 E F] (4) The respondent was entitled under r, 3 to draw his travelling allowance, and daily allowances when a Chair man performs a journey in connection therewith.

The appellant was the tenant of a shop in the demised premises. The respondent landlord filed a suit for eviction on a number of grounds including the ground that the appellant had made constructions materially altering the accommodation without his consent and that the tin shed marked by letters ABCD had been constructed by the appellant without the consent of the landlord. The trial court held that the respondent landlord was liable for eviction under section 14(c) of the U.P. Cantonment Rent Control Act, 1952. On appeal, the Additional Civil Judge set aside the trial Court 's order and dismissed the respondents suit on the findings that none of the construc tions constituted material alteration. The High Court in second appeal reversed the decision of the Additional District Judge holding that the landlord was not entitled to file a suit under section 15(c). In the appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellant that the disputed constructions were temporary in nature and did not constitute material alterations as required by section 14 (c) and that they were mere repairs which did not make any structural change. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The question whether a construction of the tin sheds or the structure, if framed, would fail within the mischief of material alteration, is a mixed question of fact and law. [975G] 2.1 The material alterations contemplated by section 15 (c), show that the expression 'materially altered ' means "a substantial change in the character, form and the structure of the building without destroying its identity". The meaning given to these two words show that a construction which converted the tenanted premises into two rooms and a tin shed with out the ceiling, instead, is to be of such a temporary nature as to materially alter the accommodation. [ 975G H] 2:2 In the instant case, the disputed construction was constructed by appellant without digging any foundation of the floor of the room nor it touched the ceiling. The partition wall was made without digging the floor. The house was made with the consent and the erstwhile landlord. It was a temporary wall of 6 feet height converting the big hall into two portions for its convenient use, it could be removed at any time without causing any damage to the building. [977A B] 2(a) The question as to what constructions could materially alter or affect the form and character of the buildings must be answered in the negative. In the absence of any legislative defi cution of the said words it would be useful to refer to the meaning given by these words to buildings, which are temporary and alterations for the convenient use of the tenanted accommodation do not materially alter its building as in spite of such constructions the front and structure of a building may remain unaffected. The essential element which needs consideration is as to whether the constructions are sub stantial in nature or they alter, the form, front and structures of the accommodation, as it can easily be removed without causing damage to building. The construction so made would furnish ground for eviction only when they bring about substantial change of substantial character either in the form or structure of building. There is no material on record to sustain the findings of the High Court that the appel lant had constructed pucca structures and alterations, as such, he was liable to be evicted under section 13(c)(f) of U. P. Cantonment Act.

The appellant company filed a suit against the respondent firm for setting aside an ex parte decree for Rs. 28,479/ passed in favour of the respondent. The trial court held that summons was not duly served on the company and it came to know about the ex parte order for the first time when its constituted attorney was presented to him at its registered office. The appellant filed a revision petition under section 115 C.P.C. before the High Court which set aside the exparte decree. The High Court held that since the respondent had no knowledge of the ex appearance of the appellant company, the application filed by it under Order 9 Rule 13 C. P.C., was within time. In this appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellant that the respondent was not a person who was entitled to be served on behalf of the company in accordance with sub clause (a) of Rule 2 of Order 29 of C.p.C.; and that the service of summons as effected in accordance therewith was mandatory under clause (b). Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The words "Principal Officer" in clause (c) of rule 2 would include managing agents and it can, under this rule, be on a juristic person. [1032C] 2.1 In Rule 17 of Order 5, it has been provided that where the defendant or his agent or any other principal officer of the corporation is valid under clause(a), he may leave the summons at the registered office of the Company and make a report to that effect. In the instant case nothing of the kind was done. It was not the case of the Respondent in its rejoinder filed in the Miscellaneous Petition that the services of the summons as affected by the ex ' parte decree were duly served upon the company because it was left at the Registered office of respondent No. 2. [ 1032E F] 2:2 The appellant under the orders of the Court had furnished bank guarantee for the decretal amount. It has agreed to continue the same till disposal of the suit. [1133G] 3. In view of the provision contained in Order 5 Rule 17 C. p.C, the High court was clearly wrong in interfering with it. [1103A] 4. The respondent No 2 had no authority or power to accept service of the summon on natural persons.

The Magistrate, after passing a preliminary order on 29th July, 1976, recorded reasons for his being satisfied that a breach of peace existed even in the final order. The Magistrate passed an order under section 145(5) Cr. P.C., holding that there was an apprehension of breach of the peace, and therefore, the final orders were bad and set aside the final Order on 17th July. 1978 declaring the appellant to be in possession of the land in dispute. Against this order, the respondents moved the High Court under section 482 Cr.P.C. for quashing the said order. A Single Judge of the High court held that as there was no clear finding by the Magistrate in the preliminary order that there existed a breach or peace, the Magistrate called upon the parties to file their written statements and then after a full enquiry as provided by section 145 the Magistrate passed the final Orders on 17.7.1978 declaring the appellants to be In possession of land in question. Against the said orders, the Respondents moved the Division Bench under section 483 Cr. The High Court found that as the respondents had failed to show that there were any apprehension of a breach, the order was bad and quashed the order of the Magistrate. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1. Under section 145 it is for the Magistrate to be satisfied regarding the existence of a disturbance of the public peace and once he records his satisfaction in the main order, he has to attend his court in person or by pleader and put in written statements of their respective claims as respects the fact of actual possession of subject of dispute. The enquiry under section145 is limited to the question to who was in actual possession on the date of preliminary order irrespective of the rights of the parties. [96C D] 1.2. In R. H. Bhutani vs Miss Mani J. Desai & Ors., ; , this Court held that once a preliminary Order drawn up by the magistrate sets out the reasons for holding that a disturbance is likely to cause breach of public peace, it is not necessary that the breach of such peace should continue at every stage of the proceedings unless there is clear evidence to show in the instant case that any prejudice was caused to any of the respondents who had the full opportunity to produce their evidence before the Court. [94D E] 1:3. The order passed by the High Courts is legally erroneous and cannot be allowed to stand. [95E F] Ramarao vs Shivram & Ors. ; , referred to.

The appellant, a registered firm carrying on business in the manufacture and sale of yarn, filed its returns for the assessment years 1941 to 1955. The appellant claimed that the profits earned by it were genuine and not genuine and that they should be added to the profits of the year in their accounts. The Income tax Officer held that the assessee was not a 'dealer ' within the meaning of section 2(c) of the Indian Companies Act, 1913, but that the sales effected by the appellant were genuine, that the transactions were sham and fictitious and that the income received by it was not liable to be added back to the amounts shown as profits in its accounts. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that they were not taxable under section 66(1) of Act. The Tribunal held that though the sales were made on these sales, the appellant had failed to pay the amount shown in its books of account and therefore it was liable to include them in its income. In reference, the High Court held that as the appellant did not have a legal evidence to support its conclusion, the Tribunal could not be said to have been bound by the conclusions of the Tribunal. On further appeal to this Court, Held: (i) The finding of the Appellate Tribunal that the intermediaries were benamidars for the appellant was bad for the reason that there was no legal evidence in support of the finding of fact. It was also not open to the High court to re examine the findings of the tribunal on the question whether those findings were perverse or not, and it was only in the former class of cases that it would be necessary to draw a distinction between transactions which were made by the intermediaries as distinct entities and those which were really historical matters. The finding that the appellant 's firms were benamis for the appellants could not stand on the same footing as that of the appellant, because, there was nothing in law to show that there had been no legal or legal evidence on the record. (ii)The Tribunal had found in its order that the assessees were benamidar for the assessee and that it had also held that there were no legal documents which showed that the appellants were benamid persons. The High Court was right in observing that the finding that they acted as benamidars was not based on any evidence, and that there is no basis for this finding. (iii)The finding of facts recorded by the Tribunal were binding on the appellant under section 11(1).

The assessee, a company carried on the business of manufacture and sale of blankets and other woollen cloth. For the assessment year 1948 49, the Income Tax Officer disallowed the claim for deduction of Rs. 75465 as commission paid to the General Manager. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income tax Officer. On further appeal, the Tribunal held that the post of General Manager carried the responsibility equal to that of the Director who was given the charge of the conduct of business after his death and that the amount of Rs, 37,732 paid to Shri J.P. Vaish was an amount laid out or expended wholly or exclusively for the purpose of the business. The High Court answered the question against the assessee. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that in the circumstances of this case the entire amount of RS. 75,465 paid to him as commission was an ex gratia payment to a charge of Rs 18,000 and not wholly for the purposes of carrying on business. HELD: (i) The question whether an amount claimed as expenditure was laid out wholly or solely for the purpo se of business, profession or vocation as required under section 10(2)(Xv) of the Act has to be decided on the facts and circumstances of each particular case. But as observed by this Court in Swadeshi Cotton Mills Co. Ltd. vs C.I.T., U.P., ; , the final conclusion on the admissibility of an allowance is one of law. [529 A B] (ii) The principle of this decision applies to the present case and it must accordingly be held that in view of the circumstances established by the assessee, the entire sum of Rs 75465 paid by him was an expenditure laid out for the business, and that he was not entitled to it. [ 530 C D] Swadesha Cotton Mills Company Ltd. V. C. I.T. Bombay, ; , applied. (iii) The High Courts were right in taking the circumstance that the entire amounts of Rs., 75465 were paid by the appellant as commission to the general manager who was giving the charge. [525 G] Swanshi Cotton mills Co. vs Commissioner of Income tax, U. P., ; and Swadesi Cotton Mills Ltd.v. C,.I. T., U .P., , referred to.

The appellant was a workman employed in the Digha factory of which he was a member. On January 13, 1954, the management and the Union filed a joint petition for compromise settling all points of disputes out of court. Prior to this date the appellant had made an application praying that D. N. Ganguli and M. P. Gupta may be allowed to represent his case before the Tribunal instead of Fateh Singh as he had no faith in him. The Tribunal passed an order fixing December 20, 1956, "for filing compromise or hearing". On January 12, 1957, the appellant filed a fresh application for time stating that D was not authorised to enter into any agreement in his case and prayed for an issue of an appropriate writ or direction quashing the Tribunal 's order. The High Court dismissed the application summarily. In appeal by special leave: Held, that the settlement between the parties was collusive and mala fide and that the Secretary of the Union had made the complaint against the appellant without prejudice to pay an ex gratia amount of Rs. 1,000/ . The proper course for the Tribunal to take note also of the fact that when an individual workman becomes a party to a dispute under the Industrial Disputes Act he is a party not independently of the union which has espoused his cause. The Union or those who have by their sponsoring turned the individual dispute into an industrial dispute can therefore claim to have a say in the conduct of the proceedings before the tribunal. The union or those workmen who have, by their sponsorship or otherwise, espoused their cause and claim to be represen ted by somebody else. The principle that the party to the dispute should have a fair hearing is not applicable to an application for a writ under article 226 of the Constitution. In the present case there were no such exceptional circumstances. It has been suggested that the Union 's Secretary was in charge of the conduct and proceedings before it, and that he had made a complaint against him which resulted in the order of dismissal. The appellant could not therefore be said to have any error in refusing the application for writ.

The appellants were the tenants of two defendants in a suit for ejectment and recovery of rent against the two defendants. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the defendants had no right to continue the appeal, but the High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (1) the provisions of r. 3 of 0. XXII of the Code of Civil Procedure were not applicable to the facts of the case as the nine appellants constituted a joint Hindu family and other members of the family were already on record, and (2) the suit for eviction was barred by section 5 of the Limitation Act. Held:(i) The appeal by the surviving appellants was competent in view of the provisions Of r. 4 of 0 XLI of the C.P.C., which provided that the judgment of the appellate court shall be in writing and shall state inter alia the relief to which the appellant is entitled in case the decree appealed against was reversed or varied. The appeal could not have been filed by any one or more defendants, as the respondents had a common right and interest in getting a decree of ejectment against defendant No. 2 and such decree could have been passed only after the death of the plaintiff respondent though the decree against him had become final. (ii)The High Court was wrong in holding that r. 33 was not applicable because the defendants constituted a Joint Hindu family, that the suit was not to be reversed or modified with respect to such rights to which section 5 Of the Limitation act applied and that the decree in favour of the respondents could not continue even after the appeal by kedar Nath had abated as all the appellants had a joint interest in letting out the property. (iii)The appeal by K, who was the widow of the deceased appellant, was incompetent in view Of r, 33 of 0 XXII of C. P.C. which provided for different contingencies. The rule is under the sub heading 'judgment in appeal '. Rule 31 dealt with a matter different from the matter dealt with by r. 9 of O. XXII and no question of its provisions overriding those of rs. 9 could arise. (iv)The decree was not therefore to be set aside on the ground common to all of them. The High Court could not, therefore, have heard the appeal of K when the appeal was filed by K. The legal representatives of the original plaintiff and the surviving appellant were not impleaded as respondents.

The appellant was the tenant of May 19, 1954. The respondent landlord filed a petition for eviction against the appellant on the ground that the respondent landlord had terminated the tenancy by notice dated January 1, 1962. The Rent Controller held that the lease was for a specified period and not one year and that the forfeiture of the tenancy caused by sub letting was invalid. On appeal, the appellate tribunal affirmed the decision of the Rent Controller. In the High Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant tenant that (i) the lease in question was for three years of the old business; (ii) the notice terminating the tenancy was for one year only and not a period of 11 months; and (iii) the respondent had no subsisting cause of action. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The requirement as to written notice in writing under section 111(g) of the Transfer of Property Act is a statutory recognition of no obligation or obligation which has been imposed by those transactions which are covered by the law by its own force. [918C] 2.1 The requirement of a notice in the ordinary law, if it is mandatory for an oral communication to determine the lease, can be said to be based on such terms as may be implied from the statute. The rule of English Law before the enactment of the Law of Property act, 1925, appears to be that a suit for ejectment is equivalent to re entry and a written notice of forfeiture must not only be in writing but also in conformity with the statutory provisions. [936F G] 2:2 In the instant case, the requirement as contained in section 111 (g) was not based on any principle of justice, equity and good conscience. The basic question is whether the notice in English law has been breached or is not a mere formality. [815C D] 3.1 Section 111(d), which is a part of the Indian Rent Act, does not require that notice must be given in writing. It is only when the landlord says so. There is no statutory requirement that notice as laid down in section III (g), should be given to him in writing and in case he chooses, he must comply with the requirements of the notice. The requirements of a written statement are not such as canon the face of it other wise than a mere institution, brought home to the lessee his election to eject on the strength of the said breach. [943C D; 919A B] 3:2.1 In the present case, there was no requirement in law for the notice under section III(g), nor was it shown that the notice was not given to the tenant in the present suit. The High Court erred in holding that the provision of a statutory notice under Section 111 (d) did not require the notice as it was not issued by the landlord. [942C D, 919D] 2 :2.2. In this case, no notice was served on the appellant in the instant suit for eviction and there is no question of any requirement requiring service of notice under sub section (g). The High court erred in its view that a notice under the section could be given only to a person who had been lawfully a tenant for and conferring upon himself of the right to eject an where he was required to pay falls within the rule of justice. [947E F] 2 .3.

The appellant was a member of the Assam Secretariat Service. He was confirmed in that post on 1st November, 1946. On 18th December, 1950 he was served with an order by the District Magistrate under Rule 30(1) of the Defence of India Rules, 1962, and after serving for about three months, he was dismissed from service with immediate effect. The appellant challenged the orders of dismissal in a writ petition before the High Court which was dismissed on the ground that the Governor had acted mala fide in passing the order of dismissal without consulting the State Public Service Commission which was compulsory under Rule 10 of the Rules and Regulation 6 of the said Rules. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that the order was passed without consultation with the State Government as required by the amended Article 311(2) of Constitution and that the impugned order was not in conformity with the provisions of the proviso to clause (2) Of article 311; and that in view of the decision of this Court in Khem Chand vs The Union of India, ; , the Governor was competent to pass an order of his dismissal without holding an inquiry. HELD:(i) The expression "as stated therein" in the amended article 311(3)(c) means "the Government may, for reasons to be recorded in writing, remove a person from service on the grounds of conduct which has led to his conviction on a criminal charge". [490 B] (ii) The words used in the proviso are wide enough to include an opportunity to deny his guilt and establish that he was not guilty of any misconduct. [491 C D] (iii) The word "as" occurring in the said clause means "to make expedient to hold the inquiry under the principal clause". It is a well settled principle of interpretation that the words used therein must be given their natural meaning. In order to enable the Governor to pass the order, the Governor has to arrive at an opinion on the question of misconduct which may be inflicted on a Government servant. [490 E] (iv) The power conferred by the proviso is not unguided or uncanalised. But it does not make it compulsory for the Commission to be consulted. It is only the Governor who can do so and the Governor 's satisfaction under cl. (2), of article 311 is final. [492 F G] Khem Chand V. Union of lndia, ; ; , followed. (v) The proviso to cl. 2(c) of article 320(3) does not confer any rights on a public servant so that the absence of consultation or any irregularity in consultation does not afford him a cause of action in a court of law, vide State of U.P. vs Manbodhan Lal Srivastava; , and Khem Chand v Union of india, [1969] Vol. I S.C.R. 892, referred to. (vi) The Governor ' s power to dismiss a Government employee is not absolute but only to give him an opportunity of showing cause against the action proposed to be taken in regard to him. The effect of such satisfaction is that the government servant is dismissed without even being told of the charges against him. When such serious consequences follow, it is necessary that the pre condition laid down by sub cl. 3(c), must be satisfied before a Government Servant can be dismissed. [493 G H] (vii) The consultation with Public Service Commis sioner in the present case was not prescribed either by the Rules or by the Regulations. The consultation, therefore, with the Public Service commission was only under article 320 (3)(a). [494 A B] Khemchand vs Union of Indian, ; and Khemchand V.

The petitioners, who were the Muslim Community, challenged the constitutional validity of the Shia community 's right to perform their religious ceremonies and functions on the grounds that they had been deprived of lawful rights to perform the religious ceremonies, practices, observances and functions in accordance with the provisions of the U.P. Muslim Waqfs Act, 1936, by the Shias 's alleged adulterations, and that the impugned order was violative of their fundamental right under article 32 of the Constitution. The High Court allowed the petition holding that the petitioners were not entitled to any of the reliefs claimed in the writ petitions. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the two sects were distinct and independent of each other, and (ii) the impugned orders passed by the Sunni community under section 144 Cr. P.C., were invalid as being violative of articles 14, 19(1)(f), 21 and 31 of the Consti tution. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Shia Community is not entitled either to any fundamental right or fundamental rights guaranteed by Article 32 of Constitution. [1134B] 2. The impugned orders were bad in law because they infringed their fundamental rights under articles 25 and 26 of the Constitu tion. They are violative of Articles 14,19(1) (f),21 and 31. [1235C D] 3. The two sectings in question, one at the time when the petition was filed, and the other at the hearing, were not based on Appendices VIII and IX annexed to the petition showing that the sects as Shia Waqfs for performance of their religious rites and functions had been registered as Shias Waqfs. [1335D E] 4. The petitioners have failed to establish their claims about the holding of the Majlis in question by virtue of the provisions contained in section 144 Criminal Procedure Code, 1973. [1436E F] 5. The order passed by a District Magistrate under section 145(2) of the Criminal Procedure Act is not a judicial or quasi judicial order and it must be pointed out that all the decisions including those of this Court are based on different facts. [1535G] 6. The orders passed under section 143 Cr.P.,C. are not in any way inconsistent with the principle analogous to res judicata. [1636B] 7. The proceedings initiated by the petitioners as regards the two Shia sects, namely, Shia Muslims and Sunni Muslims, are not illegal or without jurisdiction. [1735E F; G] 8. The fact that the section does not recognise the succession of a Shia Muslim by the respondent in his individual capacity and as such the individual members of the community cannot be allowed to take advantage of the lawful exercise of their rights in any manner by the respondents or members of Shia religion is no ground for challenging the impugned action. [1836F] 9. The petition under article 226 of the constitution is not barred by res judicata or principle analogous thereto. [1934G] 10. The question whether a Shias are entitled to perform its religious rites, practices and functions as Shiasi Muslims or to appoint a person aggrieved by any judicial or quasijudicial order passed against a of the petitioners or members belonging to the minority community is a matter which has to be decided by this Court in an appropriate case. [2034A] 11. The rights of Shias to their customary rights to performed their religious rituals and functions, on the plots and structures in question have been established and are subject to the binding effect of their legal rights and every time instead of exercising the power in aid of their right it is being exercised in suppressing their rights under the pretext of imminent danger to public tranquility. [2135B] 12. The respondents are seeking to set at naught the earlier decision of this court in Civil Appeal No.

The assessee, a limited company, was carrying on business in the assessment year 1957 58. The assessee, being a limited Company, disclosed capital gains of Rs.3,10,200 but claimed set off of capital loss of Rs 3,17,500 sustained by it during the assessment years 1957 58 and 1961 66 over sale of shares to three associate concerns. It was maintained by the Income tax Officer that the loss was sustained in the previous year relevant to the assessment for 1957 58, and that the same should be set off against the capital gains in the assess ment year 1965 66. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that there was no genuine loss; it was only a notional loss which could have been set off in accordance with the provisions of Section 24(3) of the 1922 Act. On appeal by the Revenue, the Tribunal held that the assessee was entitled to the benefit of set off under section 24(4) of 1922 Act, and accordingly set off on the footing that when in the course of assessment year, 1957 58 the loss had been claimed it was excluded in the computation of income as capital gains. In reference, the High Court held that in view of the provisions contained in Section 80 of the 1961 Act regarding intimation of losses as notional when he really meant that it was an estimate. It agreed with the conclusion of the Tribunal and found against the Revenue. Dismissing the appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1. The benefit conferred under section24 of 1922 act continued to be given effect to under the 1961 act and notwithstanding the wordings of section 80 of latter Act, the same cannot be allowed to be taken advantage of by the revenue, nor should it be used to the prejudice of the assessee. [1164E] 2.1 The benefit of setting off has been claimed in the assessments year 1965 68 to which the Act of 1961 applied. It is necessary to turn attention to the relevant provisions thereof and they are in sections 74 and 80. For convenience they are extract ed from section 80 together. Section 80 provides that where any assessee sustains a loss such as is referred to in sub section (2A) and the loss cannot be wholly set off, in accordance therewith, the portion not so set off shall be carried forward to the following year and so on. however that no loss shall be carry forward for more than eight years. [1106G H; 1166A] 2:2 The benefit under section 23 of 1922 is continued to he given effect from the 1st day of April 1961, or any earlier assessment year which is not a part of the assessment Act, but the loss could be wholly sets off in accord ance with the provi sions of that sub section.

The respondent was recruited as a Senior Scientific Officer on October 12, 1966 in the Defence Science Service. He was posted in the Directorate of Technical Development and Production (Air) (DN) and P. The Department of Defence Research & Development (DRDO) was reconstituted as Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDS). The appellant who was working in DTD & P. was transferred to the Directorate, Naval Science Service on October 1, 1979. He joined the Directorate on October 2, 1979 and was posted according to the exigency of service in any of the said three units. His services were inter changeable and inter transferable. The respondent approached the Administrative Tribunal by way of a writ petition challenging the order dated May 12, 1985, which was dismissed by the High Court holding that the re spondent was not liable to be retired at the age of 58 years his superannuation age being deemed to have been increased to 60 years in view of the OM dated 24.12.85 read with ODAS (R & D) and DoS (DNP) Rules, and that he would continue in service till he attains the age Of 60 years unless of course for some other legal reasons it becomes necessary to discontinue his services before that date. The appellant Union of India filed an appeal against the decision of the Tribunal contending that the Government had a right to prescribe different conditions of service for the members belonging to the different units and merely because the superannuation age of the members of the DRDS was increased, it could not be held that the respondent who belonged to another unit, viz. DAQAS, was entitled to the said benefit. The High Court dismissed the appeal. Dismissing the appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The question is whether the respondent was also entitled to claim the benefit of the power so exercised in the facts and circumstances of the case. [319B] 1.2 The decision of this Court in Union of india vs M/s. Air Force, ; , relied on. 1.3 The question involved in the instant appeal is not whether the Government has such power. The question was whether the respond ent was also liable to he retired at tho age of 60 years. [330C] 1:4 In view of Rule 12 of the Central Civil Services (Pension) Rules which applied to all the three units, the respondent could not claim the benefits of the enhanced superannuation age from the different unit. The decision is both proper and valid. There is no substance in the appeal preferred by the Union of lndia.

The appellant was elected to the Sangli City Municipality. The election was challenged by a petition on several grounds, one of which was that he had been guilty of publication of two pamphlets in the Official Gazette and the other of corrupt practices committed by him as alleged by the petitioner. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the two witnesses who were examined as court witnesses had been cited by the election petitioner earlier and the Judge had in the exercise of jurisdiction vested in him refused to issue summonses to them when he was asked to do so on August 21, 1968. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the procedure adopted by the trial court was wrong in that the first issue which was decided against the appellant on the first date was not maintainable; and (ii) the election petition was filed beyond time and should have been entertained. HELD: The High court was not called upon to go into this question. It is for the High Court to take a different view. But it cannot be said that there was no evidence on which the Judge could have come to the conclusion he did, The first issue was rather confusing and misleading. Instead of framing a separate issue with regard to each charge of corrupt practice raised in the petition, the learned judge framed the issue in a manner which leaves much to be desired. [975 D E] In the instant case, though the election petitioners had not been examined but during the course of the evidence led before the trial Court it became quite clear that the trial Judge was satisfied that the appellant had been personally responsible for the distribution of the first pamphlet and as such found him guilty of a corrupt practice. There is no reason to interfere with the order of the High court under article 227 of the Constitution.

The petitioner was a registered dealer under the U. P. Sales Tax Act, 1948. He was assessed to sales tax in accordance with the provisions of that Act. The contention of the petitioner was that the Validation Act was ultra vires the powers of the State Legislature under article 213(1) of the Constitution and that it was not a law which the State legislature could pass on to the purchaser. Held, that the validation Act was intra vires the State Government and was valid. The Validation Act is not ultra vires. The effect of the legislation as stated in the long title and in the preamble to the Act was to validate the impugned notification in relation to the amended section. The validating Act was passed by the legislature within its own legislative field and it was therefore ultra vires article 213 of the constitution. The State Legislature could not enact a law with retrospective operation without the saving provisions of the U P. sales Tax Act. M. P V. Sundararamier & Co. vs The State of Andhra Pradesh, ; , referred to. Held further, that there is no substance in the contention that the validating Act is ultra vires and the impugned notifications are ultra vires as they purported to validate a tax imposed by the Government on the sale of goods under entry 54 in List II of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution. The expression "in the form in which they were in force immediately before the commencement of this Act" in section 3 must be given its ordinary meaning and it is not an essential characteristic of a sales tax that the seller must have the right to pass it on to him, nor was the power of the legislature to impose a tax on the purchasers as did the U . P. General Sales Tax (Amendment) Act, 1957, which introduced section 3 in the Act into the Act, be held to be ultra vires, void and inoperative. The Union of India vs Madan Gopal, ; and M.P.

The appellant was convicted and sentenced to death under section 302 I.P.C. and the High Court affirmed it in appeal. In appeal to this Court, on behalf of the appellant it was contended that the sentence imposed by the Sessions Court was not excessive; that the extreme penalty of death was not unreasonable; that there was no pre mature incarceration which could be simplistically assumed by award of long incarceration, for, the offence committed by him was beyond doubt and that he had a young wife and a farm to look after. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The sentence of imprisonment is reduced to rigorous imprisonment for two years. [591B] 2.1 In the instant case, the appellant was in his early twenties and signs of repentance are seen. The victim and her parents have forgiven the criminal. While it is possible that the accused may procure such condonation from unwilling victim, the fact remains that the two families being close cousins are ready to take a lenient view of the situation. Of course, this does not bind the Court in any manner. [592C D] 2:2 In the circumstances of the case, in the instant cases, the sentence of death is reduced from 4 years to 2 years R.I. [593D E] Sunil Batra 's case and later that of another Bench of the High Courts on this aspect, are set aside. The sentences of imprisonment for life are maintained. [594F G] 3.1 There is no reason to sentencing the appellant to prison custody for two year R. I. [595G H] Sunil, Batra 'Silva ' vs N.K.A. Appeal allowed in part.

The respondent assessee was a limited company dealing in land. It maintained its accounts on mercantile system. By an order dated June 21, 1946 under rule 75A(1) of the Defence of India Rules read with section 19 of the , the Income tax Officer brought to tax a sum of Rs.7,24,914 in the assessee 's business income. This sum was assessed by the Income Tax Officer as compensation for the land. The respondent challenged the assessment before the Arbitrator and made an award on July 29, 1955 whereby he fixed the amount of compensation at Rs.30,10,873 on account of permanent acquisition of the land, thus enhancing the original amount of compensa tion by Rs.5,13,624. On appeal, the Arbitrator made an Award dated July 29. 1955 whereby it was determined that the income accrued to the assessee on the date of the award. The State Government appealed to the High Court and during the pendency of the appeal before the High court it deposited a sum which was allowed by the Tribunal. In second appeal by the respondent, the High COurt held that the compensation received by the assessee related to the acquisition of land which was the stock in trade of the assessee, and therefore, the amount could not be said to have accrued to it as income during the previous year ended March 31, 1956 relevant to the assessment year 1956 57. The High Court also held that since the award was made by the Arbitrator on July29, 1955 enhancing the amount, the entire amount was in dispute in the appeal filed by the State Government. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the sum of compensation received was not a receipt of a revenue nature and therefore could not have accrued as income from the previous years ending March 31 1956 relevant for the assessment years 1956 57 and 58. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The payment made by Land Acquisition Officer by his award on June 29,1955, enhancing the entire income on the basis of the final compensation was in question in the second appeal filed before the Income Tral Court. Indeed, the dispute was regarded by the Court as real and substantial, because the assessee was not permitted to withdraw the sum deposited by the Government on April 25, 1956 without furnishing a security bond for refunding the amount in the event of the Appeal being allowed. There was no absolute right to receive the amount at that stage. If the appeal was allowed in its entirety the right to payment of the enhanced compensation would have fallen altogether. This is a case which must be distinguished from that decided by this Court in Kedarnath Jute Mfg. Co. Ltd.

The appellants filed a suit against the respondents for eviction of the appellants on the ground that they had been in possession of the shop let for non residential purposes mentioned in clause (f) of section 12(1) of the Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961. The appellants pleaded that the compromise decree was void and inexecutable as being against the provisions of the Act. The trial court accepted the appellants ' objection to the execution of the decree and dismissed the execution case. A miscellaneous appeal filed by the respondents was also dismissed by the High Court. In this appeal by special leave it was contended for them that the decree was not a nullity because the decree in question was void as being inconsistent with section 13(2) of Act, 1956. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The language of section 2(2), which is somewhat different from many similar State Statutes, clearly shows that the inhibition related to the filing of the suit only. No suit can be filed for eviction except on one or more of the grounds enumerated in section 12 (11). [882 D] (2) The words "is required bona fide by the landlord for the purpose of continuing or starting his business" and "in the present case, " mean bona fide requirement by the tenant for the purposes of continuing the business. [883 E F] (3) The expression "suit" in section 2 (f), means a suit for eviction against a tenant except on the one or several of the ground enumerated in Section 12(11). A decree for eviction based on an award without anything more is not different. [884 G H] (4) In sub sections (2), (3), (5) and (6) of Section 12, certain conditions have been engrafted to show under what circumstances an order for the eviction of a tenant cannot be passed except on either or more Of the grounds mentioned in section 13 (1). A Bench of the High Courts in Bahadur Singh & Anr. vs Muni Subrat Dass & Anr., [1971] 3 S.C.R. 872, held that the words "in respect of which relief can be claimed" do not either expressly or impliedly exclude the operation of Order 23, Rule 3 because grounds for claiming relief are always limited whether the relief be claimed under the general law or a statute.

The assessee company was a limited company doing business as selling agents of a Textile Mill. For the assessment year 1955 56, the Income tax Officer disallowed an amount of Rs. 11,88,COO/ and levied additional super tax at the rate of 3 1/2% on the distributable surplus of Rs., 91,116/ . The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the loss incurred by the company was not a capital loss but a revenue loss. On reference, the High Court answered the question in favour of the assessee. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The Income tax officer took an erroneous view of the scope of section 23A(1). He should have ignored the fact that the Directors were naturally more interested in the stability of their concern rather than in increasing the tax payable to the Government. [8 4 C] Commissioner of Income tax, West Bengal vs Gangadliar Bannerjee and Co., , referred to. (ii) The High Court was right in holding that the assessee had suffered a capital losses of Rs 12 lakhs/ . In view of this the loss any reasonable body of Directors of a company would have done just what the Directors of the company did. [884 D] Commissioner, Income tax vs Williamson Diamonds Ltd., , distinguished. (iii) The loss any reasonably body of directors of a Company would have been done just as it was not expected to gamble with the future of the concern. The question is not whether the value of the shares may not go up in future but whether the Directors are justified in not declaring dividends in view of section 22(1) of the Act.

The Consolidation Officer acting under section 12(4) of the Uttar Pradesh Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1954, referred the question of title to the Civil Judge for determination. The arbitrator gave his award on May 14, 1956 and submitted it to the civil court for final decision. On May 19, 1956, the Civil judge modified the award by holding that the Civil Court was not justified under section 15 of the Act in modifying the award merely because he disagreed with the finding. He further held that the civil Judge was not right in holding that section 15(1) of that Act applied to arbitrations under the Consolidation of Holding Act and that the decision of the Civil court modifying the Award was appealable under section 39 of the . The appellant contended before the High Court that section 37 of the , did not apply because the appellants had apparently applied under section 18 of the U.P. Consolidation of holdings Act, which provides for appeals to the District Judge against the order of the civil judge. The High Court held that section 12 (6) was applicable and that section 39 was not applicable to arbitrations referred to in section 37. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that section 18 did not make any distinction between provisions like section 39 and section 15, and that therefore section 12 was not made applicable to arbitration under the consolidation of Holdings. HELD : Section 12(6) must be read with section 37 as it stood before its amendment in 1956. The effect of section 46 and section 47 is that all the provisions of the except sub section (1) thereof shall be determined in accordance with the provisions Of the . [678 D] In the instant case, the effect of sections 46 and 47 was to apply sections 15 and 39 of U. P. Consolidation Act, and section 37 was not therefore applicable to proceedings under the Act.

The petitioner, a diploma holder in Engineering and holds the post of Executive Engineer in the respondent Corporation, was appointed as Executive Engineer by the respondent corporation. Till 1974, the promotion post of Superintending Engineer was available both for diploma holders and degree holders according to merit cum seniority. This resolution was also not a regulation made under section 64 of the Maharashtra Industrial Development Act, 1961. The petitioner challenged the said resolution before the High Court which dismissed the petition. Hence this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 For the purpose of promotion, a valid classification can made among the members holding the same post on the basis of their qualification. In the instant case, the petitioner who was senior to respondent No. 2 would have been promoted to the post on that date. However, since respondent No 2 was a degree holder, he got the said Resolution and was promoted to that post on 31st October 1990. However since respondent NO.2 was a Degree holder, his promotion to the said post on 1st October, 1990 was challenged by a writ petition in the High Courts. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petition. [372A B] 1.2 In the absence of rule or regulation, the authority can prescribe service conditions by executive instructions and this is what was done till the year 1988 and is also sought to be done since 1988 by the impugned resolution. The proposition that in the absenceof the rules and regulations, the authorities can act by executive instruction finds direct support in Mysore State Road Transport Corporation vs Gopinath Gundachar char, [1968] 1 SCR 767 and vs Balasubramaniam & Ors., ; , referred to.

The petitioner, a member of the Bar Association of the State of Punjab, filed a writ petition in the High Court for quashing the order dated January 7, 1987 passed by the Chief Justice of the High Courts and the transfer of all other Judges to the Delhi High Court. The High Court held that the Judges strength of the different High Courts was not justified as the High Powered Committee had been constituted under the Constitution. The petitioner filed a petition in this Court for special leave against the order of the Chief justice of the Punjab High Court and the High court, which was granted by the Court on January 7. 1987. On behalf of the Union of India it was contended that the High Commission had acted mala fide in passing the impugned order and that the same should be quashed. The question for consideration was whether the High Commissioner 's power to appoint solely vests with the State Government or even the Central Government, as the highest judicial authority in the country, was empowered by the Constitution to appoint Judges of the Supreme Court. Allowing the writ petition, ^ HELD: 1.1 The Chief Justice has quite often both before and after he has stated that it is the exclusive responsibility of the institution of the chief justice to be recognised as of crucial importance in the matter of appointments to the Supreme court or the Supreme High Court, and that if the executive sets up a standalone by which it professes its actions to be judged it must be held to those standards. This is to say, by itself does not detract from the necessity to maintain the highest standards of judicial independence. [459E F] 1.2 The Chief justice has quite frequently both before the Parliament and before the Supreme Bench have stated that the Chief Justices of India are bound by the decisions of the Court in the context of appointment of judges. [460G] 1:3. The Chief Justices, of the States and the Chief Ministers are not constitutional functionaries having a consultative role and the power of appointment resides solely and exclusively in the Central Govern ment. The judiciary is meant to be the executive and the judiciary has been invested with the responsibility of administering justice. It is only through the great institutions of national integration that the judiciary can have a grievance but should be free to take such steps as it may think fit in the institution itself or the other. [461H] 1 :4. The independence of the judiciary is not ensured by a literal interpretation. What the framers of Part III of the Constitution do is to achieve the constitutional purpose and should not be rendered sterile by a narrow interpretation. That is why the Chief Judge of India, in his affidavit filed on behalf of Union of States and other States, has stated: "The Chief Justice, of India is the Chief Secretary, the Chief Minister of the state and such other Judges of that High Court as the Central Govt. may deem fit to consult, are merely constitutional functionaries, having a consultation with the Chief Judicial Magistrate, and the Governor of India would be competent to take any decision as to which opinion it should be formed". [463A B] 1 .5. The power to constitute a new body is vested in the President by the constitution of the Council. The composition of the Committee is not justiciable. It has to be held that a two Judge Bench of five Judges, one sitting singly and the other sitting singly, has both before it and before it, as also before the end of this year.

The respondent was a Relieving Head Cashier in the K.G. Road Branch of the appellant Bank. He was served with a memo dated August 1, 1978 by the Divisional Office of the Bank calling for his expla nation. A letter was addressed to the General Manager of the K G Road Branch on August 1.1978 asking him to furnish details of persons who traveled and the amounts received by the said firm. No reply was received from the appellant bank. The respondent sent a reply on August 10, 1978 which was not found satisfactory. Some correspondence ensued between the respondent and the appellant in this connection but finally the respondent was served a second show cause notice on August 11, 1978. The appellant challenged the order of punishment by filing a writ petition before the High Court. A Single Judge of the High court allowed the writ petition quashing the impugned order of dismissal and directed that the respondent be paid all consequential benefits. The Division Bench dismissed the appeal filed by the appellant against the said order of the Single Judge. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The respondent did not attribute any bias or mala fides to the Enquiry Officer nor did he com plain that he was in any manner prejudiced on account of the said enquiry conducted during the pendency of a departmental enquiry. [205G] 1.2 In the facts and circumstances of this case, the ends of justice would be met if instead of directing all further benefits to the appellant, the High Courts ought not have directed payment of all consequential benefit flowing from the declaration that the impugned orders were bad in law. The ends of Justice would be meet ing the ends. [206B] 1:3. The order of removal is set aside and the matter remitted to the competent Disciplinary Authority to take a fresh decision based on the report of the Enquiry officer. [207C] 1 :4. If one were to go by the charge le velled against the respondent, and the reply thereto one may carry the impression that the respond ent had made the claim on the basis of the fake receipt; whether the respondent himself was duped or not would be a different matter. The fact however remains that the order imposing punishment is bad in Law.

The respondents were owners of a building in the mainkhad, Delhi. The appellant Corporation had taken steps to acquire the land for its scheme and to make a town planning scheme. The respondents submitted their applications for sanction under section 16 of the Delhi Development Act, 1957, but did not comply with the same. The Commissioner, however, rejected the application on the ground that the proposal was covered by the Master Plan in respect of widening of the road. The High Court dismissed the writ petition filed by the appellant. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the Master plan prepared under section 7 of the Act was not in conformity with the Master plans, and (ii) the provisions of section 14 of the Development Act were violated in as much as the Master Plans were prepared in a particular manner without any material to show that any part of the land belonging to the respondents will be covered by a proposed road. HELD: The High court was justified in issuing the writ of mandamus. [174 E] (i)(a) The purpose of the development Act is to provide for the development of Delhi according to plan and for matters ancillary thereto. Section 3(2)(a), which provides that the expression "development or development area" shall include any other purpose, has no application in this case. [175 D] (b) The Master Plan and the Zonal Development Plan are prepared under sections 7 and 8. Under section 14, the Master Planning Act is an Act to provide a broad outline of what every development should be undertaken or carried out in any area by any person or body (including a department of Government). Section 15 provides for the Authority to make modifications in the Master 's plan or the Zonal development Plan under the circumstances mentioned therein. [176 E] The Master plan and the two maps relied on by the appellants do not give any indication that any portion of the property belonging to respondents will he covered by any portion thereof.

The appellant No. 1 was convicted and sentenced to various terms of imprisonment by the Special Judge, Bombay, under section 161 Indian Penal Code with a fine of Rs. 25,000/ . The High Court acquitted him but on appeal by special leave it was contended that (1) the statement made by the appellant No 1 before the Magistrate in answer to a question put to him by the Additional District Magistrate was inadmissible in evidence and (2) the statements were not recorded under section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and were therefore inadmissible in law. Held, that the statement of the accused person was admissible in evidence as it was made after he had been examined under section 342 of the Criminal Procedure Code and could not be used for any other purpose. The statement was admissible under section 162 of the Cr. P.C., but it was not a confession made by an accused person to a police officer. A confession made to an accused in answer of a question which he had put to the witness cannot be treated as a confession within the meaning of section 164 Of the Code and therefore, the statement was inadmissible under section 466 of the Indian Penal code. A.I.R. 1936 Lah. 524, referred to. The fact that the confession made before the Additional Sessions Judge was inadmissible could not affect the validity of the trial. A statement made to a Magistrate in his examination under section 313 Of the Criminal Code is admissible in terms and the accused cannot be allowed to cross examine the witness on the ground that he had no opportunity to cross examination as provided by section 162 Of the Cr Procedure Code. The evidence of an accomplice, who was not examined at the trial stage, could not have been used against him for the purpose of proving his guilt. A retracted statement is a confession and it is open to the court to examine the accused in order to see whether he has been corroborated by any other evidence or otherwise. A person may be compelled to give evidence in a proceeding which is a confidential document but this does not mean that the court cannot afford to run the risk of opprobrium even if unfounded, that they have enlisted the Magistrate and he has no such opportunity to miss for entrapping the accused into its culmination. The confession may be proved by direct evidence and it would not be sufficient to prove the offence. A conviction can be based on the uncorroborated evidence of a co accused who is in police custody and whose testimony cannot be relied upon unless it is corroborated in material particulars.

The respondent plaintiff was serving as a constable when an incident took place on 17.2.1971, which led to the prosecution of the appellant along with the Head Constable and the Sub Inspector. The charge against him was that he physically assaulted and detained one Gurdial Singh. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the suit was barred by limitation. On appeal, the first appellate court held that the impugned order of dismissal was void on the ground of arbitrariness and there fore, the bar of limitation would not apply. In second appeal, a Single Judge of the High Court allowed the respondent 's appeal in respect of the finding out the cause of action for the suit and then in that light deter mined the correct article of the Limitation Act applicable to the case. The Division Bench held that since the impugned ord er was passed by an authority not in this regard, it could not be questioned in a second appeal before the High court. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 In the instant case, the question involved in the suit should not have been lightly brushed aside by the High Courts in limine. It has been asserted on oath before this Court and not denied by the respondent that the aforesaid Kahan Singh had to be re instated in service for a short time in pursuance of the decision in the Suit as the order of his dismissal had been passed by the authority not compe tent in this case, and that later he was again dismissed. It is further asserted on behalf of the appellants that the finding of the Additional District Judge on the question of limitation is patently illegal inasmuch as the judgment assumes that no law of limitation was applicable to suits where an order is impugned as being void. [826D E] 1.2 The High Court should call for the records and decide the case finally at the motion stage itself as the case is an old one. In the event of admission of fresh evidence, the High COurt shall permit the plaintiff to file relevant rebutting evidence.

The appellant, a private limited company carrying on business in tea garden tools and requisites and also acting as agents for selling tea. The respondent entered into certain transactions with the appellant 's mills and only the delivery orders were addressed to the mills changed hands. The amount realised on sale to M/s. Lachhminarain Kenia & Co., was not appropriated to the contract so that there was no completed sale since no property passed, but only the deliveries of the goods were of a speculative character as contemplated in Explanation 2 to section 24(1) of the Income Tax Act, 1922. The appellant claimed adjustment of this loss in the computation of its income for the assessment year 1959 60. The Income tax Officer held that the transactions involving mere transfer of delivery notes and not actual delivery of the good were of such speculative character and as there were no speculation profits in that year he held that they were speculative transactions within the meaning of Explanation 2. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the income tax Officer. The High Court on reference answered the question in favour of the assessee. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that (1) the transactions were mere sales of delivery orders or sales of goods so as to bring them to charge under section 3 of the Act, and (2) the loss should be treated as business loss since no part of the sale was effected by the assessee and his transferees. HELD: The appeal must be dismissed. (i) The Explanation to section 6 of the Indian Income tax Act, 1961 enumerates the heads of income chargeable to income tax. It lays down that where an assessee sustains a loss under any of these heads in any year, he shall be entitled to have the loss set off against his income profits or gains under any other head in that years. This general provision is qualified by the first proviso which permits the set off of a loss in speculative business against the assessee 's profits and gains, i any, in a similar business only. Explanation 1 says that where the speculative transactions are of such a nature as to constitute a business, the business shall be deemed to be distinct and separate from any other business. Explanation 2 defines a speculative transaction as a transaction in which a contract for purchase and sale of any commodity is periodically or ultimately settled otherwise than by the actual delivery or transfer of the commodity. The words actual delivery in explanation 2 means real as opposed to notional delivery. For income tax purposes speculative transactions means what the definition of that expression in Explanation 1 has been qualified by first proviso to section 4(1). [184 D E] Raghunath Prasad Poddar vs Commissioner of Income tax, Calcutta, ; and State of Andhra Pradesh vs Kolla Sreeramamurthy, , referred to. (ii) The High Courts on the point were not considering the effect of the position that the property in the goods passed to the ultimate endorsee of the delivery order. It was erroneous to think that if any transfer of a commodity or the scrips had taken place, on the other hand, a transaction which is not otherwise speculative in nature may yet be speculative according to explanation 2 if there is no actual delivery meaning to that expressing for purposes of income tax only.

The appellant was declared elected to the State Legislative Assembly. The respondent challenged the election of the appellant on the ground that he had not been duly nominated and that the Returning Officer was wrong in rejecting his nomination papers. Held, that the word "subscribe" in section 33(1) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, means "to sign". The word " substitute" is used in various senses to indicate different modes of signing and it includes the placing of a mark. The General Clauses Act also says that "sign" means the signature or the making of a marks. The general words "subscribes" are not defined but they are intended to be used in both senses, namely, "to attest or confirm by adding one 's signature". The General clauses Act does not define the word 'subscribe ' and it is only used in Ch. 1 of Part V dealing with the nomination paper that the words "sign " and "subscribing" are used. The word ' subscribes ' is not defined in the General Clauses act, but it is equally clear when the Act is read as a whole along with the form in the second schedule, that "subscriptions" are to be made differently from the making or other paper in accordance with prescribed regulations where there is no signature and no mark the form would have to be rejected and their absence could not be dismissed as technical and unsubs tantial. The words " signing" and "writing" in the general sense of the word, are used in different senses to denote different modes and a stamp or other mechanical impression of a signature is good in the case of electioneering papers.

The appellants were employees of the respondent Company.
