During the pendency of the dispute relating to the re instatement of three of the union leaders who had been dismissed by the company, the company issued notices to them under section 33(A) of the , calling upon them to report for duty on or before September 18, 1972 failing which their absence would be construed as voluntary abandonment of service and their names would be struck off from the muster rolls of the Company. On October 23, 1972, the appellants sent separate communications to the respondent company intimating that they were interested in the service of the company and had neither voluntarily abandoned the service nor did they wish to do so and that they would report for work at the moment the strike was called off by their union. The appellants made a formal demand calling upon the respondent to report on July 19, 1973 but the respondent refused to do it. On September 26, 1972 the company sent separate communication to the appellants intimating them that since the strike embarked upon by the workmen was illegal and arbitrary, that they had not abandoned service, that at any rate the termination of their services could only be in terms of the appellant 's standing orders and since the standing orders did not provide for treating the workmen as having abandoned service in case they were absent in connection with the notified strike, the Company 's action was manifestly illegal and invalid. The company filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the legality of the action taken by the appellants. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the action of the appellants in removing the names of the employees from its rolls was illegal, and invalid, and that the appellants had not been abandoned or retrenched due to any reasons beyond their control. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appel lant company that the respondent 's attitude in removing them from its roll was manifestly wrong and invalid; that the failure to perform the duties pertaining to the office must be with actual or imputed intention, on the part of the officer to abandon service which in view of the ratio of Gopal Chandra Misra 's case, can be legitimately said to mean to detach, unfasten, undo or untie the binding knot or link which holds one to the official and the obligations and privileges that go with it their absence from duty was purely temporary and could by no stretch of imagination be construed to mean that detach ing, unfanten, restoring; to the company 's service, the employees had been in connection winter with notified strike; and that, therefore, the action on the side of the respondents was manifestly legal. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The period stretches over six years and Shri Sachine Chaudhary brings to our notice the fact that back wages have to be computed, if ordered in full, on a much higher scale because of two settlements which have raised the scales of wages substantially. While there is no case specifically put forward that the workmen concerned have been employed elsewhere during this period, still we take a total view the whole case and direct that for the entire period from 1972 to the date of reinstatement 75 per cent of the wages will be paid to all the workmenconcerned on the scales and revised scales as the case may be. [616C D] 2. The respondents ' absence from work was because of their peaceful strike to enforce their demand. Therefore, there was no abandonment of their service. [625E F] 3. The contention that in the circumstances of the instant case, it could not be said that the appellant had voluntarily abandoned his service cannot be countenanced. [716F G] 4. The appellant ' s absence from duties was because the respondents were peaceful strike and not imputed intention on their part to abandon their service which they did not have. [613H; 614A] 5. The notice of termination of service was not in accordance with law.

The appellant was the trustees of a public trust. The trustees executed an agreement in favour of the appellant for the sale of certain house belonging to the trust to secure repayment of the loan by monthly instalments of Rs. 100 each and in default of three instalments the entire amount remaining unpaid shall become due and recoverable from the mortgagee property. The appellant failed to pay the instalments within the time fixed by the trustees, but on the failure of the trustees to comply with the requirements of r. 89 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the appellant instituted a suit for recovery of money against the trustees. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the trustees had failed to comply and that the properties were not liable to be sold as stipulated in the decree; and that they had agreed to abandon the execution proceeding and to abandon execution proceedings. On appeal, the District Court reversed the order of the District Judge and held that the requirements under 0. 21 r.89 of the Civil Procedure Code were not complied with and that it was not open to the appellant to initiate fresh proceedings for recovery. The High Court in revision set aside the order passed by the District court and restored that of the trial court. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The High Courts have held that under section 54 of the Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950, the (Bombay Act) which was extended over the territory now forming part of the State of Gujarat ceased when a new High Court was set up in the State and it was impossible to hold that a judgment delivered by a Full Bench of a High Court after due consideration of the points before it is liable to he regarded as irrelevant by Judges of that Court on the round of some alleged irregularity in the constitution of the Full Bench. [459 C D] (2) The expression "sale" in section 36 of the Act includes execution of a decree for sale of mortgaged property, and does not include execution of the decree holder 's decree in execution of decrees. The word "credit" is used to convey a right upon the judgment debtor, even after the property is sold, to satisfy the claim of the judgment creditor and to compensate the auction purchaser by paying him 5% of the purchase money. [460 E F] (3) The words "less any amount which may be due to the decreeholder" in sub section (a) of section 54 are not intended to defeat the claim for execution of decree against property belonging to a public Trust. They are not meant to convey or take upon the Charity Commissioner 's power of the Court to execute a mortgage decree against properties belonging to private persons by virtue of a title to apply to have the sale set aside on his depositing in court, and the question of law arising before him as well as the question whether a judgment debtor is entitled to commence fresh proceedings under section 21 of the City Civil Procedure Act, 1908, does not arise. [461 F G] (4) The word 'credit ' has been used in section 165 of the Evidence Act to confer a right on the judgment debtors even after their death to apply for execution against the property belonging thereto and to prove the decree being passed by them. In the present case, the trustees have not by themselves referred the matter to the Full bench. The decision of the High Court is binding upon the appellants. [463 G H] (5) The contention that the mortgagee 's appeal was not maintainable because the judgment of the Division Bench was binding on him cannot be accepted.

The appellant, a railway employee, was compulsorily retired from service under Rule 2(2) of the Pension Rules on the ground that he had attained 30 years of qualifying serv ice. The respondent filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the order of retirement. The learned Single Judge dismissed the writ petition holding that there was no in firmity in Rule 2 (2) and as such the order could not be set aside. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Government had issued instruc tions dated July 11, 1955 and February 8, 1956 which lay down that the retirement under Rule 1(1)(a) should be effected when such retirement is necessary in public interest. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: The High Court has rightly held that Rule 2 of the pension Rules was ultra vires Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution of India. [802C] The object of Rule 2 is to chop off the dead wood. Rule 2 provides no guide line and gives absolute discretion to the Government. There is no requirement under the rule to act in 'Public Interest '. A person who joins Government service at the age of 21 years can be retired prematurely under F.R. 56(j). The Government has also the power under Rule, 2(1) to retire a servant at any time after he has completed 30 years ' qualifying service. [800F] The words "weed out unsuit able employees" cannot include the power already contained in the Pension Rule. The words 'weedout unsuitu larly ' mean that such power can only be exercised in 'public interest '. This is a statutory rule which is identical to Fundamental Rule 56(1).

The appellant assessee was an unregistered firm carrying on business of manufacture and sale of katechu under the two contracts. The sales of kutechu were effected between 26th July, 1943 to 31st March, 1943. In the accounting period the assessee had taken a risk in obtaining a profit from the selling price charged by him for the period ending 31st day of March, 1944 and paid a sum of Rs.5,600/ as tax on the sale of Katech ure. The Income Tax Officer held that there could be no profit attributable to the manufacturing activity carried on during the chargeable accounting period ending 30th March, 1942 and that there was no profit arising during the previous year ending 31th March 1944. He also held that the assessee was entitled to set off in respect of the deficiency in the profits accruing in the year 1940 41. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed this order but the Tribunal accepted the contention of the assessee that since the business carried on in Nepal on or about 23rd November, 1942 to 30th April, 1944, it could not be said that the business was carried on outside the period of the accounting year ending 30st March 1944 and therefore there was a profit attributable lo the manufacturing activities. The High Court held that as provided in the Act the assessee could not claim set off under section 7 of the Income Tax Act, 1922, on the ground that the profits earned during the relevant previous year must be computed on yearly basis in terms of the definition of "accounting period" and basic scheme of the income tax Act bearing in mind that excess profits are excess of profits which were intended to be mopped up during the war period intended to he taxed separately and differly. The Revenue appealed to this Court by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The question whether the profits in the one case could be identified with the profits of the other would be determined by reference to the period in which those accrued or arose. [608C] 2.1 The term "accountant" is the same as the expression "account ing period". In the context of the Act, it is the period beginning from 1st September 1939 ending after amendment on 31st May, 1946. So if there was any deficiency of profits in any particular period, it must be determined on that basis. [613D E] 2:2 The term 'accounting Period ' means the period commencing from 1 st April, 1943 and ending on 31th April 1944.

The Kerala Public Service Commission invited applications for filling up 130 expected vacancies in the posts of Junior Engineers in the Public Works Department as per notification dated 16th May, 1978. The qualifications specified for the posts were B.Sc. in Civil Engineering or Mechanical Engineering of the Kerala University or its equivalent as prescribed by the special rules of the State Government. The applicants had to appear in the written test conducted by the KPSC and there was a common question paper which contained, in category I, questions in Mechanical Engineering. applicants who were qualified in Civil engineering had to answer the questions in Category II. After the written examination and the interview, but before a common rank list was prepared, the Kerala Public Services Commission recommended candidates for appointment to these posts. The names of some of the aggrieved respondents in the Writ Petitions were included in the list. The State Government issued an order on 16th April, 1979 inviting applications for recruitment and preparing separate rank lists of selected applicants holding Civil Engineering degrees. The petitioners who had qualified in civil engineering challenged the validity of the order by filing a writ petition before this Court contending that they had not yet published the rank list. They also contended that the respondents had already been published as per the notification dated 15th May 1978 and that the procedure of examination and selection was challenged. Dismissing the petitions, ^ HELD: 1. The KP SC/ST candidates who have qualified in the civil engineering degree are entitled to exercise their option and then take his turn according to his rank in the common list prepared by the Public Service Commis sion. [747C] 2. Clause 4 of the Government order No. G.O.MS. 101/79/PWD&E dated 27th September, 1979 the Government constituted the Kerala Engineering Subordinate Service (General Branch) and Kerala Engineering Subse quently order that all those who have submitted unconditional options and who possess the required qualifications prescribed in the rules will be appointed by transfer to the respective service. In case where the number of officers who had submitted options is less than the number, the remaining vacancies will be provided by direct recruitment as provided in rule 9 of the respective special rules. The Chief Engineer & R will implement the orders forthwith. [750D E] 3. Clause (4) gave unconditional option to those in the Kerala Education Subordinate Service(General Branch). As stated earlier, the K PSC was not directed to prepare a common list. Common List was referred to in the earlier order in this Court through certain misapprehensions. The High Court by its order dated 23rd April, 1980 dismissed all the S.L.P. with observations that the expression "the common list preparing by the public service Commission should be deleted. [751G H] 4. Clause 5 gave unconditional options to those In the Kerala State Engineering Service (Mechanical Branch) to remain in the said branch or to choose the newly constituted Kerala Engineering subordinate Service (Civil) (General branch). As per clause 4 of Government Order No.G.O.(Ms.) 101/1979/PWD &E dated 28th September 1979, the Government of Kerala and the K.PSC was also not directed that then the petitioner 's turn comes in the Common list he is entitled to claim that post under the orders of this Court. [753A B] 5.

The respondent plaintiff filed a suit for dissolution of partnership and accounts. During his life time the business was under the control of the defendant, but on his death the defendants Nos. 1 and 2 were substituted in place of the deceased. The plaintiff claimed that he had no interest in the firm. In paragraph 16 of the plaint it was stated that he has a partner of a partnership business along with his brothers and that he is now converted into a partnership firm by a regular deed. During their life time, the business of the business started under the management of the defendants. The defendant No. 1 filed an application for dissolution stating that the plaintiff has no interest to the firm and that the suit was governed for the purpose of court fees by section 7(iv)(f) of the Court Fees Act. The trial court passed an order on 26th December, 1981 on the basis of false allegations made by the defendants and in reply to the plaintiff 's letter seeking information that he was a partner in a partnership. A suggestion to re constitute and partnership made and repeated by the plaintiff had been ignored. In reply to this, the plaintiff filed an appeal before the High Court which was dismissed. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The plaintiff respondent No. 2 is not obliged to state the exact amount which would result after taking all the accounts and he may, therefore, put a tentative valuation upon the suit, but he is not permitted to choose an unreasonable and arbitrary figure for that purpose. At page 392 of the judgment in Meenakshisundaram Chettiar vs Venkatachalam Chettiar, AIR 1936 Bombay 166, it was held that when the valuation put by the defendant appears to be arbitrary and unreasonable, the court may reject it and leave the plaintiff to correct the valuation or have the suit rejected. similar was the view taken by this Court in Meenakhisundai Chettiar vs Venkachalam, [1945] ILR XXIV Patna 334; and Ishwarappa vs Dhanji, AIR 1932 Bombay 166. 1.2 In a suit of accounts, the defendant is not required to state his exact amount as which would arise after taking every the accounts, but it is not permissible to choose any figure he likes and thus decide finally the court which shall have jurisdiction to entertain the suit without reference to the subject matter of the litigation, the nature and extent of the relief claimed or any other factor. He has not been given the absolute right or option to place any valuation whatever on such relief and where the plaintiff manifestly and deliberately under estimates the relief the court is entitled to examine the correctness of the valuation given by the Plaintiff and to revise the same if it is patently arbitrary or unreasonable. [511B C] 2. The High Court while repelling the argument that the principle underlying both clauses (c) and (f) is substantially the same and the Full Bench decision governed the case, has not accepted the contention of the plaintiff that the court was bound to accept that 'the plaintiff can give an arbitrary valuation in the plaint, and that it will be tentatively valued at Rs.50 only. The Full Bench deci sion on this point will be open to the trial court to take into consideration the statement in the pleadings that the defendant has been ousted from the partnership business. If the court comes to the conclusion that the tentative valuation of the suit would be beyond its pecuniary jurisdiction, it shall pass an appropriate order under Order VII of the Code of Civil Procedure. [512C E] 3.

The appellant company was registered as a 'dealer ' under the Madhya Pradesh General Sales Tax Act, 1958. The respondent assessee in the first two appeals had declared its factory units manufacturing and selling bidis. The company claimed exemption from payment of sales tax on the ground that the industries run by it were "traditional" industries within the meaning of section 12 of the Act. The State Government rejected the claim. In the second appeal, the High Court held that the exemption was not available to the respondent assessee because (i) the exemption granted under the notification dated 1st April 1981 was only for the period exempted from payment and (ii) the notification did not require a minimum number of industries in the category of dealers specified in column (1) or that they did not comply with the requirements of the notification. In these appeals by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the State Government had no power to exempt the respondent from sales tax under the Act and that the executive instructions issued by the Government were only clarificatory in nature and could not operate as a bar to the exemption conferred by the notification; and that even if the exemption is granted for an "tractive industry" it does not necessarily follow that the units intended to be covered by the new scheme were only those that were covered by it. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The expression "traalised industrial unit" in the notification cannot mean a certificate on the terms prescribed under the earlier notification. [615C] 2.1 The exemption granted by the State no doubt is to be construed strictly but is not confined only to the conditions exhaustive or suffi cient and may lead to abuse of power by executive author ity unless canalised by procedural guidelines and then to say that such a conclusion is borne out by the mere reference to a certificate being granted by an officer. [625E F] 2(a) The expression 'traditional industries ' in the Government notification cannot be read as one merely clarifying an ambiguity in the earlier one and hence, the exemption cannot be treated as one only of those units which do not fall under rule 14. [716B C] (b) The words "traitable industrial units" in a notification can be given their widest meaning so as to include within its ambit all categories of industries that do not come under the category enumerated in section 22D(a). [617C D] 2.(c) The exemption is only prospective operation. It does not mean that the conditions specified in the notifi cation are not exhaustive or elastic and may have been intended to operate from the construction of the words of the Notification or by necessary implication therefrom. [512E F; 624F G] (d) The notification does not authorise a person to avail of the exemption under it, only some of those categories which do no fall under Rule 14 can opt for the alternative of deter mination. [613H] 2:2. The words 'tractive industries ' are not to be given a restricted meaning and may result in abuse of powers by executive authorities unless canalising them is shown to be capricious, arbitrary or otherwise. [641A B] 3.

The Delhi Higher Judicial Service Rules, 1970 were framed by the Lt. Governor of Delhi in consultation with the High Court. The Lt. Col. (Civil) was a member of the Delhi Judicial Service and had been functioning as a full fledged strength of the High Judicial Service. In the year 1971, the Administrator of Delhi appointed under article 309 of the Constitution, the Delhi Higher judicial Service Rules 1970 were promulgated by the Lieutenant Governor in consultation therewith. The Delhi Higher Judiciary Service Rules were framed under Article 309 of Constitution. Rule 3(b) of the said Rules provided that "the seniority of direct recruits vis a vis promotees shall be determined in accordance with the respective dates of their continuous officiation as Additional District and Sessions Judges, who were functioning in the Union Territory of Delhi on deputation from other States and those whose names were recommended by the High Courts. " Rule 4(2) provides that "in the case of appointment to the service, the seniority shall be the same as in the Delhi judicial Service". The Lt Col. was appointed as a member on probation for a period of two years. He was confirmed in the post of Additional District & Sessions Judge on probation. On his attaining the age of superannuation he was promoted as Additional Distt. and Sessions Judge. In 1975, the Lt Col, who had joined the service long time back, was reverted to the post on the recommendation of the Full Court. Rule 8(2), which provides for confirmation in case of direct recruitment, provided that the seniority of the direct recruits shall be fixed by the Administrator in consultationwith the High court. The petitioners filed a writ petition before the Delhi High Court challenging the validity of Rule 8 (2) and the fixation of inter se seniority on the ground that the Lt., Col. had no power to hold the posts of District Judges, and that the direct recruitment to the Service was made by promotion from members of Delhi Judicial service. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that (1) the Lt, Col. is a member in the service as he has been appointed to the Indian Administrative Service by promotion on the basis of selection from members Central Service; (2)(a) the seniority list of promotees and direct recruits is not included in the Service; and (b) the Delhi Subordinate Judicial Service was constituted on May 15, 1971 with effect from March 13, 1972. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The contention that the petitioners were appointed to a post in the judicial service by promotion as Deputy Custodian General of Delhi is without force because the quota rule has been framed under Rule 7(1) of Rules 16 and 17 of the Rules. [387F] 2. (a) The Lt., the Lt and the Lt are not subordinate to the Government of India, Ministry of Home Affairs or to the Central Government, National Judicial Service Judges and that they have no authority in prescribing a quota for direct recruits. Rule 7 is not really a quota rule but it does not lay down any proportion, all it did. It merely indicates a ceiling on the number of vacancies to be filled by promotion. [388B C] (b). The Lt, the Lieutenant, Delhi High Courts and the Delhi Administrative Service Rules are entirely different from the rules in the instant case. Rule 4 (2), as well as rule 8(1)(a), which is a part of the non service quota, is not applicable to the direct recruit under Rule 16(1). [388C D] 3. The seniority list prepared by the Delhi Full Court is valid and rational. If appointments have to be made from two different sources, then the authorities should so plan that the recruits come from two distinct sources in time and officers from one source are not required to function substantively and effectively in the jobs which are intended to be performed by recruits of other source and face the prospect of being either pushed back or thrown out. [389E F] 4.

The appellant was a partner in a trading venture conducted by the respondent. In 1948, he filed three returns of income (i) on 4 10 1950 in respect of the assessment year 1950 51, and (ii) on 1 7 1951 in the status of an individual and claimed that the income should be assessed in the hands of L. The Income tax Officer assessed the Ambala Flour Mills in the three years of assessment in the category of "an association of persons". In appeals by the appellant to the District Court, the High Court restored the decree of the trial court and declared the partnership stood dissolved on April 29, 1948. On appeal by certificate, HELD : (i). The expression "any person" in the setting in which it appears must be confined to a person intimately connected in the aforesaid sense with the assessments of the year under appeal. "In making a direction against Debi Parshad the Tribunal did not exercise his powers qua a stranger to the assessment proceeding. [392 D] (ii). The words "any other than an appealing assessee" in section C. Prashar and another vs Vasantsen Dwarkadas and others, , explained. (iii) The expression 'any person ' in the set of which it appeared must be confine to a persons intimately related in the said sense with assessments of year under Appeal. " In the present case, the Income tax officer held that Debi Parhod was a member of an association of Persons and since the Appellate Assistant Commissioner set aside the order assessing the income in the name of the appellant, he had to give directions with regard to the assess ment of the income, provided the assessment was not barred by law.

The appellant filed a suit for partition of his share in the joint family properties and for recovery of possession. The trial court decreed the suit but on appeal the High Court set aside the decree holding that the plaint should be valued at Rs. 15,00,000 and that the proper court fees should be paid under section 7(iv)(b) of the Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that (i) the order passed by the trial court was final as the appellant had not specifically mentioned in his plaint the value for the relief sought; (ii) the High court erred in directing him to pay court fees on the basis of the valuation of Rs. 50,000 under section 8(iv) of Act and (iii) the suit should have been valued at the rate of Rs,. 15,000 as it was a joint family property and the appellant could be justly called upon to pay additional court fees in respect of the claim for partition. HELD: (i). The High Court was right in holding that section 7 of the Suits Valuation Act postulates that the plaintiff should first value his claim for the purpose of court fee and it provides for the determination of the value of court fees and that is natural enough. [1033 B] (ii).The High Court erred in holding the valuation for jurisdiction showed in the plaint to be taken to be the valuation even for purposes of jurisdiction. The plaintiff 's failure to state the amount at which he values the relief asked for is often due to the fact that in suits for partition the plaintiff attempts to obtain the benefit of article 17 B of Schedule II in the matter of payment of court Fees. Where the plaintiff seeks to pay the fixed court fee as required by the said Article, he and his advisers are apt to take the view that it is unnecessary to state a jurisdictional valuation. [ 1033 C D] (iii).The question about proper court fee leviable on the appellant 's memorandum of appeal was properly referred to the High Courts under section 5 of the Madras High Court Fees Act, 1939. The High Courts were in error in holding otherwise. [1134 F G] (iv)The High Courts should have allowed the appellant to amend his valuation for the payment of Court fees not only on the memorandum of appeals but also on the plaint.

The appellant Corporation, which was a statutory corporation, had taken a decision to approve the plans submitted by it for the construction of a multistoreyed building. The plan was sanctioned on 30th July, 1980 and the building was constructed in the same year. In the meantime, the Delhi Development Act, 1957 came into force and the Delhi Municipal Corporation Act, 1911 was brought into force from 1st April, 1988. Section 3(1) of the Act provides that no person shall, after the commencement of the Delhi Act, erects or constructs any wall within a period of two years from the date on which the provision for the demolition is made. The appellant Corporation had taken the formal sanction of the building plans in respect of the construction and refuge areas. The approval was subject to certain conditions. The respondent No. 1, who was the owner of the plot in question, filed a suit against the appellant Corporation for recovery of the amount spent on repairs. The trial court decreed the suit. On appeal, the High Court held that the objection raised by the appellant was not maintainable and allowed the appeal. In this appeal it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the design providing for refuge areas in the ratio of one sq. metre in the area was arbitrary and violative of the Bye laws; (ii) the permission to construct a wall adjoining the inner vacant space was in addition to the requirements of bye laws; and (iii) the construction was not in accordance with the bye laws, and that the appellant had failed to establish its case against the respondent No 1. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The requirement of bye law 16(4) is in addition thereto. [608C] 1.2 The purpose of refuge areas contained in Bye law 2.27 is not an externed one but is on the wall abutting the inner open space. The construction of the wall is a matter of some complexity and, in conceivable cases, one calling for expertise is the NDMC itself. [069D E] 1:3.1. The purpose for refugees in each floor is to secure protection to persons in the event of an out break of fire in a high rise building, the expression "external wall" must be construed as meaning a structure built on the walls which are reasonably connected with a hollow core. [079E F] 1.(a) The purpose underlying the provision of byelaw 16(1), namely, to provide an inflexible, rigid standard and whether the location and distribution of the refuge areas therein is violative of article 19(1)(f). [064F G] (b) The requirement that the refuge area should be a cantilever projection or designed in some other way. [085G H] (c) The construction must be of a rigid standard, and not a limitation on the power of the NDMC to satisfy itself that the building plan provides for adequate fire safety measures. [094A B] (d) The use of the word "exhibit" in Bye laws 2.28(1). in Byelaw 2.24(2) is not intended to envisage a totally different idea of the location of 'Refuge Areas ' but, prima facie, intended to suggest some feasible alterna tive to the technical design of the construc tion of the said buildings. [104C D] (e) The importance of the safety plan and the importance of finality in terms of relevant bye laws is not a matter for the decision of the Council. [115E F; 116A B]. (f) The Authority has developed its stance from time to time incurring heavy expenditure on the construction work in any particular floor, while influencing the evaluation of such safety measures which, indeed, is a matters of some complex and, therefore, it is not possible to accept them.

The joint family of the respondent was carrying on business in a grocery shop. The family also obtained a decree for partition against the appellant and his brothers, who were carrying on the motor business. The parties to the compromise entered into a compromise which provided that prior to 1942 all the accounts of the various businesses had been correctly maintained and shown that the parties had agreed to have arbitrators appointed through Court for examining the accounts from 1942 up to March 31, 1946. In July 1946, the parties entered into an agreement whereby the parties omitted to provide in the compromise about the future conduct of the motor busi ness and claimed that the motor transport business was still a joint family business and that he had a right to ask for accounts of that business subsequent to March 1, 1946, when the arrangement was changed. The appellant contended that the respondent had no real grievance in the matter regarding taking any account of the joint family businesses including the motor cycle business after March 31. 1946, and that the suit was barred by res judicata. Held, that the compromise having been found not to be vitiated by fraud, misrepresentation, mistake or misunderstanding as held by the trial court, a finding which was not interfered with by the High Court in appeal must be set aside. The joint family consisted of three brothers and was a minor and the respondent did not have any legal right to meddle with or interfere in the liquor shops which were attributable to his business. He had no legal right in the suit property as he was bound by the terms of the compromise and the consent decree following upon it.

The appellant was a factory manufacturing salt water from the sea water works in the State of U.P. The respondent firm was engaged in the manufacture of sea water into salt and used to utilise water from it for the purpose of distributing it on payment of duty. The appellant paid duty on the basis of the water supplied by the respondent. The respondents filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the levy of cess, inter alia, on the ground that the salt works were not 'manufacturing process ' within the definition of the word 'factory ' in section 2(d) of the Act and therefore the Salt Works would come within the meaning of the expression " premises" in the definition. The High Court held that the Salt works were 'manufactured ' as defined by section 2 of the , and that the process of converting sea water to salt was not a 'factory within the purview of the definition, but it was a 'manufacturer ' under the Act. On appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The expression "manufacture" in section 3(1)(m) of Act means any building or structure which is used for purposes of gain. It has been defined by the Act as meaning any premises in which salt water is carried on by way of trade or for purposes connected with the exportation of sea into salt. The process of conversion of sea waters into salt was described in the letter dated July 12, 1949, as "manufacture and not a manufacturing process". The process was not mentioned in the notification as "manufacturing" process "in relation to the manufacture " in the Salt Act, but for the dealing in the salt Works. [603 D E] (ii) The definition of 'factory" in s.2(d)(m), does not include a factory in which certain types of work is carried out by way or as part of which it is made "to carry on the operation of an industry". The processes carried out in the instant case, therefore, were not "manufactured" within the inclusive definition of "factory" and would be a factory if the work carried on was one in respect of the salt work. [507 D E; 606 A B] (iii) The process is of conversion to salt carried on on the appellant 's Salt Works comes within the term "factory". The expression 'manufactures ' in cl. (k) of section 2 means any premises which are used for the purposes of trade, or for purpose of gain and has not been subjected to a licence. [064 C D] (iv) The processes of converting the sea waters to salt were not incidental to the use of the sieves in the sense that what is made shall be a different thing from that out of which they are mixed and therefore, the rags used in the process could not come within section 2. [074 D E]. (v) The appellant ' Salt Works do come within cl. 5(i)(m)(b) of s.3 of the . [605 G] (vi) The High court was right in holding that the appellant was rightly convicted of the offence of working the factory without obtaining a licence, and that it had been rightly convicted. [706 B C].

The respondent was appointed as Instructor in the Department of Public Instructions. In 1949, he was promoted to the post of Instructor in May, 1955. He joined duty there on November 28, 1949. On June 11, 1956, he joined duty and joined duty thereafter. The respondent continued to make representations to the Government praying that his absorption should be related back to 1949 and he should also be absorbed in the department of Technical Education with effect from November 28. 1949. In 1953, the State Government issued orders reverting him to his parent Department. On July 1, 1956 the respondent was again posted on deputation as Instructor. He was asked to report for duty there after on December 1, 1949, when he was again transferred to that Department. The appellant challenged the order of reversion by a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court allowed the petition and issued a direction that his absorbed should be taken into account. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the absorption of the respondent in the post in which he was working, did not amount to reduction in rank nor a break in the continuity of his service; (ii) the respondent had no legal right to be absorbed and consequently, a writ of mandamus as prayed for by him should not be issued. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The High court was justified in granting relief to the respondent. [259 B] (2) In the special circumstances of this case, the High court had granted the relief to respondent. The State Government had acted arbitrarily and in violation of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution.

The appellant, a foreign national and the Indian Council of Social Welfare of the country, was recognised as an institution established by a social investigation in respect of the adoption of foreign parents. The respondent, who had been recognised as a social worker under the , filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the adoptions of the appellant as being violative of the provisions of the Indian children ' (Regulation of Employment and Conditions of Service) Act, 1980. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the child should be treated as an "domicile" or a "dignity agency" and that the respondent was entitled to obtain the care and custody of foreign parent. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the Indian Children Act, 1970 being a special statute, which is applicable to the child in adoption, being welfare legislation, should be construed strictly and not with a view to make sure that the children have in fact been surrendered by its biological parents or agencies. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The Indian Children 's Act is an Act intended to provide for the child 's welfare ' and provides for the care of the child. [842C] 2.1 The Indian Council has set up a National Advisory Board for giving its report to the court in respect to the adoption. It has also been provided that the appropriate Government shall take into consideration all alternatives available to the foreign parents, if they so desired and to give them an opportunity of being heard before taking any action in relation to adoption. [42D] 2(a) The Indian Act empowers the Court to issue directions for the appointment of a foreigner as guardian of a child in the courts in Bombay, Delhi and Gujarat. [46E] (b) The recognition of foreign children by foreign parents or an orphanage agency is not a legal or valid claim. It is also necessary that the recognised social or child welfare agency should be approached in appropriate cases for the purpose of inter country adoptions. [47F] 2.(c) The recognised social, educational and child welfare agencies have to be given a fair and reasonable opportunity to the foreigner who could be made liable to be adopted by the foreign parent, and if it thinks fit, verification that the foreign or the Indian parent is an orphan or abandoned child and it has not been possible for the social or children welfare agency to trace their parents or where the child is committed by a juvenile court to an institution, centre or home for committing a child under its care, the court should be able to satisfy itself that the foreigner has reached a age of mind, take steps to ensure that the said child will be given in adoption to the foreigners making the application for guardianship. [483G H] 2 (d) The foreign parents who have taken a child are not suitable in which case they can get appropriate education and training in the country of adoption. They should also be informed by the recognised Social or child Welfare agency that the social, or child health agency must satisfy itself, firstly, that there is no impediment in the way of the Child entering the country; secondly, that the travel documents for the foreign care, welfare and child security should be submitted to the Court only through a recognised social and child Welfare Agency. [493H; 494A B] 2:2. The recognition can be based on the parents ' Social or Child welfare agency 's report and other papers and documents forwarded by the social and family welfare agencies in the reply of the petitioner. [50C D] 3.1. In all cases where a child investigation is undertaken, a recognised voluntary organisation should ensure that such social or juvenile welfare agency does not indulge in any malpractice.

The appellant company, a private limited company, had its Head Office at Calcutta and its factory at Jamshedpur. It had branches in Bombay, Madras and Bangalore. The gross effective salaries and wages of its employees were Rs. 2,65,450. In the year 1965 66, the Company declared and paid bonus at 20% for the years 1965 65, 65 and 1965 66 on the basis that the workmen employed by it were only a small percentage of the wage bill. The company claimed that this amount should be deducted from gross profits as an item of expenditure under section 6 of the Act. The Tribunal accepted the claim of the Company and held that the claim was not justified and that the Tribunal had wrongly disallowed the deduction on account of extra shift allowance made by the company to its employees drawing emoluments exceeding Rs. 750 per mensem for the year 1964 65. On appeal, the High Court held that as the workmen were entitled to the bonus at the rate of 13.51% they should be paid only at the maximum of 20%. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the Tribunal was justified in adding back the amount of Rs. 25,000 for the accounting year 1965 67 on the ground that the company had not furnished the requisite particulars; and (ii) the Company should have deducted back this amount from gross profit. HELD: The Tribunal was right in disallowing the deduction claimed by the appellant. [115G] (i). The claim of deduction of Rs, 2000 lakhs made by it at the time of making available the bonus for the relevant accounting year 1964 66 on account that his salary is only Rs.750 per mensem. This amount will have to be taken into consideration for computing bonus for that year 1965 65 and not as awarded by the Tribunal. [116A B] (ii). The Tribunal had committed an error in law in making direct tax without deducting back this item of expenses from gross income. The second item relates to the claim made by workmen for repairs and renewals. The first item relates only to a sum of Rs., 18,24,047 which was claimed as extra shift allowances for the assessment year 196566 on the footing that his wages were only Rs 750 per month.

The appellant was a starving man in 1954. He was promoted as an Assistant Commercial Tax officer in 1954, next as Joint Commercial Tax Officer in 1957 and then as a Deputy Commercial Tax officers in 1962. On promotion as Deputy Commissioner of Commercial Taxes he was posted as Member of the Sales Tax Appellate Tribunal in the same cadre. On September 28, 1975, he was retired under Fundamental Rule 56(d) (i) of the Tamil Nadu General Rules for the State and Subordinate Services. His service book showed that he had an excellent record of service. He had earned several encomiums, commendations and appreciations. The various promotions gained by him during the period from September 28 to September 28 under the rule which enables the Government to retire a Government servant in the public interest after he has attained the age of SO years or after he had completed 25 years of qualifying service. One wonders whether the failure to note the result of the enquiry in the personal file led to the impugned order of November 29, 1974 of the Government. The High Court accepted the view of the Full Board and directed that all the charges framed against him should be dropped. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Government was entitled to take into consideration the entire history of the case including that part of it which was prior to his promotion, 80% of the year which was before his promotion as Joint Tax officer and not ability, seniority being considered only where merit and ability were approximately equal. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The appellant will be reinstated in service and paid arrears of salary due to him under the rules. He is entitled to his costs. [771 B] 2. The Government was right in retiring the appellant from service. The order of the Govern ment was quashed. [781 C] 3. The effect of the order of 11th January, 1974 is that the charges should be drop and proved. The rule does not say that the previous history of a Government Servant should be completely ignored once he is promoted. Sometimes past events may help to assess present conduct. But when there is nothing in the present conduct casting any doubt on the wisdom of the promotion, it is impossible to sustain the order. retiring the appel lant from service [772 D E] 4. The fact that the appellant was sincere and hard working as a Commercial Tax Offi cer in 1953, he should be promoted as Deputy Commis sioner of Commercial Tax and posted as member of Sales Tax appellate Tribunal, a prestigious post. [764 F G] 5. The post of a Deputy Commissioner is a Selection post. Under Rule 36(b)(i) the Government may retire a government servant in public interest, after he was promoted to a selection post. In the present case, the appellant had quite a strong and grim situation that his reputation was not at all good. [782 G H] 6. The State of Tamil Nadu vs M.E. Reddy & Anr., ; , State of Punjab vs Dewan Chuni Lal, ; State of Panjab vs Dewan Benoy Kumar, ; and Union of India etc. vs M/s. Educa tion Reddy & Ant., ; referred to.

The appellants were the owners of a bus owned by the respondent State. The respondent State issued a notification under section 68 C(1) of the , authorising the respondent to ply the said stage carriage on the routes in question. The appellants challenged the validity of the scheme and the High Court quashed the notifications. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the scheme was vitiated by mala fides; (ii) the notification did not disclose the existence of two groups in the Congress Party at the time of the general election; (iii) the policy direction issued by the State Government on the basis of a scheme which disclosed that the State Transport Corporation would be taken up for nationalisation, and (iv) the procedure adopted was contrary to section 68C of the Act. HELD: The scheme was valid and not in conformity with section 68 D(3). The scheme did not contravene article 19(1)(f) of Constitution as it was not in accordance with the requirements of section 68 E(1). [362 G] (i). The policy direction given by the Government on January 4, 1962, was to ensure that the transport operators operating vehicles on routes might know that they were affected by the scheme understood the words employed as the Transport Authority under section 57 D(2) and that the operators who had in fact been affected by it would be entitled to raise their objections to the adequacy of the service pro posed and similarly do not afford requisite information to the approving authority under section 69 E(3) to decide whether to approve the scheme or not. [362 F G] The scheme as promulgated was a scheme for nationalisation of transport services and not for the purpose of carrying out its object. It did not make any difference. No doubt, in a State where there is no Regional Transport Authority at all, at all that is to say superseded. But this could be done only by an order issued under section 66 D(1), as a result of which the scheme became final and enforceable. [363 A B] (ii). The schemes were not of a kind and did not amount to a failure to fix the number of vehicles to be operated or the trips they would do on the route. [364 E F] (iii). The procedure laid down by section 68 G in respect of permits issued under the Act was not followed. [365 A B]. (iv). The Regional Transport Authorities which is specifically mentioned in the scheme were not competent to entertain applications for grant of permits where the length of the route is 100 miles or over and such route is over a Trunk Road. Where, therefore, the State Road Transport Corporation had no authority at all to issue a permit under section 63(3), it could not be said that such authority was deprived of the power to issue the permit by reason of section 69F(1); (v) The scheme being a scheme of nationalisation, the scheme must be followed strictly. [366 G H; 367 A B; 368 C D].

The appellant was a dealer in respect of certain goods. In respect of the assessment year ending with 31st December 1954, the assessee had shown its gross turnover at Rs. 70,992.10 and claimed exemption under two heads namely, (i) under section 5(2)(a)(ii) of the Bengal Finance (Sales Tax) Act, 1941, for the period 1st December 1955 to 30th December 1954; and (ii) under Section 5(1)(b) of that Act for the assessment years 1955 56 to 1969 59. The Commercial Tax Officer rejected the claim on the ground that the appellant had not called for the requisite information from the dealers concerned. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the Department was responsible for preventing the assessee from furnishing the relevant documents to establish that they had issued the declaration forms to it but the said officer did not issue the requisite summons to the parties concerned. The appellant 's writ petition challenging the order of the Appellate Tribunal was dismissed by a Single Judge. On an appeal, a Division Bench of the High Court confirmed the order. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The expression "on demand" only fixes the point of time when the declaration form is to be produced; otherwise the rule would be inconsistent with section 5 (2)(b). [629 A B] (2) The words "on demands" in r. 27A(ii) do not enable the assessee to ignore a statutory condition to claim exemption. Sub rule (3) of r.27A provides that the declaration Form is to he furnished by the dealer and r. 28A says that it shall be furnished on demand, that is to say it fixes the time when a declaration forms are to be furnished. [630 D E] (3)(a) The effect of an excepting or qualifying proviso, according to the ordinary rules of construction, is to except out of the preceding portion of the enactment, or to qualify something enacted therein which but for the proviso would be within it": see 'Craies on Statute Law", 6th Edn., p. 217; referred to. (b) The object of section 5 of the Act and the rules made thereunder is self evident. While they are obviously intended to give exemption to a dealer, in respect to sales to registered dealers of specified classes of goods, it seeks also to prevent fraud and collusion in an attempt to evade tax. [625 E F] (c) The proviso to section 5.C.I.T., West Bengal Finance Act, 1942 does not enable him to ignore the statutory condition which is not helpful to the appellant. [650 A B].

The Bihar Police Act, 1951 was enacted to provide for the better administration of justice in the State. Section 3(1) provides that no person shall be deprived of his life or liberty except in accordance with the procedure established by law. Section 4(2)(d) provides for a lawyer who is not a party to a case but whose name appears in the list filed before the Magistrate or the Sessions Court, as the case may be, and whose name has been included in the List filed by the State Government. The appellant was convicted under section 395 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to imprisonment by the Sessions Judge for two years and to pay a fine of Rs. 5,000/ . He preferred an appeal before the High Court which was allowed and the conviction and sentence were set aside. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the provisions of section 3(4)(d), (e) and (g) of the Act are not applicable to the case as there is no provision in the trial prisoners ' list for minor offences and (2) the High Courts have failed to take an erroneous view of the legal position. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The State cannot be permitted to deny the constitutional right of speedy trial to the accused on he ground that the State has no adequate financial resources to incur the necessary expenditure needed for improving the administrative and judicial apparatus with a view to ensuring speedy trial. Such a procedure is not only a mandate of equal justice implicit in Article 21 but also the compulsion of the constitutional directive embodied in Article 39A. [540 G H] 2. The Court should consider the probable sentence that will follow if a conviction is obtained. The more serious the likely consequences, the greater is the probability that a lawyer should be appointed. [541 A B] 3. (a) The State has its financial constraints and its priorities in expenditure, but as pointed out by this Court in Rhem vs Malclm, ; , it is not necessary to provide a lawyer at all times for the purpose of making an application for bail. [543 D E] (b) The court should consider whether the surety is adequately secured by crime and if so, what will be the reasonable amount of just and just 'failure to do justice. If any application for a release on the personal bond is made, the Magistrate should dispose of it in accordance therewith according to broad guidelines laid down by this court. [544 E F] (c) The Court would not adopt a similar activist approach and issue to the State directions which may involve taking of positive action with a direction to the state which may include taking of negative action such as augmenting and strengthening the investigative machinery, setting up new courts, building new court houses, providing more staff and equipment to the courts, appointment of additional judges and other measures calculated to ensure speedy trial of the accused. [545 E F; 545 A B C] (d) The High Court should have the requisite information bearing on the problem. [548 G H; 548 A] 4. (i) The appellant is entitled to get a lawyer 's custody from the court as required by section 3 courts Act, and the High court should not adopt that procedure. [549 E F]. (ii) The respondent State should furnish to the Court within three weeks from today particulars as to the location of the courts of magistrates and courts of sessions in the state of Bihar together with the total number of cases pending in each of these courts as on 31st December, 1978 giving year wise breakup of such pending cases and also explaining why it has not been possible to dispose of such of those cases as have been pending for more than six months. [550 G H].

The appellant gave notice of termination of tenancy to the respondent under section 34(1) of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948. The respondent filed a suit for possession of the land on December 31, 1951, and obtained possession thereof. In the meantime an amendment was made to the Act by the insertion of sub section (2 A) to section 34 by the Amending Act No. XXXIII of 1952. By this amendment certain further restrictions were placed on the right of the landlord to terminate the tenancy. The appellant contended that the amendment did not affect any vested right of landlords till the tenancy actually stood terminated and that the right to terminate a tenancy had accrued to the landlord after the coming into force of the Amending act, which came into force on January 12, 1953. Held, that the Amending Acts were valid and did not contravene article 31(2 A). The amendment was prospective in nature meant for the protection of tenants. The Amending Act did not effect any vested rights of the landlords till December 31 12, 1951. The amendment did affect the right conferred by section 34 (1) to terminate tenancy and does not speak of any notice at all. The amending Act did affect any vesting of the tenant 's right in the landlord arising out of the notice of termina tion and therefore the Amending provisions were not applicable to notices given before the Amending Ordinance came into operation. Durlabbhai Fakirbhai vs Jhaverbhai Bhikabhai, (1933) I.L.R. LX Cal. 1037, approved.

The petitioners were displaced persons from Pakistan. The house of one Khadim Ali was allotted to them in 1952, and they applied for a declaration that the houses belonged to them. The petitioners contended that they had been wrongly deprived of their rights in the houses by the action of the Custodian. Held, that the order of January 10, 1952, was without jurisdiction so far as it affected the rights of the petitioners. A notification mentioned in section 7 of the Act had been issued and the right, title and interest of any evacuee in the evacuee property specified in the notification had not vested in the Custodian, but only affected the interests of the evacuees. The acts of the custodian in so faras they deprive the petitioners of their property cannot be upheld. Ebrahim Aboobaker vs Tek Chand Dolwani, ; , applied. Efrahim Abubakar vs Tekchand Dolwan, ; and Ebman Aboobator vs Tek Chandra Dolwar, ; referred to. The order of the Collector was without jurisdic tion so far it affected their rights. E brahim Abhimaker vs Chet Chand Dholwani, , applied to. Educa tain Singh vs State of Punjab, [1962] Supp. 1 S.C.R. 869 and Efman Abubakishaker vs Khem Chand Doyolwani ; referred. The proceedings in the present case were not a quasi judicial one and the order was without Jurisdiction so far the interest of the petitioner was concerned.

The assessee company was carrying on the business of selling agents and on its behalf paid commission to the agents. The commission received by the agents were not expenses incurred for the purpose of the business. The assessee company claimed that the two amounts in question were not profits liable to tax as they were not expenditure incurred for purposes of the trade, and that the amounts were not allowable under section 10(2)(xv) of the Income Tax Act, 1922. The High Court held that the payments were not a joint venture or a transaction with a view to division of profits; but that the assessee was entitled to deduct a sum of Rs. 25,000/ for six months as expenses incurred by the assessee company and for a lump sum deduction of Rs 50,000 under section I(2) (xv). The High court also held that in the first place it was permissible to take the stand that the amount paid was not expenditure on account of profits or business connection. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that the High Court was wrong in holding that the sums were not liable to be taxed under section 1(2), (xv) and (xv); that the agreement between the assessee and the agents with the selling agents provided for the consent of the agents not only at the beginning of the manufacture of the yarn but also at every stage in the sale of the products; that the agents had been able to secure most liberal and profitable terms, and were not entitled to any profit. HELD: (i) The agreement clearly provided for a joint responsibility on the assessee to pay commission to its selling agents but at every point in the pro ceedings of the assessee. Even at the stage of sale of products the consent was necessary. [195 G] (ii) The assessee agreed to finance the business for the year, profession or vocation and it was not bound to accept the trust to tarmovit the contract of agency. It was also not a part of the agreement which provided for any apportionment or distribution of profits simpliciter. [196 H; 197 A] (iii) The amount in question was deductible under section 2(xiii) of Income Tax, 1922, and was not liable for tax. [197 B C] (iv) The amounts in dispute were not legally deductible under the provisions of section 10 (2)(XV) of Act. (v) The payments in question did not constitute a joint enterprise or a joint concern but were made to promote or increase the commercial activity. [198 F G] Commissioner of Income tax, Bombay vs Walchand and Co., ; , referred to.

The appellant company was a private limited company. It had its accounts pertaining to the appellant company in its books of account as on March 31, 1958 showing a sum of Rs. 36,546.17. The accounts showed a net profit of Rs 18,950.98. The Income Tax Officer came to know that the assessee had been withdrawing moneys from the company and in the belief that those amounts were liable to be treated as "dividend" under section 2(6A)(e) of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922, he reopened the assessment by virtue of section 147 of the 1961 Act. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner dismissed the appeal holding that the accumulated profits of the company amounted to Rs. 1,050 only and that amount alone could be considered as "cividend". On a reference made at the instance of the assessee, the Tribunal referred the following question to the High Court: "Whether on the facts and in circumstances of this case the Appellate Tribunal was legally correct in holding that Rs. 18,0950.97 was taken into account in determining the accumulated profit as on 31st March 1958 ?" The High Court answered the first question in favour of the Revenue. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the words "accumulated profits" in section 2 (6A) (e) could not take in current profits; and (ii) the provision for payment of tax and dividend can be taken into consideration when computing the accumulated income as on 3rd March, 1958. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High court was right in answering the first questions in favour. [950C] 2. The expression "accusation" used here for convenience is in section2(6 A) (c) of Income Tax, 1961 and it is clear that current profits cannot be included in accumulated profits. It appears to be now the established law of the land.

The appellant was the Mahant of a religious institution known as Rajgunj Asthal in Burdwan. He was granted a Sanheraj Asthal to his predecessors in title long prior to the permanent settlement, and on the strength of that entry he claimed to have been holding under a Lakheraj grant made prior to his permanent settlement. The respondents contended that they had no title to them as the lands were not in their possession for a long time without payment of rent, that the appellant was entitled to fair rent and that the claim was barred by limitation. Held, that on the facts found, the Courts below were right in holding that the suits were within time under article 131 of the Limitation Act. The suit properties formed part of a permanently settled estate of Burdwan and if a grant had been made in favour of the predecessors of the defendants, it must have been made by the Maharaja of Burdwan or by the Rajgun j Asthal. But before raising such a presumption, it was necessary to establish a lost grant in favour Of the predecessors in interest of the respondents. The fact that the lands formed part Of Mauza Nala within the Zamindari of Burdwan, and if they were not actually paying rent, could not make them liable for eviction. It was only in 1931 that the defendants could be said to have asserted a hostile title and the suit properties had been settled on the Raj Roller of Burdwan. The defendants could not fall back on a presumption of lost grant by the very persons whose title they had repudiated.

The appellant plaintiff filed a suit for specific performance of a contract. The trial Court decreed the suit but in appeal, the District Judge reversed the decree and held that the plaintiff was not an agriculturist within the meaning of the Tenancy Act. On appeal by the respondent, the High Court set aside the decree holding that the appellant was not a ' agriculturist ' within the definition of agricultural land under the Tenancy act. The High Court also held that in view of section 85A of the Act, the suit was not maintainable and dismissed the suit as it would be competent to the plaintiff to recover possession of the land from the defendant. In appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: (1) The jurisdiction of the civil court to settle, decide or deal with any question which is required to be settled, decided or dealt with by a competent authority under the Act is totally ousted. [695C] (2) Section 70(a)(ii) read with sections 85 and 85A clearly contemplates that when in a suit properly instituted by a civil court, an issue arises which is requiring the plaintiff 's to be an agriculturist, it would not be competent for the legislature stepped in to avoid the conflict of jurisdiction by introducing section 85 A into the Act. [594D E] (3) The decision correctly interpreted the law as it stood before the enactment of section 5A of Tenancy Act and held inapplicable. [599F] (4) The finding of the High court that the respondent was not entitled to a decree for specific performa in his favour is set aside. [600H] (5) The view taken by the High Courts is correct. [596G] (6) The question whether a person has become a statutory owner on the tillers ' day i.e. 1st April 1957, is within the exclusive jurisdiction of a civil Court. Therefore, it is incumbent upon the Civil Court to refer the issue to the competent authority. under the tenancy Act and decide it according to law in that light. [597A B] (7) The High court was right in holding that if an issue arose during the pendency of the suit properly constituted civil suit which the civil Court is competent to decide, prima facie on a contention being raised by the party against whom the civil suit is filed. [595C D] (8) The findings of the trial Court that the defendant had become a Statutory owner on 1st March 1957 and that he was not in possession of agricultural lands are set aside by the appellate court. [593F G] (9) The plaintiff 'could not be allowed to purchase agricultural land personally. It would thus be open to the respondent to dispose of the question whether the plaintiff is an agriculturist.

The assessee, a heavy engineering concern manufacturing steam, machinery parts and for that purpose the assessee was purchasing spare parts, forgings and castings from outside. The Tribunal held that the business of the new industrial undertakings was to manufac ture those very spare parts and the jute mill division was a separate and distinct unit and that the two units were independent producing arti cles and the entire existing business in existence. In reference the High Court answered both the questions in favour of the assessee and against the Revenue. Dismissing the appeals by certificate, HELD: The Tribunal was right in holding the two undertakings as formed by reconstruction of the existing business of a company. Use by the assessee of the articles produced in its existing business or the concept of expansion are not decisive tests in construing section 15C. [764 D] (1) The High Court is not right in view of the fact that once the new undertaking is separate and independent production units ' in the sense that the commodities produced or the results achieved are commercially tangible products and the undertakings can be carried on separately without complete absorption and losing their identity in the old business, they are not to be treated as being formed by re spondents. [774 F G] (2) The Tribunal is right in answering two questions in the negative and against assessee. [775 B C] (3) The question of depreciation does not arise out of the assessment for the year 1958 59. The High court was wrong in holding that the Tribunal was entitled to the benefit of section 15 C if that section is otherwise applicable.

The inam lands were granted to the appellants for performance of services connected therewith. The inamdars were granted a lease for performance by the inamdars in favour of the hereditary office holders, and the lands were resumed by the Inamdars. The appellants claimed title to the lands under a grant from the inamdar on the footing that the inam was from year to year. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the inams comprised both melwaram and kudiwaram rights in the land. The High Court, however, allowed the appeal of the appellants. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellants that the Inam lands were personal inams burdened with services and were not resumable under section 44 B(2)(a)(i) of the Madras Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1926. HELD: (1) The inam title, if any, of all persons claiming through the inamholders to any subordinate interest in the inams stood determined. [549 E] (2) Section 44 B (2)(b) does not apply to a personal inam burdened with a condition of service and is not dependent upon sub section (1). The inamdar was entitled to resume the inam lands made under section 43 B(1) from the date of the grant. The Inamdars were lessees of the inam villages under the inamdaridars. During the continuance of the tenancy, their possession was not adverse to the inamants. [598 G H] (3) The inams in the present case were resumables under section44 B(I). The inams were granted by the appellants to the holders of hereditary offices as remuneration for services to be rendered by them and were within the purview of section 44B(2) (a)(1). [599 A C] (4) The Inam Commission confirmed the grants of the inams in favour. of the respondents. The lands were not personal inams. They were inams granted to office holders as remuneration. The amounts of assessment or melwaran 's inam were therefore very low and could not be an ade quate remuneration. [550 E F] (5) The grantees were entitled to the kudiaray rights in their lands under section 45 B(II)(a) (i). [550 G] (6) The respondents ought not to be allowed to raise at this late stage the novel contention that the lease was from month to year and that the lands had been alienated or otherwise lost to the institution or service to which it once belonged or on the ground that the terms of the grants were not observed.

The Indore City Municipal Act, 1909 was repealed by the Madhya Bharat Municipalities Act, 1954. The Indore City Municipality was governed by the Indore City municipal Act, 1911. Under section 2(c) of that Act a tax on houses or buildings shall be levied on the annual letting value and that in assessing such tax a sum equal to 10% of such valuation shall be deducted therefrom. Section 79(1) provided that where a municipality adopts a previously prepared list for any subsequent year, it can be done subject to the provisions of sections 75 and 76. The appellant Corporation was assessed to tax on the basis of gross annual letting values at the rate of 7% of its gross annual tenancy value. The respondent Municipality preferred an appeal against the assessment to the High Court which dismissed the same. In appeal by special leave, it was contended that the tax imposed on the income of the appellant was inconsistent with section 73 under which the annual rent would be the gross annual rent and not 10% statutory allowance in lieu of the costs of repairs or on any other account whatsoever. HELD: The High Court was right in decreeing the suit. [131 B] Section 2(C) provides expressly that when a municipality adopted a previously framed list for an earlier year, the provisions Of sections 75 to 77 shall be applicable as if they were made, and the time has to be fixed for lodging objections against the entries therein. After such objections are heard and disposed of by the assessment list has to he authenticated as provided by section 76(6). Sub section (6) of section 76 lays down that the provisions in sub section (2) shall be applied if a new assessment list had been completed at the commencement of that particular official year. The word "if" appearing in sub sec. 2 of sec. 79 is obviously a mistake and must be read as "as if" because the word "on" standing by itself makes no sense at all. [132 E F] In order to prevent such a result the legislature has provided by sub section 2 of section 79 that where, on an assessment list prepared in an earlier one is adopted it becomes the list for such subsequent year subject to its procedure laid down in secs. 75 and 77. The list so adopted has therefore to be published, has to invite objections and has to comply with the provisions contained in sec. 73(2) of the Act.

The assessee company carried on the business of manufacturing matches till the account year ending April 30, 1941. During that period there was a sale of chemicals and raw materials for manufacture of matches, and it had also resulted in a substantial profit. The assessee company sold these chemicals to different parties. In a confidential report made by the Income tax Officer, the assessee admitted that the profit from the sale of the chemicals and the raw materials was not sold in the course of ordinary trading but in a reali sation sale after the company had been wound up. The Income tax officer held that the assessee company was liable to income tax on a profit of Rs. 2 lakhs arising from this sale. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income Tax Officer. On further appeal, the Tribunal found that the business had not completely ceased to exist since the assessee Company was carrying on its business as wine and spirit merchants. The High Court held that by the sale no business was done and that the amount obtained was only by way of realisation sale and was not therefore liable to tax. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The question whether a particular transaction is one or the other depends upon the facts of each case, but they do not arise in the present case, which can be decided on the narrow ground whether a transaction is a revenue sale or not with a view to trading in chemicals and manufacturing the products. [967 D] (ii) The fact that the clause in the Memorandum gave power to the company to Bell chemicals cannot be used in this connection because the evidence clearly showed that the company was keeping the factory going, not on its own behalf but entirely on behalf of the buyer. One cannot fairly say, therefore, that a sale is a slump transaction with which a woolen Syndicate is paid and no portion is attributable to the stockivoir of chemicals through the years were too petty in themselves to afford evidence of a continued or sustained trading In chemicals. [969 E F] (iii) The High Courts have held that there was evidence on which the Commissioners could arrive at their finding that trading was not a revenue transaction and that, therefore. the excess represented capital appreciation and not a trading profit.
